name: Tomato

season.transplant: After last frost, when nights stay above 50°F
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through first frost

seed.desc: Plant seed ¼" deep in moist seed-starting mix. Keep at 70–80°F. Use a humidity dome to retain moisture.

germination.desc: Seed coat splits and the radicle emerges first. Keep soil moist but not waterlogged. Bottom heat helps.

seedling.desc: First true leaves appear after cotyledons. Begin light feeding with diluted fertilizer. Thin to one per cell.

young.desc: Transplant outdoors after last frost when nighttime temps stay above 50°F. Stake or cage immediately. Water deeply.

adult.desc: Flowers form then fruit sets. Prune suckers for indeterminate varieties. Consistent watering prevents blossom end rot.

care.water: Deep water 1–2 inches per week. Water at the base — avoid wetting foliage to prevent fungal disease. Mulch to retain moisture.
care.light: Full sun — minimum 6–8 hours per day. More sun = more fruit.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining with lots of organic matter. pH 6.0–6.8. Amend with compost before planting.
care.spacing: 18–36 inches apart depending on variety. Indeterminate types need more room.
care.fertilizer: High phosphorus at planting for root development. Switch to balanced or low-nitrogen once flowering begins.
care.notes: Rotate crops every 3 years to prevent soil-borne disease. Bury stems deep when transplanting — roots form along buried stem.

container.notes: Determinate (bush) varieties are best for containers. Ensure drainage holes. Water more frequently than in-ground.

propagation.desc: Primary method. Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in seed-starting mix.
Take 4–6 inch suckers, remove lower leaves, root in water or moist soil. Produces clone of parent plant.

harvest.when: When fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. Tomatoes continue ripening off the vine.
harvest.how: Twist gently or cut stem with clean snips. Never pull — damages the vine.
harvest.storage: Store at room temperature stem-side down. Never refrigerate — destroys flavor and texture.
harvest.yield: Indeterminate varieties produce continuously until frost. Expect 10–15 lbs per plant in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Planting out too early — cold soil stunts growth and cold nights cause flower drop.
Inconsistent watering — causes blossom end rot and fruit cracking.
Over-fertilizing with nitrogen — produces lush foliage but few fruits.
Not staking early enough — damages roots when done after plant is established.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated (heirloom varieties). Hybrid seeds won't breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Let fruit fully ripen on vine past eating stage until very soft and starting to wrinkle.
seed_saving.method: Scoop seeds into jar with water. Ferment 2–3 days at room temp — stir daily. Viable seeds sink, gel coating breaks down.
seed_saving.drying: Rinse fermented seeds through strainer. Spread on non-stick surface (glass, ceramic) and dry 1–2 weeks. Do NOT use paper towels — seeds stick.
seed_saving.storage: Store in cool, dark, dry place in paper envelope or glass jar. Label with variety and year.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate heirloom varieties by 25+ feet to prevent cross-pollination with other tomato varieties.

good.why: Repels aphids, whitefly, and tomato hornworm. Some growers report improved flavor.
Root secretions deter nematodes. Flowers attract beneficial insects.
Loosens soil around tomato roots. Tomato foliage shades carrots in hot climates.
Deters tomato hornworm. Attracts pollinators. Adds trace minerals when chopped and dropped.

bad.why: Releases allelopathic chemicals that stunt tomato growth.
Compete heavily for nutrients and can harbor shared pests.
Both attract corn earworm / tomato fruitworm. Plant far apart.

culinary: One of the world's most versatile vegetables. Eaten raw in salads, roasted, sun-dried, sauced, pureed, and fermented. Foundation of Italian, Spanish, Mexican, and Indian cuisines. Rich in umami when cooked.
medicinal: High in lycopene — a powerful antioxidant linked to reduced risk of prostate and breast cancers. Rich in vitamins C and K. Lycopene bioavailability increases significantly when cooked with olive oil.

pests.name: Tomato Hornworm
pests.desc: Large green caterpillar up to 4 inches. Can fully defoliate a plant in days. Look for dark droppings on leaves.
pests.control: Hand-pick and drop in soapy water. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray is highly effective and organic.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Tiny soft-bodied insects clustering under leaves and at growing tips. Secrete sticky honeydew that leads to sooty mold.
pests.control: Blast with water spray. Neem oil solution. Encourage ladybugs and lacewings.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Tiny white flying insects that cloud up when plant is disturbed. Weaken plants and spread viral disease.
pests.control: Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil. Reflective silver mulch disorients adults.

pests.name: Early Blight
pests.desc: Fungal disease causing dark concentric rings on lower leaves. Spreads upward in warm humid weather.
pests.control: Remove affected leaves immediately. Improve airflow. Copper fungicide spray. Avoid overhead watering.

pests.name: Blossom End Rot
pests.desc: Calcium deficiency caused by inconsistent watering. Dark sunken patch on blossom end of fruit.
pests.control: Consistent deep watering. Mulch to retain moisture. Calcium spray as short-term fix.

varieties.name: Cherokee Purple
varieties.description: Large beefsteak heirloom. Deep purple-brown skin, complex smoky sweet flavor. One of the most popular heirlooms.
varieties.notes: Best flavor of all tomatoes according to many growers.

varieties.name: San Marzano
varieties.description: Classic Italian paste tomato. Elongated, meaty, low moisture. The authentic pizza sauce tomato.
varieties.notes: DOP protected in Italy. Best for sauce and canning.

varieties.name: Sun Gold
varieties.description: Orange cherry tomato. Incredibly sweet — one of the sweetest tomatoes available. Prolific producer.
varieties.notes: Most popular cherry tomato among serious gardeners.

varieties.name: Brandywine
varieties.description: Large pink beefsteak heirloom. Rich complex flavor. Potato-leaf foliage. Slow but worth the wait.
varieties.notes: The benchmark heirloom tomato for flavor.

varieties.name: Black Krim
varieties.description: Russian heirloom. Dark reddish-brown skin, rich smoky flavor. Medium-large beefsteak.
varieties.notes: Excellent in hot climates where other heirlooms struggle.

varieties.name: Mortgage Lifter
varieties.description: Enormous pink beefsteak — can reach 2 lbs. Developed by M.C. Byles who paid off his mortgage selling seedlings.
varieties.notes: Great story and great flavor. Low acidity.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: drooling, lethargy, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea
pet_toxicity.notes: Ripe fruit generally safe in small amounts. Leaves and stems contain solanine and tomatine — keep pets out of the garden.

transplant.deep_note: Bury up to 2/3 of stem — roots form all along buried stem, creating a stronger plant.

name: Basil
growing_zones: 2–11 (grown as annual; perennial only in zones 10–11)

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is consistently warm (65°F+)
season.harvest_window: Early summer through first frost — harvest continuously

seed.desc: Sow seeds on surface of moist starting mix and press lightly — basil needs light to germinate. Do not cover deeply.

germination.desc: One of the fastest germinators in warm conditions. Needs soil temperature of 65°F+. Seedlings emerge in a cluster.

seedling.desc: Very fragile at this stage. Avoid overwatering — susceptible to damping off. Thin to one plant per 6 inches.

young.desc: Begin pinching growing tips once plant has 3–4 sets of leaves. Forces bushy growth and delays flowering.

adult.desc: Harvest leaves regularly from the top. Pinch flower buds the moment they appear — flowering triggers bitterness.

care.water: Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged. Basil wilts quickly when thirsty. Water at the base.
care.light: Full sun — 6 or more hours daily. Insufficient light causes leggy, weak plants with poor flavor.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, fertile soil. pH 6.0–7.0. Add compost for best results.
care.fertilizer: Light feeding with balanced fertilizer monthly. Too much nitrogen reduces essential oil concentration and flavor.
care.notes: Bring indoors or harvest fully at first sign of frost — basil dies at 50°F. Excellent container plant.

container.min_size: 6-inch pot minimum. Wider is better for multiple plants.
container.notes: Thrives on a sunny windowsill. One of the best herbs for indoor growing. Keep away from cold drafts.

propagation.desc: Fast and reliable. Surface sow in warm conditions — germinates in 5–7 days.
Cut 4-inch stem just below a leaf node. Remove lower leaves and place in water. Roots form in 1–2 weeks. Plant in soil once roots are 1 inch long.

harvest.when: As soon as plant has 6+ leaves. Begin harvesting regularly once established.
harvest.how: Pinch or cut stems just above a pair of leaves. This forces two new shoots to grow from that point, doubling future yield.
harvest.storage: Store fresh stems in water at room temperature like cut flowers. Do not refrigerate — turns black. For longer storage, blend with olive oil and freeze in ice cube trays.
harvest.yield: A single plant harvested regularly can produce continuously for the whole season.

common_mistakes: Letting it flower — once basil flowers, leaves become bitter and plant declines rapidly. Pinch buds immediately.
Overwatering seedlings — damping off kills young plants. Allow soil surface to dry slightly between waterings.
Refrigerating fresh basil — causes blackening within hours. Keep at room temperature.
Harvesting from the bottom — always harvest from the top to encourage bushy growth.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Most sweet basil varieties cross freely with each other.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower spikes to fully develop and dry on the plant. Seeds are in the dried calyxes at the base of each flower.
seed_saving.method: Cut dried flower spikes when calyxes are brown and papery. Place upside down in a paper bag and shake to release seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Seeds dry naturally inside the flower spike. Spread any remaining moist seeds on a paper plate for 1–2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Store in sealed envelope or small glass jar in a cool dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate different basil varieties by 150+ feet or use mesh bags over flower heads to ensure pure seed.

good.why: Classic pairing. Repels aphids, whitefly, and possibly hornworm. Mutually beneficial.
Basil repels aphids and spider mites common to pepper plants.
Similar growing needs. Oregano's strong scent helps confuse pest insects.

bad.why: Sage inhibits basil growth when planted in close proximity.
Thyme prefers drier conditions — conflicting water needs cause one to suffer.
Fennel is allelopathic to most herbs including basil.

culinary: Essential herb in Italian, Thai, Vietnamese, and Mediterranean cuisines. Foundation of pesto. Pairs perfectly with tomato, mozzarella, lemon, and garlic. Best used fresh — heat destroys volatile aromatic oils. Thai basil holds up better to heat.
medicinal: Anti-inflammatory compounds including eugenol. Antibacterial properties effective against E. coli and Staphylococcus. Traditional digestive aid — relieves bloating and stomach cramps. High in vitamin K.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cluster under leaves and at new growth tips. Spread quickly in warm weather.
pests.control: Neem oil spray. Blast with water. Plant near marigolds as a decoy crop.

pests.name: Japanese Beetle
pests.desc: Skeletonize leaves rapidly. Metallic green and copper coloring.
pests.control: Hand-pick in early morning when cold and sluggish. Neem oil. Row covers over young plants.

pests.name: Fusarium Wilt
pests.desc: Fungal soil disease causing sudden wilting and brown discoloration inside stem.
pests.control: No cure once infected. Remove plant immediately. Use disease-resistant varieties. Solarize soil.

pests.name: Damping Off
pests.desc: Fungal disease that kills seedlings at soil level — stems thin and collapse.
pests.control: Use sterile seed-starting mix. Do not overwater. Improve airflow. Chamomile tea as mild antifungal drench.

varieties.name: Genovese
varieties.description: The classic Italian pesto basil. Large cupped leaves, intense flavor. Standard for Italian cooking.
varieties.notes: The variety to grow for authentic pesto.

varieties.name: Purple Ruffles
varieties.description: Deep purple, ruffled leaves. Ornamental as well as culinary. Makes beautiful purple basil vinegar.
varieties.notes: Striking in the garden and in the kitchen.

varieties.name: Spicy Globe
varieties.description: Compact globe-shaped plant. Tiny leaves, very spicy flavor. Excellent for containers and edging.
varieties.notes: Most compact basil variety — stays naturally tidy.

varieties.name: Lettuce Leaf
varieties.description: Enormous crinkled leaves up to 4 inches. Ideal for wrapping food — like rice paper rolls.
varieties.notes: Best for fresh wraps and large salads.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Basil is non-toxic and safe for dogs and cats. Many cats enjoy the scent.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot. Crown at soil level.

name: Lavender

season.start_indoors: 8–10 weeks before last frost — cold stratify seed first
season.direct_sow: Early spring or fall in mild climates
season.transplant: Spring after last frost or early fall
season.harvest_window: Late spring to midsummer when half the buds on a spike are open

seed.desc: Cold stratify seeds for 3–6 weeks in damp paper towel in the fridge before sowing. Sow on surface — needs light to germinate.

germination.desc: Notoriously slow and irregular. Keep at 65–70°F with consistent moisture. Germination rate is typically low — sow extras.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Very prone to damping off. Do not overwater. Lavender is drought-adapted from the start.

young.desc: Transplant to final location with excellent drainage. Full sun critical. Will not bloom first year from seed.

adult.desc: Harvest stems when approximately half of buds on a spike are open — this is when essential oil content peaks.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water deeply but very infrequently. Overwatering is the primary cause of lavender death.
care.light: Full sun — 8+ hours daily. Does poorly in shade or with overhead obstructions.
care.soil: Sandy, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.5–7.5. Amend heavy clay with sand and gravel. Raised beds ideal.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. Good airflow between plants prevents root rot and botrytis.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Too much nitrogen produces lush growth with poor fragrance. Light spring compost top-dress is sufficient.
care.notes: Hard prune by one-third after first flowering to maintain shape. Do not cut into old wood — will not regenerate.

container.min_size: 12-inch pot minimum with excellent drainage holes.
container.notes: Use a gritty, well-draining mix — half potting soil, half perlite or coarse sand. Terracotta pots are ideal as they wick excess moisture.

propagation.desc: Far more reliable than seed. Take 3-inch softwood cuttings in spring, or semi-hardwood in late summer. Dip in rooting hormone, plant in gritty mix. Roots in 3–4 weeks.
Slow and unreliable. Cold stratify first. Many cultivars won't breed true from seed.
Bend a low stem to the ground, pin it down, and cover with soil. Roots form at the buried node in 4–6 weeks. Sever and transplant.

harvest.when: When approximately half the buds on each flower spike have opened. Essential oil content is highest at this point.
harvest.how: Cut stems with sharp snips, leaving at least 2 inches of green growth on the stem. Never cut into woody growth.
harvest.storage: Bundle stems with rubber band and hang upside down in a warm, dark, airy space for 2–4 weeks. Store dried bundles in paper bags.
harvest.yield: An established plant can produce dozens of stems per harvest. Harvest twice per season in warm climates.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — lavender rots quickly in wet soil. When in doubt, don't water.
Heavy clay soil — must amend with grit or grow in raised beds. Clay kills lavender.
Cutting into old woody growth when pruning — it won't regrow from wood. Only prune green growth.
Growing in shade — insufficient sun produces weak plants with little fragrance and poor bloom.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. However many cultivars are hybrids or vegetatively propagated — seeds may not breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower spikes to dry completely on the plant. Seed is contained inside the dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower spikes between palms over a bowl. Winnow lightly to separate seeds from chaff.
seed_saving.drying: Seeds dry naturally on plant. If harvesting before fully dry, spread on screen in warm airy location for 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Cool, dark, dry location in paper envelope.
seed_saving.viability: 1–2 years. Germination rate drops sharply after year one.
seed_saving.notes: Propagation from cuttings is far more reliable and produces true-to-parent plants.

good.why: Lavender repels aphids and black spot fungus. Classic cottage garden pairing.
Identical growing conditions. Sage also repels cabbage moths and attracts pollinators.
Both Mediterranean drought-tolerant herbs with similar soil and water needs.
Attracts the same beneficial pollinators — bees and butterflies.

bad.why: Mint is invasive and prefers moist conditions — overwatering from mint's needs will kill lavender.
Hostas prefer shade and moisture — opposite of lavender's requirements.

culinary: Key ingredient in Herbes de Provence. Used in baked goods, shortbread, honey infusions, lemonade, and teas. Pairs with lamb, duck, and stone fruits. Very strong flavor — use sparingly or it becomes soapy.
medicinal: Proven anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) effects. Promotes sleep quality. Topical application relieves headaches, minor burns, and insect bites. Antimicrobial and antifungal. Safe for children in diluted topical application.

pests.name: Spittlebug
pests.desc: Foamy white mass on stems — larva inside. Mainly cosmetic damage.
pests.control: Blast mass off with water jet. Rarely requires further treatment.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: Fungal disease from overwatering or poor drainage. Roots turn brown and mushy.
pests.control: Improve drainage immediately. Reduce watering drastically. Remove and destroy infected plants.

pests.name: Botrytis
pests.desc: Gray mold fungus on stems and flowers in wet conditions.
pests.control: Remove affected material. Improve airflow and spacing. Avoid overhead watering.

varieties.name: Hidcote
varieties.description: Compact 12-18 inch plant. Deep purple flowers. Most cold-hardy English lavender. Excellent for edging.
varieties.notes: Best for colder climates. Zone 4 hardy with protection.

varieties.name: Munstead
varieties.description: Compact, very hardy, earlier bloomer than most. First English lavender to bloom each season.
varieties.notes: Most reliable for cold climates. Zone 4 hardy.

varieties.name: Vera
varieties.description: Large robust plant. Very high essential oil content. The commercial oil production variety.
varieties.notes: Best for essential oil extraction and drying.

varieties.name: Phenomenal
varieties.description: Heat AND cold tolerant. More humidity resistant than other lavenders. Zones 5–8.
varieties.notes: Best for humid climates where other lavenders struggle.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — linalool and linalyl acetate
pet_toxicity.symptoms: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite
pet_toxicity.notes: Cats are more sensitive than dogs. The essential oil is much more concentrated and dangerous than the plant itself. Dried lavender sachets pose a risk if ingested. The plant in the garden is low risk if pets just sniff it.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Ensure crown is not buried — crown rot is the #1 killer.
transplant.mulch: gravel or pea shingle (NOT organic — lavender needs drainage)

name: Carrot

season.start_indoors: Not recommended — taproots don't transplant well
season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring. Again in late summer for fall harvest.
season.harvest_window: Spring sowing: midsummer. Fall sowing: late fall through early winter

seed.desc: Sow directly outdoors ¼ inch deep in rows 12 inches apart. Mix seed with sand for even distribution.

germination.desc: Very slow germinator. Soil surface MUST stay moist the entire time. Cover rows with burlap and mist daily.

seedling.desc: Thin aggressively to 2–3 inches apart when seedlings are 2 inches tall. Weeding is critical — carrots cannot compete.

young.desc: Root development underway. Side-dress with low-nitrogen, high-potassium fertilizer to encourage root growth over leaf growth.

adult.desc: Ready when shoulder is ½–¾ inch in diameter. Flavor improves after a light frost — cold converts starch to sugar.

care.water: Consistent 1 inch per week. Irregular watering causes roots to crack or fork. Drip irrigation ideal.
care.light: Full sun preferred but tolerates partial shade.
care.soil: Loose, deep, sandy loam is essential. Remove all stones to 12 inches depth. pH 6.0–6.8.
care.spacing: 2–3 inches between plants after thinning. Rows 12 inches apart.
care.fertilizer: Low nitrogen — produces lush tops and small roots. Use high-potassium, high-phosphorus fertilizer.
care.notes: Loosen soil to 12 inches depth before planting. In heavy clay use raised beds or ball-type varieties.

container.min_size: 12 inches deep minimum. Use short or ball-type varieties like Chantenay or Thumbelina.
container.notes: Depth is more important than width. A tall narrow container works better than a wide shallow one.

propagation.desc: Only method. Direct sow — carrots produce a taproot immediately and cannot be transplanted.

harvest.when: 60–80 days from sowing. Shoulder of root visible at soil surface at ½–¾ inch diameter. Taste test is the best guide.
harvest.how: Loosen soil with a fork alongside the row first. Pull gently by the greens while wiggling side to side. Avoid snapping the root.
harvest.storage: Remove tops immediately after harvest — greens draw moisture from the root. Store unwashed in damp sand or sealed bag in fridge for up to 3 months.
harvest.yield: Typically 1–2 lbs per foot of row in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Letting the soil surface dry out during germination — even one dry day can kill germinating seeds.
Not thinning aggressively — crowded carrots produce forked, stunted, unusable roots.
Rocky or compacted soil — always loosen and remove debris to full depth before sowing.
Using high-nitrogen fertilizer — causes forked roots and excessive top growth with small roots.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — carrots don't flower until their second year. Open-pollinated varieties required.
seed_saving.harvest: Leave selected plants in ground over winter. Plants bolt and flower in year two. Allow seed umbels to turn brown and dry.
seed_saving.method: Cut seed heads when most seeds are brown. Place in paper bag upside down. Shake when fully dry to release seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Dry seed heads in paper bags in a warm airy space for 2–3 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Store in paper envelope in cool dry location.
seed_saving.notes: Carrots cross-pollinate with wild Queen Anne's Lace and other carrot varieties. Isolate by ½ mile or bag individual flower heads.

good.why: Tomato foliage shades carrot roots in hot weather. Carrots aerate soil around tomato roots.
Repels carrot fly — the primary carrot pest. Strong aromatic confusion.
Onion scent confuses carrot fly. Carrots repel onion fly in return — classic mutualism.
Lettuce shades carrot row reducing surface drying and weed pressure.

bad.why: Dill stunts carrot growth when mature. Small dill is fine but let it mature elsewhere.
Same family — attracts the same pests and diseases. Don't grow adjacent.

culinary: Eaten raw as snack, roasted (caramelizes beautifully), in soups, stews, stocks, and stir-fries. Juiced for sweetness and nutrition. Used in cakes and baked goods. One of the most universally eaten vegetables.
medicinal: Extraordinarily high in beta-carotene which converts to vitamin A — essential for eye health and immune function. Soluble fiber (pectin) feeds beneficial gut bacteria and lowers LDL cholesterol. Rich in biotin for hair and nail strength.

pests.name: Carrot Fly
pests.desc: Adult lays eggs at base of plant. Larvae tunnel into roots leaving brown channels.
pests.control: Row covers from germination prevent adults laying eggs. Rosemary and onion as companion plants.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Can carry carrot motley dwarf virus which causes stunting and yellowing.
pests.control: Neem oil spray. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering plants nearby.

pests.name: Wireworm
pests.desc: Larvae of click beetles live in soil for years. Tunnel into roots.
pests.control: Crop rotation essential. Beneficial nematodes applied to soil.

pests.name: Carrot Weevil
pests.desc: Adult notches leaf margins. Larvae tunnel into crown and tap root.
pests.control: Crop rotation. Remove all carrot debris after harvest. Row covers.

varieties.name: Nantes
varieties.description: Cylindrical, blunt-ended. Extremely sweet and crisp. The most popular home garden carrot.
varieties.notes: Best for heavy soil — shorter than Imperator types.

varieties.name: Chantenay
varieties.description: Short, broad, cone-shaped. Best for heavy clay or shallow soils where long carrots can't penetrate.
varieties.notes: The container and clay soil carrot.

varieties.name: Imperator
varieties.description: Long, tapered, classic supermarket shape. Needs deep loose soil to develop properly.
varieties.notes: Only practical in very deep, loose, stone-free soil.

varieties.name: Dragon
varieties.description: Purple skin, orange flesh. Striking appearance. Anthocyanins fade when cooked — best eaten raw.

varieties.name: Atomic Red
varieties.description: Deep red when cooked (lycopene content). Mild sweet flavor. Colour intensifies when cooked — opposite of Dragon.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Carrots are safe and healthy for dogs and cats. Good low-calorie treat. Cut into small pieces for smaller pets.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown ¼ inch deep (surface sow). Never transplant — taproot is immediate.
transplant.mulch: light straw or burlap until germination

name: Sunflower

season.start_indoors: 2–3 weeks before last frost in individual peat pots — dislikes transplanting
season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil reaches 55°F
season.transplant: If started indoors, transplant carefully — taproots are sensitive
season.harvest_window: Late summer to fall — 80–120 days from sowing depending on variety

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep, 6 inches apart after last frost. Direct sow preferred — sunflowers grow a long taproot early and transplant poorly.

germination.desc: Among the fastest germinators. Requires soil temperatures of 55°F+. Seedling pushes up with seed coat still attached.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Thin to final spacing. Needs minimal water — deep but infrequent watering encourages deep taproot development.

young.desc: Plant tracks the sun throughout the day (heliotropism). Very drought tolerant at this stage.

adult.desc: Head faces permanently east when fully mature. Harvest seeds when back of head turns yellow-brown and seeds are plump.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Deep, infrequent watering (once per week) encourages the deep taproot. Avoid overhead watering — can cause mold on seed heads.
care.light: Full sun — minimum 6 hours. 8+ hours produces the largest heads and best seed yield.
care.soil: Tolerates poor soils well. Well-draining is important. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.spacing: 6 inches for small varieties, 18–24 inches for giant varieties.
care.fertilizer: Avoid high-nitrogen — causes lots of leafy growth and small heads. Balanced or phosphorus-heavy fertilizer.
care.notes: Sunflowers are phytoremediation plants — they absorb heavy metals from contaminated soil. Do NOT eat seeds from plants grown for remediation.

container.min_size: 5-gallon for dwarf varieties. Standard and giant varieties need in-ground growing.
container.notes: Only dwarf varieties (under 24 inches) are practical in containers. Ensure very sturdy pot — tall plants become top-heavy.

propagation.desc: Only method. Direct sow after last frost is strongly preferred. Taproots resent disturbance.

harvest.when: When the back of the seed head turns from green to yellow-brown. Seeds should be plump with full black-and-white striped shells. Test by rubbing a few seeds — they should come free easily.
harvest.how: Cut head with 12 inches of stem attached. If leaving on plant to fully dry, protect from birds with loose mesh bag.
harvest.storage: Hang heads upside down in dry, airy space 3–4 weeks. Then rub seeds free over a bucket. Store in airtight container in cool dry place.
harvest.yield: A single large head can yield 500–2000 seeds depending on variety.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too early — seeds need to fully mature and dry on the plant for best flavor and viability.
Overhead watering — causes gray mold on developing seed heads.
Over-fertilizing with nitrogen — produces massive leafy plants with small heads and poor seed yield.
Not protecting from birds — sparrows and finches will strip a seed head in hours.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties breed true. Many commercial types are hybrids — seed from these won't produce same plant.
seed_saving.harvest: Leave seed head on plant until fully mature — back of head turns brown. Seeds should be plump and show full coloring.
seed_saving.method: Cut head with 12 inches of stem. Hang upside down in dry airy space covered loosely with paper bag to catch seeds as they dry.
seed_saving.drying: Hang 3–4 weeks in warm airy location. Seeds should rattle and pull free easily.
seed_saving.storage: Store seeds in paper envelope or mesh bag — needs some airflow. Cool, dry, dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Protect drying heads from birds — lightweight mesh bag over the head while still on plant works well.

good.why: Sunflowers provide climbing structure and partial shade for cucumbers in hot afternoon sun.
Sunflower draws aphids away from squash as a trap crop. Both thrive in full sun.
Nasturtium is a ground cover that retains moisture. Both attract pollinators.

bad.why: Sunflowers produce allelopathic compounds that stunt potato growth.
Sunflower root chemicals inhibit bean growth and nitrogen fixation.

culinary: Seeds roasted and salted for snacking. Cold-pressed sunflower oil used widely in cooking. Seeds ground into sunflower seed butter — allergen-free alternative to peanut butter. Petals edible in salads. Sprouts eaten as microgreens.
medicinal: Seeds extremely high in vitamin E — one of the richest plant sources. Magnesium for heart health. Selenium for thyroid function. Phytosterols lower LDL cholesterol. Seeds high in tryptophan — precursor to serotonin.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Colonies on stems and under leaves. Can be significant on young plants.
pests.control: Ladybugs are a natural predator. Blast with water. Neem oil.

pests.name: Cutworm
pests.desc: Moth larvae that sever seedlings at ground level overnight.
pests.control: Cardboard collar pushed into soil around stem base. Diatomaceous earth ring.

pests.name: Sunflower Moth
pests.desc: Larvae bore into seed heads and consume developing seeds.
pests.control: Monitor from early flowering. Remove and destroy affected heads. Bt spray.

pests.name: Birds
pests.desc: Will harvest your seeds before you do — especially sparrows and finches.
pests.control: Loose mesh netting over seed heads as they mature. Harvest slightly early and dry indoors.

varieties.name: Mammoth Russian
varieties.description: Classic giant sunflower — grows 10–12 feet tall with 12-inch seed heads. The archetypal sunflower.
varieties.notes: Best for seed production and the classic tall statement plant.

varieties.name: Autumn Beauty
varieties.description: Branching plant with multiple flowers in mixed colors — gold, bronze, burgundy, and bicolor.
varieties.notes: Best for cut flowers — long season of blooms.

varieties.name: Teddy Bear
varieties.description: Dwarf 2–3 foot plant with fluffy double golden flowers. Excellent for small gardens and containers.

varieties.name: Lemon Queen
varieties.description: Pale lemon-yellow flowers on branching plants. Very different from standard golden yellow.
varieties.notes: Best for arrangements — unusual soft color.

varieties.name: Pro Cut Gold
varieties.description: Bred for cut flower production — single stem, no pollen (doesn't stain), very long vase life.
varieties.notes: The professional cut-flower sunflower. Pollen-free is a selling point for allergy sufferers.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Sunflowers are non-toxic to dogs and cats. Sunflower seeds (without shells, unsalted) are a safe treat in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep. Can transplant when very small if careful.

name: Rosemary
growing_zones: 7–11 (grow as annual or container plant in colder zones)

season.start_indoors: 10–12 weeks before last frost — slow from seed
season.harvest_window: Year-round in zones 7+ once established

seed.desc: Surface sow on moist mix — needs light. Germination is notoriously slow and inconsistent. Start many extras.

germination.desc: Slow to emerge. Keep at 65–70°F. Do not overwater while waiting — roots rot easily before sprouting.

seedling.desc: Grows very slowly in first months. Ensure bright light. Pinch tips once 4 inches tall to encourage branching.

young.desc: Transplant to final spot in full sun with excellent drainage. Begin harvesting lightly once plant is 6 inches tall.

adult.desc: Woody perennial. Prune after flowering to maintain shape. Gets better each year — established plants are very productive.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water deeply then let soil dry completely. Overwatering is the number one killer.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours minimum. More sun = stronger fragrance and flavor.
care.soil: Sandy, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.0–7.0. Amend clay soils heavily or use raised beds.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. Plants can spread 3–4 feet wide when mature.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Light compost in spring only. Over-fertilizing reduces essential oil content and flavor.
care.notes: In cold climates, grow in containers and bring indoors for winter. Prune by one-third each spring to prevent woodiness.

container.min_size: 12-inch pot minimum. Terracotta preferred for moisture wicking.
container.notes: Excellent container plant. Use fast-draining mix. Bring indoors in winter in zones below 7 — place in sunniest window.

propagation.desc: Most reliable method. Take 3–4 inch softwood cuttings in spring or summer. Strip lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, plant in gritty mix. Roots in 3–4 weeks.
Slow and unreliable — germination rate is low. Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant date and expect losses.
Bend a flexible stem to the ground, pin with a wire staple, and cover the middle section with soil. Roots in 4–6 weeks. Sever and transplant.

harvest.when: Once plant is at least 6 inches tall and well established. Harvest any time during the growing season.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with sharp scissors, never removing more than one-third of the plant at once. Cut above a leaf node to encourage branching.
harvest.storage: Fresh sprigs last 2 weeks wrapped in damp paper towel in the fridge. Dry bundles hung upside down in 1–2 weeks. Freeze whole sprigs — use directly from frozen.
harvest.yield: An established plant can provide continuous harvests throughout the season. One plant is usually enough for a household.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — rosemary evolved in dry Mediterranean conditions. Wet roots rot quickly. When in doubt, don't water.
Poor drainage — must have fast-draining soil. Heavy clay will kill it.
Cutting into old woody growth — only prune green growth. Old wood won't regenerate.
Not enough sun — less than 6 hours produces weak, flavorless plants prone to disease.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Seeds viable but germination rates are low.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flowers to dry fully on the plant. Seeds are tiny and contained in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried flower stems over a paper bag. Seeds fall out easily when fully dry.
seed_saving.drying: Flowers dry on the plant naturally. Spread harvested seeds on paper for 1 week.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings are far more reliable than seed for getting true-to-parent plants quickly.

good.why: Repels carrot fly with its strong aromatic oils.
Deters cabbage moth and cabbage butterfly.
Similar growing needs. Both are Mediterranean herbs that attract beneficial insects.
Rosemary repels bean beetles when planted nearby.

bad.why: Mint prefers moist soil — the watering needs directly conflict with rosemary's drought preference.
Cucumbers need consistent moisture that would overwater rosemary.

culinary: Cornerstone of Mediterranean cooking. Pairs with lamb, chicken, roasted potatoes, focaccia, and olive oil. Used in marinades, infused oils, and compound butters. Pairs well with garlic and lemon. Flowers are edible and make beautiful garnishes. Strong flavor — use sparingly with delicate dishes.
medicinal: Improves circulation and memory — active compound rosmarinic acid shown to inhibit acetylcholinesterase, potentially supporting cognitive function. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory. Traditionally used for digestive complaints, headaches, and hair loss (scalp massage with rosemary oil shown to rival minoxidil in some studies). Antimicrobial.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional on new growth, especially in humid conditions.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil spray. Usually not severe on established plants.

pests.name: Spittlebug
pests.desc: Foamy white masses on stems in spring. Larvae inside the foam.
pests.control: Wipe or blast off with water. Minimal damage — mainly cosmetic.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: Fungal disease from overwatering or poor drainage. Plant wilts and dies suddenly.
pests.control: Prevention only — ensure excellent drainage. Remove and destroy infected plants.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White powdery coating on leaves in humid conditions or with poor airflow.
pests.control: Improve airflow between plants. Neem oil spray. Remove affected growth.

varieties.name: Tuscan Blue
varieties.description: Upright, fast-growing, excellent flavor. Large deep blue flowers. Most popular culinary variety.
varieties.notes: The best all-around rosemary for cooking.

varieties.name: Prostrate / Trailing
varieties.description: Low spreading form — reaches 2 feet tall and 4–8 feet wide. Cascades beautifully over walls.
varieties.notes: Excellent for slopes, walls, and containers where it can trail.

varieties.name: Arp
varieties.description: Most cold-hardy rosemary — survives zone 6 and sometimes zone 5 with protection.
varieties.notes: The variety to grow in colder climates where rosemary normally dies.

varieties.name: Miss Jessop's Upright
varieties.description: Very upright, tall (5–6 feet) and narrow. Best for hedges and formal gardens.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: possible GI upset in very large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small culinary amounts. Very large quantities theoretically could cause issues — not a realistic concern. Rosemary essential oil should not be used on or around cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Excellent drainage essential.

name: Thyme

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil reaches 60°F
season.harvest_window: Year-round in mild climates. Spring through fall in colder zones.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Press gently into moist mix. Keep at 65–70°F.

germination.desc: Slow and irregular. Keep consistently moist but not wet. Thin to strongest seedling per cell.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly. Pinch tips at 4 inches to encourage bushy habit. Ensure bright light to prevent leggy growth.

young.desc: Transplant to final position. Full sun, excellent drainage. Begin light harvest once established.

adult.desc: Woody perennial that improves with age. Prune by one-third after flowering. Divide every 3–4 years to rejuvenate.

care.water: Drought tolerant. Water only when soil is dry. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. More sun = more essential oils = stronger flavor.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean, slightly alkaline. pH 6.0–8.0. Poor soil actually produces more aromatic plants than rich soil.
care.fertilizer: Avoid fertilizing — rich soil reduces essential oil concentration. Lean soil produces the most flavorful thyme.
care.notes: Semi-evergreen in most climates. Cut back hard in spring to remove winter-killed wood and encourage fresh growth.

container.min_size: 6-inch pot. Excellent on a sunny windowsill.
container.notes: One of the best herbs for containers. Use fast-draining mix. Excellent combined with rosemary and oregano in a Mediterranean herb pot.

propagation.desc: Best method. Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring or summer, strip lower leaves, root in moist sand or perlite. Roots in 2–3 weeks.
Dig up established plant in spring, split root ball into sections, replant immediately. Water well until re-established.
Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Germination slow and uneven — start extras.
Pin stems to soil and cover with a thin layer of compost. Roots form in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: Any time once plant is established. Best flavor just before or during flowering.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with scissors, leaving at least two-thirds of the plant intact. Strip leaves from stems by running fingers downward.
harvest.storage: Fresh in fridge wrapped in damp paper towel for 1–2 weeks. Dry in bundles or on screens — retains flavor excellently when dried. Freeze in ice cube trays with olive oil.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest possible all season. One plant produces more than most households can use.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — thyme is Mediterranean and expects dry periods. Soggy soil causes root rot quickly.
Too much fertilizer — reduces essential oil content and produces bland, weak-flavored plants.
Not pruning — unpruned plants become woody and unproductive. Prune hard after flowering each year.
Growing in shade — thyme needs sun to produce aromatic oils. Shade-grown thyme is nearly flavorless.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Many cultivars are hybrids and won't breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on the plant. Tiny seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower heads between palms over a bowl. Winnow to remove chaff.
seed_saving.drying: Flowers dry on plant naturally. Spread harvested seeds for 1 week on paper.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings and division give true-to-parent plants much more reliably than seed.

good.why: Repels cabbage worm, whitefly, and cabbage looper.
Repels tomato hornworm. Attracts beneficial predatory insects.
Thyme repels worms and pests that affect strawberries. Both enjoy similar dry conditions.
Same Mediterranean growing requirements. Together create a pollinator-friendly planting.

bad.why: Mint needs constant moisture — the opposite of thyme's preference. One will suffer.
Basil prefers richer, moister soil than thyme. Competing water needs.

culinary: Essential in French cuisine — a key component of bouquet garni and herbes de Provence. Pairs with chicken, lamb, fish, roasted vegetables, soups, and stews. Holds up well to long cooking unlike softer herbs. English thyme is the standard culinary variety. Lemon thyme adds citrus note.
medicinal: Thymol — thyme's primary essential oil — is a proven antimicrobial and antifungal used in commercial mouthwashes and antiseptics. Strong expectorant for coughs and bronchitis. European Commission has approved thyme preparations for upper respiratory infections. Antispasmodic for digestive cramps.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: From overwatering or poor drainage. Most common cause of thyme death.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering. Plant in raised beds or containers with gritty mix.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional on soft new growth in spring.
pests.control: Blast with water. Usually self-limiting — predators keep populations in check.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions — tiny mites cause stippled, yellowing leaves.
pests.control: Increase humidity around plant. Neem oil spray. Predatory mites as biological control.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: possible mild GI upset in large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in culinary amounts. Essential oils concentrated — avoid using thyme essential oil around cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Ensure crown is not buried — prefers lean dry conditions.

name: Mint

season.direct_sow: After last frost — but cuttings or divisions are far faster
season.harvest_window: Spring through fall. Year-round indoors.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Germination unreliable from seed. Starting from cuttings or divisions is much preferred.

germination.desc: Irregular germination. Keep at 65–70°F and consistently moist.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly once established. Thin to strongest plants. Begin pinching tips to encourage bushiness.

young.desc: Contains vigorously. Plant in a buried container or dedicated bed — will spread aggressively via underground runners.

adult.desc: Very vigorous spreader. Harvest frequently to keep contained and prevent flowering, which reduces leaf quality.

care.water: Prefers consistently moist soil. Does not tolerate drought well. Water regularly, especially in containers.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Tolerates more shade than most herbs. Too much sun in hot climates causes scorching.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Not fussy about soil quality.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches — but contain with buried barriers. Runners spread aggressively.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer monthly. Not heavy feeder.
care.notes: ALWAYS grow in containers or with root barriers — mint will take over a garden bed within one season. Divide every 2–3 years to keep vigorous.

container.min_size: 8-inch pot minimum. Containers are actually the ideal way to grow mint.
container.notes: Containers are the best way to grow mint — they contain the aggressive spreading runners. Repot every 1–2 years as roots fill the pot. Excellent on a kitchen windowsill.

propagation.desc: Easiest method. Cut 4-inch stem tip, remove lower leaves, place in water. Roots form in 1–2 weeks. Transfer to soil.
Dig up a clump in spring or fall, divide into sections ensuring each has roots, replant immediately.
Mint spreads via underground stolons. Dig up a runner section with roots attached and transplant directly.
Possible but slow and unreliable. Many mint varieties don't breed true from seed.

harvest.when: As soon as plant has multiple stems and is growing vigorously. Harvest before flowering for best flavor.
harvest.how: Cut stems back by half, just above a leaf node. This forces two new shoots and keeps the plant bushy. Harvest frequently.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water like cut flowers at room temp for 5–7 days. Wrap in damp paper towel in fridge for 2 weeks. Freeze whole leaves on a tray then bag. Dry in bundles — loses some flavor but still useful.
harvest.yield: Extremely productive. One plant in good conditions can supply more than most people need.

common_mistakes: Not containing it — mint planted in open ground will spread uncontrollably via underground runners within one season.
Letting it flower — flowering triggers bitter flavor and signals plant to put energy into seed rather than leaves.
Underwatering in containers — mint in pots dries out quickly and wilts fast. Check daily in summer.
Not dividing — old mint clumps become congested and less productive. Divide every 2–3 years.

seed_saving.type: Most culinary mint varieties are sterile hybrids or don't breed true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant if saving seed from true open-pollinated varieties.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower heads over a bowl to release tiny seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Dry flower heads in paper bag for 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Propagation via cuttings or division is the standard method — reliable, fast, and true-to-parent.

good.why: Strongly repels cabbage moth, aphids, and flea beetles.
Deters aphids and spider mites. Keep in a container nearby to control spreading.
Repels aphids that commonly attack pea plants.

bad.why: Rosemary needs dry soil — mint's moisture requirements will cause conflict.
Same conflict — lavender is drought-adapted, mint is not.
Mint can out-compete and eventually crowd out chamomile.

culinary: Used in teas, cocktails (mojito, mint julep), lamb dishes, Middle Eastern cuisine (tabbouleh, fattoush), desserts, chocolate, ice cream, and fresh salads. Spearmint is the standard culinary variety. Peppermint is stronger and used more in teas and confectionery. Fresh is always superior to dried.
medicinal: Menthol — mint's active compound — is a proven muscle relaxant and cooling agent. Peppermint oil capsules are a medically recognized treatment for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Relieves nausea, headaches (topical application to temples), and indigestion. Clears nasal congestion. Antimicrobial properties.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Can appear on new growth in clusters. Usually controlled by predatory insects.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Encourage ladybugs.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions — cause stippled yellowing on leaves.
pests.control: Increase moisture. Neem oil spray. Mist leaves regularly.

pests.name: Mint Rust
pests.desc: Orange pustules on undersides of leaves — fungal disease.
pests.control: Remove and destroy infected leaves. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering.

pests.name: Flea Beetles
pests.desc: Tiny black beetles create small holes in leaves.
pests.control: Row covers. Diatomaceous earth around base. Neem oil.

varieties.name: Spearmint (M. spicata)
varieties.description: The standard culinary mint. Milder than peppermint. Used in cooking, teas, and cocktails worldwide.
varieties.notes: The mint most people mean when they say 'mint'.

varieties.name: Chocolate Mint
varieties.description: Peppermint type with a genuine chocolate undertone. Dark brown stems. Striking in teas and desserts.
varieties.notes: One of the most popular specialty mints.

varieties.name: Apple Mint
varieties.description: Soft fuzzy leaves with a mild apple-mint flavor. Less aggressive spreader than other mints.
varieties.notes: Best mint for fresh eating — soft leaves pleasant in salads.

varieties.name: Mojito Mint (M. × villosa)
varieties.description: The authentic mojito cocktail mint. Large crinkled leaves. Very fragrant.
varieties.notes: If you make mojitos, grow this variety specifically.

varieties.name: Pennyroyal (M. pulegium)
varieties.description: Ground-covering mint. Historically used as insect repellent. Strongly medicinal. Avoid during pregnancy.
varieties.notes: Do not consume during pregnancy — uterotonic compounds.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: pennyroyal mint is severely toxic — avoid
pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea in large amounts; pennyroyal causes liver failure
pet_toxicity.notes: Common spearmint and peppermint are safe in small amounts. PENNYROYAL MINT (Mentha pulegium) is severely toxic to cats and dogs — can cause liver failure and death. Never use pennyroyal essential oil on pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Plant in a container sunk into ground to prevent spreading.

name: Oregano

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall. Year-round in mild climates.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Tiny seeds. Press gently into moist starting mix. Keep at 65–70°F.

germination.desc: Relatively reliable germinator in warm conditions. Seedlings are tiny at first — be patient.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly initially. Pinch tips at 4 inches to encourage bushy growth. Ensure good airflow to prevent damping off.

young.desc: Begins vigorous growth. Harvest lightly once plant reaches 6 inches. Full flavor develops as plant matures.

adult.desc: Perennial that gets more flavorful with age. Prune hard after flowering. Divide every 3–4 years.

care.water: Drought tolerant. Water when soil is dry. Lean, dry conditions actually produce more aromatic and flavorful plants.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Essential for strong flavor.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean, slightly alkaline preferred. pH 6.0–8.0. Poor soil = more flavor.
care.fertilizer: Avoid fertilizing — rich soil and high nitrogen produce lush, tasteless plants.
care.notes: Greek oregano is far more flavorful than common oregano. Flavor intensifies when dried. Semi-evergreen in mild winters.

container.notes: Excellent container herb. Use fast-draining mix. Perfect companion in a Mediterranean herb pot with thyme and rosemary.

propagation.desc: Take 3-inch stem tip cuttings in spring or summer. Root in moist sand or perlite in 2–3 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring every 3–4 years. Dig up, split, replant sections immediately.
Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Reliable germinator in warm conditions.

harvest.when: Once plant is 6 inches tall. Best flavor just before flowers open — essential oil content is highest at this stage.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips, leaving at least two-thirds of the plant. Strip leaves by running fingers downward along the stem.
harvest.storage: Dries exceptionally well — flavor actually intensifies when dried. Bundle and hang in warm airy space 1–2 weeks. Store dried leaves in airtight jar. Freeze fresh leaves in olive oil.
harvest.yield: Very productive. One established plant typically produces more than a household can use.

common_mistakes: Over-fertilizing — produces lush growth with very little flavor or aroma.
Overwatering — oregano is drought-adapted. Wet soil leads to root rot and bland flavor.
Buying the wrong variety — common oregano sold in garden centers often has little flavor. Seek out Greek or Italian oregano specifically.
Not pruning after flowering — leads to woody, unproductive plants.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Greek oregano breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry completely on the plant.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower heads over a bowl. Tiny seeds fall out easily.
seed_saving.drying: Spread on paper for 1 week after harvest.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Flavor varies between seed-grown plants. Taste before selecting parent plants for seed saving.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites. Improves tomato flavor according to many growers.
Oregano's aromatic oils confuse and deter pepper pests.
Similar growing needs. Both deter common vegetable garden pests.
Traditional Mediterranean pairing — oregano planted under vines deters insects.

bad.why: Mint's aggressive spreading and moisture needs conflict with oregano.
Fennel inhibits growth of most herbs including oregano.

culinary: Indispensable in Italian, Greek, Mexican, and Middle Eastern cooking. Essential on pizza and in tomato sauce. Pairs with lamb, chicken, seafood, and roasted vegetables. One of the few herbs that is better dried than fresh — drying concentrates the essential oils. Za'atar spice blend is built on oregano.
medicinal: Carvacrol and thymol — oregano's primary active compounds — are among the most potent naturally occurring antimicrobials. Oregano oil shows activity against drug-resistant bacteria in lab studies. Anti-inflammatory, antifungal, and antioxidant. Used traditionally for respiratory infections, digestive complaints, and as a topical antiseptic.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional on new growth. Usually minor on healthy plants.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Predatory insects usually manage populations naturally.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot, dry, dusty conditions. Cause speckling and yellowing of leaves.
pests.control: Mist leaves to increase humidity. Neem oil spray.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: From overwatering or poorly draining soil.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering frequency. Remove and destroy affected plants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset, vomiting in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in tiny culinary amounts — a lick of something with oregano is fine. Large amounts can cause GI upset. Essential oil is concentrated and should be kept away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Lean soil preferred — don't bury crown.

name: Parsley

season.direct_sow: 4 weeks before last frost — tolerates light frost
season.transplant: Early spring — cold hardy to 20°F when established
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through fall. Overwinters in mild climates.

seed.desc: Soak seeds in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to speed germination. Sow ¼ inch deep.

germination.desc: Notoriously slow germinator. Keep consistently moist. Soil temperature of 65°F+ speeds germination considerably.

seedling.desc: Thin to 6–8 inches apart. Seedlings grow slowly at first — be patient. Transplant carefully as taproots dislike disturbance.

young.desc: Growth accelerates once root system is established. Begin harvesting outer leaves once plant has 5+ stems.

adult.desc: Biennial — bolts and flowers in year two. In year one, harvest leaves continuously. Roots become edible in year two.

care.water: Consistently moist but well-draining. Does not tolerate drought or waterlogging. Even moisture is key.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Tolerates more shade than most herbs — good for partly shaded gardens.
care.soil: Rich, deep, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Amend with compost for best results.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly during growing season. Benefits from regular feeding unlike drought-adapted herbs.
care.notes: Slow to establish but very cold hardy once it is. Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool.

container.min_size: 8-inch pot minimum — needs depth for taproot. 12 inches preferred.
container.notes: Good container plant but needs consistent watering. Taproot needs at least 8 inches of depth. Water more frequently than in-ground plants.

propagation.desc: Primary method. Soak seeds 24 hours in warm water to break dormancy. Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant or direct sow 4 weeks before last frost.
Rarely done but possible in early spring. Parsley develops a taproot that makes division difficult — handle roots carefully.

harvest.when: Begin when plant has at least 5 stems. Harvest outer stems first, leaving center stems to grow.
harvest.how: Cut outer stems at the base — not the tips. This encourages the plant to produce new growth from the center. Never take more than one-third at a time.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water like cut flowers — lasts 1–2 weeks on the counter. Refrigerate in damp paper towel for up to 2 weeks. Freeze chopped in ice cube trays with water. Dried parsley loses much of its flavor.
harvest.yield: One plant produces a continuous supply throughout the season when harvested correctly.

common_mistakes: Impatient with germination — parsley takes 2–4 weeks to germinate. It's not dead, it's slow.
Not soaking seeds before sowing — dry seeds can take 4+ weeks. Soaking cuts time to 1–2 weeks.
Harvesting from the top — always harvest outer stems from the base. Harvesting tips reduces total yield.
Letting it bolt in year two — once it flowers, leaf quality drops sharply. Remove flower stems to prolong harvest.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — flowers and sets seed in year two. Open-pollinated varieties breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Leave selected plants to overwinter. In year two they bolt, flower, and set seed. Harvest seed heads when brown.
seed_saving.method: Cut seed heads when half the seeds are brown. Bag and hang to dry — seeds shatter when fully dry.
seed_saving.drying: Hang cut stems upside down in paper bag for 2–3 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Parsley crosses with other parsley varieties and with related wild plants. Isolate by 300 feet for pure seed.

good.why: Attracts predatory wasps that parasitize tomato pests. Both enjoy similar growing conditions.
Classic companion. Parsley repels asparagus beetles. Both benefit each other.
Parsley improves rose fragrance according to traditional companion planting lore. Repels rose beetles.
Same family — but parsley attracts beneficial insects that help carrots. Keeps some distance.

bad.why: Onions, garlic, and chives stunt parsley growth when planted too closely.
Parsley can inhibit lettuce germination when planted very close.

culinary: One of the most widely used culinary herbs globally. Two main types: flat-leaf (Italian) has stronger flavor, curly-leaf is milder and used as garnish. Essential in tabbouleh, chimichurri, gremolata, persillade, and fines herbes. Rich, fresh flavor pairs with almost everything. Flat-leaf preferred for cooking.
medicinal: Exceptionally high in vitamin K — critical for blood clotting and bone health. Very high in vitamin C — a handful of fresh parsley contains as much vitamin C as an orange. Rich in iron. Volatile oils apiol and myristicin shown to have antitumor activity in research. Traditional use as a diuretic and for kidney stones. Chewing fresh parsley neutralizes bad breath.

pests.name: Parsleyworm
pests.desc: Striking green caterpillar with black and yellow bands — larvae of the black swallowtail butterfly.
pests.control: Hand pick if population is large. Consider leaving some — they become beautiful butterflies. Plant extra parsley to share.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cluster on stems and under leaves. Especially problematic on young plants.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Encourage predatory insects by planting flowers nearby.

pests.name: Carrot Fly
pests.desc: Same pest as attacks carrots — parsley is in the same family. Larvae damage roots.
pests.control: Row covers. Companion plant with onion or chive to confuse adults.

pests.name: Crown Rot
pests.desc: Fungal disease causing collapse at soil level in wet conditions.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Ensure airflow around plant base.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: spring parsley (Cymopterus watsonii) — different plant is toxic
pet_toxicity.symptoms: photosensitization possible in very large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Common garden parsley (Petroselinum) is safe in small amounts. Excellent breath freshener for dogs. Very large amounts can cause photosensitization. Pregnant animals should avoid — uterine stimulant.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Direct sow preferred — taproot dislikes disturbance.

name: Cilantro

season.direct_sow: 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring. Again in late summer for fall harvest. Every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply.
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Bolts quickly in summer heat.

seed.desc: The 'seed' is actually a fruit containing two seeds. Crush lightly before sowing to improve germination. Sow ¼ inch deep.

germination.desc: Germinates relatively quickly in cool soil (55–65°F). Warm soil dramatically slows or prevents germination.

seedling.desc: Thin to 4–6 inches apart. Does not transplant well — thin in place by snipping with scissors rather than pulling.

young.desc: Grow rapidly in cool weather. Begin harvesting outer leaves at 4–6 inches tall. Watch for bolting triggers — heat or long days.

adult.desc: Bolts rapidly when temperatures exceed 75°F or days lengthen. Collect coriander seeds when plant flowers and sets seed.

care.water: Moderate and consistent moisture. Does not tolerate drought or waterlogging. Water at the base.
care.light: Full sun in cool climates. Partial shade in warm climates to slow bolting.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.2–6.8.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen fertilizer promotes leafy growth and delays bolting slightly.
care.notes: Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest. Choose slow-bolt varieties like 'Slow Bolt' or 'Santo'.

container.min_size: 8-inch pot minimum — needs depth for taproot.
container.notes: Possible in containers but bolts faster than in-ground. Place in a cool spot and water consistently. Use deep containers.

propagation.desc: Only practical method. Crush the round 'seed' (fruit) lightly before sowing. Direct sow — does not transplant well. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks.

harvest.when: Begin harvesting when plants are 4–6 inches tall. Harvest regularly to delay bolting.
harvest.how: Cut outer leaves and stems at the base. Alternatively cut the whole plant back by half. Once it begins to bolt, harvest everything immediately — flavor deteriorates fast after bolting.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water at room temperature for 5–7 days. Refrigerate in damp paper towel for 1–2 weeks. Freeze whole leaves on a tray then transfer to bags. Does not dry well — loses most flavor.
harvest.yield: Each plant produces for 3–4 weeks before bolting in warm weather. Succession sowing is essential for continuous supply.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer heat — cilantro is a cool-season herb that bolts rapidly above 75°F. Plant in spring or fall.
Transplanting seedlings — cilantro has a sensitive taproot. Always direct sow.
Not succession sowing — a single planting provides only a few weeks of harvest. Sow new seeds every 2–3 weeks.
Letting it bolt without harvesting seeds — when it does bolt, let it go to seed for coriander spice. Free harvest from a 'failed' plant.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow plants to bolt and flower. Seeds (coriander) are ready when they turn from green to tan-brown.
seed_saving.method: Cut seed heads into a paper bag. Shake vigorously when fully dry to release seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Hang cut stems upside down in paper bag for 1–2 weeks. Seeds dry quickly.
seed_saving.storage: Airtight jar — coriander seeds are used as a spice and store well this way.
seed_saving.notes: The seeds ARE the coriander spice. Let some plants bolt intentionally to collect coriander for cooking. Two herbs from one plant.

good.why: Both cool-season crops with similar timing. Cilantro provides light shade for spinach in warm spells.
Cilantro attracts beneficial insects including hoverflies that prey on aphids.
Anise is said to improve cilantro germination when planted nearby.
Cilantro attracts beneficial insects that control pepper pests.

bad.why: Fennel inhibits cilantro growth and the two compete aggressively.
Lavender's dry soil preference conflicts with cilantro's moisture needs.

culinary: Essential in Mexican, Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, and Middle Eastern cuisines. Used in salsa, guacamole, curries, pho, tacos, chutneys, and ceviche. The seeds are coriander — a completely different flavor used as a spice in curry, bread, and pickling. About 4–14% of people have a gene that makes cilantro taste soapy.
medicinal: Rich in antioxidants including quercetin. Shown to have heavy metal chelating properties — may help remove lead and mercury from the body. Anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial. Digestive aid — reduces bloating and gas. Coriander seeds specifically shown to lower blood sugar and LDL cholesterol.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Common on new growth. Can spread rapidly in cool conditions.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Beneficial insects usually manage populations.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Clouds of white insects when plant is disturbed. Weaken plants.
pests.control: Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray.

pests.name: Bacterial Leaf Spot
pests.desc: Dark water-soaked spots on leaves in wet conditions.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Remove affected leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats. Many cats are indifferent; some show interest. Good source of vitamins.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow only — taproot makes transplanting nearly impossible.

name: Chives

season.direct_sow: As soon as soil can be worked in early spring — very cold tolerant
season.harvest_window: Early spring through late fall. One of the first herbs up in spring.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Fresh seed germinates much better than old seed — use seeds from the current or previous year.

germination.desc: Reliable and relatively quick in cool moist conditions. Tiny grass-like shoots emerge first.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly in first year. Thin to 4–6 inches. Avoid heavy harvest in year one to allow root development.

young.desc: Clumps begin to fill out. Light harvest is fine once plants are 6 inches tall.

adult.desc: Vigorous perennial clumps that expand each year. Divide every 3–4 years. Lavender-pink flowers are edible and attractive to bees.

care.water: Moderate and consistent moisture. More tolerant of drought than many herbs but best with regular watering.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. One of the most shade-tolerant alliums.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0. Not fussy.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring. Not a heavy feeder.
care.notes: One of the easiest perennial herbs. Cut back to 2 inches several times per season to keep productive and prevent woodiness. Flowers are edible.

container.notes: One of the best herbs for indoor growing. Very adaptable. Divide and repot every 2 years as clumps fill the container.

propagation.desc: Easiest and fastest method. Dig up clump in spring or fall, split into sections of 6–10 bulbs, replant 4–6 inches apart. Establishes quickly.
Sow fresh seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow in early spring. Use fresh seeds — viability drops quickly.

harvest.when: Once plants reach 6 inches tall. Begin light harvest in year one, heavy harvest from year two.
harvest.how: Cut leaves with scissors to within 2 inches of the ground. The plant regrows from the base. Harvest every 4–6 weeks or as needed. Flowers are also edible — harvest just as they open.
harvest.storage: Fresh chives wilt quickly. Use within a few days. Refrigerate in damp paper towel. Freeze chopped in ice cube trays. Dried chives lose most of their flavor.
harvest.yield: Very productive perennial. One established clump provides continuous harvest all season for years.

common_mistakes: Using old seed — chive seeds lose viability quickly. Use fresh seeds from the current season for reliable germination.
Not cutting back — chives that are never cut hard become weak and hollow. Cut to 2 inches several times per season.
Not dividing — old congested clumps become less productive. Divide every 3–4 years.
Expecting heavy harvest in year one — let plants establish their root systems before heavy harvesting.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some flower heads to dry completely on the plant. Black seeds visible in dried seed heads.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried seed heads into a paper bag.
seed_saving.drying: Seeds dry naturally on the plant. Further dry indoors for 1 week.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place. Use within 1–2 years.
seed_saving.viability: 1–2 years — viability drops off faster than most herbs.
seed_saving.notes: Division is the preferred propagation method — faster and more reliable than seed.

good.why: Chives repel carrot fly with their allium scent. Classic companion combination.
Repels aphids and black spot fungus. Traditional rose garden companion.
Repels apple scab. Plant chives around the base of apple trees.
Deters aphids and spider mites. Improves tomato flavor according to many growers.

bad.why: Alliums including chives inhibit bean and pea growth. Keep well separated.
Chives stunt pea growth when planted in proximity.

culinary: Mild onion flavor. Used as a garnish and flavoring in soups, salads, baked potatoes, eggs, cream cheese, dips, and sauces. Flowers are edible with a mild onion flavor — beautiful in salads. Garlic chives (A. tuberosum) have a distinct garlic flavor and are used extensively in Asian cuisines.
medicinal: Member of the allium family — shares health benefits with garlic and onion. Contains allicin and quercetin with antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. Supports cardiovascular health. Rich in vitamin K and vitamin C. Mildly antibacterial.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.desc: Tiny insects cause silvery streaking on leaves.
pests.control: Neem oil spray. Reflective mulch. Encourage predatory insects.

pests.name: Onion Fly
pests.control: Row covers. Crop rotation. Remove affected bulbs.

pests.name: Downy Mildew
pests.desc: Gray fuzzy coating on leaves in wet humid conditions.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Remove affected growth.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, Heinz body anemia
pet_toxicity.notes: All alliums including chives are toxic. Chives are often grown in pots within reach — be careful. Cats are especially sensitive.

transplant.deep_note: Plant clumps at nursery depth. Division transplants easily.

name: Sage

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm soil
season.transplant: Spring after last frost or early fall
season.harvest_window: Spring through fall. Semi-evergreen in mild climates.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep in moist starting mix. Germinates best at 60–70°F.

germination.desc: Moderate germination rate. Keep moist and warm. Thin to strongest seedlings.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in early stages. Ensure bright light. Begin pinching at 4 inches for bushy growth.

young.desc: Transplant outdoors in good sun with excellent drainage. Begin light harvest once well established.

adult.desc: Woody perennial. Prune hard after flowering each spring. Replace every 4–5 years as plants become overly woody.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water deeply but infrequently. Overwatering causes root rot quickly.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Essential for strong flavor and fragrance.
care.soil: Well-draining, sandy or loamy, slightly alkaline. pH 6.0–7.0. Does not tolerate wet feet.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. Plants spread to 2–3 feet wide.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Light spring compost. Over-fertilizing reduces essential oil content.
care.notes: Semi-evergreen. Cut back hard by one-third in early spring to prevent woodiness. Replace every 4–5 years.

container.notes: Does well in containers. Use well-draining mix. Bring indoors in zones below 4 for winter. Ensure full sun placement.

propagation.desc: Best method. Take 3–4 inch softwood cuttings in spring, strip lower leaves, root in moist sand in 3–4 weeks.
Divide established plants in spring every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Replant sections immediately.
Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Moderate germination. Many cultivars don't breed true.
Pin low branches to soil and cover with compost. Roots form in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: Once plant is well established — at least 6 inches tall. Best flavor just before and during flowering.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with scissors, never removing more than one-third of the plant. Strip leaves from stems as needed.
harvest.storage: Fresh in fridge for 1 week. Dries very well — bundle and hang in warm airy space. Dried sage retains good flavor for 1 year. Freeze whole leaves for longer storage.
harvest.yield: One established plant provides abundant harvest throughout the growing season.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — sage evolved in dry Mediterranean conditions. Wet roots rot rapidly.
Not pruning after flowering — plants become unproductive and overly woody without annual pruning.
Keeping plants too long — sage declines after 4–5 years. Replace with fresh plants from cuttings.
Growing in shade — shade-grown sage has little flavor or fragrance.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated common sage breeds true. Many ornamental cultivars are hybrids.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on the plant. Seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower heads between palms over a bowl.
seed_saving.drying: Spread on paper for 1 week after harvest.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings are the preferred propagation method for named cultivars.

good.why: Strongly repels cabbage moth, cabbage looper, and whitefly.
Repels carrot fly. Classic combination in the vegetable garden.
Identical growing conditions. Both attract beneficial insects and pollinators.
Sage deters tomato hornworm and flea beetles.

bad.why: Sage inhibits basil growth when planted too close.
Sage is believed to stunt cucumber growth.

culinary: Classic in Italian cuisine — saltimbocca, brown butter and sage pasta. Essential in traditional stuffing and Thanksgiving dishes. Pairs with pork, poultry, game, beans, and winter squash. Strong flavor — use sparingly with delicate dishes. Fried sage leaves are a simple, elegant garnish.
medicinal: One of the most studied medicinal herbs. 'Salvia' comes from Latin for 'to save.' Proven to improve memory and cognitive function in clinical trials. Antimicrobial — traditional use for sore throats (gargle with sage tea). Reduces hot flashes in menopausal women (clinical evidence). Anti-inflammatory. Reduces excessive sweating.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions — cause stippling and yellowing.
pests.control: Neem oil spray. Increase humidity around plant. Predatory mites.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: From overwatering — most common cause of sage death.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering. Ensure excellent soil drainage.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: In warm conditions or when grown indoors.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Small culinary amounts safe for dogs. Cats more sensitive — avoid large amounts. Sage essential oil toxic to cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Good drainage critical.

name: Dill

season.direct_sow: 2–3 weeks before last frost. Succession sow every 3–4 weeks for continuous harvest.
season.harvest_window: Early summer through fall from successive sowings

seed.desc: Direct sow ¼ inch deep. Do not start indoors — taproot dislikes transplanting. Scatter seeds thinly and cover lightly.

germination.desc: Reliable and fast in moderately warm soil. Thin to 12 inches for best leaf production or 18 inches for seed production.

seedling.desc: Feathery foliage appears quickly. Thin early — crowded dill bolts sooner and produces less.

young.desc: Rapid upright growth. Begin harvesting feathery leaves (dill weed) once plant is 8 inches tall.

adult.desc: Bolts and flowers — flower heads (dill heads) used for pickling. Seeds (dill seed spice) follow. Self-seeds freely.

care.water: Moderate moisture. Tolerates brief drought but consistent moisture delays bolting. Water at the base.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 5.8–6.5. Not fussy.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer. Avoid excess nitrogen — promotes leafy growth but delays seed production.
