care.notes: Self-seeds prolifically — allow some plants to go to seed for a self-sustaining patch. Tall stems may need staking in windy spots.

container.notes: Dill is tall (3–5 feet) with a deep taproot — containers are challenging. Dwarf varieties like 'Fernleaf' are more practical in large deep pots.

propagation.desc: Only method. Direct sow — cannot be transplanted successfully. Dill self-seeds so prolifically that it often establishes its own presence in the garden with no effort.

harvest.when: Harvest leaves (dill weed) from 8 inches tall. Flower heads for pickling just as they open. Seeds when dry and brown.
harvest.how: Cut feathery leaf stems with scissors. For dill heads, cut entire flower head with stem. For seeds, cut heads into a bag as they dry.
harvest.storage: Fresh dill weed lasts 1 week in the fridge in damp paper towel. Freeze chopped dill in ice cube trays — retains flavor better than drying. Dill seeds store for years in an airtight jar.
harvest.yield: Highly productive. One plant provides leaves for several weeks. Let go to seed for dill seed spice as a bonus harvest.

common_mistakes: Starting indoors — dill has a taproot that strongly resents transplanting. Always direct sow.
Planting near fennel — dill and fennel cross-pollinate and can hybridize, affecting both flavor and seed quality.
Not succession sowing — a single planting bolts and is done within weeks. Sow every 3–4 weeks for continuous harvest.
Planting near carrots when mature — young dill is fine near carrots but mature dill stunts them.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Self-seeds readily. Seeds are also the dill seed spice.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow plants to flower and set seed. Harvest seed heads when seeds turn from green to tan-brown.
seed_saving.method: Cut seed heads into a paper bag. Shake vigorously when dry to release seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Hang cut stems in paper bag for 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Airtight jar — dill seeds are a culinary spice and store like any spice.
seed_saving.notes: Do not plant near fennel — they cross-pollinate. Allow some plants to self-seed for a self-sustaining dill patch.

good.why: Repels aphids, spider mites, and cabbage looper when young.
Dill attracts beneficial insects that prey on lettuce pests.
Dill attracts predatory wasps and other beneficials. Improves cucumber flavor according to some growers.
Dill and onion grow well together without interference.

bad.why: Young dill is fine but mature dill stunts carrot growth and the two can hybridize.
Cross-pollinate with each other — both lose flavor integrity. Keep far apart.
Mature dill stunts tomato growth. Young dill is acceptable as a companion.

culinary: Two distinct products from one plant — dill weed (feathery leaves) and dill seed (spice). Dill weed essential in Scandinavian, Eastern European, and Middle Eastern cooking. Used in pickles, gravlax, potato salad, borscht, tzatziki, and egg dishes. Dill seed used as a spice in pickles, breads, and spice blends.
medicinal: Traditionally used to relieve colic in infants — gripe water historically contained dill. Digestive aid that reduces gas and bloating. Seeds contain flavonoids with antioxidant properties. Antimicrobial compounds. Rich in calcium and manganese.

pests.name: Parsleyworm
pests.desc: Same caterpillar that attacks parsley — larvae of the swallowtail butterfly. Striking green with black bands.
pests.control: Hand pick if necessary. Consider leaving them — they become beautiful butterflies. Plant extra dill to share.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Can appear on soft new growth.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Beneficial insects attracted by dill's flowers usually manage populations.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves in humid conditions.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats in small amounts. Good digestive herb for dogs.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow preferred — taproot is immediate and dislikes transplanting.

name: Chamomile

season.start_indoors: 4–6 weeks before last frost — but direct sowing is easier
season.direct_sow: Early spring — 2 weeks before last frost. Also fall sow in mild climates.
season.transplant: Spring, with care — does not transplant well
season.harvest_window: Early summer through fall from successive sowings

seed.desc: Surface sow — seeds need light to germinate. Scatter on moist soil surface and press gently. Do not cover.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable in cool moist conditions. Tiny seedlings resemble grass initially.

seedling.desc: Thin to 8–10 inches. Feathery, aromatic foliage develops quickly. Smells strongly of apple when touched.

young.desc: Rapid growth toward first flowers. Branching, bushy habit. Flower buds visible before plant is 12 inches tall.

adult.desc: Covered in small daisy-like flowers from early summer. Harvest daily at peak. Self-seeds prolifically — let some go to seed.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates brief drought once established. Water at the base — overhead watering promotes fungal disease on flowers.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Very adaptable.
care.soil: Average, well-draining. pH 5.6–7.5. Not fussy — thrives in poor soil. Rich soil produces lots of foliage but fewer flowers.
care.fertilizer: Avoid fertilizing — lean soil promotes better flower production. Too much nitrogen = leaves, not flowers.
care.notes: Self-seeds so readily it becomes a permanent garden resident after the first year. Thin volunteers as needed.

container.notes: Good container plant. Use lean, well-draining mix. Avoid over-fertilizing. Will self-seed into adjacent containers and garden beds.

propagation.desc: Primary method. Surface sow — needs light. Direct sow in early spring or fall. Self-seeds so readily that after the first year it usually establishes itself without effort.
Allow some plants to go to seed and chamomile will naturalize in the garden, returning year after year without replanting.

harvest.when: Harvest flowers when petals are fully open and beginning to reflex (bend back). This is when essential oil content is highest.
harvest.how: Pinch or snip individual flower heads. A chamomile comb or wide-toothed fork speeds harvesting considerably. Harvest every few days to keep plants producing.
harvest.storage: Dry flowers in a single layer on a screen in a warm, airy, dark space for 1–2 weeks. Do not pile up — they mold. Store dried flowers in airtight jar away from light. Use within 1 year for best potency.
harvest.yield: One plant produces hundreds of flowers over the season when harvested regularly. A small patch produces more chamomile than most households can use.

common_mistakes: Covering seeds when sowing — chamomile seeds need light to germinate. Surface sow only.
Harvesting flowers too early or too late — harvest when petals are fully open and just beginning to reflex backward for maximum essential oil content.
Drying in thick layers — flowers in piles mold rather than dry. Single layer on a screen is essential.
Over-fertilizing — produces lush leafy plants with very few flowers.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Self-seeds prolifically. Seeds tiny.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some flowers to dry completely on the plant. Tiny seeds in the dried center of the flower head.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried flower heads between palms over a bowl. Seeds are tiny — winnow carefully.
seed_saving.drying: Flowers dry on plant naturally. Further dry on paper for 1 week.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark location.
seed_saving.notes: Chamomile self-seeds so easily that deliberate seed saving is rarely necessary. Simply allow some plants to go to seed.

good.why: Chamomile attracts beneficial hoverflies and wasps that prey on cabbage pests.
Attracts pollinators and beneficial insects to the vegetable garden.
Chamomile is said to improve onion flavor and growth when planted nearby.
Traditional orchard companion — attracts beneficial insects, improves tree health in folk tradition.

bad.why: Mint's aggressive growth can crowd out chamomile.
Fennel's allelopathic compounds inhibit chamomile growth.

culinary: Primarily used as a tea — one of the world's most popular herbal teas. Light, apple-scented flavor. Used in desserts, infused honey, syrups, and cocktails. Pairs with vanilla, lemon, honey, and apple. Chamomile syrup is a popular mixer in craft cocktails.
medicinal: One of the most extensively studied medicinal herbs with thousands of years of documented use. Proven anti-inflammatory and antispasmodic. Clinical evidence for reducing anxiety — comparable to some pharmaceutical anxiolytics in mild-moderate anxiety. Promotes sleep. Topical use for wound healing, eczema, and skin irritation. Chamomile tea as antifungal drench for seedling damping off is a well-known organic gardening remedy.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional on new growth. Chamomile's strong scent repels many pests naturally.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Beneficial insects attracted by chamomile flowers usually manage populations.

pests.name: Mealybug
pests.desc: White cottony clusters on stems, mainly in humid conditions or indoors.
pests.control: Neem oil. Isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab for spot treatment.

pests.name: Gray Mold (Botrytis)
pests.desc: Fuzzy gray mold on flowers and stems in wet conditions.
pests.control: Harvest flowers promptly. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Remove affected material.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — bisabolol, chamazulene, anthemic acid, tannic acid
pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, allergic reactions, internal bleeding with long-term use
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists chamomile as toxic to dogs and cats. Despite being used in herbal teas for humans, it can cause problems in pets — especially cats. Avoid.

transplant.deep_note: Surface sow — seeds need light. Transplants shock easily. Direct sow preferred.

name: Thai Basil

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Early summer through first frost

seed.desc: Surface sow on moist starting mix. Needs warmth — 70°F+ for reliable germination.

germination.desc: Fast in warm conditions. Tiny seedlings emerge in clusters.

seedling.desc: Thin to 6 inches. Pinch tips early for bushy growth.

young.desc: Pinch flower buds to delay bolting. More heat-tolerant than sweet basil.

adult.desc: Purple flower spikes are attractive but trigger leaf bitterness. Pinch or allow to flower for ornamental use.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Slightly more drought tolerant than sweet basil.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Loves heat more than sweet basil.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced monthly. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: More heat and humidity tolerant than sweet basil. Holds up much better when cooked — ideal for stir-fries and curries.

container.notes: Excellent container herb. Great on a sunny patio in summer.

propagation.desc: Surface sow in warm conditions. Germinates in 5–7 days.
4-inch stem cuttings root in water in 1–2 weeks.

harvest.when: Once plant has 6+ leaves and multiple stems.
harvest.how: Pinch stems just above a leaf node. Harvest from the top down.
harvest.storage: Store stems in water at room temperature. Freeze in oil for longer storage.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest all season when pinched regularly.

common_mistakes: Treating it like sweet basil — Thai basil tolerates more heat and can handle brief cooking.
Not pinching flower spikes — flowering reduces leaf quality though is slower to bitter than sweet basil.
Refrigerating — turns black quickly. Keep at room temperature.
Under-watering in containers — wilts fast in pots in summer heat.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Crosses with other basil varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow purple flower spikes to dry. Seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried spikes over a bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate from other basil varieties by 150+ feet for pure seed.

good.why: Repels aphids and whitefly. Classic pairing.
Both love heat. Basil deters pepper pests.

culinary: Essential in Thai cuisine — pad kra pao (Thai basil stir-fry), green and red curries, pho, and Vietnamese dishes. Anise-clove flavor is more complex than sweet basil and holds up to heat. Stems and flowers also edible. Cannot be substituted with sweet basil in authentic Thai cooking.
medicinal: Adaptogenic properties. Rich in eugenol — anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial. Traditional use in Ayurvedic medicine for stress, coughs, and skin conditions. Antioxidant-rich.

pests.name: Damping Off
pests.control: Sterile mix. Good airflow. Don't overwater.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as standard basil — safe for dogs and cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Lemon Basil

season.harvest_window: Early summer through first frost

seed.desc: Surface sow on warm moist mix. Needs 70°F+ for germination.

germination.desc: Fast in warm conditions. Smells strongly of lemon from first true leaves.

seedling.desc: Delicate at this stage. Avoid overwatering. Thin to 6–8 inches.

young.desc: Pinch tips to encourage bushy growth. White flowers appear earlier than other basils.

adult.desc: Smaller, more compact plant than sweet basil. Harvest frequently.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Don't let soil dry out completely.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced feeding monthly.
care.notes: Smaller plant than sweet basil. White flowers are very attractive. Bolts faster in heat.

container.notes: Compact size makes it ideal for containers. Great on a kitchen windowsill.

propagation.desc: Surface sow in warm conditions.
Root 4-inch cuttings in water in 1–2 weeks.

harvest.when: Once plant has multiple stems and 6+ leaves.
harvest.how: Pinch from the top above a leaf node.
harvest.storage: Stems in water at room temperature. Freeze in oil.
harvest.yield: Compact but productive with regular harvesting.

common_mistakes: Expecting sweet basil flavor — the lemon note changes which dishes it suits.
Letting it bolt — bolts faster than sweet basil. Pinch buds aggressively.
Overwatering seedlings — very susceptible to damping off.
Using dried — loses almost all lemon fragrance when dried.

seed_saving.type: Hybrid — seeds may not breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow white flower spikes to dry on plant.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry spikes into a paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Being a hybrid, propagation via cuttings is preferred to preserve characteristics.

good.why: Repels aphids. Lemon scent adds additional pest confusion.
Traditional pairing in Southeast Asian cuisine — plant near the kitchen for easy access.

culinary: Fragrant lemon-basil scent ideal for fish, seafood, salads, desserts, teas, and cocktails. Popular in Indonesian, Thai, and Lao cuisine. Used in lemon basil chicken, rice dishes, and herb teas. Pairs beautifully with lemon curd, shortbread, and fruit salads. Use fresh only — loses fragrance completely when cooked or dried.
medicinal: Similar to sweet basil — anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial. Lemon-scented essential oils shown to have mild anxiolytic and mood-lifting properties. Digestive aid.

pests.name: Damping Off
pests.control: Sterile mix. Good airflow. Avoid overwatering.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Holy Basil (Tulsi)

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm soil
season.transplant: When nights above 55°F — more cold-sensitive than sweet basil
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through first frost

seed.desc: Surface sow on warm moist mix. Needs 70–75°F for reliable germination.

germination.desc: Moderate germinator. Keep consistently warm and moist.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly at first. Distinctive clove-pepper aroma from early stage.

young.desc: Pinch tips for bushy growth. Purple or green stems depending on variety.

adult.desc: Vigorous and heat-loving. Allowed to flower in Ayurvedic tradition — flowers are used medicinally.

care.water: Moderate and consistent. Slightly more drought tolerant than sweet basil.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours. Loves heat.
care.soil: Well-draining, fertile. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Minimal — medicinal potency is higher in lean soil.
care.notes: Sacred in Hindu tradition — often grown near temples and homes for spiritual and medicinal purposes. More heat-tolerant than sweet basil.

container.notes: Traditionally grown in terracotta pots near the entrance of homes. Does very well in containers.

propagation.desc: Surface sow in warm conditions 6–8 weeks before transplant.
Root 4-inch cuttings in water in 1–2 weeks. Easy and reliable.

harvest.when: Once plant is established with multiple stems. In Ayurvedic tradition leaves are harvested in the morning.
harvest.how: Pinch leaves and stems from the top. In medicinal use the whole plant including flowers and seeds is used.
harvest.storage: Dry leaves on screens — retains medicinal compounds better than sweet basil when dried. Store in airtight jar.
harvest.yield: Very productive in warm conditions.

common_mistakes: Treating like sweet basil — Holy basil is not a culinary substitute for sweet basil. Very different flavor.
Planting out too early — extremely cold sensitive. Wait until soil is thoroughly warm.
Over-fertilizing — reduces medicinal compound concentration.
Discarding flowers — in Ayurvedic use, flowers and seeds are as valuable as leaves.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower spikes to dry fully on plant. Tiny seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried spikes between palms over a bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Seeds are used medicinally (sabja seeds) — soak in water and they form a gel used in drinks and Ayurvedic preparations.

good.why: Repels pests. Sacred plant believed to bring good energy to the garden.
Both love heat. Deters pests.

culinary: Used differently from sweet basil — clove-pepper-anise flavor is much stronger. Used in Thai dishes, particularly in authentic pad kra pao. Tulsi tea is a primary use — whole leaves steeped fresh or dried. Not typically used raw in salads.
medicinal: Considered the most medicinally important basil. Classified as an adaptogen — helps body adapt to stress. Extensive clinical research supports anxiolytic, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and antidiabetic effects. Lowers cortisol. Supports thyroid function. Antimicrobial against a wide range of bacteria and fungi. One of Ayurveda's most revered herbs.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Peppermint

season.start_indoors: Start from cuttings or divisions — seed not reliable
season.harvest_window: Spring through fall. Year-round indoors.

seed.desc: Peppermint is a sterile hybrid — does not produce viable seed. Start from cuttings or divisions only.

germination.desc: Not applicable — propagate vegetatively.

seedling.desc: Cuttings root quickly. New growth appears within 2 weeks.

young.desc: Contain immediately — spreading runners emerge quickly. Plant in buried container or dedicated bed.

adult.desc: Vigorous spreader. Strong menthol scent. Harvest frequently to keep productive.

care.water: Prefers consistently moist soil. Does not tolerate drought well.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More shade tolerant than most herbs.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer monthly.
care.notes: Much stronger menthol content than spearmint. Must be contained — spreads aggressively via underground stolons.

container.notes: Containers are the best way to grow peppermint. Repot every 1–2 years as roots fill the container.

propagation.desc: Cut 4-inch stem, remove lower leaves, place in water. Roots in 1–2 weeks.
Dig up clump, divide into sections with roots, replant immediately.
Dig up underground stolons with roots attached and transplant directly.

harvest.when: Once plant is actively growing with multiple stems.
harvest.how: Cut stems back by half above a leaf node. Harvest before flowering for strongest menthol content.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water 5–7 days. Freeze whole leaves. Dry in bundles — retains flavor well.
harvest.yield: Extremely productive. One plant provides abundant harvest all season.

common_mistakes: Not containing it — peppermint spreads even more aggressively than spearmint.
Expecting it to come true from seed — sterile hybrid. Must propagate vegetatively.
Letting it flower before harvesting — menthol content peaks just before flowering.
Confusing with spearmint — peppermint has much higher menthol content and different flavor profile.

seed_saving.type: Sterile hybrid — does not produce viable seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Not applicable.
seed_saving.method: Not applicable.
seed_saving.notes: Propagate only via cuttings, division, or runners.

good.why: Deters aphids and spider mites. Keep in container nearby.
Strongly repels cabbage moth and aphids.
Peppermint's strong scent confuses and deters a wide range of pests.

bad.why: Lavender is drought-adapted — mint's moisture needs will cause conflict.

culinary: Stronger and more intensely menthol-flavored than spearmint. Used in teas, hot chocolate, mojitos, confectionery, chocolate, ice cream, and desserts. Peppermint extract and oil are widely used in baking. Not typically used in savory cooking — menthol is too dominant. Essential for peppermint tea.
medicinal: Menthol is a powerful muscle relaxant and cooling agent. Peppermint oil enteric-coated capsules are a clinically validated treatment for IBS — reduces abdominal pain and bloating. Topical application to temples relieves tension headaches as effectively as acetaminophen in studies. Relieves nausea. Clears nasal congestion. Antimicrobial.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions. Stippled yellowing leaves.
pests.control: Neem oil. Increase humidity. Mist leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy in cats; GI upset in dogs
pet_toxicity.notes: The plant is less dangerous than the essential oil. Cats lack the liver enzymes to metabolize many essential oil compounds. Peppermint essential oil can cause serious toxicity in cats — never diffuse near cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth in a buried container to contain spreading.

name: Lemon Thyme

season.start_indoors: 6–8 weeks before last frost — cuttings preferred
season.direct_sow: Not recommended — grow from cuttings for true lemon flavor
season.harvest_window: Spring through fall

seed.desc: Can be grown from seed but may not breed true for lemon flavor. Cuttings preferred.

germination.desc: Slow and variable. Keep at 65–70°F and consistently moist.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Lemon scent develops as plant matures.

young.desc: Begin light harvest. Full lemon-thyme flavor develops as essential oils concentrate.

adult.desc: Low, spreading perennial. More compact than common thyme. Pink flowers very attractive to bees.

care.water: Drought tolerant. Water when soil is dry. Overwatering is the primary killer.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours for best flavor and fragrance.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean. pH 6.0–8.0.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil produces the most aromatic plants.
care.notes: More compact and lower-growing than common thyme. Beautiful edging plant. Variegated forms available.

container.notes: Excellent container plant. Works beautifully cascading over the edge of a pot.

propagation.desc: Best method to ensure true lemon flavor. Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring, root in moist sand in 2–3 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring every 3–4 years.
Pin stems to soil. Roots form in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: Any time once established. Best flavor before and during flowering.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with scissors leaving two-thirds of plant intact.
harvest.storage: Fresh in fridge 1–2 weeks. Dries well — hang in bundles. Freeze in olive oil.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest all season from one established plant.

common_mistakes: Growing from seed expecting strong lemon flavor — seed-grown plants vary. Take cuttings from proven plants.
Overwatering — same drought tolerance as common thyme.
Not pruning after flowering — becomes woody and unproductive.
Confusing with common thyme in cooking — lemon thyme adds a distinct citrus note.

seed_saving.type: Hybrid — does not breed true from seed. Cuttings are the correct propagation method.
seed_saving.harvest: Not reliable for seed saving.
seed_saving.method: Not applicable for true-to-parent plants.
seed_saving.notes: Always propagate lemon thyme from cuttings to preserve the lemon character.

good.why: Repels hornworm. Lemon scent adds additional pest confusion.
Repels aphids. Beautiful ornamental pairing.
Repels worms and pests. Tolerates similar growing conditions.

culinary: Citrus-thyme flavor works beautifully with fish, chicken, seafood, and summer vegetables. Used in marinades, herb butters, salad dressings, and cocktails. Pairs with lemon, garlic, and white wine. Excellent with roasted fish and grilled vegetables. Substitute for common thyme when a brighter, citrus note is wanted.
medicinal: Same antimicrobial and antispasmodic compounds as common thyme plus lemon-derived compounds. Traditionally used for respiratory infections and digestive complaints. Thymol content may be slightly lower than common thyme.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: From overwatering. Most common cause of failure.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Garlic Chives

season.direct_sow: Early spring as soon as soil can be worked
season.harvest_window: Early spring through late fall

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Use fresh seed — viability drops quickly. Germinates reliably in cool moist conditions.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool conditions. Flat, grass-like shoots emerge first.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in first year. Distinct garlic aroma from early stage. Avoid heavy harvest year one.

young.desc: Clumps begin to fill out. Begin moderate harvest. White star-shaped flowers are edible.

adult.desc: Very vigorous perennial. White flower clusters very attractive to pollinators. Divide every 3–4 years.

care.water: Moderate moisture. Slightly more drought tolerant than common chives.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Light spring feeding. Not a heavy feeder.
care.notes: Can self-seed aggressively if flowers are allowed to set seed — deadhead or harvest flowers before seed sets to control spread.

container.notes: Excellent container herb. White flowers are beautiful. Deadhead in containers to prevent aggressive self-seeding.

propagation.desc: Fastest method. Divide clumps in spring or fall every 3–4 years.
Sow fresh seeds. Germinates reliably in cool conditions. Use seeds from current season.

harvest.when: Once plant reaches 6 inches. Harvest leaves and flowers. Flower buds and open flowers are particularly prized.
harvest.how: Cut leaves with scissors to within 2 inches of the ground. Harvest flower buds for stir-fries or open flowers for garnish.
harvest.storage: Fresh in fridge 2–3 days. Freeze chopped. Dried loses most flavor.
harvest.yield: Very productive perennial. Flowers are an additional valuable harvest.

common_mistakes: Letting flowers go to seed — self-seeds very aggressively. Deadhead or harvest flowers before seed sets.
Not dividing — congested clumps become less productive after several years.
Using old seed — garlic chive seeds lose viability faster than most vegetables.
Confusing with common chives — the garlic flavor requires adjusting the quantities used in recipes.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some flower heads to dry completely. Black seeds visible in dried pods.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried heads into paper bag.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so readily that deliberate seed saving is rarely necessary.

good.why: Repels aphids and black spot. Beautiful garden pairing.
Garlic scent repels carrot fly.
Deters aphids and spider mites.

culinary: Essential in Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese cuisines. Used in dumplings (jiaozi), stir-fries, noodle dishes, kimchi, and as garnish. Flat leaves have stronger garlic-onion flavor than common chives. Flower buds stir-fried are a delicacy. Seeds used as a spice in some Asian cuisines.
medicinal: Stronger medicinal properties than common chives due to higher allicin content. Cardiovascular support, antimicrobial, and antioxidant properties similar to garlic. Digestive aid. Rich in vitamin C, vitamin K, and folate.

pests.name: Leaf Miner
pests.control: Remove affected leaves. Yellow sticky traps.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, Heinz body anemia
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as regular garlic — all alliums toxic to dogs and cats. Keep away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Greek Oregano

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm soil
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Keep at 65–70°F. More reliable than common oregano seed.

germination.desc: More reliable germinator than common oregano. Distinct peppery aroma from first leaves.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Fuzzy white-haired leaves develop — characteristic of Greek oregano.

young.desc: Full flavor develops as plant matures. Harvest once well established at 6 inches.

adult.desc: More compact and lower-growing than common oregano. White flowers. Very drought tolerant.

care.water: Very drought tolerant. Water only when soil is completely dry.
care.light: Full sun — 8+ hours for maximum flavor. The most sun-demanding oregano.
care.soil: Lean, sandy, well-draining, alkaline preferred. pH 6.5–8.0. Poor soil = best flavor.
care.fertilizer: Never fertilize — reduces essential oil content dramatically.
care.notes: The most flavorful oregano for cooking — far superior to common oregano. Fuzzy leaves are distinctive. White flowers rather than pink.

container.notes: Thrives in containers. Use very lean, gritty mix. Terracotta preferred. Full sun location essential.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. More reliable germinator than common oregano.
Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring or summer. Root in gritty mix in 3 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring every 3–4 years.

harvest.when: Just before or during flowering — highest essential oil content.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips leaving two-thirds of plant. Strip leaves from stems.
harvest.storage: Dries superbly — flavor actually intensifies when dried. Bundle hang 1–2 weeks. Store in airtight jar for up to 1 year.
harvest.yield: Highly productive. One plant more than sufficient for a household.

common_mistakes: Buying common oregano when Greek is intended — the flavor difference is enormous.
Fertilizing — immediately reduces the essential oil concentration that makes Greek oregano valuable.
Growing in rich soil — lean, poor soil produces far more flavorful plants.
Overwatering — extremely drought adapted. Wet roots rot quickly.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow white flower heads to dry on plant. Seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried heads over a bowl. Winnow lightly.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Taste leaves before selecting parent plants — flavor varies between individuals.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites. Improves tomato flavor.
Aromatic oils deter pepper pests.
Traditional Mediterranean companion under vines.

culinary: The true cooking oregano of Mediterranean cuisine. What most people taste on pizza and in Italian-American food is Greek oregano. Essential in Greek salad, moussaka, souvlaki, and tomato-based sauces. Much more pungent and peppery than common oregano — use less. Drying concentrates and improves its flavor.
medicinal: Higher carvacrol and thymol content than common oregano — among the most potent natural antimicrobials known. Oregano oil supplements typically standardized from Greek oregano. Shown active against drug-resistant bacteria, Candida, and parasites in vitro. Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as standard oregano. Fine in tiny amounts, problematic in large amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Roman Chamomile

season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall — flowers over a longer period than German chamomile

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Keep at 55–65°F. Prefers cooler germination than German chamomile.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool conditions. Apple scent present from earliest stage.

seedling.desc: Low, mat-forming growth habit develops early. Quite different from the upright German chamomile.

young.desc: Spreads horizontally via runners. Can be used as a ground cover or lawn substitute.

adult.desc: Perennial ground cover 3–6 inches tall. Flowers over a long season. Releases apple scent when walked on.

care.water: Moderate. More drought tolerant than German chamomile once established.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, sandy, slightly acidic. pH 5.6–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil promotes better flower production.
care.notes: Can be used as a lawn substitute — tolerates light foot traffic. Releases beautiful apple scent when walked on. 'Treneague' is a non-flowering lawn variety.

container.notes: Good in wide shallow containers or window boxes. Cascades nicely over pot edges.

propagation.desc: Easiest for perennial clumps. Divide in spring or fall.
Spreads naturally via surface runners. Detach rooted runners and transplant.
Surface sow in cool conditions. 'Treneague' lawn variety is sterile and must be propagated by division.

harvest.when: When flower petals are fully open and beginning to reflex. Smaller flowers than German chamomile.
harvest.how: Pinch or snip individual flower heads. Harvest regularly to keep plants producing.
harvest.storage: Dry in single layer on screens in warm dark airy space. Store in airtight jar for up to 1 year.
harvest.yield: Produces over a longer season than German chamomile but fewer flowers per plant.

common_mistakes: Confusing with German chamomile — Roman chamomile is perennial and mat-forming. German is annual and upright.
Expecting identical medicinal properties — Roman chamomile contains different compounds and is used differently.
Not allowing to spread — Roman chamomile is a ground cover and needs space to spread.
Mowing before flowering — if using as a lawn, allow to flower occasionally for best fragrance and health.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated (except Treneague which is sterile). Breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds in dried flower center.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried heads between palms over a bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Treneague non-flowering lawn variety cannot be seed saved — propagate by division only.

good.why: Attracts beneficial insects that prey on cabbage pests.
Traditionally said to improve onion health and flavor.
Traditional orchard companion — attracts beneficial insects.

culinary: Same uses as German chamomile — primarily as a tea. Slightly more bitter and complex flavor than German chamomile. Used in herbal tea blends, infused honey, and syrups. Less commonly used than German chamomile for culinary purposes.
medicinal: Contains different active compounds than German chamomile — notably isobutyl angelate and isoamyl angelate rather than alpha-bisabolol. Traditional use for anxiety, insomnia, digestive complaints, and menstrual cramps. Used extensively in aromatherapy — Roman chamomile essential oil is considered more valuable than German for emotional and nervous system support.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, contact dermatitis
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as common chamomile — listed as toxic by ASPCA for dogs and cats.

transplant.deep_note: Surface sow or plant divisions at nursery depth.

name: French Lavender

season.start_indoors: 10–12 weeks before last frost — cuttings preferred
season.direct_sow: Not recommended — very slow from seed
season.harvest_window: Almost year-round in mild climates — one of the longest-blooming lavenders

seed.desc: Very slow and unreliable from seed. Cuttings strongly preferred.

germination.desc: Slow. Keep at 65–70°F. Low germination rates — sow many extras.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Serrated (dentata) leaf margin becomes visible as plant matures.

young.desc: Transplant to sunny, well-drained location. Will not bloom well in first year from seed.

adult.desc: Blooms almost continuously in mild climates. Distinctive tufted flower heads with petal-like bracts. Less cold hardy than English lavender.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water deeply but infrequently.
care.light: Full sun — 8+ hours.
care.soil: Sandy, well-draining, alkaline preferred. pH 6.5–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Light spring compost only.
care.notes: More heat and humidity tolerant than English lavender. Less cold hardy. Excellent for warmer climates where English lavender struggles. Nearly ever-blooming.

container.notes: Excellent container plant in cooler zones — bring indoors for winter. Requires very sunny position.

propagation.desc: Strongly preferred. Take 3-inch softwood cuttings in spring or summer. Root in gritty mix in 3–4 weeks.
Very slow and unreliable. Not recommended for practical purposes.

harvest.when: When flower buds are showing color but not fully open.
harvest.how: Cut flower stems above the foliage. Do not cut into woody stems.
harvest.storage: Bundle and hang to dry. Distinctive flowers hold their shape and color well when dried — excellent for crafts.
harvest.yield: Abundant flowers over a very long season in mild climates.

common_mistakes: Planting in zones below 8 without protection — much less cold hardy than English lavender. Will die in hard freezes.
Overwatering — same drought preference as all lavenders.
Cutting into old wood — only prune green growth.
Expecting identical properties to English lavender — French lavender has lower essential oil content.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated but rarely sets seed reliably. Cuttings are the standard propagation method.
seed_saving.harvest: Rarely necessary — cuttings preferred.
seed_saving.method: N/A
seed_saving.notes: Propagate exclusively from cuttings for reliable, true-to-parent plants.

good.why: Classic pairing. Lavender repels aphids and adds fragrance.
Similar growing conditions. Both attract pollinators.
Mediterranean companions with matching care needs.

bad.why: Mint's moisture needs conflict with lavender's drought preference.
Shade and moisture lovers — opposite of lavender's needs.

culinary: Less commonly used in cooking than English lavender due to stronger, more camphorous scent. Flowers used as garnish and in herbal teas. In warm climates where it grows prolifically, used similarly to English lavender in small quantities.
medicinal: Similar but milder medicinal properties to English lavender. Lower linalool content reduces its potency as an anxiolytic. Still useful for aromatherapy, topical wound healing, and insect repellent. Camphor content makes it better for respiratory complaints than English lavender.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: nausea, vomiting
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as standard lavender — cats more sensitive. Avoid essential oils around cats entirely.

transplant.deep_note: Same as English lavender — crown at soil level, gravel mulch for drainage.

name: Vietnamese Coriander

season.start_indoors: Start from cuttings — does not grow from seed reliably
season.transplant: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: All season in warm climates. Summer through frost in colder zones.

seed.desc: Rarely grown from seed. Start from stem cuttings rooted in water — the standard method.

germination.desc: Propagate from cuttings, not seed.

seedling.desc: Cuttings root very quickly in water. Distinctive pointed leaves with dark chevron markings develop.

young.desc: Grows rapidly in warm conditions. Begin harvesting once plant is established with multiple stems.

adult.desc: Vigorous spreader in warm conditions. More heat tolerant than true cilantro — an advantage in summer gardens.

care.water: Prefers consistent moisture. More tolerant of wet conditions than Mediterranean herbs.
care.light: Partial shade to full sun. Tolerates more shade than true cilantro.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced monthly feeding.
care.notes: The summer substitute for cilantro — tastes similar but tolerates heat without bolting. Vigorous spreader in warm climates — may need containing.

container.notes: Excellent container plant. Bring indoors in winter in zones below 9. Grows well on a warm windowsill.

propagation.desc: Only practical method. Cut 4-inch stem, place in water — roots form in 3–5 days. Transfer to soil once roots are 1 inch long.

harvest.when: Once plant has multiple stems. Harvest continuously.
harvest.how: Pinch or cut stem tips. Plant regrows quickly from nodes.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water at room temperature 5–7 days. Freeze whole leaves. Does not dry well.
harvest.yield: Extremely productive in warm conditions. One plant provides continuous harvest.

common_mistakes: Trying to grow from seed — propagate from cuttings only for reliable results.
Using it in cold dishes expecting true cilantro flavor — slight difference, particularly noticeable raw.
Letting it dry out — prefers more moisture than Mediterranean herbs.
Exposing to frost — kill it quickly below 40°F. Bring indoors early.

seed_saving.type: Rarely sets seed outside of tropical climates.
seed_saving.harvest: Not practical outside tropical regions.
seed_saving.method: Propagate exclusively from cuttings.
seed_saving.notes: One cutting from a friend or market is all you need — roots in days and grows vigorously.

good.why: Attracts beneficial insects. Provides ground cover in hot weather.
Both enjoy heat and humidity. Vietnamese coriander thrives in conditions peppers love.

bad.why: Lavender is drought-adapted — Vietnamese coriander needs more moisture.

culinary: Staple herb in Vietnamese, Malaysian, Singaporean, and Cambodian cuisines. Used in Vietnamese pho, laksa, salads, and as a table herb. Flavor is similar to cilantro but with a stronger, more peppery note and slight lemongrass undertone. Does not bolt in summer heat — makes it invaluable when true cilantro is unavailable. Also called rau ram or laksa leaf.
medicinal: Traditional use in Southeast Asian medicine for digestive complaints, reducing libido (monks traditionally consumed it), anti-inflammatory effects, and skin conditions. Shown to have antimicrobial activity. Rich in flavonoids and polyphenols.

pests.name: Slug
pests.desc: In moist conditions — rasp holes in leaves.
pests.control: Diatomaceous earth around base. Beer traps. Remove by hand at night.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Not related to regular coriander but similarly safe in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Bell Pepper

season.transplant: After last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through first frost

seed.desc: Plant ¼ inch deep in warm starting mix. Needs 75–85°F soil — bottom heat mat strongly recommended.

germination.desc: Slow without bottom heat. Keep consistently warm. Germination drops sharply below 70°F.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly. Bright light prevents leggy seedlings. Thin to one per cell.

young.desc: Transplant once nights stay above 55°F. Peppers sulk in cold soil.

adult.desc: Flowers self-pollinate. Green peppers are unripe — allow to fully color for maximum sweetness and nutrition.

care.water: Consistent deep watering 1–2 inches per week. Irregular watering causes blossom drop and bitterness.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours minimum.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 6.0–6.8.
care.fertilizer: High phosphorus at planting. Switch to calcium-rich balanced fertilizer once flowering.
care.notes: Black plastic mulch warms soil and boosts yields significantly. Stake when laden with fruit.

container.notes: Excellent container plant — containers warm faster than garden soil. One plant per pot.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with bottom heat.
Take stem cuttings before frost to overwinter. Root in moist mix. Overwintered plants produce earlier the following year.

harvest.when: Green: 70 days. Colored: 20–30 days additional ripening on the plant.
harvest.how: Cut with scissors — never pull. Leave a short stem on fruit.
harvest.storage: Room temperature 1 week. Refrigerate 2 weeks. Roast and freeze for long-term storage.
harvest.yield: 8–10 peppers per plant in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Planting out too early — cold soil below 60°F stunts peppers for the entire season.
Skipping bottom heat for germination — rate drops dramatically without it.
Picking only green — colored peppers have more nutrition. Wait for full color.
Inconsistent watering — causes blossom drop and cracked fruit.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Crosses freely with other Capsicum annuum.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow peppers to fully ripen and begin to wrinkle.
seed_saving.method: Cut pepper open, scrape seeds onto paper plate. Rinse and dry on non-stick surface.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate sweet peppers from hot peppers by 300+ feet.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites.
Similar needs. Tomatoes provide wind protection.
Deters nematodes and soil pests.

bad.why: Compete for nutrients and share pests.

culinary: One of the world's most consumed vegetables. Eaten raw, roasted, stuffed, stir-fried, pickled, and preserved. Red peppers have three times more vitamin C than green. Essential in Mediterranean, Mexican, Hungarian, and Asian cuisines.
medicinal: Extremely high in vitamin C — one red bell pepper contains twice the daily requirement. Rich in antioxidants including beta-carotene and lycopene. Anti-inflammatory. Vitamin B6 for brain health.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cluster on new growth and undersides of leaves.

pests.name: Blossom Drop
pests.desc: Flowers fall without setting fruit — temperature extremes or stress.
pests.control: Consistent watering. Avoid cold nights below 55°F or hot days above 90°F.

varieties.name: California Wonder
varieties.description: The classic blocky 4-lobed bell pepper. Thick walls, mild sweet flavor. Turns red at maturity.
varieties.notes: Most reliable bell pepper for home gardens.

varieties.name: Chocolate Beauty
varieties.description: Brown-skinned bell pepper with sweet flavor. Unusual color — turns from green to deep chocolate brown.
varieties.notes: Unique color for salads and charcuterie boards.

varieties.name: Purple Beauty
varieties.description: Deep purple bell pepper. Turns green as it ripens further. High anthocyanin content.
varieties.notes: Most ornamental bell pepper. Color fades when cooked.

varieties.name: Lemon Dream
varieties.description: Bright lemon-yellow when ripe. Exceptionally sweet, thin walls. Excellent fresh eating.

varieties.name: Mini Sweet Mix
varieties.description: Small 2–3 inch peppers in mixed red, yellow, and orange. Snack-sized, very sweet, prolific.
varieties.notes: Best for snacking and lunchboxes. Very productive.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Ripe sweet peppers are safe for dogs and cats. Avoid feeding large quantities. Remove seeds and stem.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot. Peppers don't root from stems like tomatoes.

name: Jalapeño Pepper

season.transplant: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through first frost

seed.desc: Plant ¼ inch deep. Needs 75–85°F for reliable germination. Bottom heat mat recommended.

germination.desc: Faster than bell pepper in warm conditions.

seedling.desc: Grow quickly once germinated. Ensure bright light. Stocky seedlings transplant best.

young.desc: Prolific flowering plant. Warm soil critical.

adult.desc: Green jalapeños at 75 days. Allow to turn red for sweeter, hotter, more complex flavor. Corking (white lines) is normal.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1 inch per week. Drought stress increases capsaicin and heat level.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Well-draining, fertile. pH 6.0–6.8.
care.fertilizer: Balanced at planting. Low nitrogen once flowering.
care.notes: More productive and heat-tolerant than bell pepper. Water stress deliberately used to increase heat level.

container.notes: Very well suited to containers. Compact plant that produces abundantly.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with bottom heat.
Overwinter cuttings indoors to get a head start the following season.

harvest.when: Green: 75 days. Red: 30+ days additional. Corking is normal.
harvest.how: Cut with scissors leaving a short stem.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 1–2 weeks. Pickle, dry, smoke (chipotle), or freeze.
harvest.yield: 25–35 peppers per plant in a good season.

common_mistakes: Planting in cold soil — stunts growth for the entire season.
Overwatering — reduces capsaicin content.
Removing corked peppers prematurely — corking is normal.
Not saving overwintered plants — jalapeños are perennial in frost-free climates.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties breed true. Crosses with other Capsicum annuum.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow peppers to fully redden and begin to wrinkle.
seed_saving.method: Wear gloves. Scrape seeds from fully ripe red peppers. Rinse and dry.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Wear gloves — capsaicin is concentrated in seeds and white pith.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites.
Similar needs. Provides wind protection.

culinary: World's most widely consumed hot pepper. Essential in Mexican, Tex-Mex cuisine. Used fresh in salsa, guacamole. Pickled jalapeños are a global condiment. Smoked and dried = chipotle. Red jalapeños sweeter and more complex than green.
medicinal: High capsaicin — proven pain reliever when applied topically. Boosts metabolism. Anti-inflammatory. Very high vitamin C especially when red.

varieties.name: Classic Jalapeño M
varieties.description: The standard commercial jalapeño. Consistent heat (2,500–8,000 SHU), medium size.

varieties.name: Mucho Nacho
varieties.description: Larger jalapeño — up to 4 inches. Milder heat. Excellent for poppers and stuffing.

varieties.name: TAM Jalapeño
varieties.description: Very mild jalapeño — developed at Texas A&M for low heat. Full jalapeño flavor without the burn.
varieties.notes: Best for heat-sensitive people who want jalapeño flavor.

varieties.name: Purple Jalapeño
varieties.description: Starts purple, ripens to red. Slightly hotter than standard. Ornamental and culinary.
varieties.notes: Beautiful in the garden. High anthocyanin content.

varieties.name: Chipotle (Morita)
varieties.description: Red-ripe jalapeños smoked to make chipotle. Allow to fully redden on plant then smoke over pecan or mesquite.
varieties.notes: Grow any jalapeño to red maturity for chipotle.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: oral irritation, pawing at mouth, drooling, vomiting from capsaicin
pet_toxicity.notes: Capsaicin causes discomfort and GI upset. Not toxic but will cause significant irritation. Keep away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot.

name: Cucumber

season.direct_sow: 1 week after last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep in warm soil. Cold soil causes rot before germination.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil (65°F+). One of the quicker vegetables to germinate.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Provide trellis immediately if vining type.

young.desc: Vines extend quickly. Separate male and female flowers appear.

adult.desc: Harvest frequently — overripe cucumbers signal the plant to slow production.

care.water: Consistent deep watering 1–2 inches per week. Inconsistent watering causes bitter cucumbers. Mulch to retain moisture.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, warm. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 12 inches on trellis. 36 inches for bush types.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early, switch to phosphorus-potassium once flowering.
care.notes: Trellis vining types — improves airflow, reduces disease, easier harvest.

container.notes: Bush varieties work best. Train vining types up a trellis. Water very frequently.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or start indoors briefly. Do not start too early — roots dislike being pot-bound.

harvest.when: Slicing: 6–8 inches. Pickling: 2–4 inches. Pick before yellow coloration.
harvest.how: Cut stem — never pull.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate up to 1 week. Deteriorates rapidly — use fresh.
harvest.yield: 10–20 cucumbers per plant.

common_mistakes: Planting in cold soil — cucumbers rot rather than germinate.
Allowing fruit to overripen — signals plant to stop producing. Harvest every 1–2 days.
Inconsistent watering — primary cause of bitter cucumbers.
Not trellising vining types — more disease and harder to harvest.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Crosses easily with other cucumbers.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow fruits to fully ripen past eating stage — skin yellows.
seed_saving.method: Scoop seeds, rinse off gel, spread on paper to dry.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate by 500 feet or hand-pollinate.

good.why: Provides climbing structure and partial afternoon shade.
Attracts beneficial predatory insects.
Deters cucumber beetles and nematodes.

culinary: Eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, as crudités. Pickled as dill pickles and gherkins. Used in tzatziki, raita, and cold soups. English cucumbers are mild and thin-skinned. Persian cucumbers small and crisp.
medicinal: 96% water — excellent for hydration. Contains cucurbitacins with anti-inflammatory activity. Vitamin K for bone health. Silica for skin and joint health.

pests.name: Cucumber Beetle
pests.control: Row covers until flowering. Hand-pick. Neem oil.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White powdery coating — very common in humid conditions.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Cucumber is safe and even beneficial for dogs — hydrating and low calorie. Remove skin for sensitive pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at or just slightly deeper than nursery pot depth.

name: Zucchini

season.direct_sow: 1 week after last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost — extremely productive

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep in warm soil. Large seed — easy to handle. Needs 60°F+.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable in warm conditions.

seedling.desc: Grows very rapidly. Requires full sun from day one.

young.desc: Sprawling plant needs significant space. Male and female flowers appear — bees needed.

adult.desc: Notoriously prolific. Harvest every 1–2 days or zucchini become marrows.

care.water: Deep watering 1–2 inches per week. Water at base — wet leaves promote powdery mildew.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. Amend generously with compost.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early. Balanced once flowering. Calcium prevents blossom end rot.
care.notes: One or two plants is usually enough. Succession plant to avoid glut.

container.notes: Very large and sprawling — in-ground strongly preferred.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after last frost or start briefly indoors.

harvest.when: 6–8 inches for best flavor. Flowers edible when harvested young.
harvest.how: Cut stem with sharp knife — never twist or pull. Check daily.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate up to 1 week. Freeze grated for baking.
harvest.yield: Can produce 6–10 zucchini per week at peak.

common_mistakes: Planting too many — one or two plants is sufficient.
Not checking daily — grows enormous overnight.
Watering overhead — promotes powdery mildew.
Not hand-pollinating when bee activity is low.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Crosses readily with other Cucurbita pepo squash.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow one zucchini per plant to fully mature — grows enormous with hardened skin.
seed_saving.method: Scoop seeds. Rinse well. Dry on glass or ceramic.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with summer squash, pumpkins, and some ornamental gourds. Isolate by 500+ feet.

good.why: Trap crop for aphids. Attracts pollinators.
Nitrogen fixation benefits heavy-feeding zucchini.
Deters squash bugs and nematodes.

culinary: Eaten raw, sautéed, grilled, roasted, stuffed, baked (zucchini bread), and as pasta substitute. Flowers are a delicacy. Mild flavor takes on the character of whatever it's cooked with.
medicinal: Low calorie and high water content. Rich in vitamin C, B6, and riboflavin. Antioxidants lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health. High fiber from the skin.

pests.name: Squash Vine Borer
pests.desc: Larvae tunnel into stem base causing sudden wilting.
pests.control: Row covers until flowering. Wrap stem base with foil.

pests.name: Squash Bug
pests.desc: Gray-brown bug and egg masses on leaf undersides.
pests.control: Hand-pick eggs and adults daily. Neem oil.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating — almost universal late season.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Zucchini is safe for dogs and cats. Cooked or raw. Very bitter 'cucurbitacin' occasionally found in some plants can cause GI upset — taste before feeding.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth on a slight mound for drainage.

name: Lettuce

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Again in late summer.
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Bolts in summer heat.

seed.desc: Surface sow — seeds need light to germinate. Germinates poorly above 80°F.

germination.desc: One of the fastest vegetable germinators in cool conditions.

seedling.desc: Thin to proper spacing. Outer leaves can be harvested very early.

young.desc: Fast-growing in cool weather. Begin cut-and-come-again harvesting.

adult.desc: Head types form firm heads. Loose leaf types harvest continuously. All bolt in heat.

care.water: Consistent light moisture. Shallow roots dry out quickly. Mulch to keep roots cool.
care.light: Full sun in cool weather. Partial shade in warm weather to extend season.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 6 inches for loose leaf. 12 inches for head types.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen. Liquid feed every 2 weeks.
care.notes: Succession sow every 2 weeks. Many varieties — loose leaf easiest to grow.

container.notes: One of the best vegetables for containers. Great for balcony gardens.

propagation.desc: Surface sow. Fast and easy. Succession sow every 2 weeks.

harvest.when: Loose leaf: from 30 days, outer leaves. Head types: when head feels firm.
harvest.how: Cut-and-come-again: cut outer leaves leaving center. Head types: cut entire head at base.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 5–7 days. Do not wash until ready to eat.
harvest.yield: Loose leaf most productive — multiple harvests per plant.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer heat — bolts rapidly above 75°F.
Not succession sowing — a single planting lasts only 2–3 weeks.
Covering seeds — needs light to germinate.
Inconsistent watering — causes tip burn and bitterness.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Some crossing between varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow to bolt and set seed. Fluffy white pappus like dandelion.
seed_saving.method: Cut seed heads when half have formed pappus. Shake into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate varieties by 25 feet for reasonably pure seed.

good.why: Lettuce shades carrot row, reducing moisture loss.
Mature and harvested before lettuce needs the space.
Repels aphids that commonly attack lettuce.

bad.why: Can inhibit lettuce germination when very close.

culinary: Backbone of salads worldwide. Many types — romaine, butterhead, iceberg, loose leaf. Used in wraps, sandwiches, spring rolls. Braised lettuce traditional in French cuisine.
medicinal: Dark green varieties far more nutritious than pale iceberg. Rich in vitamins K and A. Romaine has significant vitamin C. High folate for cell division.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cluster in leaf folds and growing tips.

pests.name: Slug
pests.control: Beer traps. Diatomaceous earth. Hand-pick at night.

pests.name: Tip Burn
pests.desc: Brown leaf edges — calcium deficiency from inconsistent watering.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: All lettuce types are safe for dogs and cats. High water content. Good low-calorie treat.

transplant.deep_note: Very shallow — plant so crown is just at or barely below soil level.

name: Spinach

season.direct_sow: 6–8 weeks before last frost. Late summer for fall crop.
season.harvest_window: Early spring and fall. Bolts in summer.

seed.desc: Sow ½ inch deep. Prefers cool soil 45–75°F. Germinates poorly in warm soil.

germination.desc: Quick in cool conditions. Slow or fails in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Thin to 3–4 inches. Begin harvesting baby leaves.

young.desc: Rapid growth in cool weather. Harvest outer leaves regularly.

adult.desc: Full rosette. Bolts rapidly with heat or long days.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Drought causes bolting. Mulch to keep soil cool.
care.light: Full sun in cool weather. Part shade extends season.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.5–7.5. Sensitive to acidic soil.
care.spacing: 3–4 inches for baby leaf. 6 inches for full-sized.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen. Side-dress 3 weeks after germination.
care.notes: Withstands temperatures down to 20°F when established.

container.notes: Excellent container vegetable. Grow baby spinach in window boxes.

propagation.desc: Direct sow in cool soil. Succession sow every 2 weeks. Pre-soak 24 hours to speed germination.

harvest.when: Baby leaves from 25 days. Full leaves from 40 days. Before any flower stalk.
harvest.how: Cut outer leaves leaving center growing point.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 5–7 days. Blanch and freeze for long-term.
harvest.yield: 4–6 weeks of harvest before bolting.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer — bolts almost immediately.
Not succession sowing — single planting lasts only 4–6 weeks.
Growing in acidic soil — spinach is pH sensitive.
Letting it bolt — harvest aggressively.

seed_saving.type: Dioecious — separate male and female plants. Wind-pollinated.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow to bolt. Harvest before seeds shatter.
seed_saving.method: Thresh by rubbing stalks between hands over a bucket.
seed_saving.drying: Dry seed stalks in paper bag 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Wind-pollinated — isolate by 1 mile for pure seed.

good.why: Spinach as living mulch. Both cool-season crops.
Peas fix nitrogen. Both cool-season — perfect partners.
Quick maturing — harvested before spinach needs space.

culinary: One of the most nutritionally dense leafy greens. Eaten raw, sautéed, wilted, in smoothies, pasta, quiche, spanakopita, saag. Baby spinach mild for raw use. Mature spinach stronger flavor, better cooked.
medicinal: High in vitamin K, A, folate, and iron. Nitrates lower blood pressure. Lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health. Calcium and magnesium for bone health.

pests.name: Leaf Miner
pests.desc: Larvae tunnel in leaves creating winding trails.

pests.name: Downy Mildew
pests.desc: Yellow patches on upper surface with gray fuzz below.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: kidney stress with very large quantities due to oxalic acid
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. High oxalate content means large quantities can contribute to kidney stones in susceptible animals. Avoid feeding regularly to pets with kidney issues.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery depth. Direct sown seedlings thinned in place.

name: Kale

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Late summer for fall and winter harvest.
season.harvest_window: Nearly year-round. Best flavor after fall frosts.

seed.desc: Sow ¼–½ inch deep. Tolerant germinator across wide temperature range.

germination.desc: Reliable. Fast in warm soil too.

seedling.desc: Cold hardy. Watch for slugs and cabbage worms.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Begin harvesting outer leaves once plant has 8+ leaves.

adult.desc: Very productive long-season plant. Gets better after frost sweetens the leaves.

care.water: Consistent 1–1.5 inches per week. Drought causes tough bitter leaves.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. High organic matter.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen. Side-dress every 4–6 weeks.
care.notes: Flavor sweetens dramatically after frost. Can be harvested through winter in many zones.

container.notes: Good in large containers. Ornamental kale varieties beautiful in pots.

propagation.desc: Reliable and easy. Start indoors or direct sow.

harvest.when: When plant has 8+ leaves. Harvest outer leaves leaving at least 4 inner.
harvest.how: Snap or cut outer leaves at the base.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 1–2 weeks. Blanch and freeze. Kale chips for snacking.
harvest.yield: One plant produces continuously for 6+ months in mild climates.

common_mistakes: Harvesting inner leaves — always harvest outer leaves first.
Not waiting for frost — taste dramatically improves after frost.
Not controlling caterpillars — devastate kale rapidly.
Planting too late in spring — bolts in summer.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Crosses with all Brassica oleracea.
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter, flower in year two. Harvest seed pods when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow from dried pods.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts. Isolate by 1 mile.

good.why: Trap crop for aphids.
Deters cabbage worms and nematodes.
Attracts parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage caterpillars.

culinary: Versatile superfood. Raw (massaged salad), sautéed, steamed, roasted (kale chips), soups, stir-fries, grain bowls. Dinosaur kale most tender raw. Curly kale best for chips.
medicinal: Among most nutritious vegetables. High vitamins K, A, C. Glucosinolates produce sulforaphane — potent anticancer activity. Lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health. Cholesterol-lowering when steamed.

pests.name: Imported Cabbageworm
pests.desc: Velvety green caterpillar. Chews large holes.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Gray-green cabbage aphid in tight colonies.

pests.name: Flea Beetle
pests.control: Row covers. Diatomaceous earth. Neem oil.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset, gas, Heinz body anemia in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Small amounts safe. Large quantities can cause GI issues and in extreme cases blood cell damage. Not a food to give regularly.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot.

name: Potato

season.start_indoors: Chit seed potatoes 4–6 weeks before planting
season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost — soil temp 45°F minimum
season.harvest_window: Early summer (new potatoes) through fall

seed.desc: Plant certified seed potato pieces (each with 1–2 eyes) 4 inches deep. Chitting before planting speeds emergence.

germination.desc: Shoots emerge and break through soil. Keep hilling soil up around emerging shoots.

seedling.desc: Continue hilling — mound soil up around stems as they grow.

young.desc: Vines grow and flower. Flowers signal tubers forming below.

adult.desc: Vines yellow and die back — tubers are mature. New potatoes can be harvested 2 weeks after flowering.

care.water: Consistent 1–2 inches per week. Stop once vines die back.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Loose, well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 5.0–6.5. Acidic soil reduces scab.
care.spacing: 12 inches between pieces. 30 inches between rows.
care.fertilizer: High potassium and phosphorus. Avoid fresh manure — promotes scab.
care.notes: Hill consistently — any tubers exposed to light turn green and toxic.

container.notes: Potato grow bags are ideal — easy harvesting without digging. Fill gradually as plants grow.

propagation.desc: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes. Cut into pieces each with 1–2 eyes. Cure cut pieces 24–48 hours before planting.

harvest.when: New potatoes: 2 weeks after flowering. Mature: 2–3 weeks after vines die back completely.
harvest.how: Use garden fork, insert 12 inches from plant. Lift carefully.
harvest.storage: Cure in dark at 50–65°F for 1–2 weeks. Store in dark, cool, humid location.
harvest.yield: 5–10 pounds per pound of seed potato.

common_mistakes: Using supermarket potatoes — may carry disease and are often treated to inhibit sprouting.
Allowing tubers to be exposed to light — produces toxic solanine.
Not hilling consistently.
Planting in alkaline soil — increases potato scab.

seed_saving.type: Propagated vegetatively from tubers.
seed_saving.harvest: Save small healthy tubers from your harvest.
seed_saving.method: Store separately from eating potatoes.
seed_saving.notes: Replace with certified seed every 3–5 years to avoid disease buildup.

good.why: Nitrogen fixation. Beans repel Colorado potato beetle.
Repels Colorado potato beetle.
Deters nematodes and soil pests.

bad.why: Same family — shares blight. Plant far apart.

culinary: World's most consumed vegetable. Boiled, baked, roasted, fried, mashed, in soups. Waxy varieties best for salads. Starchy varieties (Russet) best for mashing. Yukon Gold all-purpose.
medicinal: High potassium — more than bananas. Significant vitamin C in skin. B6 for neurotransmitter production. Resistant starch in cooled potatoes feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

pests.name: Colorado Potato Beetle
pests.desc: Yellow and black striped beetle — defoliates plants.

pests.name: Late Blight
pests.desc: Dark lesions in wet cool weather — same pathogen as Irish famine.
pests.control: Copper fungicide. Remove infected plants. Avoid overhead watering.

pests.name: Potato Scab
pests.desc: Rough corky patches on skin from alkaline soil.
pests.control: Acidify soil below pH 5.5. Avoid fresh manure.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: green skin, leaves, stems, raw flesh (solanine)
pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, weakness, tremors
pet_toxicity.notes: Green or raw potatoes contain solanine — toxic to both dogs and cats. Fully cooked plain potato is safe in small amounts. Keep plants out of reach — all green parts are toxic.

transplant.deep_note: Plant seed potatoes 4 inches deep. Hill soil up over emerging stems — this triggers more tuber formation.

name: Garlic

season.direct_sow: Plant cloves in fall (October–November) for summer harvest
season.harvest_window: Early to midsummer — when lower leaves begin to brown

seed.desc: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep, pointed end up, in fall. Choose largest cloves for biggest harvests.

germination.desc: Green shoots emerge in fall. Plant overwinters. Cold period essential for bulb development.

seedling.desc: Slow winter growth. Mulch heavily after ground freezes. Resumes vigorous growth in spring.

young.desc: Rapid spring growth. Hardneck varieties produce scapes — remove them to direct energy to the bulb.

adult.desc: Harvest when lower third of leaves have turned brown.

care.water: Moderate spring watering. Stop 2 weeks before harvest.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, loose, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 6 inches between cloves. 12 inches between rows.
care.fertilizer: Nitrogen-rich in spring. Stop feeding in late spring.
care.notes: Hardneck varieties produce scapes — harvest when they curl for a bonus crop. Softneck stores longer.

container.notes: Possible in deep containers. Needs to overwinter outdoors in cold climates.

propagation.desc: Separate bulb into cloves just before planting. Plant largest cloves for largest bulbs.

harvest.when: When lower one-third of leaves have turned brown. Typically June–July.
harvest.how: Loosen soil with fork, lift gently. Do not pull by the tops.
harvest.storage: Cure in warm dry airy spot out of direct sun for 3–4 weeks. Store in cool dry location. Hardneck: 4–6 months. Softneck: 6–12 months.
harvest.yield: One clove planted = one bulb harvested.

common_mistakes: Planting in spring — needs cold vernalization period to form bulbs.
Planting small cloves — size directly predicts bulb size.
Not removing hardneck scapes — reduces bulb size by 20–30%.
Harvesting too early or too late.

seed_saving.type: Propagated vegetatively from cloves.
seed_saving.harvest: Reserve largest cloves from best bulbs at harvest.
seed_saving.method: Store as you would eating garlic until fall planting.
seed_saving.notes: Selecting largest cloves from best bulbs over generations improves your strain.

good.why: Repels aphids and black spot fungus.
Deters spider mites and aphids.
Garlic repels carrot fly.

culinary: Used in virtually every cuisine on Earth. Raw, roasted (becomes sweet and mild), sautéed, pickled, fermented (black garlic), and dried. Forms the aromatic base of most savory cooking.
medicinal: One of the most extensively researched medicinal plants. Allicin is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial. Meta-analyses show significant blood pressure reduction. Reduces LDL cholesterol. Antifungal. Immune-stimulating.

pests.name: White Rot
pests.desc: Devastating fungal disease. White fluffy growth at base. Persists in soil for decades.
pests.control: Remove and destroy. Long rotation. No cure.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, pale gums, Heinz body anemia, rapid breathing
pet_toxicity.notes: Garlic is significantly more toxic than onion pound for pound. Cats are more sensitive than dogs. Even small amounts can cause Heinz body anemia — destruction of red blood cells. No safe amount. Keep all alliums out of reach.

transplant.deep_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep, pointed end up.

name: Onion

season.direct_sow: Very early spring — 8 weeks before last frost
season.transplant: As soon as soil can be worked
season.harvest_window: Midsummer when tops fall over

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Long growing season requires early start.

germination.desc: Grass-like shoots emerge. Tuck any that fall over back upright.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly. Trim tops to 3 inches. Transplant outdoors as soon as possible.

young.desc: Bulbing begins when day length triggers it. Long-day vs short-day varieties critical.

adult.desc: Necks soften and tops fall over naturally — the sign to harvest.

care.water: Consistent 1 inch per week. Stop in final 2 weeks.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, loose, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early. Switch to potassium-phosphorus once bulbing begins.
care.notes: Day length critical — long-day for north of 36° latitude, short-day for south.

container.notes: Better for green onions than large storage onions.

propagation.desc: Most variety selection. Start early.
Fastest and easiest. Limited variety choice.

harvest.when: When 50–75% of tops have fallen over naturally.
harvest.how: Gently loosen soil with fork and lift.
harvest.storage: Cure 2–4 weeks in warm dry airy location. Store in net bags in cool dry ventilated location.
harvest.yield: One large onion per plant.

common_mistakes: Planting wrong day-length variety.
Using sets that are too large — prone to bolting.
Over-fertilizing with nitrogen during bulbing.
Harvesting before tops fully fall.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Wind and insect pollinated.
seed_saving.harvest: In year two plants bolt and flower. Bag individual heads as they mature.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other onions and wild Allium. Isolate by 1 mile.

good.why: Classic mutualism — onion repels carrot fly, carrot confuses onion fly.
Repels aphids and spider mites.

culinary: Foundational aromatic in almost every world cuisine. Raw, caramelized, pickled, dried. Yellow most versatile. Red for raw use. Sweet for fresh eating.
medicinal: Quercetin — one of the most potent natural anti-inflammatories. Lowers blood pressure and LDL cholesterol. Prebiotic fiber. Antimicrobial.

pests.name: White Rot
pests.desc: Devastating fungal — persists in soil decades.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, pale gums, Heinz body anemia
pet_toxicity.notes: All forms of onion are toxic. Cooked onion is equally dangerous. Cats are more sensitive than dogs. Thiosulfates cause Heinz body anemia. Cumulative toxicity — small amounts over time are also harmful.

transplant.deep_note: Plant sets or transplants 1 inch deep. Bulbing occurs at soil level — don't plant too deep.

name: Green Bean

season.direct_sow: 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil is 60°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through fall

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep. Needs warm soil — cold causes rot. Inoculate with Rhizobium for nitrogen fixation.

germination.desc: Seedling pushes up with cotyledons above ground. Fast in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Bush beans compact. Pole beans begin vining — provide trellis immediately.

young.desc: Rapid growth and flowering. Self-pollinating. Pods develop quickly.

adult.desc: Harvest when pods snap cleanly. Seeds barely visible through pod.

care.water: Consistent 1 inch per week especially during flowering.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Moderately fertile, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 3–4 inches for bush. 6 inches for pole.
care.fertilizer: Minimal — beans fix their own nitrogen. Over-fertilizing produces foliage not beans.
care.notes: Two types: bush (compact, once harvest) and pole (continuous, needs support). Inoculate seed with Rhizobium.

container.notes: Bush beans work well in containers.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks.

harvest.when: Pods finger-thick and snap cleanly. Before any yellowing.
harvest.how: Hold vine, snap or cut pod. Never yank.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 5–7 days. Blanch and freeze. Pickle as dilly beans.
harvest.yield: Bush: harvest over 2–3 weeks. Pole: continuous 2–3 months.

common_mistakes: Planting in cold soil — rot before germinating.
Over-fertilizing — beautiful plants with few pods.
Not harvesting frequently — overripe pods stop production.
Not succession sowing bush beans.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Primarily self-pollinating.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow pods to dry completely on the plant.
seed_saving.method: Shell dried pods by hand.
seed_saving.notes: One of the easiest for seed saving — largely self-pollinating.

good.why: Beans fix nitrogen for carrots.
Classic Three Sisters. Beans climb corn and fix nitrogen.
Classic Three Sisters.

culinary: Eaten fresh, steamed, roasted, stir-fried, pickled, canned. Used in salads, stews, casseroles. Yellow wax beans same flavor, different color.
