medicinal: Good plant protein and fiber. Rich in folate and vitamin K. Fiber slows glucose absorption. Antioxidant flavonoids.

pests.name: Mexican Bean Beetle
pests.desc: Copper-colored beetle and spiny larvae skeletonize leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Green beans are a healthy low-calorie treat for dogs. Safe for cats. Plain only — no added salt, butter, or seasonings.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown 1 inch deep. Transplants rarely needed.

name: Garden Pea

season.direct_sow: 4–6 weeks before last frost. Also late summer for fall.
season.harvest_window: Late spring through early summer.

seed.desc: Sow 1 inch deep. Inoculate with Rhizobium. Soak overnight to speed germination.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool moist soil. Germinates at 40–75°F.

seedling.desc: Tendrils emerge. Provide trellis immediately.

young.desc: Climbs rapidly. Self-pollinating.

adult.desc: Pods fill quickly. Harvest snow peas flat, snap when plump, garden peas when full.

care.water: Moderate and consistent. Water at base — overhead promotes mildew.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Minimal — fix own nitrogen. High phosphorus and potassium at planting.
care.notes: Plant as early as possible — done producing once temps exceed 80°F consistently.

container.notes: Dwarf and bush varieties most practical.

propagation.desc: Direct sow as early as possible. Cold-tolerant.

harvest.when: Garden peas: pods plump but not starchy. Snow peas: flat. Snap peas: plump and snapping.
harvest.how: Hold vine, snap or snip pod. Harvest every 2–3 days.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate immediately. Use within 3–5 days. Shell and freeze for long-term.
harvest.yield: 2–3 months before heat ends production.

common_mistakes: Planting too late — every week reduces harvest.
Not providing support.
Not harvesting frequently.
Not inoculating seed.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Primarily self-pollinating.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow pods to dry completely on the vine.
seed_saving.method: Shell dried pods.
seed_saving.notes: Self-pollinating — no isolation required.

good.why: Peas fix nitrogen. Both cool-season.
Peas fix nitrogen for carrots.
Same cool season timing.

culinary: Garden peas fresh or frozen. Sugar snap eaten whole. Snow peas in stir-fries. Dried split peas in soups. Pea shoots a gourmet green.
medicinal: Good plant protein — 8g per cup. High fiber. Rich in vitamins K, C, and thiamine. Folate for cell division.

pests.name: Pea Moth
pests.control: Row covers during flowering. Early planting.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — sweet peas (Lathyrus) are toxic, garden peas (Pisum) are safe
pet_toxicity.symptoms: none for garden peas
pet_toxicity.notes: Garden peas (Pisum sativum) are safe. Do NOT confuse with sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) which are toxic. Snow peas and snap peas also safe.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown 1 inch deep. Cool soil preferred.

name: Broccoli

season.direct_sow: Not recommended for spring. Fall: 85–100 days before first frost.
season.harvest_window: Late spring or fall. Prefers cool weather.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Very reliable germinator.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable. One of the easiest brassicas.

seedling.desc: Transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost. Cold-hardened seedlings tolerate light frost.

young.desc: Large blue-green leaves develop. Central head develops 30–40 days after transplanting.

adult.desc: Harvest before yellow flowers open. Side shoots develop after main head harvest.

care.water: Consistent 1–1.5 inches per week. Drought causes bitter heads and premature flowering.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen throughout. Calcium prevents hollow stem.
care.notes: Fall crops generally superior — cooler weather means larger sweeter heads.

container.notes: Very large plants — in-ground strongly preferred.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant.

harvest.when: While head is deep green and tight. Any yellowing means it's opening.
harvest.how: Cut main stem 5–6 inches below head. Leave plant — side shoots develop for weeks.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 3–5 days. Blanch and freeze.
harvest.yield: One large central head plus weeks of side shoots.

common_mistakes: Planting too late for spring crop.
Waiting too long to harvest — flavor deteriorates rapidly.
Removing plant after main head — side shoots are a bonus.
Inconsistent watering — causes hollow stem.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Crosses with all Brassica oleracea.
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter, flower in spring. Harvest pods when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with cabbage, kale, Brussels sprouts. Isolate by 1 mile.

good.why: Trap crop for aphids.
Attracts parasitic wasps for caterpillar control.
Repels cabbage moths.

culinary: Raw with dip, steamed, roasted, stir-fried, pasta, soups. Roasting caramelizes natural sugars. Stems edible — peel outer layer if tough.
medicinal: Sulforaphane — one of the most potent natural anticancer compounds. Indole-3-carbinol supports hormone balance. Very high vitamin C and K. Chopping and resting 40 minutes before cooking maximizes sulforaphane.

pests.name: Imported Cabbageworm
pests.desc: Pale green caterpillar. Chews large holes.

pests.name: Cabbage Aphid
pests.desc: Dense gray-green colonies — can infest florets.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI irritation in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Small amounts safe and nutritious. Large quantities (over 10% of diet) cause GI irritation from isothiocyanates. Florets safer than stems.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot.

name: Sweet Corn

season.direct_sow: 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 60°F
season.harvest_window: Midsummer to fall

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep. Sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination — single rows produce poorly.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil. Slow or rots below 60°F.

seedling.desc: Rapid growth with adequate nitrogen. Thin to 12 inches.

young.desc: Can grow 2–3 inches per day. Tassels (male) appear first, then silks (female).

adult.desc: Ears ready 18–24 days after silks appear. Test by piercing a kernel — milky juice = perfect.

care.water: Consistent 1–1.5 inches per week. Critical during tasseling and silking.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 5.8–6.8.
care.spacing: 12 inches between plants. 30 inches between rows. Minimum 4 rows.
care.fertilizer: Heavy nitrogen feeder. Side-dress when 12 inches tall and again when tasseling.
care.notes: Must grow in blocks — wind-pollinated. Each silk connects to one kernel.

container.notes: Requires blocks for pollination. Grows 5–8 feet tall.

propagation.desc: Direct sow in blocks after last frost.

harvest.when: 18–24 days after silks appear. Pierce kernel — milky juice = perfect.
harvest.how: Grip ear and pull down and twist. Harvest in morning for best sweetness.
harvest.storage: Eat immediately. Refrigerate up to 3 days. Blanch and freeze.
harvest.yield: 1–2 ears per stalk.

common_mistakes: Planting in single rows — needs blocks for pollination.
Planting different varieties close together — cross-pollination ruins flavor.
Harvesting too late — sweetness peaks for only 1–3 days.
Under-watering during tasseling.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated (heirloom) breeds true. Hybrid does not.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow ears to dry completely on stalk — far past eating stage.
seed_saving.method: Shell kernels by hand or rubbing cobs together over bucket.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with all other corn by wind — isolate heirloom by 500+ feet.

good.why: Classic Three Sisters. Beans fix nitrogen for corn.
Classic Three Sisters. Ground cover suppresses weeds.

culinary: One of the world's most important crops. Eaten fresh, canned, frozen, dried into cornmeal, polenta, masa. Used in chowder, cornbread, tamales, tortillas.
medicinal: Fiber, B vitamins, magnesium. Lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health. Resistant starch feeds gut bacteria. Purple corn high in anthocyanins.

pests.name: Corn Earworm
pests.control: Apply mineral oil to silk channel. Bt spray on silks.

pests.name: Corn Borer
pests.desc: Larvae tunnel into stalks and ears.
pests.control: Bt spray at early silk stage. Remove stalks after harvest.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: intestinal obstruction from swallowed cob pieces
pet_toxicity.notes: Corn kernels are safe. The COB is a serious choking and obstruction hazard for dogs — can require emergency surgery. Never give a dog a corn cob.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown 1 inch deep in blocks. Transplanting disrupts roots — direct sow only.

name: Eggplant

season.transplant: After last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost

seed.desc: Plant ¼ inch deep. Needs 75–85°F soil. Bottom heat mat essential.

germination.desc: Slow without heat. Keep consistently warm.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly. Strong light needed. Very cold-sensitive.

young.desc: Purple star-shaped flowers appear. Self-pollinating.

adult.desc: Harvest while skin is still shiny — dull = overripe and bitter.

care.water: Consistent deep watering. Drought stress causes bitter fruit.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, warm. pH 5.8–6.5.
care.fertilizer: Balanced at planting. High potassium once fruiting.
care.notes: Most heat-loving nightshade. Black plastic mulch significantly improves yields.

container.notes: Containers warm faster — advantage for heat-loving eggplant.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant with bottom heat.
Take cuttings before frost to overwinter indoors.

harvest.when: When skin is shiny and full-sized. Press gently — should spring back.
harvest.how: Cut stem — do not twist. Stems often thorny.
harvest.storage: Room temperature 3–4 days. Refrigerate 1 week. Roast and freeze.
harvest.yield: 4–8 eggplants per plant.

common_mistakes: Planting too early — most cold-sensitive common vegetable.
Harvesting overripe — dull skin = bitter.
Not providing enough heat.
Skipping bottom heat for germination.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Crosses possible.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow fruit to fully ripen past eating — skin yellows.
seed_saving.method: Scrape seeds into water. Good seeds sink. Rinse and dry.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate varieties by 300 feet.

good.why: Repels aphids and thrips.
Deters nematodes and soil pests.

culinary: Essential in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian, East Asian cuisines. Baba ganoush, moussaka, ratatouille, eggplant parmesan, Japanese nasu dengaku. Absorbs flavors exceptionally well.
medicinal: Nasunin in purple skin protects brain cell membranes. Chlorogenic acid — anti-inflammatory and antiviral. Fiber for gut health.

pests.name: Flea Beetle
pests.desc: Shothole pattern on leaves — worst on young plants.
pests.control: Row covers on transplants. Diatomaceous earth. Neem oil.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy
pet_toxicity.notes: Plant parts are toxic. Ripe eggplant flesh is safe in small amounts but avoid feeding — some animals are sensitive. Keep plants out of reach.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot.

name: Beet

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Again late summer.
season.harvest_window: Early summer and fall

seed.desc: Seed cluster contains 2–4 seeds. Sow ½ inch deep. Soak 24 hours before planting.

germination.desc: Multiple seedlings emerge per cluster. Thin to strongest one early.

seedling.desc: Thin to 3–4 inches. Thinnings edible as baby beet greens.

young.desc: Root begins developing. Harvest greens without pulling root.

adult.desc: Harvest when roots 1½–3 inches diameter. Larger roots become tough and woody.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Irregular watering causes cracking.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Loose, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.5–7.5. Boron deficiency causes black heart.
care.fertilizer: Moderate balanced. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: Two crops in one — roots and nutritious greens (taste like Swiss chard).

container.notes: Good container vegetable. Deep containers for best root development.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only. Each cluster produces multiple seedlings — thin early.

harvest.when: When roots 1½–3 inches diameter. Baby beets from 1 inch.
harvest.how: Loosen soil, lift gently. Twist off greens leaving 1 inch of stem.
harvest.storage: Remove greens. Refrigerate 2–4 weeks. Pickle or freeze.
harvest.yield: One root per thinned seedling.

common_mistakes: Not thinning — crowded beets produce no usable root.
Harvesting too large — woody and bitter above 3 inches.
Not eating the greens — highly nutritious.
Letting soil dry out.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Crosses with Swiss chard and sugar beet.
seed_saving.harvest: Harvest seed stalks when brown and dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with Swiss chard. Isolate by ½ mile.

good.why: Mutual pest deterrence.
Compatible cool-season crops.

culinary: Roasted, pickled, juiced, in soups (borscht). Golden and candy-stripe varieties milder. Beet greens sautéed like chard. Beet hummus and chocolate cake popular.
medicinal: Very high in nitrates — lowers blood pressure and improves exercise performance clinically. Betaine protects liver. Betalain pigments powerful antioxidants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: kidney stress from oxalates in large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. High in oxalates — avoid in pets with kidney disease. Beet greens also safe in moderation.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown ½ inch deep. Thinnings are edible. Transplants poorly.

name: Radish

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Every 2 weeks. Again late summer.
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall — bolts in summer

seed.desc: Sow ½ inch deep. Among the most cold-tolerant vegetable seeds.

germination.desc: Among the fastest-germinating vegetables. Useful as row marker.

seedling.desc: Thin to 2 inches immediately. Crowded radishes produce only tops.

young.desc: Root develops rapidly. Check regularly — mature fast.

adult.desc: Harvest promptly. Left too long bolt and become hollow and very pungent.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Irregular watering causes cracking and extreme pungency.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Loose, well-draining. pH 5.8–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Not needed — grows too fast.
care.notes: Excellent for succession sowing. Use as row markers for slow crops like carrot.

container.notes: Perfect container vegetable. Great for children's gardens.

propagation.desc: Direct sow. Succession sow every 2 weeks.

harvest.when: ¾–1 inch diameter. 25–35 days from sowing.
harvest.how: Pull by grasping root at soil level.
harvest.storage: Remove tops immediately. Refrigerate 1–2 weeks.
harvest.yield: One radish per seed. Multiple successions per season.

common_mistakes: Not thinning — requires proper spacing.
Planting in summer — bolts almost immediately.
Not harvesting promptly — pithy and hot within days.
Forgetting to succession sow.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Crosses with other radishes.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow bolted plants to flower and set seed pods. Harvest when dry.
seed_saving.method: Shell pods or thresh in bag.
seed_saving.notes: Bolts and flowers quickly — easy to save seed. Isolate by 300 feet.

good.why: Loosen soil for carrots. Harvested before carrots need space.
Perfect interplanting — harvested while lettuce still small.
Repels cucumber beetles.

culinary: Eaten raw in salads, as crudités, pickled, cooked. French Breakfast mild, Cherry Belle medium, Black Spanish very hot. Tops edible — peppery raw or sautéed.
medicinal: Glucosinolates produce isothiocyanates with anticancer properties. Digestive stimulant. Diuretic. High vitamin C. Anthocyanins in red varieties are antioxidants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: possible gas and GI upset from glucosinolates
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats in small amounts. Peppery taste usually deters pets naturally.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown ½ inch deep. Too fast to transplant.

name: Swiss Chard

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Again late summer.
season.harvest_window: Nearly year-round in mild climates.

seed.desc: Each seed cluster contains 2–4 seeds. Sow ½ inch deep, 6 inches apart.

germination.desc: Reliable and fast in cool conditions.

seedling.desc: Thin to one per spot. Beautiful rainbow stems visible from seedling stage.

young.desc: Begin cut-and-come-again harvest of outer leaves.

adult.desc: Highly productive long-season plant. Rainbow varieties provide colorful stems.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Tolerates brief drought better than spinach.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. One of the most shade-tolerant leafy vegetables.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced every 4–6 weeks.
care.notes: More heat-tolerant than spinach, more cold-tolerant than basil. Near year-round producer. Ornamental enough for flower beds.

container.notes: Excellent container vegetable. Rainbow chard ornamental enough for decorative pots.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or start indoors. Reliable germinator.

harvest.when: Begin outer leaf harvest once plant has 8+ leaves.
harvest.how: Cut or snap outer leaves at base. Leave at least 4 inner.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 5–7 days. Blanch and freeze. Reduces dramatically in volume when cooked.
harvest.yield: One plant can produce 6+ months in mild climates.

common_mistakes: Harvesting inner leaves — stops production.
Growing in full shade — tolerates it but produces less.
Not succession sowing — single spring planting bolts in summer.
Letting it bolt.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Same species as beet — crosses freely.
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter, flower in year two. Harvest seed stalks when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with beets. Isolate by ½ mile.

good.why: Repels pests that attack chard.
Compatible cool-season companions.

culinary: Raw in salads, sautéed with garlic and olive oil, quiches, frittatas, pasta, soups. Interchangeable with spinach. Stems can be pickled.
medicinal: Very high in vitamins K, A, C. Rich in magnesium. Betalain antioxidants in colored stems. Syringic acid regulates blood sugar.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: kidney stress from oxalates
pet_toxicity.notes: Same as spinach — safe in small amounts, avoid in pets with kidney issues due to oxalic acid content.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery depth, crown at soil level.

name: Cabbage

season.direct_sow: 90 days before first fall frost for fall crop.
season.transplant: Very cold hardy — transplant 4 weeks before last frost
season.harvest_window: Late spring or fall through winter

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Germinates at 40°F — very cold tolerant.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable across a wide temperature range.

seedling.desc: Cold hardy. Watch for damping off indoors.

young.desc: Outer leaves develop first. Head forms from inside. Consistent water prevents splitting.

adult.desc: Harvest when firm when squeezed. Harvest before it splits.

care.water: Consistent 1–1.5 inches per week. Inconsistent watering causes heads to split.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.5–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Heavy nitrogen feeder. High nitrogen early, balanced once heading.
care.notes: Fall cabbages are generally superior. Cover with row cover to exclude cabbage butterflies.

container.notes: Not practical in containers.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting.

harvest.when: When head is firm when squeezed.
harvest.how: Cut stem at base. Leave outer leaves — small secondary heads often form.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 1–2 months. Root cellar 3–4 months. Ferment as sauerkraut or kimchi for indefinite storage.
harvest.yield: One head per plant.

common_mistakes: Inconsistent watering — heads split.
Planting too late for spring.
Not controlling caterpillars.
Harvesting too early — heads should be very firm.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Crosses with all Brassica oleracea.
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter small plants. Replant in spring. Harvest when seed pods dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh and winnow.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with broccoli, kale, Brussels sprouts. Isolate by 1 mile.

good.why: Repels cabbage moth and whitefly.
Attracts parasitic wasps for caterpillar control.
Repels cabbage moths.
Attracts beneficial insects.

bad.why: Brassicas and tomatoes inhibit each other.

culinary: Raw in coleslaw, fermented as sauerkraut and kimchi, braised, stuffed (cabbage rolls), in soups. Red cabbage higher anthocyanin content. Savoy most tender for stuffing.
medicinal: Glucosinolates produce cancer-fighting compounds. Vitamin C and K. Raw cabbage juice used for stomach ulcers. Sauerkraut is a powerful probiotic.

pests.name: Clubroot
pests.control: Raise pH. Long rotation. Resistant varieties.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: gas and GI upset in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Can cause significant gas. Cooked is easier to digest than raw.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery pot.

name: Butternut Squash

season.direct_sow: 1 week after last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Fall — after first light frost sweetens the flesh

seed.desc: Plant 1 inch deep in warm soil. Needs 60°F+ soil.

germination.desc: Fast in warm conditions.

seedling.desc: Very fast growth. Needs significant space.

young.desc: Long vines. Male flowers before female. Bees required.

adult.desc: Tan skin as it ripens. Stem begins to dry and cork — sign of maturity.

care.water: Deep watering 1–2 inches per week.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Heavy feeder. High nitrogen early, switch to phosphorus-potassium once flowering.
care.notes: Needs long warm season. Excellent storage squash — 3–6 months.

container.notes: Very large vining plant.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after last frost.

harvest.when: Skin hard and tan, stem dry and corky, thumbnail cannot pierce skin.
harvest.how: Cut stem leaving 2–3 inches. Handle carefully.
harvest.storage: Cure at 80–85°F for 10–14 days. Store at 50–60°F for 3–6 months. Do not refrigerate.
harvest.yield: 4–6 squash per vine.

common_mistakes: Planting too early in cold soil.
Harvesting too early — skin must be fully tan.
Not curing — stores poorly.
Not leaving stem — creates entry point for rot.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated breeds true. Less crossing risk than C. pepo varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow to fully mature on vine. Scoop seeds from mature squash.
seed_saving.method: Rinse seeds, spread on glass to dry.
seed_saving.notes: C. moschata more isolated from other squash species.

good.why: Classic Three Sisters. Squash ground cover reduces weeds.
Beans fix nitrogen.
Trap crop for aphids. Attracts pollinators.

culinary: Roasted, pureed into soup, risotto, pasta, curries. Naturally sweet — pairs with sage, nutmeg, cinnamon. Seeds roasted like pumpkin seeds. Excellent storage life.
medicinal: Very high in beta-carotene. Potassium for heart health. Vitamin C. Fiber for gut health. Anti-inflammatory carotenoids.

pests.name: Squash Vine Borer
pests.desc: Larvae tunnel into stem base causing sudden collapse.
pests.control: Row covers until flowering. Aluminum foil around stem base.

pests.name: Squash Bug
pests.desc: Gray-brown bugs and egg masses on leaf undersides.
pests.control: Hand-pick adults and eggs. Neem oil.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — seeds and raw skin difficult to digest
pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset from raw skin or seeds
pet_toxicity.notes: Plain cooked butternut squash is safe and nutritious. Remove seeds and skin before feeding. A good source of fiber.

transplant.deep_note: Plant on a slight mound for drainage. Set at nursery pot depth.

name: Leek

season.transplant: 6 weeks before last frost — very cold hardy
season.harvest_window: Fall through winter — frost improves flavor

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Tiny grass-like shoots emerge. Long season requires early start.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool conditions.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly indoors. Trim tops to 3 inches. Plant in 6-inch deep holes — drop seedling in, water but don't fill hole.

young.desc: Hole-planting blanches (whitens) the shank naturally. Earthing up extends blanched area.

adult.desc: Harvest after frost. Can overwinter through hard frosts.

care.water: Consistent 1 inch per week.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen throughout for thick shanks.
care.notes: Unique hole-planting technique creates long white blanched shank.

container.notes: Needs deep planting for blanching.

propagation.desc: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting.

harvest.when: When shanks 1+ inch diameter. Can harvest at any size.
harvest.how: Loosen soil with fork. Pull gently.
harvest.storage: Leave in ground until needed. Refrigerate 2 weeks after harvesting.
harvest.yield: One leek per plant.

common_mistakes: Not starting early enough indoors.
Not blanching properly — hole-planting key to long white shank.
Harvesting before frost — frost dramatically improves flavor.
Planting too shallowly.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter. Crosses with other leeks.
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter, flower in year two. Cut dry seed heads into paper bag.
seed_saving.method: Shake to release seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Leek seeds viable shorter time than most vegetables.

good.why: Classic mutualism — leek repels carrot fly, carrot repels leek moth.
Both benefit from each other.

culinary: Mild sweet allium. Essential in vichyssoise, cock-a-leekie, quiche, gratins, braised dishes. Welsh national symbol. Milder than onion.
medicinal: Quercetin, allicin, kaempferol — anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular benefits. Folate. Prebiotic fiber. Vitamin K for bone health.

pests.name: Leek Moth
pests.desc: Larvae create transparent windows in leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: same as garlic and onion — Heinz body anemia
pet_toxicity.notes: Leeks belong to the allium family and are toxic like garlic and onion. Avoid all alliums for pets.

transplant.deep_note: Drop transplant into a 6-inch hole — do not fill hole, just water. The deep planting blanches the white stem naturally.

name: Arugula

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Every 2 weeks. Again late summer.
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Bolts in summer.

seed.desc: Surface sow or ¼ inch deep. Tiny seeds. Very fast to germinate.

germination.desc: Extremely fast. One of the quickest salad greens.

seedling.desc: Thin to 4–6 inches. Thinnings edible immediately.

young.desc: Harvest can begin as soon as leaves are 2 inches long.

adult.desc: Full peppery flavor. Bolts in heat — harvest everything when flower stalk appears.

care.water: Consistent moisture — drought accelerates bolting.
care.light: Full sun in cool. Part shade in warm to slow bolting.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen.
care.notes: One of the fastest crops from seed to harvest. Succession sow every 2 weeks.

container.notes: Perfect container salad green. Among the easiest and fastest.

propagation.desc: Surface sow directly. Too fast to bother starting indoors.

harvest.when: From 21 days, when leaves 2–4 inches. Young leaves mild, older hotter.
harvest.how: Cut 1 inch above soil for regrowth. Or harvest individual outer leaves.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 5–7 days. Very perishable.
harvest.yield: 3–4 cut-and-come-again harvests.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer — bolts within days.
Not succession sowing — weekly sowing needed.
Harvesting too late — large old leaves very bitter.
Overwatering in cool weather.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Crosses with other arugula and wild relatives.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow to bolt and flower. Harvest pods when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dried pods over bucket.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds readily — allow some to bolt for a self-sustaining patch.

good.why: Ideal salad garden companion.
Both fast cool-season crops.

culinary: Peppery, slightly bitter salad green. On pizza after baking, in pasta, sandwiches. Pairs with parmesan, lemon, prosciutto. Flowers edible. Staple of Italian cuisine.
medicinal: High in glucosinolates — anticancer isothiocyanates. High vitamin K. Nitrates for cardiovascular health. Low in oxalates — calcium more bioavailable than spinach.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none in small amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Peppery taste usually deters excessive eating naturally.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown — barely covered. Transplants rarely needed.

name: Broad Bean (Fava Bean)

season.direct_sow: Fall in mild climates for overwintering. Early spring 4 weeks before last frost.
season.harvest_window: Late spring through early summer

seed.desc: Large seeds — plant 2 inches deep. Germinates in cool soil 35–75°F.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool conditions.

seedling.desc: Cold-hardy plants withstand hard frosts.

young.desc: Black and white flowers appear. Black bean aphids love this stage — monitor closely.

adult.desc: Pods fill and become firm. Harvest while green for fresh use.

care.water: Moderate moisture. Tolerates cool wet conditions.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Minimal — nitrogen fixer.
care.notes: Cool-season crop. Chop and drop spent plants to add nitrogen to soil.

container.min_size: Tall plants need significant root space.
container.notes: In-ground preferred.

propagation.desc: Direct sow early spring or fall. Soak overnight.

harvest.when: Fresh: pods fat and beans bright green. Dried: pods brown and papery.
harvest.how: Pull pods downward — snap cleanly.
harvest.storage: Fresh: refrigerate 5 days or blanch and freeze. Dried: airtight container for years.
harvest.yield: 3–5 lbs per 10-foot row.

common_mistakes: Planting in warm weather — cool-season crop only.
Not pinching out aphid-infested growing tips.
Waiting too long for fresh beans — starchy and mealy.
Not inoculating with Rhizobium.

seed_saving.type: Partly self-pollinating. Crosses with other fava varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow pods to dry completely on plant.
seed_saving.method: Shell when dry.
seed_saving.notes: One of the most ancient crops — seed saving deeply rooted in cultural tradition.

good.why: Beans fix nitrogen for potatoes.
Nitrogen fixation benefits carrots.
Both cool-season crops.

culinary: Essential in Middle Eastern (ful medames), Italian, Spanish cuisines. Eaten fresh, dried, canned, roasted, pureed. Double-podding fresh beans gives most tender result.
medicinal: High protein — 26g per 100g dried. Rich in folate, iron, manganese. L-dopa precursor to dopamine. Note: people with G6PD deficiency (favism) must avoid.

pests.name: Black Bean Aphid
pests.desc: Dense black colonies on growing tips.
pests.control: Pinch out infected tips. Neem oil. Parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Chocolate Spot
pests.desc: Brown spots from Botrytis in wet weather.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, lethargy
pet_toxicity.notes: Broad beans (fava beans) are toxic to dogs and cats. Can cause severe GI distress and in large amounts hemolytic anemia. Do not feed.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sown 2 inches deep. Direct sow preferred over transplanting.

name: Sweet Potato

season.start_indoors: Start slips 6–8 weeks before last frost
season.transplant: 2 weeks after last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Fall — 90–120 days after planting slips

seed.desc: Not grown from seed. Start from slips — sprouts from a sweet potato tuber. Place tuber halfway in water to sprout.

germination.desc: Slips emerge from tuber in 4–6 weeks. Separate when 6 inches long.

seedling.desc: Slips establish slowly. Once established vines spread rapidly.

young.desc: Vines spread aggressively as ground cover. Tubers developing underground.

adult.desc: Vines begin to yellow as tubers mature. Harvest before heavy frost.

care.water: Moderate — more drought tolerant than regular potatoes.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Needs heat.
care.soil: Loose, well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 5.5–6.5. Sandy loam ideal.
care.fertilizer: Low nitrogen. High potassium and phosphorus.
care.notes: Needs long warm season. Black plastic mulch dramatically improves yields.

container.notes: Very large spreading vines make containers impractical.

propagation.desc: Place tuber halfway in water until 6-inch sprouts develop. Twist off and plant.
Cut 12-inch sections, strip lower leaves, plant in moist soil. Roots in 2 weeks.

harvest.when: 90–120 days after planting. Before first frost. Vines begin to yellow.
harvest.how: Loosen with garden fork 12 inches from plant. Dig carefully — tubers spread widely.
harvest.storage: Cure at 85–90°F and 90% humidity for 1–2 weeks. Store at 55–60°F for 4–6 months.
harvest.yield: 5–10 lbs per plant in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Planting too early in cold soil.
Over-fertilizing with nitrogen — beautiful vines, tiny roots.
Not curing — lacks sweetness and stores poorly.
Damaging tubers during harvest — cuts allow rot.

seed_saving.type: Propagated vegetatively from tubers or vine cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: Keep a few well-formed tubers for next year's slip production.
seed_saving.method: Store carefully until spring.
seed_saving.notes: Store slip-production tubers separately from eating tubers.

good.why: Nitrogen fixation. Both love heat.
Deters nematodes attacking roots.
Repels whitefly and root pests.

bad.why: Both vigorous spreading vines — compete aggressively.

culinary: Baked, roasted, mashed, fried, in soups, curries, casseroles, pies, and desserts. Used in Japanese, West African, and American Southern cuisines.
medicinal: Extremely high in beta-carotene. More fiber per calorie than regular potato. Purple varieties high in anthocyanins. Resistant starch when cooled feeds gut bacteria. Potassium for blood pressure.

pests.name: Sweet Potato Weevil
pests.desc: Most serious pest. Larvae tunnel into tubers.
pests.control: Use certified clean slips. Crop rotation. Remove all debris after harvest.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Clouds on leaves in warm conditions.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset from leaves if consumed
pet_toxicity.notes: Plain cooked sweet potato is safe and nutritious for dogs. Leaves and vines contain toxins — keep pets away from the plant. Raw sweet potato can cause GI upset.

transplant.deep_note: Plant slips with the node just below soil level. Deeper is fine — 1-2 inches.

name: Catnip

season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall

seed.desc: Surface sow or barely cover — needs light. Cold stratify for 1–2 weeks in fridge to improve germination rates.

germination.desc: Slow and variable. Keep moist at 60–70°F. Germination improves significantly after stratification.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly at first. Pinch tips to encourage bushy growth. Protect from cats at this stage — they will roll on and destroy young plants.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. Begin light harvest. Catmint (ornamental cousin) is less attractive to cats.

adult.desc: Vigorous spreader. Prune hard after first flush of flowers to encourage second bloom. Divide every 3 years.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water deeply but infrequently. Overwatering causes root rot.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More fragrant in full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean to moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0. Poor soil actually intensifies nepetalactone content.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. Spreads via self-seeding and underground runners.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil produces more potent essential oils.
care.notes: Protect young transplants with wire cloches — cats will seek out and destroy seedlings. Established plants are more resilient.

container.notes: Containers are a great way to protect young plants from cat damage. Easy to move indoors.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Cold stratify first for better germination.
Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring. Root in moist sand in 2–3 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring or fall every 3 years.

harvest.when: Just before or during flowering — highest nepetalactone content.
harvest.how: Cut stems back by one-third. Strip leaves from stems to dry separately.
harvest.storage: Dry in bundles hung upside down in warm airy space. Store dried herb in airtight jar away from light — potency fades over time.
harvest.yield: Very productive. One plant provides abundant harvest for humans and cats alike.

common_mistakes: Not protecting young transplants — cats destroy seedlings. Use wire cloches until established.
Letting it self-seed unchecked — can spread aggressively in favorable conditions.
Harvesting after full flowering — potency of nepetalactone peaks just before and during early flowering.
Over-fertilizing — reduces essential oil content that gives catnip its medicinal and feline properties.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried heads between palms over a bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so readily that deliberate saving is often unnecessary.

good.why: Repels flea beetles that devastate eggplant.
Deters squash bugs and aphids.
Repels aphids and flea beetles.

bad.why: Competing moisture needs and both spread aggressively — give each space.

culinary: Leaves used in herbal teas. Mild minty-lemony flavor. Used in some traditional recipes as a seasoning in Italy and parts of Europe. Young leaves edible raw in salads. Much less commonly used culinarily than medicinally.
medicinal: Nepetalactone — the compound that attracts cats — is a mild sedative and insect repellent in humans. Traditional use for anxiety, insomnia, headaches, and digestive complaints including colic. Antispasmodic. Mild diaphoretic (promotes sweating) used traditionally for fevers and colds. Insect repellent — nepetalactone shown to repel mosquitoes more effectively than DEET in some studies.

pests.name: Cats
pests.desc: The primary pest — cats roll on, chew, and destroy plants especially when young.
pests.control: Wire cloches over young transplants. Established plants are more resilient. Accept some cat damage as normal.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Ironically, catnip repels aphids from nearby plants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: euphoric rolling/rubbing in cats — intended reaction, not toxicity
pet_toxicity.notes: Completely safe for both dogs and cats. Cats experience euphoria from nepetalactone — completely harmless and temporary. Dogs show no reaction. Can eat freely.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Protect immediately with wire cloche — cats will destroy young transplants.

name: Lemon Balm

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall. Multiple harvests per season.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Do not cover. Keep at 65–70°F.

germination.desc: Slow and variable. Keep moist. Lemon scent present from earliest stage.

seedling.desc: Grow slowly initially. Bright crinkled leaves distinctive. Begin pinching at 4 inches.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. Begin harvest once plant is bushy and well established.

adult.desc: Vigorous perennial. Cut back hard after flowering to prevent self-seeding and encourage fresh growth.

care.water: Moderate moisture. More tolerant of wet conditions than Mediterranean herbs but overwatering causes root rot.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Partial shade in hot climates prevents scorching and extends season.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.5. Not fussy.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. Self-seeds and spreads — contain if needed.
care.fertilizer: Light feeding. Avoid excess nitrogen — reduces essential oil content.
care.notes: Can self-seed aggressively — deadhead after flowering or cut back hard to prevent spread. Drought-stressed plants have the most intense lemon scent.

container.notes: Excellent container herb. Containment in pots prevents aggressive self-seeding. Good on a sunny patio.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors. Slow germinator — start early.
Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring or summer. Root in moist mix in 2–3 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring or fall. Very easy — vigorous root system divides readily.

harvest.when: Just before flowering for maximum essential oil content. Harvest in the morning after dew has dried.
harvest.how: Cut stems back by one-third to one-half. Never strip the plant bare.
harvest.storage: Fresh leaves lose aroma quickly — use same day. Dry quickly in single layer on screens. Freeze in ice cube trays with water for best flavor preservation. Dried lemon balm loses significant aroma.
harvest.yield: Multiple cuts per season from established plants. Very productive.

common_mistakes: Expecting strong lemon flavor when dried — lemon balm loses most of its aroma when dried. Use fresh for best results.
Letting it self-seed unchecked — can become invasive. Deadhead or cut back after flowering.
Harvesting after full flowering — essential oil content drops sharply once flowers fully open.
Not enough sun — plants in deep shade produce little fragrance.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried heads into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so readily after first year that deliberate saving is rarely necessary.

good.why: Attracts pollinators and beneficial insects. Lemon scent may deter some pests.
Attracts pollinators needed for fruit set.
Excellent under fruit trees — attracts pollinators during flowering.

bad.why: Both spread aggressively and compete for space.

culinary: Mild lemon flavor used in teas, salads, desserts, fruit salads, cocktails, lemonade, pesto, and as a garnish. Pairs with fish, chicken, and summer vegetables. Used to flavor vinegars and oils. Essential in some traditional lemon herb blends. Best used fresh — loses most aroma when dried or heated.
medicinal: One of the most clinically studied medicinal herbs for anxiety and sleep. Multiple randomized controlled trials show significant reduction in anxiety and improved sleep quality. Rosmarinic acid inhibits GABA transaminase — similar mechanism to some anti-anxiety medications. Antiviral — cream containing lemon balm extract clinically proven to treat and prevent cold sores (herpes labialis). Cognitive enhancement shown in healthy adults. Antispasmodic for digestive complaints.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating in humid conditions or shady spots.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Move to sunnier position. Neem oil.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats. Mild calming effect. Not to be confused with lemon verbena which can cause GI issues.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Stevia
plant_type: Perennial (grown as annual in most zones)

season.transplant: After last frost when soil is thoroughly warm
season.harvest_window: Summer through fall. Harvest before flowering for sweetest leaves.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Fresh seed critical — viability drops dramatically within 6 months. Germination unreliable even from fresh seed.

germination.desc: Variable and often poor even with fresh seed. Start many extras. Keep at 70–75°F.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Bright light essential. First true leaves are distinctively sweet — taste test to confirm identity.

young.desc: Growth accelerates in warm weather. Begin light harvest. Pinch tips for bushier plant.

adult.desc: Harvest leaves before flowering — sweetness is highest before plants bolt. Flowering dramatically reduces stevioside content.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Does not tolerate drought or waterlogging. Even moisture is key.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Requires warmth.
care.soil: Well-draining, slightly acidic, rich. pH 6.5–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly. Adequate nutrition improves leaf yield.
care.notes: Day length sensitive — flowers in response to short days in late summer. Harvest heavily before this occurs. In frost-free zones overwinters as a perennial.

container.notes: Good container plant — can bring indoors to overwinter in cold zones. Place in sunniest indoor location.

propagation.desc: Most reliable method. Take 3–4 inch cuttings in summer. Root in moist sand in 2–3 weeks. Provides true-to-parent plants.
Unreliable germination even from fresh seed. Many commercial seeds have very low viability. Use fresh seed only.

harvest.when: Just before flowering — stevioside content peaks. Harvest leaves and small stems throughout the season.
harvest.how: Cut stems back by one-third. Strip leaves and dry separately. Harvest the whole plant before first frost in cold climates.
harvest.storage: Dry leaves quickly in a single layer at low heat or in a dehydrator. Dried leaves retain sweetness for 1–2 years in airtight jar. Grind dried leaves into powder for use as a sweetener.
harvest.yield: One established plant can produce 100–200g of dried leaves per season in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Using old seed — stevia seed viability drops rapidly. Only fresh seed (less than 6 months old) gives reasonable germination.
Letting it flower — sweetness drops significantly once flowering begins. Monitor and harvest aggressively before bolting.
Exposing to frost — extremely cold sensitive. Bring indoors or harvest entirely before first frost.
Overwatering — causes root rot. Consistent moisture is needed but not waterlogging.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated but germination is notoriously poor even from fresh seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds with pappus like dandelion.
seed_saving.method: Collect dry seed heads and gently rub to release seeds.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place. Use within 3–6 months.
seed_saving.viability: 3–6 months only — one of the shortest-lived herb seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings are far more reliable than seed for propagation.

good.why: Attracts beneficial insects.
Similar growing conditions — both love warmth.

culinary: The world's premier natural zero-calorie sweetener. Dried and powdered leaves are 200–300 times sweeter than sugar with no calories and no glycemic impact. Used in teas, baking, beverages, and as a sugar substitute. Fresh leaves can be chewed or added directly to tea. Slight licorice-like aftertaste in concentrated form. Use sparingly — a little goes a very long way.
medicinal: Stevioside and rebaudioside — the active glycosides — have no caloric value and do not raise blood sugar. Clinically shown to modestly lower blood pressure. Safe for diabetics — does not affect insulin response. Anti-inflammatory. Antimicrobial properties. Extensively studied and approved as a food additive globally. Traditionally used in Paraguay for centuries as a sweetener and medicinal plant.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Common when grown indoors or in warm sheltered conditions.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: From overwatering or poorly draining soil.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering. Remove affected plants.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — not to be confused with xylitol (artificial sweetener)
pet_toxicity.symptoms: none from natural stevia plant
pet_toxicity.notes: Natural stevia plant is safe for dogs and cats. Do NOT confuse with commercial sweeteners containing xylitol which is severely toxic to dogs. The plant itself is safe.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Very cold sensitive — transplant only after soil is warm.

name: Valerian

season.harvest_window: Roots harvested fall of second year. Leaves any time.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Cold stratify for 2–4 weeks for better germination. Fresh seed preferred.

germination.desc: Slow and variable. Keep moist at 60–65°F. Patience required.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in first year. Develops only foliage — roots used medicinally are harvested in year two.

young.desc: Rosette of pinnate leaves develops. Tap root growing deeper. Distinctive unpleasant smell from roots when disturbed.

adult.desc: In year two sends up tall flowering stems (4–6 feet) with clusters of small pale pink-white flowers. Highly attractive to cats and pollinators.

care.water: Moderate to moist. More tolerant of wet conditions than most herbs. Do not let dry out completely.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Moist, rich, well-draining. pH 5.5–7.0. Deep soil for taproot development.
care.fertilizer: Moderate balanced fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: The tall flowering stems may need staking. Cats are attracted to valerian roots similarly to catnip — protect dug roots.

container.min_size: Very deep container needed for taproot.
container.notes: Not well suited to containers — deep taproot needs significant soil depth. In-ground strongly preferred.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Cold stratify first.
Divide established plants in spring or fall. Very easy — clumps expand readily.
Take root sections in fall. Replant immediately.

harvest.when: Roots: fall of second year after first frost, when valerenic acid content is highest. Leaves: any time during the growing season.
harvest.how: Dig up roots with a garden fork in fall. Wash thoroughly. Roots smell unpleasant when fresh — this is normal and indicates potency.
harvest.storage: Dry roots at low temperature (below 104°F) to preserve valerenic acid. Cut into small pieces for faster drying. Store in airtight jar. Dried roots smell less unpleasant than fresh. Tincture preserved in alcohol for long-term storage.
harvest.yield: Mature plant produces significant root mass by end of year two.

common_mistakes: Harvesting roots in year one — roots need two growing seasons to develop adequate medicinal compounds.
Drying roots at high heat — destroys valerenic acid. Dry slowly at low temperature.
Expecting pleasant-smelling roots — fresh valerian root smells strongly unpleasant. This is normal and expected.
Confusing with red valerian (Centranthus ruber) — that is a different and non-medicinal plant despite the similar name.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Seeds have feathery pappus and disperse readily.
seed_saving.method: Collect seed heads just before fully ripe and dry in paper bag.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds readily when established. Collect before seeds disperse.

good.why: Attracts earthworms to the soil area according to traditional companion planting.
Root exudates said to stimulate root growth of neighboring plants.
Traditional companion — said to improve rose health and vigor.

bad.why: Valerian is generally considered beneficial to other plants.

culinary: Not a culinary herb — the taste is extremely unpleasant. Roots occasionally used in herbal preparations but not in food. The name comes from the Latin 'valere' (to be strong) not from any food use.
medicinal: One of the most extensively researched herbal sleep aids. Valerenic acid inhibits GABA breakdown — same neurotransmitter targeted by benzodiazepines, but through a gentler mechanism. Multiple clinical trials support efficacy for insomnia and sleep quality improvement. Reduces time to fall asleep. Anti-anxiety effects. Used for restlessness, nervous tension, and stress. Generally considered safe for short-term use. Takes 2–4 weeks of regular use for full effect. European Medicine Agency approves for sleep disturbances.

pests.name: Cats
pests.desc: Attracted to the roots similarly to catnip — will dig up and roll on recently harvested roots.
pests.control: Protect dug roots from cats. Established plants rarely disturbed by cats.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: In humid conditions on lower leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: cats may experience catnip-like euphoria from the roots
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for both dogs and cats. Cats are attracted to valerian root similarly to catnip — the reaction is harmless. Small sedative effect in dogs similar to human use.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Echinacea

season.start_indoors: 8–10 weeks before last frost — cold stratify seed first
season.direct_sow: Fall (natural stratification over winter) or very early spring
season.harvest_window: Flowers mid-summer. Roots harvested fall of year 3+.

seed.desc: Cold stratify for 4–8 weeks in damp paper towel in fridge before sowing. Surface sow — needs light.

germination.desc: Improved dramatically by cold stratification. Without it germination is slow and poor.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in first year. Mainly root development. May not flower in year one.

young.desc: First flowering possible in year two. Purple daisy-like flowers with prominent orange-brown cone appear.

adult.desc: Fully established perennial. More flowers each year. Roots harvested for medicine from year 3 onward for sustainability.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Deep but infrequent watering. Very resilient.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More blooms in full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.0. Tolerates poor soil well.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Too much nitrogen produces lots of foliage and few flowers.
care.notes: Leave seed heads standing over winter — goldfinches rely on them for food. Cut back in early spring. Divides and self-seeds to form colonies.

container.min_size: Large deep container possible but limits root development.
container.notes: Better in the ground — deep taproot needs space. Not practical in containers long-term.

propagation.desc: Cold stratify first. Surface sow in fall or early spring. Self-seeds once established.
Divide established clumps in spring or fall every 4–5 years to maintain vigor.
Take 3-inch root sections in fall. Plant horizontally 2 inches deep.

harvest.when: Flowers: when fully open and petals beginning to reflex — highest alkylamide content. Roots: fall of year 3+ after leaves die back.
harvest.how: Cut flower stems at base. For roots: dig carefully with fork, harvest only outer roots leaving center plant intact for sustainability. Never harvest all roots.
harvest.storage: Dry flowers on screens. Dry root sections at low heat. Tincture in alcohol for most effective preservation of active compounds. Dried herb loses potency over 1–2 years.
harvest.yield: Multiple flower harvests per season from year 2 onward. Root harvest from year 3 — sustainable partial harvest only.

common_mistakes: Not cold stratifying seed — without it germination is poor. This step is non-negotiable.
Harvesting roots too early — roots need at least 3 years to develop meaningful medicinal compound levels.
Harvesting all roots — always leave the crown and some roots. Take only 25–30% per harvest for sustainability.
Deadheading all seed heads — goldfinches depend on them in winter. Leave some for wildlife.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true but crosses between Echinacea species.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed heads to dry on plant. Seeds are inside the spiky cone.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried cone between gloved hands over a bowl to dislodge seeds.
seed_saving.drying: Dry cones further in paper bag 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Cold stratify saved seeds before sowing. Echinacea species cross if grown together.

good.why: Attracts the same pollinators — bees and butterflies. Beautiful combination.
Complementary bloom time and pollinator attraction.
Both drought-tolerant perennials that attract beneficial insects.

bad.why: Echinacea is generally considered beneficial to garden ecology.

culinary: Not used in cooking. Occasionally used in teas and infusions though flavor is unremarkable.
medicinal: One of the most widely sold herbal supplements globally. Clinical evidence supports modest reduction in duration and severity of the common cold when taken at onset. Stimulates innate immunity — increases phagocytosis and natural killer cell activity. Alkylamides (in root and fresh flower) are the primary active compounds — cause distinctive tingling sensation on the tongue when fresh. Anti-inflammatory. Topical wound healing. Most effective when taken immediately at first sign of illness. E. purpurea, E. angustifolia, and E. pallida have different compound profiles and uses.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.control: Blast with water. Natural predators usually manage populations.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves especially late season.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Remove affected leaves. Usually not serious on established plants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none in normal amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats. Sometimes used as an immune supplement for pets under veterinary guidance. No known toxicity.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Establishes slowly — be patient.

name: Feverfew

season.direct_sow: After last frost — or fall for spring germination
season.harvest_window: Leaves: spring through fall. Flowers: midsummer.

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Press gently into moist mix. Keep at 65–70°F.

germination.desc: Fairly reliable in warm conditions. Tiny seedlings — be careful not to overwater.

seedling.desc: Grows relatively quickly. Distinctive chrysanthemum-like deeply cut aromatic leaves.

young.desc: Branching, compact plants. Begin leaf harvest once established.

adult.desc: Covered in small white daisy-like flowers midsummer. Short-lived perennial — replace every 3 years as vigor declines. Self-seeds readily.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates brief drought once established. Do not overwater.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–6.7. Not fussy.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil produces more medicinally potent leaves.
care.notes: Short-lived perennial — individual plants decline after 3 years but self-seeding keeps the colony going. Strongly aromatic — repels many insects.

container.notes: Good container plant. Self-seeding into adjacent pots is possible.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant. Self-seeds readily once established.
Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring. Root in moist mix in 2–3 weeks.
Divide clumps in spring every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.

harvest.when: Leaves: any time but highest parthenolide content just before flowering. Flowers: when fully open.
harvest.how: Cut leaves and stems as needed. Never remove more than one-third of the plant.
harvest.storage: Fresh leaves used medicinally and in cooking. Dry quickly — parthenolide is volatile and levels drop in dried material. Freeze fresh leaves for medicinal use to better preserve active compounds.
harvest.yield: Productive throughout the season. One plant provides sufficient leaf harvest for regular use.

common_mistakes: Eating fresh leaves without preparation — direct consumption of fresh leaves causes mouth ulcers in many people. Use in sandwiches (between two slices of bread to buffer direct contact) or as a tincture.
Relying on poorly dried herb — parthenolide degrades with drying and storage. Fresh or frozen is more effective.
Expecting immediate migraine relief — feverfew is a preventative, not an acute treatment. Must be taken daily for prevention.
Stopping suddenly after long-term use — can cause post-feverfew syndrome (rebound headaches, anxiety, insomnia). Taper gradually.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry heads into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Often self-sustaining once established through self-seeding.

good.why: Repels aphids and rose beetles. Traditional rose companion.
Strong aromatic scent repels many fruit tree pests.
Repels cabbage moth and whitefly.

bad.why: Feverfew's aromatic compounds generally benefit surrounding plants by repelling pests.

culinary: Occasionally used in salads and sandwiches but strong bitter flavor limits culinary use. Traditional use in egg dishes and herb butters in some European cuisines. Primarily a medicinal herb.
medicinal: Parthenolide — the primary active compound — inhibits platelet aggregation and prostaglandin synthesis. Multiple clinical trials support efficacy for migraine prevention when taken daily — reduces frequency by up to 50% in some studies. Must be used as a preventative (daily) not an acute treatment. Anti-inflammatory. Traditional use for fever (hence the name), arthritis, and menstrual pain. European scientific literature supports migraine prevention use. Important: do not use during pregnancy — uterine stimulant.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional. The plant's aromatic oils generally deter aphids.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, contact dermatitis, mouth ulcers
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists feverfew as toxic to dogs and cats. Same compound (parthenolide) that causes mouth ulcers in humans when eaten raw causes similar issues in pets. Keep away from animals.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Borage

season.start_indoors: Not recommended — taproot sensitive to transplanting
season.direct_sow: 2–3 weeks before last frost. Succession sow every 4 weeks.
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost from successive sowings

seed.desc: Direct sow ½ inch deep. Large seed — easy to handle. Does not transplant well due to taproot.

germination.desc: Reliable in moderately warm soil. Fast in warm conditions.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Large, hairy, cucumber-scented leaves develop quickly.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Flower buds appear. Begins sprawling — needs space or support.

adult.desc: Covered in stunning blue star-shaped flowers. Self-seeds prolifically — becomes a permanent garden resident.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates brief drought once established. Overwatering causes root rot.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Thrives in lean soil — rich soil produces fewer flowers.
care.fertilizer: None needed. Rich soil reduces flowering and increases floppy growth.
care.notes: Self-seeds so prolifically it becomes a permanent garden resident after first year. Thin or transplant volunteers — but transplant when very small due to taproot.

container.notes: Taproot makes containers challenging. Plants sprawl and become large. In-ground strongly preferred.

propagation.desc: Direct sow in place. Does not transplant well once established. Self-seeds so reliably that after the first year it typically maintains itself.

harvest.when: Flowers: when fully open, in the morning. Leaves: young leaves before they become too hairy. Seeds: when black and dry on plant.
harvest.how: Pinch individual flowers. Cut young leaves with scissors. Shake seed heads into bag when dry.
harvest.storage: Flowers best used fresh — freeze in ice cubes for preservation. Leaves used fresh only. Seeds dry on plant naturally.
harvest.yield: One plant produces hundreds of flowers over the season. Self-seeding provides indefinite supply.

common_mistakes: Starting indoors — taproot makes transplanting very difficult. Always direct sow.
Planting only once — self-seeds but consider succession sowing for earlier and later harvests in year one.
Not supporting sprawling plants — tall stems become top-heavy and can fall over. Stake or plant near a fence.
Eating mature leaves — young leaves are palatable; older leaves are very hairy and unpleasant to eat raw.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect black seeds from plant before they drop. Seeds shatter when fully dry.
seed_saving.method: Collect individual seeds or shake dry plant over paper bag.
seed_saving.drying: Use immediately or dry 1 week on paper.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so readily that deliberate saving is unnecessary for garden continuity.

good.why: Repels tomato hornworm. Attracts pollinators. Adds trace minerals when chopped and dropped as mulch.
Repels strawberry pests. Attracts pollinators at critical fruiting time.
Attracts pollinators essential for fruit set. Deters squash bug.
Repels cabbage worm. Traditional brassica companion.

bad.why: Borage is considered universally beneficial in the garden.

culinary: Bright blue star-shaped flowers are the most important use — edible and stunning. Used as garnish for salads, cocktails, punches, and desserts. Frozen in ice cubes for drinks. Candied as cake decorations. Young leaves have a cucumber flavor and used in salads, dips (especially in Germany), cold soups, and as a cooked green. Used in the Italian liqueur Fascia di Boragine. Traditional ingredient in Pimm's Cup cocktail.
medicinal: Seed oil high in gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) — an omega-6 fatty acid with anti-inflammatory properties. GLA shown to help rheumatoid arthritis symptoms. Traditional anti-inflammatory and adrenal tonic use — 'borage for courage' was a medieval saying. Leaves contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids — avoid large quantities internally. Seed oil does not contain PAs and is safer for internal use. Topical use for eczema and skin inflammation.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Can appear in large numbers but borage attracts predatory insects that quickly control them.
pests.control: Usually self-limiting. Blast with water. Borage is often used as a trap crop specifically for aphids.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.control: Remove most affected plants by late summer. Allow to self-seed for next year.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, possible liver damage with chronic exposure
pet_toxicity.notes: Pyrrolizidine alkaloids are potentially hepatotoxic with repeated exposure. Occasional incidental ingestion unlikely to cause harm but not a plant to allow pets to graze on regularly.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow only — taproot is immediate. Does not transplant well.

name: Hyssop

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm soil
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Germinates best at 60–70°F. Surface sow or very shallow cover.

germination.desc: Moderate germinator. Keep moist and cool to moderate temperature.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Upright, slightly woody from early stage. Strong aromatic scent from first leaves.

young.desc: Begin light harvest. Deep blue-purple (or white/pink) flower spikes appear in late summer. Highly attractive to bees.

adult.desc: Semi-evergreen perennial. Prune hard in spring. Replace every 4–5 years as plants become too woody.

care.water: Drought tolerant. Water when soil is dry. Overwatering causes root rot.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours for best flavor and flowering.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean, alkaline preferred. pH 7.0–8.0. Poor soil produces more aromatic plants.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil produces the most aromatic and flavorful plants.
care.notes: Semi-evergreen in mild winters. Prune hard in spring to prevent woodiness. Excellent bee plant — one of the most popular with honeybees.

container.notes: Good container plant. Use lean, well-draining mix. Full sun position essential.

propagation.desc: Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant.
Take 3-inch softwood cuttings in spring or summer. Root in gritty mix in 3–4 weeks.
Divide established clumps in spring every 3–4 years.

harvest.when: Just before or during flowering for maximum essential oil content.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with scissors. Leave two-thirds of plant intact.
harvest.storage: Dry quickly in bundles. Store dried herb in airtight jar. Retains flavor reasonably well when dried.
harvest.yield: Multiple harvests per season from established plants.

common_mistakes: Growing in wet or heavy soil — must have excellent drainage.
Not pruning — becomes woody and unproductive without annual hard pruning in spring.
Keeping plants too long — decline after 4–5 years. Replace from cuttings.
Growing near radishes — hyssop specifically inhibits radish growth.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower spikes to dry on plant. Seeds in dried calyxes.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried spikes between palms over bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Seed-grown plants may vary slightly in flower color.

good.why: Repels cabbage moth and whitefly.
Traditional vineyard companion — attracts beneficial insects and repels pests.
Repels aphids and attracts pollinators.

bad.why: Hyssop specifically inhibits radish growth — one of the few documented negative companions.

culinary: Used sparingly in soups, stews, stuffings, and meat dishes. Traditional flavoring in Chartreuse liqueur and other herbal liqueurs. Pairs with fatty meats (lamb, pork) where its bitterness cuts through richness. Used in herb blends for game birds. Strong, bitter, minty flavor — use very sparingly. Flowers edible as garnish.
medicinal: Traditional expectorant and antispasmodic for respiratory conditions — coughs, bronchitis, and asthma. Anti-inflammatory rosmarinic acid. Antiviral properties — shown active against herpes simplex in vitro. Digestive stimulant. The liqueur Chartreuse was originally made by monks as a medicinal preparation. Important: avoid therapeutic doses during pregnancy — uterine stimulant.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional. Hyssop generally deters aphids from nearby plants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, loss of coordination
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists hyssop as toxic to dogs and cats. Keep out of reach.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Needs good drainage.

name: Marjoram
plant_type: Perennial (grown as annual in cold zones)

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost. Year-round in mild climates.

seed.desc: Surface sow — tiny seeds need light. Keep at 65–70°F. Germinates best in warm conditions.

germination.desc: Reliable in warm conditions. Tiny seedlings — avoid overwatering.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Delicate appearance but more cold sensitive than oregano.

young.desc: Begin light harvest once plant is bushy and 6 inches tall. Pinch tips for compact growth.

adult.desc: Compact and mounding. Small white or pink flowers attract beneficial insects. Harvest before full flowering.

care.water: Moderate. More moisture-sensitive than oregano. Do not overwater or let dry out completely.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–8.0.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced feeding. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: Sweeter and more delicate than oregano. Cold sensitive — treat as annual in zones below 9. More commonly used fresh than dried.

container.notes: Excellent container herb. Bring indoors to overwinter in cold zones. Sunny windowsill.

propagation.desc: Surface sow indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant.
Take 3-inch tip cuttings in spring or summer. Root in 2–3 weeks.
Divide in spring in mild climates where plants overwinter.

harvest.when: Just before flowering for most complex flavor. Any time during the growing season.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips, leaving two-thirds of plant.
harvest.storage: Fresh best. Dries reasonably well — hang in bundles. Flavor more delicate than oregano when dried. Freeze in olive oil.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest all season with regular cutting.

common_mistakes: Confusing with oregano — marjoram is sweeter and more delicate. Not directly interchangeable in recipes.
Treating as frost hardy — much more cold sensitive than oregano. Protect or bring indoors at first frost warning.
Harvesting after full flowering — flavor becomes more bitter and intense post-flowering.
Overwatering — more susceptible to root rot than oregano.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry on plant. Tiny seeds.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried heads over bowl.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Save seeds in warm climates where plant overwinters. In cold zones save before first frost.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites. Similar to oregano's benefits.
Aromatic oils deter pepper pests.
Similar growing needs. Both deter garden pests.

culinary: The sweeter, more delicate cousin of oregano. Essential in French cuisine — herbes de Provence, bouquet garni, fines herbes. Pairs beautifully with eggs, chicken, lamb, mushrooms, and tomatoes. Used in sausages, stuffings, and vegetable dishes. Less pungent than oregano — better for delicate preparations. German cuisine uses it extensively in sausages and pork dishes (called 'Wurstkraut' — sausage herb).
medicinal: Similar medicinal properties to oregano but milder. Contains carvacrol and thymol — antimicrobial and antifungal. Antispasmodic for digestive complaints. Traditionally used for headaches (topical oil application) and respiratory infections. Warming herb — improves circulation. Mild anxiolytic properties.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset, vomiting
pet_toxicity.notes: Mildly toxic in large amounts. ASPCA lists marjoram as toxic to cats and dogs. Small incidental exposure unlikely to cause harm.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Tarragon (French)

season.start_indoors: Start from divisions or cuttings — true French tarragon doesn't grow from seed
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall

seed.desc: French tarragon is sterile — produces no viable seed. MUST be propagated vegetatively. Russian tarragon (inferior flavor) can be grown from seed but is not recommended.

germination.desc: Not applicable — French tarragon does not produce viable seed.

seedling.desc: Divisions and cuttings establish in 2–4 weeks. Anise-like aroma present from earliest growth.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. Upright stems with narrow, glossy leaves. Begin light harvest once well established.

adult.desc: Vigorous perennial. Dies back in winter, returns reliably in spring. Divide every 3 years to maintain vigor.

care.water: Moderate. Drought tolerant once established. Do not overwater — susceptible to root rot.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Well-draining, sandy, lean. pH 6.0–7.5. Rich soil reduces essential oil content.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Over-fertilizing produces bland flavor.
care.notes: French tarragon is the only culinary variety — do not buy Russian tarragon seeds. Flavor is completely different. Loses flavor when dried — always use fresh or frozen.

container.notes: Good container plant. Bring indoors in zones below 4. Needs to experience cool temperatures to die back and return in spring.

propagation.desc: Primary method. Divide established clumps in spring every 3 years. Each section with roots plants immediately.
Take 3-inch stem cuttings in spring or early summer. Root in moist sand in 3–4 weeks.
Pin stems to soil and cover midsection. Roots form in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: Once plant is well established. Best before and during early flowering — highest essential oil content.
harvest.how: Cut stem tips with scissors. Never take more than one-third.
harvest.storage: Fresh best — flavor deteriorates significantly when dried. Freeze whole sprigs on a tray then bag. Infuse in vinegar (tarragon vinegar) for long-term flavor preservation. Store infused vinegar for up to 6 months.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest all season from established plants.

common_mistakes: Buying Russian tarragon seed — this is not the culinary herb. Russian tarragon tastes like dried grass. French tarragon cannot be grown from seed.
Drying tarragon — loses almost all flavor when dried. Always use fresh or frozen.
Not dividing — plants decline after 3–4 years without division.
Harvesting in late summer and expecting regrowth — plants begin going dormant. Stop harvesting in late summer and let the plant prepare for winter.

seed_saving.type: French tarragon is sterile — produces no viable seed. Propagate exclusively by division or cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: Not applicable.
seed_saving.method: Not applicable.
seed_saving.notes: If a plant labeled 'tarragon' produces seed, it is Russian tarragon and lacks culinary value.

good.why: Traditional companion — said to improve eggplant growth.
Tarragon has a reputation as a general garden beneficial — may deter some pests.

bad.why: Tarragon generally considered neutral to beneficial.

culinary: One of the four classic French fine herbs (with chervil, chives, and parsley). Essential in béarnaise sauce, chicken tarragon, fish dishes, compound butters, cream sauces, and vinaigrettes. Distinctive anise-like flavor that softens when cooked. Used in herb mustard, pickles, and to flavor vinegar. Indispensable in classical French cooking. Pairs with chicken, fish, eggs, asparagus, and cream.
medicinal: Traditionally used as a digestive aid and appetite stimulant. Estragole (the main essential oil) has antifungal and antimicrobial properties. Contains compounds shown to regulate blood sugar. Topical use for toothache — numbing effect similar to cloves. Antioxidant. Caution: estragole has shown carcinogenic properties in high doses in animal studies — normal culinary use considered safe.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: Most common problem — from overwatering or poor drainage.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering. Plant in raised bed or well-amended soil.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite
pet_toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic by ASPCA for dogs and cats. The compound estragole (also found in basil) may have carcinogenic properties. Small culinary amounts in food unlikely to cause issues but avoid intentional feeding.

transplant.deep_note: Plant divisions at nursery depth. French tarragon propagated by division only.

name: Comfrey

season.start_indoors: Start from root divisions — seed is slow
season.direct_sow: Possible but slow. Root divisions are much faster.
season.harvest_window: Leaves: spring through fall, multiple cuts per year. Roots: fall of year 2+.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Cold stratify for improved germination. Slow to establish from seed — root divisions are far better.

germination.desc: Slow and variable from seed. Root divisions establish in 2–3 weeks and grow rapidly.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly from seed in year one. From root division: rapid growth, large leaves by midsummer.

young.desc: Large, hairy, deep green leaves develop. Purple tubular flowers attractive to bumblebees. Roots grow very deep.

adult.desc: Extremely vigorous perennial. Almost impossible to eradicate once established — every root fragment regenerates. Choose placement carefully.

care.water: Tolerates both drought and wet conditions. Very adaptable. More productive with adequate moisture.
care.light: Full sun to heavy shade. One of the most shade-tolerant garden plants.
