care.soil: Almost any soil. Very deep taproot accesses nutrients other plants cannot reach. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.spacing: 24–36 inches. Plants spread and are very difficult to remove.
care.fertilizer: None needed — mines nutrients from deep in the soil.
care.notes: Bocking 14 is the sterile hybrid variety — does not self-seed, preventing invasive spread. Strongly recommended over common comfrey for garden use. The leaves are one of the best organic fertilizers available — high nitrogen, potassium, and trace minerals.

container.notes: The deep taproot makes containers impractical. In-ground only. Choose location permanently — nearly impossible to move once established.

propagation.desc: Cut roots into 2-inch sections. Plant 3–4 inches deep. Each section grows into a new plant. Spring or fall.
Slow and unreliable. Root divisions strongly preferred. Bocking 14 is sterile and cannot be grown from seed.

harvest.when: Cut leaves when 18–24 inches tall. Up to 4–5 cuts per season in good conditions.
harvest.how: Cut stems 2 inches above ground with sickle or shears. Plant regrows vigorously. Wear gloves — hairs cause skin irritation.
harvest.storage: Fresh leaves used immediately as mulch or liquid fertilizer (comfrey tea). Dry leaves for topical poultice use. Do not consume internally — pyrrolizidine alkaloids are hepatotoxic.
harvest.yield: One mature plant can yield over 100 lbs of leaves per season. Extremely productive.

common_mistakes: Planting common comfrey instead of Bocking 14 — common comfrey self-seeds aggressively and is nearly impossible to eradicate. Always use Bocking 14.
Planting in the wrong location — once established this plant is permanent. You cannot easily move it or remove it.
Consuming internally — pyrrolizidine alkaloids in comfrey are hepatotoxic (liver-damaging). For external use only in modern herbal practice.
Not wearing gloves when harvesting — the fine hairs cause significant skin irritation.

seed_saving.type: Common comfrey is open-pollinated. Bocking 14 is sterile — cannot be seed saved.
seed_saving.harvest: Not applicable for Bocking 14.
seed_saving.method: Collect seed from common comfrey if using that variety.
seed_saving.notes: Always propagate Bocking 14 from root cuttings only.

good.why: Planted around base of trees, the deep taproot mines minerals and the chop-and-drop leaves fertilize the soil. Essential in permaculture orchards.
Comfrey leaves used as mulch around potatoes suppress weeds and add potassium — a primary potato nutrient.
Comfrey tea (liquid fertilizer) is excellent for tomatoes — high potassium promotes fruiting.

bad.why: Comfrey grows very large and shades out smaller neighbors. Give it space.

culinary: Not used in modern cooking — pyrrolizidine alkaloids make internal use unsafe. Historically used as a vegetable before the toxicity was understood. External use only.
medicinal: Allantoin — the primary active compound — accelerates cell proliferation and wound healing. Clinically proven for sprains, bruises, muscle pain, and osteoarthritis when applied topically. Approved in Germany for topical use. Anti-inflammatory rosmarinic acid. EXTERNAL USE ONLY — pyrrolizidine alkaloids cause cumulative liver damage when consumed internally. One of the most effective topical herbs for musculoskeletal injuries. Traditional use for broken bones ('knitbone') — allantoin's cell proliferation effects may explain this.

pests.name: Slugs
pests.desc: Young plants can be damaged by slugs.
pests.control: Beer traps. Diatomaceous earth around young plants. Established plants are too vigorous to be seriously harmed.

pests.name: Comfrey Moth
pests.desc: Caterpillars of the scarlet tiger moth — beautiful larvae sometimes found on leaves.
pests.control: Leave them — the moth is beautiful and not significantly harmful to established plants.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — especially roots — pyrrolizidine alkaloids
pet_toxicity.symptoms: liver damage, vomiting, lethargy — cumulative toxicity
pet_toxicity.notes: Pyrrolizidine alkaloids cause cumulative liver damage in dogs and cats. Chronic exposure dangerous. Keep pets away from comfrey plants, especially the roots. For external use on pets, avoid — many vets advise against it.

transplant.deep_note: Plant root sections 3-4 inches deep. CHOOSE LOCATION CAREFULLY — permanent planting, nearly impossible to remove.

name: Calendula

season.direct_sow: 2–4 weeks before last frost. Again in late summer for fall bloom.
season.transplant: Tolerates light frost — plant out early
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost. Flowers continuously.

seed.desc: Sow ¼–½ inch deep. Unusual curved seeds resemble tiny caterpillars. Prefers cooler germination.

germination.desc: Reliable in cool to moderate conditions. Prefers 60–70°F — may be slower in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Grows fairly quickly. Sticky aromatic foliage from early stage.

young.desc: Rapid growth and early flowering. Deadhead to encourage continuous bloom.

adult.desc: Covers itself in orange and yellow flowers from early summer until hard frost. Self-seeds reliably for next year.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates brief drought. Overwatering causes root rot and powdery mildew.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More flowers in full sun.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. pH 5.5–7.0. Thrives in lean soil — too rich means more leaves and fewer flowers.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Lean soil promotes best flower production.
care.notes: One of the easiest and most rewarding herbs to grow. Deadhead regularly to extend blooming season. Self-seeds reliably. Edible flowers.

container.notes: Excellent container plant. Compact varieties especially good. Regular deadheading essential in containers.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or start indoors. Very reliable germinator. Self-seeds prolifically after first year.

harvest.when: Flowers: when fully open in the morning. Harvest frequently to keep plants producing.
harvest.how: Pinch or cut individual flower heads at the base of the stem. Daily harvesting keeps plants blooming.
harvest.storage: Dry flower heads in a single layer on screens in a warm dark airy space. Petals can be separated from green base for better drying. Store dried flowers in airtight jar away from light. Use within 1 year. Infuse in oil for topical preparations.
harvest.yield: A small planting of calendula provides an almost unlimited supply of flowers for topical preparations.

common_mistakes: Not deadheading — undeadheaded plants set seed and stop flowering. Harvest or deadhead every few days.
Drying in piles — flowers mold. Single layer on screens only.
Confusing with marigold (Tagetes) — not the same plant. Tagetes cannot be substituted for Calendula medicinally.
Planting in summer heat without shade — flowers and declines in intense heat. Better as spring and fall crop.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some flower heads to dry on plant. Distinctive curved seeds clearly visible.
seed_saving.method: Collect seeds by hand when dry and brown.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so readily it becomes permanent in the garden after first year.

good.why: Repels whitefly, aphids, and nematodes. Attracts pollinators and beneficial insects.
Repels asparagus beetle.
Attracts beneficial insects that prey on carrot pests.
Calendula is one of the most beneficial companion plants in the vegetable garden — attracts beneficials and repels pests broadly.

bad.why: Calendula is considered universally beneficial in the garden.

culinary: Petals edible — used as a saffron substitute for color (called 'poor man's saffron'). Petals add yellow-orange color to rice, soups, and stews. Used fresh in salads as a garnish. Added to cheese, butter, and vinegars. Dried petals used in herbal teas. Mild, slightly bitter, faintly peppery flavor. Petals only — the green base is bitter.
medicinal: One of the most important topical medicinal plants. Calendula cream and ointment clinically proven for wound healing, diaper rash, skin inflammation, radiation dermatitis (used in cancer care), and surgical wound healing. Triterpene saponins and flavonoids are primary active compounds. Anti-inflammatory, antifungal, and antimicrobial. Internal use: anti-inflammatory, menstrual regulation, digestive complaints. Infused oil is the standard preparation for topical use — infuse dried flowers in olive oil for 4–6 weeks.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Common — calendula is sometimes used as a trap crop specifically to draw aphids away from vegetables.
pests.control: Blast with water. Allow natural predators to manage. Ironically beneficial as a trap crop.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: Common in humid conditions or late season.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Remove affected plants by late summer. Allow to self-seed for next year.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, skin irritation (contact dermatitis)
pet_toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic by ASPCA for dogs and cats. Primarily causes GI upset and skin irritation. Widely used in pet topical products but internal ingestion should be avoided.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow or transplant at nursery pot depth.

name: St. John's Wort

season.start_indoors: 8–10 weeks before last frost — cold stratify first
season.direct_sow: Fall for spring germination. Early spring.
season.harvest_window: Midsummer — just as flowers begin to open

seed.desc: Surface sow — tiny seeds need light. Cold stratify for 4–6 weeks. Fresh seed preferred.

germination.desc: Slow and variable. Cold stratification significantly improves rate. Keep at 60–65°F.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in year one. Mainly root and foliage development. May not flower until year two.

young.desc: Distinctive oval leaves with translucent oil glands visible when held to light — a key identification feature. Yellow flowers appear in midsummer.

adult.desc: Established perennial flowering reliably each midsummer. Spreads via rhizomes and self-seeding.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Prefers dry to moderate conditions.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Best flower production in full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean to moderately fertile. pH 5.5–7.0. Thrives in poor soil.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Poor soil produces more medicinally potent plants.
care.notes: Considered invasive in some western US states — check local regulations before planting. Crush a flower bud between fingers — should produce red-purple stain from hypericin. This is the key quality indicator.

container.notes: Rhizomatous spreading habit makes containers impractical long-term. In-ground preferred.

propagation.desc: Cold stratify first. Surface sow in fall or early spring.
Divide spreading rhizomes in spring or fall.
Softwood cuttings in early summer root in 3–4 weeks.

harvest.when: CRITICAL: Harvest when flowers are just beginning to open — 25–50% of buds open. This is when hypericin and hyperforin content peaks. The traditional harvest date is around St. John's Day (June 24).
harvest.how: Cut flowering tops — top 6 inches of stems with flowers and buds. Crush a few buds to check for red-purple stain confirming hypericin presence.
harvest.storage: Dry quickly in single layer in dark airy space. Hypericin is light-sensitive — dry in dark to preserve potency. Store in dark glass airtight container. Make oil infusion or tincture immediately from fresh flowers for maximum potency.
harvest.yield: Harvest tops once per season at peak flowering. One established planting provides significant harvest.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too early or too late — the 25–50% open flower window is critical for maximum medicinal potency.
Drying in light — hypericin is photosensitive. Dry in dark to preserve medicinal compounds.
Not checking for red-purple stain — always crush a bud to confirm identity and quality before harvesting.

Ignoring drug interactions — St. John's Wort is a significant inducer of CYP3A4 enzymes and reduces efficacy of many medications including contraceptives, antivirals, and blood thinners. Inform a doctor before use.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds and spreads via rhizomes.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed capsules to dry on plant. Tiny seeds.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried capsules into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Often self-sustaining once established.

good.why: Both thrive in dry, lean, well-drained soil. Complementary flower colors.
Both medicinal perennials that attract pollinators. Similar growing conditions.

bad.why: St. John's Wort does not significantly harm neighboring plants.

culinary: Not a culinary herb. Occasionally used in herbal teas for its mild flavor but primarily a medicinal plant.
medicinal: One of the most studied herbal antidepressants. Multiple meta-analyses confirm efficacy comparable to standard antidepressants for mild to moderate depression with significantly fewer side effects. Hypericin and hyperforin are the primary active compounds. Inhibits reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. Antiviral properties — shown active against enveloped viruses. Topical use for wound healing and nerve pain. CRITICAL DRUG INTERACTIONS: induces CYP3A4 liver enzyme — reduces effectiveness of contraceptives, cyclosporine, HIV antivirals, warfarin, digoxin, and many other medications. Always consult a doctor before use with any medications.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.control: Blast with water. Natural predators usually manage.

pests.name: Chrysolina Beetle
pests.desc: Metallic green-gold beetle — a natural biocontrol agent used against invasive St. John's Wort in some regions.
pests.control: Not usually a problem in gardens. If population is large, hand-pick.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: photosensitization, skin lesions, nervous system effects
pet_toxicity.notes: Hypericin causes photosensitization — light-colored pets that ingest and are exposed to sunlight can develop skin lesions. Also causes nervous system effects. Keep away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Lovage

season.harvest_window: Early spring through fall. One of the first perennial herbs up in spring.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep with fresh seed — viability drops quickly. Cold stratify for 2–4 weeks for better germination.

germination.desc: Improved significantly with fresh seed and cold stratification.

seedling.desc: Grows steadily. Distinctive celery-like aroma from first leaves.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Can reach 3–4 feet in first year. One of the larger herbs.

adult.desc: Very large perennial — 5–7 feet tall when flowering. Yellow flowers on tall umbels. One plant is usually sufficient for most households.

care.water: Moderate to moist. More moisture-tolerant than Mediterranean herbs. Does not tolerate drought well.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Tolerates more shade than most herbs.
care.soil: Rich, moist, deep, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Deep soil for extensive root system.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring. Benefits from richer soil than most herbs.
care.notes: One plant is usually enough for a whole household — extremely productive. Cut flower stalks before they fully develop to extend leaf production.

container.notes: Grows 5–7 feet tall with extensive root system. In-ground only.

propagation.desc: Use fresh seed only. Cold stratify for best germination. Sow indoors or direct sow in fall.
Divide established clumps in spring or fall every 4–5 years.

harvest.when: Young leaves from early spring — one of the first harvests of the year. Harvest leaves and stems throughout the season before plant flowers.
harvest.how: Cut outer stems and leaves at the base. Cut flower stalks before they bloom to extend leaf season. Seeds harvested when turning from green to tan.
harvest.storage: Fresh leaves wilt quickly — use same day. Freeze leaves in bags for later use. Dry seeds in paper bag. Stems can be used like celery immediately — do not store well.
harvest.yield: One large established plant produces far more than most households can use. Extremely productive.

common_mistakes: Planting too many — one plant is genuinely sufficient for most households.
Using old seed — viability drops dramatically after 1 year. Use fresh seed only.
Not cutting flower stalks — allowing to flower reduces leaf quality. Cut scapes before flowering to extend leaf season.
Underestimating the size — lovage grows 5–7 feet tall. Plan accordingly.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Use fresh seed — viability drops quickly.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some umbels to dry on plant. Seeds turn from green to tan-brown.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry umbels into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place. Use within 1 year.
seed_saving.viability: 1 year — one of the shortest-lived herb seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Sow fresh seed immediately for best results. Sow in fall for spring germination.

good.why: Attracts beneficial insects and pollinators when flowering.
Large plant provides beneficial insect habitat. Root exudates said to stimulate surrounding plants.

culinary: Tastes exactly like strong celery — all parts are edible and used as a celery substitute. Leaves and stems used in soups, stews, salads, and stocks. Hollow stems used as drinking straws for Bloody Mary cocktails. Seeds used as a spice in breads, cheeses, and spice blends (similar to celery seed). Roots cooked as a vegetable. Young blanched shoots eaten like celery. Maggi seasoning sauce flavor is largely derived from lovage.
medicinal: Traditional diuretic and digestive aid. Butylidenephthalide in the root shown to have smooth muscle relaxant properties explaining its traditional use for digestive spasms and menstrual cramps. Anti-inflammatory. Expectorant for respiratory complaints. Root used traditionally for urinary tract infections. Antirheumatic. Caution: avoid during pregnancy — uterine stimulant. Avoid with kidney disease.

pests.name: Celery Leaf Miner
pests.desc: Winding tunnels in leaves — same pest as attacks celery (same plant family).
pests.control: Remove affected leaves. Row covers on young plants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset, possible photosensitization
pet_toxicity.notes: Like all Apiaceae (carrot family) members, lovage contains furanocoumarins that can cause photosensitization. Large amounts can cause GI issues. Incidental garden exposure unlikely to harm.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Allow space — grows 5-7 feet tall.

name: Marigold

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost — blooms continuously

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Large seeds easy to handle. Needs warmth — 65°F+.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable. One of the quickest flowers from seed.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly. Pinch tips at 4 inches for bushier plants.

young.desc: Flower buds appear early. Deadhead spent blooms to keep producing.

adult.desc: Blooms continuously until hard frost. Prolific and self-cleaning in most varieties.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates brief drought once established. Overwatering causes root rot and poor flowering.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. More sun = more flowers.
care.soil: Average, well-draining. pH 5.8–7.0. Not fussy — thrives in lean soil.
care.spacing: 6–18 inches depending on variety. French marigolds 6–8 inches, African 12–18 inches.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Too much nitrogen produces foliage at the expense of flowers.
care.notes: One of the most valuable companion plants in the vegetable garden. Root secretions repel nematodes. Deadhead regularly for continuous bloom.

container.min_size: 6-inch pot for French types. 10-inch for African types.
container.notes: Excellent container plant. Use lean mix — rich soil reduces flowering.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks early. Self-seeds moderately.
Stem cuttings root easily in water in 1–2 weeks. Useful for overwintering favorite colors.

harvest.when: Flowers harvested for arrangements when just opening. Deadhead spent blooms to extend season.
harvest.how: Pinch or cut flower stems just above a leaf node. Deadhead by removing entire spent flower head.
harvest.storage: Fresh cut flowers last 7–10 days in water. Dry flower heads for potpourri and seed saving.
harvest.yield: One plant produces hundreds of flowers over the season with regular deadheading.

common_mistakes: Over-fertilizing — produces lush green plants with very few flowers. Lean soil is better.
Not deadheading — spent flowers signal the plant to stop producing. Remove them regularly.
Overwatering — marigolds prefer to dry out slightly between waterings.
Planting in shade — they simply will not bloom well without full sun.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated French and African varieties breed true. Many hybrids will not.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow some flower heads to fully dry on the plant. Seeds inside the dried base of the flower head.
seed_saving.method: Pull seeds from dried flower heads by hand. Each petal base contains one seed.
seed_saving.drying: Dry harvested seeds on paper for 1 week.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: African and French marigolds cross-pollinate. Isolate by 500 feet for pure seed.

good.why: Root secretions repel root-knot nematodes. Flowers attract beneficial insects.
Deters aphids and other rose pests.
Repels squash bugs and cucumber beetles.
Broad-spectrum nematode suppression in soil. One of the most universally beneficial companions.

bad.why: Some evidence that marigolds inhibit bean growth when planted very close.

culinary: Petals of Tagetes tenuifolia (signet marigold) are edible — used as garnish and in salads. Standard garden marigolds are not typically eaten. Petals used as saffron substitute in some Eastern European cuisines.
medicinal: Anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds in the flowers. Not to be confused with Calendula officinalis (pot marigold) which has much stronger medicinal properties. Tagetes species used topically for insect bites and minor skin irritation in traditional medicine.

varieties.name: French Marigold (Tagetes patula)
varieties.description: Compact 6–12 inch plants. Most effective for nematode suppression. Best for tight spaces and container growing.
varieties.notes: Best companion plant of the two types.

varieties.name: African Marigold (Tagetes erecta)
varieties.description: Large 18–36 inch plants with big pompom flowers. More dramatic in the garden.
varieties.notes: Needs more space but more showy.

varieties.name: Signet Marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia)
varieties.description: Lacy foliage, tiny flowers, strongly lemon-scented. Edible flowers.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions. Stippled yellowing leaves.
pests.control: Neem oil. Increase humidity. Predatory mites.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Occasional — ironic given marigold's reputation as a pest repeller.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Ladybugs.

pests.name: Botrytis
pests.desc: Gray mold in wet conditions on spent flowers.
pests.control: Deadhead promptly. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: mild GI upset, drooling, skin irritation from sap contact
pet_toxicity.notes: Tagetes marigolds cause mild GI irritation and skin irritation from the sap. Not severely toxic. Do not confuse with Calendula (pot marigold) which has different properties.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Nasturtium

season.start_indoors: Not recommended — taproot sensitive. Direct sow is better.
season.direct_sow: 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost

seed.desc: Large seeds — nick the seed coat with sandpaper or soak 24 hours to improve germination. Sow 1 inch deep.

germination.desc: Reliable in warm soil. Large seedling pushes up quickly once started.

seedling.desc: Round distinctive leaves appear. Fast grower. Thin to proper spacing.

young.desc: Vining types begin to sprawl or climb. Bushy types mound up. First flower buds appear.

adult.desc: Covered in orange, yellow, and red flowers. All parts edible. Self-seeds freely.

care.water: Moderate. Tolerates drought well. Overwatering or rich soil produces lots of leaves with few flowers.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Tolerates more shade than most flowering annuals.
care.soil: Poor to average, well-draining. pH 6.0–8.0. Rich soil = foliage, no flowers. One of few plants that thrives in genuinely poor soil.
care.spacing: 10–12 inches for bushy types. 18–24 inches for trailing/vining types.
care.fertilizer: Never fertilize — this is one of the very few plants where fertilizing actively harms flowering.
care.notes: Two main types: bushy (mounding, good for containers) and trailing (vining, excellent as ground cover or to cascade from containers). Both edible entirely.

container.notes: Trailing types cascade beautifully from hanging baskets. Use lean mix without added fertilizer.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after last frost. Nick or soak seed coat first. Self-seeds prolifically — often returns year after year.

harvest.when: Flowers: when fully open. Leaves: any time. Seeds: when plump and green for pickling, or when tan and dry for next year.
harvest.how: Pinch flowers, leaves, and stems as needed. Harvest seeds before they fall.
harvest.storage: Flowers and leaves used fresh immediately. Green seeds pickled in vinegar — used as caper substitute. Dry seeds stored in paper envelope.
harvest.yield: Extremely productive. One plant provides continuous harvest of flowers and leaves all season.

common_mistakes: Fertilizing — the single most common mistake. Rich soil or added fertilizer produces lush all-green plants with no flowers.
Starting indoors — the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Always direct sow.
Expecting immediate flowers — takes 55+ days. Don't pull plants thinking they've failed.
Not eating them — most gardeners don't realize the entire plant is edible and delicious.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Self-seeds so prolifically it often establishes itself permanently.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect plump round seeds from the plant before they fall. They drop readily when ripe.
seed_saving.method: Pick seeds by hand when tan-green. Dry on paper.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.viability: 5–7 years — one of the longest-lived flower seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Allow some plants to self-seed for a permanent nasturtium patch.

good.why: Trap crop for aphids — aphids prefer nasturtium, keeping them off tomatoes.
Trap crop for aphids and cucumber beetles.
Repels squash bugs. Ground cover retains soil moisture.
Trap crop for cabbage aphids and whitefly.

bad.why: Nasturtium is universally beneficial as a trap crop and pollinator attractor.

culinary: One of the most edible ornamental plants — flowers, leaves, stems, and unripe seeds all eaten. Flowers have a peppery, slightly sweet flavor — excellent in salads, as garnish, and stuffed with cream cheese. Young leaves used like watercress in salads and sandwiches. Unripe green seeds pickled as caper substitute. Seed paste used as mustard substitute.
medicinal: High in vitamin C — historically used by sailors to prevent scurvy. Antimicrobial and antifungal compounds — traditionally used for urinary tract infections and respiratory infections. Glucosinolates broken down to isothiocyanates with antibiotic properties. Anti-inflammatory.

varieties.name: Alaska Mix
varieties.description: Variegated cream and green leaves. Compact bushy habit. Excellent for containers.
varieties.notes: Most ornamental foliage of all nasturtiums.

varieties.name: Empress of India
varieties.description: Deep scarlet flowers on dark blue-green foliage. Compact. Very striking.

varieties.name: Jewel Mix
varieties.description: Semi-trailing type in mixed warm colors. Most common garden nasturtium.
varieties.notes: Best all-rounder for both ornament and edibility.

varieties.name: Moonlight
varieties.description: Pale cream to yellow flowers on trailing vines. Unusual soft color.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Deliberately used as a trap crop — aphids prefer nasturtium to other plants. Large colonies are expected and useful.
pests.control: Leave colonies to draw aphids away from vegetables. If overwhelming, blast with water.

pests.name: Caterpillar
pests.control: Hand-pick. Bt spray if severe. Leave some damage — nasturtium is resilient.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: possible mild GI upset from the peppery compounds
pet_toxicity.notes: Nasturtium is non-toxic and the flowers and leaves are edible. Peppery taste naturally deters most pets from eating large amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow only — taproot. Plant 1/2 inch deep.
transplant.mulch: none (lean soil preferred, mulch traps moisture)

name: Zinnia

season.start_indoors: 4 weeks before last frost — brief start only
season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm (65°F+)
season.harvest_window: Early summer through frost

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Large flat seeds easy to handle. Need warmth — 70°F+ for fast germination.

germination.desc: Very fast in warm conditions. One of the quickest cut flowers from seed.

seedling.desc: Pinch growing tip when 6 inches tall to encourage multiple stems and more flowers.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Flower buds appear quickly. Heat-loving — grows faster as summer warms.

adult.desc: Non-stop bloomer. Cut flowers to encourage more. Extremely heat-tolerant — blooms when other flowers stop.

care.water: Moderate. Water at the base — overhead watering causes powdery mildew. Allow to dry slightly between waterings.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours minimum. Loves heat.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. pH 5.5–7.5. More tolerant of rich soil than nasturtium.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly. Moderate feeder.
care.notes: One of the top butterfly-attracting flowers. Monarch butterflies particularly attracted. Excellent cut flower — lasts 7–10 days in a vase.

container.min_size: 6-inch pot for dwarf varieties. 10-inch for standard.
container.notes: Compact and dwarf varieties best for containers. Need frequent deadheading in pots.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after last frost or start 4 weeks indoors. Do not start too early — dislikes being root-bound.

harvest.when: Cut when flower is fully open but before center turns yellow-brown. Test by holding stem 8 inches from head — if it droops, wait another day.
harvest.how: Cut stem at a 45° angle with sharp scissors. Cut long stems, just above a leaf node, to encourage branching.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water up to 10 days. Re-cut stems every 2–3 days. Keep out of direct sunlight indoors.
harvest.yield: One plant produces 20–50 flowers over the season with regular cutting.

common_mistakes: Starting too early indoors — zinnias grow so fast that starting more than 4 weeks early leads to root-bound stunted plants.
Overhead watering — causes powdery mildew that disfigures plants late in season. Always water at base.
Not cutting — plants that aren't cut for flowers or deadheaded slow down dramatically. Cut frequently.
Planting in shade or cool weather — zinnias are true heat lovers and simply will not perform in cool conditions.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties breed true. Many modern varieties are hybrids.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower heads to dry completely on the plant — center turns brown and dry.
seed_saving.method: Pull dry petals apart — long thin seeds attached to each petal base.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Zinnias cross-pollinate readily — isolate different colors by 300 feet for pure seed.

good.why: Attracts whitefly predators and beneficial wasps. Beautiful combination.
Attracts pollinators and beneficial insects at critical fruiting time.
Excellent pollinator attractor — particularly monarchs and swallowtails.

bad.why: Zinnias are universally beneficial as pollinator attractors.

culinary: Petals are technically edible — used as a garnish. No significant culinary tradition. Focus is on ornamental use.
medicinal: Traditional use in some cultures for digestive complaints and as a mild antiseptic. Not a significant medicinal plant in modern herbalism.

varieties.name: Benary's Giant
varieties.description: Large 4–6 inch flowers on tall 3–4 foot stems. Best for cut flowers. Heat and mildew resistant.
varieties.notes: The gold standard for cutting garden zinnias.

varieties.name: Profusion Series
varieties.description: Compact 12–18 inch plants covered in small flowers. Extremely disease resistant. Best for bedding.

varieties.name: Thumbelina
varieties.description: Dwarf 6–8 inch plants. Best for edging and containers.
varieties.notes: Ideal for small spaces and pots.

varieties.name: Envy
varieties.description: Unusual lime-green double flowers. Unique color in the garden.
varieties.notes: Excellent for arrangements — rare green flower.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White powdery coating on leaves — nearly universal late in season.
pests.control: Water at base only. Improve airflow. Remove severely affected plants. Choose resistant varieties like Profusion.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In hot dry conditions. Stippled yellowing leaves.
pests.control: Neem oil. Increase humidity. Predatory mites.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Zinnias are non-toxic to dogs and cats. Safe garden flower.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Don't start too early — transplant shock common.

name: Rose

season.start_indoors: Not applicable — plant bare-root or container roses
season.direct_sow: Plant bare-root roses in early spring. Container roses any time after last frost.
season.harvest_window: Flowers: late spring through fall depending on variety. Hips: after first frost.

seed.desc: Most roses are not grown from seed — plant bare-root or container specimens. Seeds require 4–16 weeks cold stratification and take 2–3 years to bloom.

germination.desc: If growing from seed: very slow and unreliable. Stratify seeds 4 months in damp mix in refrigerator.

seedling.desc: Seedlings grow very slowly. Most gardeners start with bare-root or container plants which establish in one season.

young.desc: First year: focus on root establishment. Light pruning only. May produce some flowers. Do not over-harvest.

adult.desc: Established roses bloom prolifically. Prune in early spring when forsythia blooms. Deadhead throughout season for reblooming varieties.

care.water: Deep watering 1–2 inches per week. Water at the base — wet foliage promotes black spot and powdery mildew. Drip irrigation ideal.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. 8 hours produces the healthiest plants with most flowers.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 6.0–6.5. Amend with compost generously before planting.
care.spacing: 18 inches to 6 feet depending on variety. Hybrid teas 24–36 inches. Shrub roses 4–6 feet.
care.fertilizer: Feed every 4–6 weeks during growing season with rose-specific or high-potassium fertilizer. Stop feeding 6 weeks before first frost.
care.notes: Choose disease-resistant varieties to minimize spray programs. Mulch 3–4 inches around base — keeps roots cool, retains moisture, reduces disease splash. Never plant a new rose where an old rose died — replant disease.

container.min_size: 15-gallon minimum for hybrid teas. Patio and miniature roses in 5–10 gallon.
container.notes: Miniature and patio roses bred specifically for containers. Water and feed more frequently than in-ground roses.

propagation.desc: Take 6-inch semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, plant in moist sand/perlite mix. Roots in 4–8 weeks.
Most economical way to buy roses. Plant in early spring before leafing out. Soak roots 12–24 hours before planting.
Commercial method of grafting a desired variety onto a vigorous rootstock. Not practical for home gardeners.

harvest.when: Flowers: in the cool of the morning when buds are just beginning to open (showing color but not fully open). Rose hips: after first frost when fully red and slightly soft.
harvest.how: Cut stems at 45° angle with clean sharp pruners, just above an outward-facing leaf with 5 leaflets. Remove thorns and lower leaves immediately. Rose hips: cut stem with scissors.
harvest.storage: Fresh cut roses in deep water for 6–12 hours before arranging. Last 7–14 days in water changed every 2 days. Rose hips dried on screens or used fresh for tea and preserves.
harvest.yield: Reblooming varieties produce flushes throughout the season. Once-blooming varieties have a single spectacular flush in late spring/early summer.

common_mistakes: Overhead watering — the primary cause of black spot and powdery mildew. Always water at base.
Planting too shallow or too deep — bud union (knobby graft point) should be at or just below soil level depending on climate.
Not pruning — unpruned roses become unproductive and disease-prone. Prune hard in early spring.
Choosing disease-prone varieties — old hybrid teas require heavy spray programs. Modern shrub roses and Knock Out types are nearly disease-free.

seed_saving.type: Species roses breed true from seed. Hybrid roses do not — seeds produce unpredictable offspring.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow hips to ripen fully after frost — fully red and slightly soft. Extract seeds from inside hip.
seed_saving.method: Cut hip open, extract seeds, clean off pulp. Cold stratify 4–16 weeks in damp mix in refrigerator before sowing.
seed_saving.storage: Stratify then sow. Do not store dry.
seed_saving.viability: Sow after stratification — viability drops quickly.
seed_saving.notes: Growing roses from seed is a 2–3 year process and produces variable results except with species roses.

good.why: Repels aphids and black spot. Classic cottage garden pairing.
Repels aphids, black spot fungus, and Japanese beetles. Plant bulbs around rose base.
Repels aphids. Allium scent confuses pests.
Deters nematodes and aphids. Attracts beneficial insects.
Repels aphids and Japanese beetles.
Attracts beneficial insects. Traditional rose companion.

bad.why: Compete for nutrients and can share fungal diseases.
Allelopathic to most plants including roses.

culinary: Rose petals edible — used in Middle Eastern (rose water, Turkish delight), Indian (gulkand), and European (rose hip jam, rose syrup) cuisines. Only use petals from unsprayed roses. Remove white heel at base of petal which is bitter. Rose hips extremely high in vitamin C — used in teas, jams, and syrups. Rose water used in baking and beverages globally.
medicinal: Rose hip tea one of the highest natural vitamin C sources — 20x more per weight than oranges. Anti-inflammatory galactolipid (GOPO) in rose hips shown to reduce osteoarthritis pain in clinical trials. Rose water anti-inflammatory topically. Petals used in aromatherapy for anxiety and depression. Traditional use for menstrual irregularity and digestive complaints.

varieties.name: Knock Out Series
varieties.description: Extremely disease-resistant shrub roses. Bloom continuously from spring to frost with almost no maintenance. Best for low-maintenance gardens.
varieties.notes: Virtually disease-free. The most popular rose in the US.

varieties.name: David Austin English Roses
varieties.description: Old-fashioned cupped, quartered, or rosette flowers with modern repeat-blooming. Rich fragrance. Wide range of colors.
varieties.notes: Best fragrance of modern roses. Some disease susceptibility depending on variety.

varieties.name: Hybrid Tea
varieties.description: Classic long-stemmed exhibition roses. Large single blooms on upright plants. Best for cutting.
varieties.notes: Requires more maintenance and spray program than modern shrub roses.

varieties.name: Climbing Rose
varieties.description: Long flexible canes trained to trellises, arbors, and fences. Some once-blooming, some repeat.
varieties.notes: Once-bloomers (like 'New Dawn') are extremely vigorous and cold-hardy.

varieties.name: Miniature Rose
varieties.description: Compact plants under 18 inches. All the features of larger roses in small scale. Excellent for containers.
varieties.notes: Often more disease-resistant than hybrid teas.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Clusters on buds and new growth. Ants farm them — control ants to control aphids.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Ladybugs. Plant garlic and chives nearby.

pests.name: Black Spot
pests.desc: Circular black spots on leaves causing defoliation. Most common and serious rose disease.
pests.control: Water at base only. Remove fallen leaves. Copper or sulfur fungicide. Choose resistant varieties.

pests.name: Japanese Beetle
pests.desc: Skeletonize petals and leaves. Metallic green and copper.
pests.control: Hand-pick in morning. Neem oil. Trap crops nearby (not directly adjacent).

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White powdery coating on new growth in humid conditions.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Baking soda spray. Remove affected growth. Resistant varieties.

pests.name: Rose Sawfly
pests.desc: Pale green caterpillar-like larvae skeletonize leaves from undersides.
pests.control: Hand-pick from undersides. Neem oil spray on undersides of leaves.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: puncture wounds from thorns, GI upset from rose hips in large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Rose petals, hips, and leaves are non-toxic. The thorns are a physical hazard. Rose hips in large quantities may cause GI upset. Roses treated with pesticides are dangerous — only allow pets near untreated roses.

transplant.deep_note: Bud union (grafting knob) at or just below soil level in cold climates, above soil in warm. Bare roots: crown 2 inches below in cold zones.
transplant.mulch: wood chips or bark (3-4 inches, away from canes)

name: Cosmos

season.start_indoors: Not recommended — direct sowing is faster and easier
season.direct_sow: After last frost. Can also sow in early fall in mild climates.
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost

seed.desc: Scatter seeds on surface and rake in lightly. Or sow ¼ inch deep. Very easy and forgiving.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable. Ferny foliage emerges first — very distinctive.

seedling.desc: Feathery lacy foliage grows quickly. Thin to 12 inches.

young.desc: Rapid tall growth. Pinch tips at 12 inches for branching and more flowers.

adult.desc: Tall airy plants covered in daisy-like flowers in pink, white, red, and bicolor. Self-seeds prolifically.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Overwatering or rich soil produces tall floppy plants with few flowers.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Poor to average, well-draining. pH 6.0–8.0. Like nasturtium, thrives in lean soil.
care.fertilizer: Never fertilize — produces rank leafy growth and few flowers in rich conditions.
care.notes: One of the easiest flowers to grow from seed. Self-seeds so readily it becomes permanent. Excellent for filling large areas quickly and cheaply.

container.min_size: 10-inch deep container for standard types. Dwarf varieties in smaller pots.
container.notes: Tall varieties may need staking. Dwarf varieties like 'Sonata' bred specifically for containers.

propagation.desc: Scatter directly after last frost. Self-seeds so readily it maintains itself year after year once established.

harvest.when: Cut when flower is just fully open or even in bud — it opens in the vase.
harvest.how: Cut long stems to just above a leaf node to encourage branching.
harvest.storage: 7–10 days in water. Change water every 2 days.
harvest.yield: Extremely prolific cut flower. One plant produces dozens of blooms over the season.

common_mistakes: Fertilizing — produces tall floppy plants with almost no flowers. Never feed cosmos.
Planting in rich soil — same result as fertilizing. They genuinely thrive in poor, lean soil.
Starting indoors — direct sowing is faster and produces better plants due to taproot.
Not pinching — pinching the growing tip at 12 inches dramatically increases flower production.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Self-seeds prolifically. Long thin seeds.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds form after petals fall. Harvest when seeds are dry and brown on the plant.
seed_saving.method: Shake or strip dry seed heads into a paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so freely that deliberate saving is usually unnecessary.

good.why: Attracts beneficial insects including parasitic wasps that prey on tomato pests.
Excellent beneficial insect habitat. Attracts predatory wasps, hoverflies, and bees.

bad.why: Cosmos is universally beneficial for attracting beneficial insects.

culinary: Petals technically edible but no significant culinary tradition. Occasional use as a colorful garnish.
medicinal: Traditional use in some cultures for fever and malaria (Cosmos sulphureus). C. bipinnatus used in some Mexican traditional medicine. Not a significant medicinal plant in modern herbalism.

varieties.name: Sensation Mix
varieties.description: Classic tall 3–4 foot plants in mixed pink, white, and carmine. The standard garden cosmos.
varieties.notes: Best for back of border and cutting garden.

varieties.name: Sonata Mix
varieties.description: Compact 18–24 inch plants. Same flower colors. Best for smaller gardens and containers.

varieties.name: Chocolate Cosmos (C. atrosanguineus)
varieties.description: Deep maroon-brown flowers with genuine chocolate scent. Perennial in zones 7+.
varieties.notes: A different species. Truly smells of chocolate — extraordinary.

varieties.name: Xanthos
varieties.description: Pale yellow flowers — unusual color for cosmos. Compact plants.
varieties.notes: First yellow cosmos variety. Very different look.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.control: Blast with water. Natural predators usually manage — cosmos attracts them.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.desc: Cause distorted petals and silvery streaking.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Cosmos is non-toxic to dogs and cats. Safe garden flower.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow or transplant at nursery pot depth.

name: Black-Eyed Susan

season.direct_sow: Early spring — cold stratification by frost helps germination
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through fall — long bloom period

seed.desc: Surface sow — needs light. Cold stratify for 4 weeks or direct sow in early spring to let frost do the stratifying naturally.

germination.desc: Improved by cold stratification. Variable without it.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly initially. Hairy leaves characteristic from early stage.

young.desc: Flower stems emerge from rosette. First year plants sometimes don't bloom if started late.

adult.desc: Golden-yellow daisy flowers with prominent dark brown center cone. Blooms for months. Self-seeds and spreads to form colonies.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. One of the most drought-resistant native flowers.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Tolerates partial shade but fewer flowers.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Tolerates clay soil better than most flowers.
care.fertilizer: None needed. Fertilizing produces weak floppy stems.
care.notes: North American native — excellent for wildlife gardens and low-maintenance landscapes. Leave seed heads standing in winter for bird food. Self-seeds to form beautiful naturalized colonies.

container.notes: Better in the ground — spreads naturally and is more impactful in mass plantings.

propagation.desc: Cold stratify first. Direct sow in fall or early spring. Self-seeds reliably.
Divide established clumps in spring or fall every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

harvest.when: Cut flowers when petals are fully open but before center cone softens.
harvest.how: Cut long stems at 45°. Condition in water for 12 hours before arranging.
harvest.storage: 7–10 days in water as cut flower.
harvest.yield: One established plant produces dozens of flowers over the season.

common_mistakes: Not cold stratifying seed — germination is much better with cold treatment.
Removing seed heads — birds rely on the seeds through winter. Leave them standing.
Planting in rich soil or fertilizing — produces weak floppy stems that require staking.
Treating as a true perennial — R. hirta is a short-lived perennial that self-seeds to maintain itself. Don't expect the original plant to live more than 2–3 years.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Breeds true. Self-seeds prolifically.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed heads to dry completely on the plant. Seeds inside the cone.
seed_saving.method: Rub dried cone between palms over a bowl. Small dark seeds fall out.
seed_saving.drying: Dry cones in paper bag 2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds to maintain a permanent colony. Birds will spread seeds for you.

good.why: Both native prairie plants with complementary bloom times. Create a long-season pollinator garden.
Similar drought tolerance. Complementary colors — yellow and purple.
Attracts beneficial insects including native bees and parasitic wasps.

bad.why: Native plant — generally beneficial to garden ecology.

culinary: Not a culinary plant. Seeds occasionally eaten by humans but not a food tradition.
medicinal: Traditional Native American medicine used root tea for worms and colds, leaf poultice for snakebite and sores. Contains immunostimulant compounds similar to Echinacea (same family). Used in some herbal preparations for immune support. Primarily an ecological and ornamental plant in modern use.

varieties.name: Indian Summer
varieties.description: Extra-large 6-inch flowers. AAS winner. Very showy.

varieties.name: Prairie Sun
varieties.description: Golden-yellow flowers with green center — no dark eye. Very different look. Sterile so blooms longer.
varieties.notes: Unique among rudbeckias for the golden center.

varieties.name: Cherry Brandy
varieties.description: Unusual copper-orange-burgundy flowers. Very different from typical yellow.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves late in season.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Usually not serious enough to treat.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.control: Blast with water. Natural predators manage.

pests.name: Septoria Leaf Spot
pests.control: Remove affected leaves. Avoid overhead watering.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: mild GI upset if large amounts consumed
pet_toxicity.notes: Generally considered non-toxic. May cause mild GI upset if eaten in large quantities due to the aromatic compounds.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Develops a taproot — transplant when small.

name: Dahlia
growing_zones: 8–11 perennial. 2–11 as annual with tuber storage.

season.start_indoors: Start tubers indoors in pots 4–6 weeks before last frost to get earlier blooms
season.transplant: Plant tubers after last frost when soil is warm
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost — blooms best in late summer and fall

seed.desc: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep, eye (growth point) facing up. Do not water until shoots emerge — tubers rot if kept wet in cold soil.

germination.desc: Shoots emerge from tuber. Do not water until you see growth above soil.

seedling.desc: Rapid growth once started. Stake immediately — stems become top-heavy. Pinch tip when 12 inches tall for more flowers.

young.desc: Bushy growth with large lush leaves. Flower buds appear. Disbudding (removing side buds) creates larger single blooms.

adult.desc: Spectacular blooms in an enormous range of forms and colors. Best performance in warm weather — peak bloom late summer to frost.

care.water: Consistent deep watering — 1–2 inches per week once growing. Do not water until shoots emerge from tubers.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 6.0–7.0. Heavy feeder.
care.spacing: 12–36 inches depending on variety. Dinnerplate dahlias need 36 inches.
care.fertilizer: Low nitrogen (causes leafy growth over flowers), high phosphorus and potassium. Feed every 3–4 weeks once blooming.
care.notes: Tubers must be dug and stored before frost in zones below 8. Dig after light frost kills tops, dry 24 hours, pack in peat or sawdust at 40–50°F.

container.min_size: 5-gallon for dwarf types. 15-gallon for dinner-plate types.
container.notes: Patio dahlias bred specifically for containers. Compact 12–18 inch plants with proportionate flowers.

propagation.desc: Divide tubers in spring — each division must have at least one eye (growth bud) attached to the neck. Divisions without an eye will not grow.
Take 3–4 inch cuttings from shoots emerging from tubers in spring. Root in moist mix in 3 weeks. Exact clones of parent.
Only for dahlia species and some bedding dahlias. Named varieties are vegetatively propagated.

harvest.when: Cut in the cool of morning or evening when flower is fully open. Dahlias do not open further after cutting.
harvest.how: Cut long stems at 45° angle with clean sharp pruners. Remove all leaves below waterline. Immediately place in deep cold water.
harvest.storage: Condition in cold water for 12 hours. Lasts 5–8 days in vase. Change water every 2 days. Keep in cool location.
harvest.yield: One tuber produces 10–30+ flowers over the season depending on variety and disbudding practice.

common_mistakes: Watering tubers before shoots emerge — tubers planted in cool wet soil rot before growing. Wait for green shoots.
Not staking early — dahlia stems snap in wind. Stake at planting time before stems emerge.
High nitrogen fertilizer — produces massive plants with few flowers. Use low nitrogen, high potassium formula.
Leaving tubers in ground below zone 8 — they are frost-tender and will die. Must be dug and stored.

seed_saving.type: Named varieties must be propagated vegetatively (tubers or cuttings). Seed produces highly variable offspring.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed heads to ripen after petals fall. Seeds inside the dried flower head.
seed_saving.method: Pull apart dried heads to extract seeds.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Growing dahlias from seed produces exciting unknowns — good for breeding new varieties.

good.why: Deters nematodes. Complementary warm colors.
Both prefer lean soil. Complementary textures.

bad.why: Dahlias generally get along well with most plants.

culinary: Tubers of some dahlia species edible — similar flavor and texture to water chestnuts. Not commonly eaten in modern Western cuisine. Dahlia tubers were considered a food source in Mexico before they became ornamental plants. Petals edible and used as garnish.
medicinal: Traditional Aztec medicinal plant — used for epilepsy and other conditions. Contains inulin (a prebiotic fiber) in tubers. Not a significant modern medicinal plant.

varieties.name: Dinner Plate Dahlia
varieties.description: Enormous blooms 8–12 inches across. Require staking and disbudding. Most spectacular garden dahlia.
varieties.notes: The showiest flowers in the garden. Require the most work.

varieties.name: Ball Dahlia
varieties.description: Perfectly round double flowers 2–4 inches. Very formal and symmetrical. Excellent for cutting.

varieties.name: Cactus Dahlia
varieties.description: Pointed quilled petals giving a spiky appearance. Very different texture from other dahlias.

varieties.name: Pom Pom Dahlia
varieties.description: Small perfectly round globe flowers under 2 inches. Extremely prolific.
varieties.notes: Best for repeated cutting — most flowers per plant.

varieties.name: Bishop of Llandaff
varieties.description: Stunning dark bronze-black foliage with vivid red peony-form flowers. Classic cottage garden variety.
varieties.notes: The most striking foliage of any dahlia.

pests.name: Earwig
pests.desc: Chew ragged holes in petals overnight.
pests.control: Trap in rolled newspaper. Hand-pick at night. Diatomaceous earth.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Clusters on buds and growing tips.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves late in season.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: mild vomiting, diarrhea, skin irritation
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists dahlias as toxic to dogs and cats. Causes mild to moderate GI upset and skin irritation. Tubers stored indoors in fall are a particular risk. Keep pets away.

transplant.deep_note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep, eye facing up. Do NOT water until shoots emerge — tubers rot in cold wet soil.

name: Monstera (Swiss Cheese Plant)

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage. Fruit possible indoors on mature plants given enough light.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagate from stem cuttings.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in water or moist mix in 3–5 weeks.

seedling.desc: New growth from cuttings emerges slowly.

young.desc: First few leaves are solid with no splits. Fenestrations (splits and holes) develop as the plant matures.

adult.desc: The iconic large split-leaf tropical. The splits and holes (fenestrations) are adaptations to allow wind to pass through without damaging the leaf in its native rainforest habitat. One of the most popular houseplants worldwide. Provide a moss pole for larger leaves. In ideal conditions outdoors, produces edible fruit (Monstera deliciosa — the 'fruit salad plant').

care.water: Allow top 1–2 inches to dry between waterings. Consistent moisture but never waterlogged.
care.light: Medium to bright indirect light. Direct sun burns the leaves. Very low light causes slow growth with no fenestrations (splits).
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix amended with perlite. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Provide a moss pole or trellis for climbing — this produces much larger, more fenestrated leaves.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly during spring and summer.
care.notes: Monstera develops larger, more deeply fenestrated leaves when given: bright indirect light, a moss pole to climb, and appropriate pot size (not too large). Yellow leaves = overwatering. Brown leaf tips = low humidity or dry air. Aerial roots are normal — tuck them into a moss pole or let them hang. Wipe large leaves monthly.

container.notes: Large floor containers with moss poles allow the most dramatic growth.

propagation.desc: Cut below a node that includes an aerial root. Place in water. Roots in 3–5 weeks. One of the most satisfying propagations — you can watch the roots develop.
Dip in rooting hormone. Insert in moist mix. Cover with plastic bag for humidity. Roots in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: The fruit (Monstera deliciosa) takes 12+ months to ripen and must be fully ripe to eat — unripe fruit contains calcium oxalate crystals.
harvest.how: Harvest when the green scales begin to separate and the fruit smells intensely tropical.
harvest.storage: Allow to ripen at room temperature. Refrigerate after ripening.
harvest.yield: Fruit production requires mature plants (5+ years) and significant light.

common_mistakes: No moss pole — leaves stay small and few fenestrations develop without climbing support.
Overwatering — yellowing leaves with wet soil.
Too little light — solid small leaves with no splits. Move to brighter location.
Low humidity causing brown edges — mist regularly or use a humidifier.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by stem cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Stem cuttings in water.
seed_saving.notes: Water propagation is one of the most satisfying and visual houseplant propagations.

good.why: Similar care and tropical aesthetic.
Both easy-care tropical vines.

bad.why: Monstera needs more moisture and humidity.

culinary: Unripe fruit severely toxic. Fully ripe Monstera deliciosa fruit edible — tastes of pineapple, banana, and vanilla mixed. One of the most unusual edible tropical fruits. Requires 12+ months to ripen after flowering.
medicinal: Traditional Mexican use of the roots for arthritis. Not in modern Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — especially unripe fruit; calcium oxalate crystals
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Oral irritation, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists Monstera as toxic. Calcium oxalate crystals cause significant oral pain. Unripe fruit is more toxic. Keep pets away from all plant parts.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 1–2 years in spring when rootbound. Go up one pot size. Add a moss pole at transplanting — much easier than adding one later.

varieties.name: Monstera deliciosa (standard)
varieties.description: Classic large split leaves. The iconic houseplant.

varieties.name: Monstera adansonii (Swiss Cheese Vine)
varieties.description: Smaller leaves with more holes than splits. More compact and trailing.
varieties.notes: Best for smaller spaces. Excellent in hanging baskets.

varieties.name: Variegata (Thai Constellation/Albo)
varieties.description: White or cream variegated leaves. Extraordinarily expensive and highly sought after.
varieties.notes: Most valuable and rarest. Requires more light for variegation.

varieties.name: Monstera Peru
varieties.description: No fenestrations — thick, deeply textured rugose leaves. Very unusual.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown waxy bumps on stems and leaf undersides.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton. Horticultural oil.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.control: Increase humidity. Wipe leaves. Neem oil.

name: Bok Choy

season.direct_sow: 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring. Late summer for fall crop.
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Bolts rapidly in summer heat.

seed.desc: Sow ¼ inch deep. Very cold tolerant — germinates at 45°F. Fast and reliable.

germination.desc: One of the fastest vegetable germinators. Even in cool soil.

seedling.desc: Thin to proper spacing. Grows rapidly in cool weather. Watch for flea beetles.

young.desc: Leaves and stems develop the characteristic texture. Begin harvesting outer leaves or baby bok choy plants.

adult.desc: Full heads form. Harvest before warm weather causes bolting. Fall-planted bok choy is often superior — cooler temps = sweeter, crunchier stems.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1 inch per week. Drought or irregular watering triggers premature bolting.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More shade-tolerant than most brassicas.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. Benefits from high nitrogen.
care.spacing: 6 inches for baby bok choy. 12 inches for full-sized plants.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen for leafy growth. Side-dress with nitrogen every 3 weeks.
care.notes: One of the fastest cool-season vegetables. Excellent succession crop — sow every 2–3 weeks. Baby bok choy (harvested at 4 weeks) is a specialty market crop.

container.notes: Excellent container vegetable. Grow baby bok choy in window boxes. Water consistently — containers dry out fast.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or start indoors briefly. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest.

harvest.when: Baby bok choy: 4 weeks at 4–6 inches tall. Full size: 45–60 days when heads are firm but before bolting.
harvest.how: Baby: cut entire plant at soil level. Full size: cut at base or harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again. Once flower stalk appears, cut entire plant immediately.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed for 1 week. Very perishable once cut. Blanch and freeze for longer storage.
harvest.yield: Very productive. Succession sowing gives continuous supply.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer heat — bolts within days above 75°F. Spring and fall only.
Not succession sowing — a single planting bolts all at once. Sow new seeds every 2–3 weeks.
Ignoring flea beetles on seedlings — can devastate young plants quickly. Row covers on transplants.
Not harvesting promptly — once the central flower stalk begins to appear, harvest immediately or lose the plant.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Crosses freely with other Brassica rapa — turnip, napa cabbage, mizuna.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow plants to bolt and flower. Harvest seed pods when tan and dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dried pods over bucket. Small round seeds.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with turnip, napa cabbage, and other B. rapa plants. Isolate by 1 mile for pure seed.

good.why: Attracts parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage caterpillars.
Deters cabbage worms and nematodes.
Repels cabbage moths with allium scent.
Trap crop for aphids and cabbage white butterflies.

bad.why: Brassicas and tomatoes inhibit each other.

culinary: Staple vegetable in Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Southeast Asian cuisines. Stir-fried with garlic (the most common preparation), added to soups (pho, ramen, wonton soup), steamed, braised, and eaten raw in salads. The white stems and green leaves have different textures — stems need more cooking time. Baby bok choy is more tender and milder. Napa cabbage (also B. rapa) is a close relative used similarly.
medicinal: High in vitamins C, K, and A. Glucosinolates break down to sulforaphane and indole-3-carbinol — anticancer compounds shared with broccoli and kale. Calcium and magnesium for bone health. Anti-inflammatory. Antioxidant flavonoids. One of the most nutritious brassicas calorie-for-calorie.

varieties.name: Shanghai Green
varieties.description: The most common variety. Light green stems, dark green leaves. Mild flavor. Standard supermarket bok choy.

varieties.name: Baby Bok Choy
varieties.description: Harvested young at 4–6 inches. More tender and milder. Popular in restaurants.
varieties.notes: Harvest entire plant — grows many per packet.

varieties.name: Choy Sum
varieties.description: Related plant with edible flowering shoots. The flowering stem and buds are the prized part.
varieties.notes: Different plant from bok choy but closely related and prepared the same way.

varieties.name: Toy Choy
varieties.description: Miniature variety — stays small even at maturity. Ideal for containers and small gardens.

pests.name: Flea Beetle
pests.desc: Tiny black beetles create shothole pattern on leaves — especially devastating on seedlings.
pests.control: Row covers on transplants. Diatomaceous earth. Neem oil. Protect until plants are established.

pests.name: Imported Cabbageworm
pests.desc: Pale green caterpillar from cabbage white butterfly.
pests.control: Bt spray. Row covers. Hand-pick eggs and larvae.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cabbage aphids in gray-green colonies on leaves and growing tip.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Clubroot
pests.desc: Swollen distorted roots from soil-borne pathogen.
pests.control: Raise soil pH. Long crop rotation. Resistant varieties.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset in large quantities
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Like all brassicas, large quantities can cause GI irritation.

transplant.deep_note: Shallow planting — crown at soil level.

name: Brazilian Pepper (Dedo de Moça)

season.start_indoors: 10–12 weeks before last frost — longer season needed
season.transplant: After last frost when soil is thoroughly warm
season.harvest_window: Late summer through frost. Perennial in frost-free zones.

seed.desc: Plant ¼ inch deep. Capsicum baccatum needs higher germination temps than annuum — 80–85°F. Bottom heat mat essential.

germination.desc: Slower than C. annuum. Keep consistently warm. Patience required — worth the wait.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Requires long warm season — start early. Bright light critical.

young.desc: Distinctive white flowers with green/yellow spots — characteristic of C. baccatum. More branching than annuum peppers.

adult.desc: Prolific fruiting. Long thin peppers in clusters. In zones 10+, plant overwinters and becomes a woody shrub producing for years.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Slightly more drought tolerant than bell pepper once established.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–6.8.
care.spacing: 24–36 inches. Plants become large and bushy, especially in warm climates.
care.fertilizer: Balanced at planting. Low nitrogen once flowering. High potassium promotes fruiting.
care.notes: In frost-free climates this plant becomes a woody perennial shrub lasting many years and producing thousands of peppers. Prune hard in winter to rejuvenate.

container.notes: Good container plant in cooler climates — bring indoors to overwinter as a perennial. Can last years in a large container.

propagation.desc: Start 10–12 weeks before last frost with bottom heat. Longer head start needed than C. annuum.
Take 4–6 inch stem cuttings before frost. Root in moist mix. Overwinter indoors. This is the standard method in Brazil for keeping prized plants.

harvest.when: Green: 90 days. Red (fully ripe): 30+ additional days. Red fruit is sweeter, more complex, and has higher capsaicin.
harvest.how: Cut with scissors leaving short stem. Never pull — damages plant.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 2 weeks. Dry whole (hanging clusters traditional in Brazil). Pickle. Make hot sauce. Freeze.
harvest.yield: Extremely productive once established. A single mature plant can produce hundreds of peppers per season.

common_mistakes: Not starting early enough — needs 10–12 weeks indoors, not the standard 8.
Cold soil at transplant — even more cold-sensitive than annuum peppers. Wait for truly warm soil.
Pulling out in fall — in zones 9+ bring indoors or mulch heavily. This plant is a perennial worth saving.
Harvesting only green — red ripe baccatum peppers have dramatically superior flavor.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. C. baccatum does not cross with C. annuum — safe to grow near jalapeños.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow peppers to fully redden and begin to wrinkle on plant.
seed_saving.method: Scrape seeds from ripe fruit. Wear gloves — hot varieties.
seed_saving.drying: Dry on glass or ceramic surface 1–2 weeks.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: One of the few Capsicum species that does NOT cross with standard garden peppers — excellent for seed savers.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites.
Deters nematodes and soil pests.
Loosens soil around pepper roots.

culinary: The defining pepper of Brazilian cuisine. 'Dedo de moça' means 'lady finger' — named for the long elegant fruit shape. Used fresh in vinaigrette (the ubiquitous Brazilian table condiment), in moqueca (fish stew), with farofa, and in countless regional dishes. Moderate heat (5,000–15,000 SHU) with a fruity, citrusy flavor characteristic of C. baccatum species. The pepper is served whole in restaurants so diners can squeeze juice onto food. Essential in malagueta sauce.
medicinal: Capsaicin content provides the same benefits as other hot peppers — pain relief, metabolism boost, cardiovascular support. The fruity flavor compounds in C. baccatum (distinctive from other species) are currently studied for their unique antioxidant profile. Traditional Brazilian use for digestion and circulation.

varieties.name: Dedo de Moça (Classic)
varieties.description: The traditional Brazilian variety. Long thin bright red pepper, 4–5 inches. Fruity heat, 5,000–15,000 SHU. The definitive Brazilian table pepper.
varieties.notes: What Brazilians mean when they say 'pimenta'. Iconic.

varieties.name: Aji Amarillo
varieties.description: Peruvian C. baccatum. Orange-yellow when ripe. Fruity, raisin-like flavor with substantial heat (30,000–50,000 SHU). The defining pepper of Peruvian cuisine.
varieties.notes: Indispensable in Peruvian cooking — used in ceviche, aji de gallina, and causa.

varieties.name: Aji Limon
varieties.description: Bright yellow, lemon-shaped. Strong citrus flavor with heat. Beautiful in the garden and on the plate.
varieties.notes: The most citrusy Capsicum variety available.

varieties.name: Bishop Crown (Joker's Hat)
varieties.description: Unusual flattened shape resembling a bishop's crown. Mild to medium heat. Distinctive and beautiful — often grown ornamentally.
varieties.notes: One of the most visually distinctive peppers. Often used stuffed.

varieties.name: Aji Crystal
varieties.description: Large, pale yellow-cream when ripe. Very mild baccatum — 5,000 SHU or less. Fruity flavor with minimal heat. Excellent for those wanting baccatum flavor without intense heat.
varieties.notes: The mild baccatum — all the flavor, little heat.

varieties.name: Malagueta
varieties.description: The most famous Brazilian pepper after dedo de moça. Small (1–2 inch), extremely hot (60,000–100,000 SHU). Used in the traditional malagueta pepper sauce that accompanies every Brazilian dish.
varieties.notes: Actually C. frutescens, not baccatum — but the defining Brazilian hot pepper alongside dedo de moça.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: oral and GI irritation from high capsaicin content
pet_toxicity.notes: High capsaicin content. Not classically toxic but causes significant discomfort. Malagueta variety is extremely hot — strong deterrent naturally.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Habanero Pepper

season.transplant: After last frost when soil is warm — very heat-loving
season.harvest_window: Late summer through frost

seed.desc: Plant ¼ inch deep at 80–85°F. C. chinense is the slowest Capsicum species to germinate. Bottom heat essential.

germination.desc: Notoriously slow. Keep consistently warm at 80°F+. Germination can take up to 4 weeks even with perfect conditions.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly. Needs full sun and warmth. Much slower than annuum peppers.

young.desc: White flowers appear. Self-pollinating but heat and humidity can cause blossom drop. Long time to first fruit.

adult.desc: Lantern-shaped fruit develops. Color changes from green through orange to red depending on variety. Heat at this stage is intense.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Drought stress increases capsaicin but reduces yield.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours. Needs more heat than most peppers.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–6.8.
care.fertilizer: Balanced at planting. Low nitrogen once flowering.
care.notes: One of the hottest commercially available peppers (100,000–350,000 SHU). Handle with extreme care — wear gloves. Do not touch eyes.

container.notes: Good container plant. Bring indoors before frost — can overwinter and be more productive in year two.

propagation.desc: Start 10–12 weeks before last frost with bottom heat at 80°F+.
Root stem cuttings before frost to overwinter the plant.

harvest.when: When fully colored — orange or red depending on variety. Do not harvest green except in emergencies.
harvest.how: Cut with scissors. WEAR GLOVES. Avoid touching face.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 2 weeks. Freeze whole. Dry. Make hot sauce.
harvest.yield: 20–50 peppers per plant in a long warm season.

common_mistakes: Not starting early enough — needs 10–12 weeks. One of the longest-season vegetables.
Insufficient heat — habaneros need hot summers. In cool climates use black plastic mulch and cloches.
Handling without gloves — capsaicin causes intense and long-lasting burning on skin and eyes.
Harvesting green — habaneros are dramatically hotter and more flavorful when fully ripe to orange or red.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. C. chinense crosses with other chinense varieties (scotch bonnet, ghost pepper) but NOT with C. annuum.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow to fully ripen and soften slightly.
seed_saving.method: Scrape seeds wearing gloves. Rinse well. Dry on glass.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Does not cross with jalapeños or bell peppers — safe to grow near them.

good.why: Repels aphids and spider mites.
Deters nematodes.

culinary: The backbone of Caribbean, Yucatecan, and West African cuisines. Essential in Belizean habanero sauce, Yucatecan salsa roja, and jerk seasoning. Fruity, floral flavor beneath the extreme heat — distinctive among hot peppers for its aroma. Used in hot sauces, salsas, marinades, and curries. Pairs with tropical fruits — mango habanero is a classic combination.
medicinal: Among the highest capsaicin content of commonly grown peppers (100,000–350,000 SHU). All the cardiovascular, analgesic, and metabolic benefits of capsaicin in concentrated form. Used in high-potency topical pain relief products.

varieties.name: Orange Habanero
varieties.description: The standard habanero. Bright orange when ripe, wrinkled lantern shape. 100,000–350,000 SHU.
varieties.notes: The classic. What most people mean by 'habanero'.

varieties.name: Red Savina
varieties.description: Selectively bred for extreme heat — held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper. 350,000–577,000 SHU. Deep red.
varieties.notes: One of the hottest habanero varieties. Intense fruit flavor beneath the heat.

varieties.name: Chocolate Habanero (Congo Black)
varieties.description: Deep brown-chocolate ripe color. Smoky, earthy flavor with intense heat. 300,000+ SHU.
varieties.notes: More complex flavor than orange habanero. Used in mole and complex sauces.

varieties.name: White Habanero
varieties.description: Pale ivory-white when ripe. Slightly milder than orange. Clean fruity flavor without smokiness.

varieties.name: Peach Habanero
varieties.description: Soft peach-salmon color when ripe. Slightly sweeter fruit flavor. Similar heat to standard habanero.
varieties.notes: Most attractive habanero for ornamental growing.

varieties.name: Scotch Bonnet
varieties.description: Same species as habanero but different shape — flattened bonnet shape. Essential in Jamaican cuisine and jerk seasoning. Similar heat.
varieties.notes: Scotch bonnet and habanero share similar heat but different flavor profiles.

pests.name: Blossom Drop
pests.desc: Flowers fall without setting fruit — heat or cold stress.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: severe oral burning, vomiting, diarrhea from extreme capsaicin
pet_toxicity.notes: Extremely high capsaicin. Not toxic but causes intense discomfort. Pets typically self-deter.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

name: Asparagus

season.harvest_window: Year 3 onward — spring spear emergence

seed.desc: Plant 1-year-old crowns (not seed) 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench 18 inches wide. Crown spikes facing up.

germination.desc: Spears emerge in spring. Do NOT harvest in year 1 or 2 — let fern develop to feed crown.

seedling.desc: Ferny foliage develops through summer. Feeds the underground crown. Leave completely alone.

young.desc: Year 2: resist harvesting. Small light harvest only at end of year 2 season if plants look vigorous.

adult.desc: Year 3+: harvest spears for 4–6 weeks in spring. Stop when spears thin below pencil thickness. Let fern grow for rest of year.

care.water: Consistent moisture during establishment. Drought-tolerant once established. Deep watering encourages deep root system.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours. Asparagus needs sun to produce well.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining, sandy loam. pH 6.5–7.5. Prepare bed deeply — asparagus will be here 20+ years.
care.spacing: 18 inches between crowns. 5 feet between rows.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen in spring after harvest. Balanced in fall. Top-dress with compost annually.
care.notes: Asparagus is a 20-year investment. Prepare the bed extremely well before planting. All-male hybrid varieties (Jersey Knight, Jersey Giant) produce more spears.

container.min_size: Not practical — deep roots and perennial habit.
container.notes: Asparagus needs permanent in-ground planting.

propagation.desc: Purchase 1-year-old crowns from reputable supplier. Plant in spring. Seeds take 3 years to produce usable crowns.

harvest.when: Year 3: when spears are 6–9 inches tall with tight tips.
