harvest.how: Snap or cut at soil level. Stop when spears become thin (under pencil thickness).
harvest.storage: Refrigerate upright in 1 inch of water for 3–5 days. Blanch and freeze for long-term storage.
harvest.yield: 1–2 lbs per plant per year from established beds. A family of 4 needs 25–50 crowns.

common_mistakes: Harvesting in year 1 or 2 — weakens crowns for life. Be patient.
Cutting fern after harvest — the fern feeds next year's crop. Let it grow all season.
Poor soil preparation — asparagus occupies the same ground for 20 years. Prepare deeply with compost.
Choosing female plants — all-male hybrids produce 3x more spears.

seed_saving.type: Dioecious — separate male (no berries) and female (red berries) plants.
seed_saving.harvest: Red berries on female plants contain seeds.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from red berries. Cold stratify 6 weeks before sowing.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Buying 1-year crowns is far more practical than growing from seed.

good.why: Classic companion — asparagus beetle repelled by tomatoes. Parsley near asparagus improves both.
Traditional companion that improves asparagus vigor.
Repels asparagus beetle.

bad.why: Same soil depth — compete for resources.

culinary: Eaten steamed, roasted, grilled, in risotto, pasta, soups, stir-fries. White asparagus (blanched by mounding soil) is prized in European cuisine. Green asparagus more common in North America. Pairs with hollandaise, eggs, prosciutto, parmesan, and lemon. Brief cooking preserves flavor and nutrition.
medicinal: Rich in folate — critical for fetal neural tube development. High in vitamin K. Asparagine is a natural diuretic — causes the distinctive urine odor in those who carry the detection gene. Prebiotic inulin feeds beneficial gut bacteria. Anti-inflammatory. Glutathione — a powerful antioxidant.

pests.name: Asparagus Beetle
pests.desc: Blue-black beetle and gray larvae eat spears and fern. Most serious asparagus pest.
pests.control: Hand-pick adults and egg clusters. Neem oil. Plant tomatoes and basil nearby as deterrents.

pests.name: Rust
pests.desc: Orange powdery pustules on fern. Weakens crowns over time.
pests.control: Resistant varieties. Remove infected material. Copper fungicide.

varieties.name: Jersey Knight
varieties.description: All-male hybrid. High yield. Disease resistant. Widely adapted.
varieties.notes: Best all-around asparagus for most gardens.

varieties.name: Purple Passion
varieties.description: Purple spears sweeter and more tender than green. Turns green when cooked.
varieties.notes: Eat raw to preserve color and sweetness.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset from the plant itself in large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Garden asparagus spears are safe. The ornamental 'asparagus fern' (a different plant sold in shops) IS toxic. Raw asparagus can cause GI upset — cooked is easier to digest.

transplant.deep_note: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in a prepared trench. Crown spikes face up. This deep planting is essential for 20-year establishment.

name: Celery

season.start_indoors: 10–12 weeks before last frost — one of the earliest starts
season.direct_sow: Not practical — very long growing season
season.transplant: 2–3 weeks before last frost — tolerates light frost
season.harvest_window: Late summer through fall

seed.desc: Surface sow — tiny seeds need light. Soak overnight. Keep at 70°F. Notoriously slow and challenging germinator.

germination.desc: Very slow. Keep moist and warm consistently. One of the most difficult vegetables to germinate reliably.

seedling.desc: Grows very slowly. Needs consistent moisture. Celery seedlings are fragile and sensitive to drying out.

young.desc: Growth accelerates in cool weather. Begin blanching if desired — wrap stems with paper or cardboard to exclude light for milder flavor.

adult.desc: Harvest outer stalks first as needed. Full head harvest when stalks are thick and firm.

care.water: Extremely consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week minimum. Never let soil dry out. Drip irrigation ideal. Celery is 95% water and needs constant supply.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining, high organic matter. pH 6.0–7.0. Heavily amended with compost.
care.fertilizer: Heavy feeder. High nitrogen throughout. Side-dress every 3 weeks with balanced fertilizer.
care.notes: One of the most demanding vegetables to grow well. Needs consistently cool, moist conditions. Much easier to grow as a fall crop.

container.notes: Possible in containers but requires extremely consistent watering — containers dry out fast and celery cannot tolerate drought.

propagation.desc: Surface sow 10–12 weeks before transplant. Soak seeds overnight. Keep consistently moist at 70°F. Expect patchy germination.

harvest.when: When stalks are 12–18 inches tall and firm. Outer stalks harvestable from about 85 days.
harvest.how: Cut outer stalks at base leaving center to continue growing. Or cut entire plant at soil level.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate wrapped in foil for 2–3 weeks. Freezes well when chopped for cooking.
harvest.yield: One plant provides several weeks of harvest of outer stalks.

common_mistakes: Inconsistent watering — causes hollow, pithy stalks and bitterness.
Starting too late — needs 10–12 weeks before last frost, not the standard 6–8.
Planting in summer heat — celery prefers cool conditions. Best as a fall crop.
Expecting easy germination — celery is one of the hardest vegetables from seed.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — must overwinter to flower. Open-pollinated varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow plants to overwinter and flower in year 2. Harvest seed heads when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dried seed heads in paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.viability: 5–8 years — one of the longest-lived vegetable seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other celery and celeriac. Isolate by ½ mile.

good.why: Traditional companion — both benefit from each other.
Attracts beneficial insects.
Traditional companion pairing.

bad.why: Same family — attracts same pests. Keep somewhat separated.

culinary: Celery stalks eaten raw as crudités, in salads, soups, stocks (the holy trinity of French cooking with onion and carrot), stews, stir-fries, and Waldorf salad. Seeds used as a spice. Celery salt is a classic condiment. All parts used — stalk, leaves (more intense flavor), and seeds. Essential in Bloody Mary.
medicinal: Phthalides lower blood pressure by relaxing arterial muscles (clinically studied). Anti-inflammatory. High in vitamin K. Apigenin — a potent anti-inflammatory and potentially anticancer flavonoid. Traditional use as a diuretic. Celery seeds shown to reduce uric acid — traditional gout remedy.

pests.name: Celery Leaf Miner
pests.desc: Winding tunnels in leaves from fly larvae.
pests.control: Remove affected leaves. Row covers on young plants.

pests.name: Early Blight
pests.desc: Brown spots on leaves with yellow halos.

varieties.name: Utah 52-70 R Improved
varieties.description: The classic supermarket celery type. Tall green stalks, reliable producer.
varieties.notes: Most widely grown celery variety in North America.

varieties.name: Giant Red
varieties.description: Red-tinged stalks with excellent flavor. More ornamental than green types.
varieties.notes: Beautiful in the garden and at the table.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs and cats. Cut into small pieces for dogs to prevent choking. High water content — good low-calorie treat.

transplant.deep_note: Plant slightly deeper than nursery pot. Blanch by hilling soil up around stems as they grow.

name: Fennel

season.direct_sow: After last frost for fall bulb harvest. Or early spring for foliage herb.
season.harvest_window: Fall (bulb fennel). Year-round (herb fennel).

seed.desc: Sow directly ¼ inch deep. Germinates best in cool to moderate soil. Two types: bulb fennel (grown for swollen base) and herb fennel (grown for leaves and seeds).

germination.desc: Reliable in moderately warm soil. Fine feathery shoots emerge.

seedling.desc: Feathery anise-scented foliage develops quickly. Thin to proper spacing.

young.desc: For bulb fennel: the base swells at soil level. Hill soil around the base when it reaches golf ball size to blanch and sweeten.

adult.desc: Bulb ready when tennis ball sized. Harvest before flower stalk forms. Herb fennel: harvest fronds any time, flowers and seeds when mature.

care.water: Consistent moisture — especially important for bulb development. Drought causes premature bolting.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.spacing: 12 inches for bulb fennel. 18 inches for herb fennel.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer. Avoid excess nitrogen for bulb types.
care.notes: WARNING: fennel is allelopathic to most vegetables and herbs — it inhibits growth of tomatoes, peppers, beans, and most herbs. Grow in isolation or in a dedicated fennel bed.

container.min_size: 12-inch deep for herb fennel. 15-inch for bulb fennel.
container.notes: Herb fennel works well in containers. Bulb fennel needs deeper soil for bulb development.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only — taproot dislikes transplanting. Succession sow every 3 weeks for bulb fennel.

harvest.when: Bulb: when swollen base is 3–4 inches across, before flower stalk appears. Herb: fronds any time. Seeds: when dry and brown on plant.
harvest.how: Cut bulb at soil level leaving fronds. Fronds: snip as needed. Seeds: shake dry umbels into paper bag.
harvest.storage: Bulb refrigerates 1–2 weeks. Fronds wilt quickly — use same day or freeze. Seeds in airtight jar for years.
harvest.yield: One plant produces one bulb. Herb types produce abundant fronds all season.

common_mistakes: Planting near other vegetables — fennel allelopathic chemicals inhibit nearly everything nearby.
Harvesting bulb after bolting — bolt causes woody texture and bitter flavor. Harvest before any flower stalk appears.
Confusing with dill — similar appearance but very different flavor. Cannot substitute for each other.
Growing bulb fennel in spring — bolts too quickly in long days. Fall crop is far superior.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Crosses readily with other fennel varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow plants to flower and set seed in year 2 (herb types) or let bolt (bulb types). Harvest seed heads when brown.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry umbels into paper bag.
seed_saving.storage: Airtight jar — fennel seeds are also a culinary spice.
seed_saving.notes: Do not plant near dill — they cross-pollinate and both lose flavor integrity.

good.why: Fennel is broadly allelopathic. Best grown in isolation or with other fennel plants.

bad.why: Cross-pollinate and ruin each other's seed quality.
Same family — shares pests and diseases.

culinary: All parts edible — bulb, fronds, flowers, seeds, and pollen. Bulb eaten raw (salads, slaws), braised, roasted, and grilled. Fronds used as herb with fish, seafood, and salads. Seeds used as spice in Italian sausage, bread, and spice blends. Fennel pollen is a gourmet spice. Essential in Italian cuisine. Pairs with fish, pork, citrus, and apple.
medicinal: Anethole — fennel's primary essential oil — is antispasmodic (relieves digestive cramps), expectorant (loosens mucus), and mildly estrogenic. Traditional digestive remedy — fennel tea relieves bloating, gas, and colic. European Medicines Agency approves fennel preparations for digestive complaints and coughs. Antimicrobial. Mild galactagogue (promotes breast milk production).

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Green or black aphids on flowers and new growth.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Natural predators — fennel flowers attract beneficial insects.

pests.name: Parsleyworm
pests.control: Leave them — they become swallowtail butterflies. Plant extra fennel to share.

varieties.name: Florence Fennel (Finocchio)
varieties.description: The bulb-forming type. Large swollen base, mild anise flavor. The culinary fennel of Italian cooking.
varieties.notes: Grow this for the bulb. Sow in late summer for fall harvest.

varieties.name: Bronze Fennel
varieties.description: Stunning bronze-purple feathery foliage. Grown as an herb and ornamental. No significant bulb.
varieties.notes: Most beautiful fennel. Excellent in flower borders.

varieties.name: Sweet Fennel
varieties.description: Herb type with green foliage. Grown for leaves and seeds. More vigorous than Florence fennel.
varieties.notes: Best for seed saving and herbal use.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: none in moderate amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for dogs. Fennel is sometimes used medicinally for dogs to ease digestion. Cats generally tolerate it well.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Direct sow preferred — taproot dislikes transplanting.

name: Sweet Pea

season.direct_sow: As early as soil can be worked — 6 weeks before last frost. Fall sow in mild climates.
season.transplant: Early spring — very cold hardy seedlings
season.harvest_window: Spring through early summer. Stops in heat.

seed.desc: Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak 24 hours — hard seed coat inhibits germination. Sow 1 inch deep. Prefers cool soil.

germination.desc: Reliable after seed coat scarification. Cool soil preferred (55–65°F).

seedling.desc: Pinch growing tip when 4 inches tall to encourage branching and more flowering stems.

young.desc: Climbs rapidly with tendrils. Provide support from seedling stage. Feed regularly.

adult.desc: Covered in intensely fragrant flowers. Cut frequently — stopping seed set is essential for continuous bloom. Stops producing in summer heat.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Never let dry out — causes bud drop. Mulch to keep roots cool.
care.light: Full sun in cool climates. Afternoon shade in warm climates to extend season.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 7.0–7.5. Add lime if soil is acidic.
care.spacing: 6 inches. Provide support — wire, trellis, netting, or twiggy branches.
care.fertilizer: High potassium feed every 2 weeks once growing. Avoid high nitrogen — all leaves, few flowers.
care.notes: Sweet peas are for fragrance — arguably the best scent of any garden flower. Pick flowers every 2–3 days to prevent seed set which stops blooming. They hate heat — plant early.

container.notes: Good in containers with adequate support. Keep roots cool with mulch or double-potting.

propagation.desc: Nick seed coat with sandpaper, soak 24 hours, then sow. Direct sow or start indoors.

harvest.when: When lowest flower on the stem has just fully opened.
harvest.how: Cut long stems with scissors — taking stems encourages more. Never leave dead flowers on the plant.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water — lasts 5–7 days. The fragrance fills a room.
harvest.yield: Prolific cut flower when picked regularly. One planting produces for 6–8 weeks.

common_mistakes: Not scarifying seeds — very hard seed coat inhibits germination. Always nick or soak.
Not picking regularly — seed set stops blooming completely within days.
Planting too late — sweet peas hate heat. Early planting is everything.
Not pinching — unpinched plants produce one stem with few flowers.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated heirlooms breed true. Modern varieties often crosses.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow pods to dry completely on plant. Pods turn tan and papery. Seeds rattle.
seed_saving.method: Shell dried pods.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Do not eat sweet pea seeds — mildly toxic. Not the same as edible garden peas.

good.why: Sweet peas fix nitrogen (legume) and their height provides wind protection.
Sweet peas provide light shade for lettuce as temperatures warm.

bad.why: Sweet peas are generally beneficial — nitrogen-fixing legumes.

culinary: NOT edible — sweet pea seeds are mildly toxic. Do not confuse with edible garden peas.
medicinal: Not medicinal. Mildly toxic if ingested in quantity. For ornamental and fragrance use only.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Common on growing tips and flower buds. Can be heavy in spring.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Ladybugs.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating late in season when heat arrives.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Usually indicates end of season has arrived.

varieties.name: Spencer Mix
varieties.description: Large ruffled flowers in mixed colors. The classic sweet pea. Excellent fragrance.

varieties.name: Old Spice Mix
varieties.description: Heirloom varieties with stronger fragrance than modern types. Smaller flowers.
varieties.notes: Best fragrance of all sweet peas — what gardeners mean when they say 'old-fashioned sweet peas'.

varieties.name: Cupani
varieties.description: The original wild sweet pea from Sicily. Bicolor purple and maroon. Extraordinary fragrance. Oldest named variety (1699).
varieties.notes: The fragrance benchmark. All modern sweet peas descend from this variety.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — especially seeds — aminopropionitrile, beta-aminopropionitrile
pet_toxicity.symptoms: weakness, lethargy, tremors, paralysis, seizures (lathyrism)
pet_toxicity.notes: Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are seriously toxic — can cause lathyrism, a neurological condition causing paralysis. Seeds are the most dangerous part. Do NOT confuse with edible garden peas (Pisum sativum). Keep strictly away from all pets and children.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep. Transplants possible when very small — handle gently.

name: Peony

season.start_indoors: Not applicable — plant bare roots or divisions
season.transplant: Fall (September–October) is ideal. Spring also works but first bloom delayed.
season.harvest_window: Late spring — brief but spectacular 1–3 week bloom period.

seed.desc: Plant bare-root divisions with 3–5 eyes (red buds) facing up, 1–2 inches below soil surface. Deeper planting is the #1 reason peonies fail to bloom.

germination.desc: Red shoots emerge in spring. Do not be alarmed — peonies emerge late and grow fast.

seedling.desc: Year 1: modest growth, possibly no flowers. Do not fertilize heavily. Establish the root system.

young.desc: Year 2: fuller growth, possibly some flowers. Stake flower buds — heavy blooms require support.

adult.desc: Year 3+: full bloom. Peonies improve every year and live 50–100 years in one spot. Do not move them.

care.water: Moderate. Drought tolerant once established. Good drainage is critical — crown rot in wet soil.
care.light: Full sun to light shade. Full sun produces the most flowers. At least 6 hours.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.5–7.0. Excellent drainage essential — wet crown causes rot.
care.spacing: 3–4 feet. Peonies are long-term — give them permanent space.
care.fertilizer: Low nitrogen. High potassium and phosphorus for bloom. Top-dress with compost in fall.
care.notes: Plant at correct depth — 1–2 inches below soil surface in cold climates. Too deep = no bloom. Do not move established plants. Cut foliage to ground in fall to prevent disease overwintering.

container.min_size: Not suitable — deeply rooted perennial needing permanent location.
container.notes: Peonies are long-lived perennials that resent disturbance. Not suitable for containers.

propagation.desc: Divide in fall when dormant. Each division needs 3–5 eyes (red buds). Replant immediately at correct depth.
Extremely slow — takes 3–5 years to first bloom. Not practical for most gardeners.

harvest.when: For cutting: when buds show color but are still in the 'marshmallow' stage — soft but not yet opening.
harvest.how: Cut long stems in the morning. Remove leaves below waterline.
harvest.storage: Fresh in cool water for 7–10 days. Harvest in bud stage and refrigerate dry in bags for up to 6 weeks for later arrangements.
harvest.yield: 3–7 stems per plant depending on age and variety. Increases annually.

common_mistakes: Planting too deep — the most common reason peonies fail to bloom. Maximum 2 inches below soil.
Moving established plants — peonies resent disturbance and may not bloom for 3 years after moving.
Removing foliage before it yellows — the foliage feeds next year's blooms. Leave until frost.
Not staking — heavy double blooms collapse in rain without support.

seed_saving.type: Blooms true to species but hybrids produce variable seedlings.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow pods to ripen after bloom — football-shaped pods split to reveal shiny seeds.
seed_saving.method: Collect seeds when pods split. Cold stratify (3 months warm, 3 months cold) before sowing.
seed_saving.drying: Sow fresh — do not allow to dry out completely.
seed_saving.storage: Stratify in damp perlite in refrigerator.
seed_saving.notes: Peony from seed is a 3–5 year project to first bloom. Division is far more practical.

good.why: Ornamental alliums bloom at same time as peonies — beautiful combination.
Fills gaps between peonies after bloom with long-season color.
Complementary bloom time. Classic cottage garden combination.

bad.why: Peonies are generally not allelopathic. Main concern is competition for space.

culinary: Petals edible and used in Chinese cuisine — crystallized as sweets, used in teas, and as garnish. Not commonly eaten in Western cuisine.
medicinal: Paeoniflorin — peony root's active compound — is anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antispasmodic. Used in Traditional Chinese Medicine for 2,000+ years for menstrual pain, muscle cramps, arthritis, and fever. Clinically studied for rheumatoid arthritis — positive results in reducing inflammation. Root preparations used extensively in East Asian medicine.

pests.name: Botrytis Blight
pests.desc: Gray mold on stems and buds in wet cool conditions. Most serious peony disease.
pests.control: Improve airflow. Remove infected material immediately. Copper or sulfur fungicide. Cut foliage to ground in fall.

pests.name: Ants
pests.desc: Ants on peony buds are common and harmless — they feed on nectar and do not harm the plant.
pests.control: No treatment needed. Shake blooms before bringing indoors.

varieties.name: Sarah Bernhardt
varieties.description: Classic pink double peony. Outstanding fragrance. One of the most popular peonies for over 100 years.

varieties.name: Karl Rosenfield
varieties.description: Deep crimson-red double. Strong stems that don't need staking. Excellent cut flower.
varieties.notes: Best red peony for cutting gardens.

varieties.name: Bowl of Beauty
varieties.description: Japanese form — single ring of pink petals surrounding a cream center. Unusual and elegant.
varieties.notes: Most distinctive peony form. Less common than doubles.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, depression
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists peonies as toxic to dogs and cats. Primarily causes GI upset. Not severely toxic but should be kept away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: CRITICAL: eyes (red buds) must be 1-2 inches below soil level — NO DEEPER. Planting too deep is the #1 reason peonies fail to bloom.

name: Strawberry

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root plants in early spring
season.harvest_window: June-bearing: 2–3 week intense harvest in June. Everbearing: smaller crops spring and fall. Day-neutral: continuous spring through fall.

seed.desc: Purchase bare root plants — bareroot 'crowns' from nurseries are the standard. Remove all flowers in the first year to build a strong root system. The temptation to harvest first-year fruit is significant, but removing flowers dramatically improves long-term productivity.

germination.desc: If growing from seed (not typical): cold stratify 4 weeks. Germination unreliable.

seedling.desc: First year: allow runners to establish daughter plants but remove all flowers.

young.desc: Runners create daughter plants. Allow 2–4 runners per plant to root, then cut remaining runners.

adult.desc: Full production in year 2+. A strawberry bed is most productive in years 2–4, then declines. Renovate or replant every 3–4 years by dividing runners into a new bed.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture and keep fruit off soil.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 5.5–6.5.
care.spacing: 12–18 inches for matted row. 8–10 inches for hill system.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer before planting. Light nitrogen after harvest. Avoid excess nitrogen — promotes leaves over fruit.
care.notes: Mulch is essential — straw mulch under plants keeps fruit clean and prevents disease. The traditional name 'straw-berry' refers to the straw mulch historically used. Net or use bird scare devices — birds and slugs are the primary pest. Everbearing and day-neutral varieties are more productive per plant; June-bearing varieties produce the largest single crop.

container.min_size: Strawberry pots or any 8+ inch container.
container.notes: Outstanding container plant. Hanging baskets, window boxes, strawberry towers, raised beds. Day-neutral varieties best for containers.

propagation.desc: Allow runners to root into soil or small pots of soil placed nearby. Sever from mother plant when rooted. Free unlimited plants.

harvest.when: Fully red (or white for pineapple varieties), slightly soft, and fragrant. Twist and pull gently.
harvest.how: Twist and pull with the calyx attached. Handle gently.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed up to 5 days. Freeze well. Jam and preserves.
harvest.yield: 1 quart per plant per season (June-bearing). Less but more spread out for everbearing.

common_mistakes: Not removing flowers year 1 — hurts long-term productivity
No mulch — fruit rots on soil
Birds and slugs — net and use iron phosphate bait
Not renovating — beds decline after year 4

seed_saving.type: Propagated by runners — free and unlimited.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Allow runners to root.
seed_saving.notes: Runner propagation is so easy there is no reason to save seed.

good.why: Deters pests, attracts pollinators, companion planting tradition.
Repels slugs and worms.
Good space-sharing ground cover companion.
Deters aphids.

culinary: Fresh eating — unrivaled when vine-ripened. Strawberry jam — the most beloved preserve. Strawberry shortcake. Strawberry daiquiri. Chocolate-dipped strawberries. Strawberry vinegar. Dried strawberries. The flavor difference between garden-fresh and store-bought is extraordinary.
medicinal: Very high in vitamin C. Ellagic acid with anticarcinogenic properties. Fisetin — a flavonoid being studied for senolytic properties (clearing senescent cells) and longevity effects. Traditional use for whitening teeth and treating skin conditions.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — strawberries are safe for pets.
pet_toxicity.notes: Strawberries are completely safe for pets. One of the pet-friendliest fruits.

transplant.deep_note: The crown (base of the leaves) must be exactly at soil level. Too deep: crown rot. Too shallow: roots dry out. This is the most important planting detail for strawberries.
transplant.mulch: straw (traditional — keeps fruit clean and prevents disease)

varieties.name: Jewel
varieties.description: June-bearing. Very large, very sweet berries. The most widely planted commercial and home variety in the Northeast.
varieties.notes: Best June-bearing for flavor and size.

varieties.name: Seascape
varieties.description: Day-neutral. Excellent flavor. Reliable production from spring through fall.

varieties.name: Ozark Beauty
varieties.description: Everbearing heirloom. Very sweet. Reliable in many climates.

varieties.name: Albion
varieties.description: Day-neutral. Excellent disease resistance. Large firm berries.

varieties.name: Pineapple (White)
varieties.description: White berries with pineapple-vanilla flavor. Birds don't recognize them as ripe — pest protection built in.
varieties.notes: Most unusual flavor. Natural bird resistance.

pests.name: Birds
pests.desc: The primary problem — take ripe fruit immediately.
pests.control: Bird netting from when fruit begins to color.

pests.name: Slugs
pests.control: Iron phosphate bait (Sluggo). Straw mulch reduces slug habitat.

pests.name: Botrytis (Gray Mold)
pests.desc: Ripe fruit rots rapidly in wet conditions.
pests.control: Good air circulation, avoid overhead watering, harvest frequently.

pests.name: Spotted Wing Drosophila
pests.desc: Tiny fly lays eggs in ripe fruit.

name: Mandevilla
growing_zones: 9–11 perennial. 2–11 as annual or container plant.

season.start_indoors: Start from nursery transplant — not typically grown from seed
season.transplant: After last frost when nights stay above 50°F
season.harvest_window: Blooms continuously from late spring through frost

seed.desc: Mandevilla is purchased as a nursery transplant. Seeds rarely available and very slow. Purchase established plants for same-season blooms.

germination.desc: If starting from seed (rare): sow ¼ inch deep at 75–80°F. Germination slow and unreliable. Cuttings are far more practical.

seedling.desc: Young plants establish quickly in warm conditions. Provide trellis support from the start — vines reach for support immediately.

young.desc: Rapid vining growth begins. Large trumpet-shaped buds form. Pinch growing tips to encourage branching and more flowers.

adult.desc: Covered in large 3–5 inch trumpet flowers in pink, red, white, or bicolor. Blooms continuously without deadheading. Can reach 10–20 feet in one season.

care.water: Consistent moisture during the growing season — 1–2 inches per week. Allow top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Reduce significantly in winter if overwintering indoors. Overwatering is the most common cause of yellowing leaves.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. More sun = more blooms. Will survive in partial shade but flowering is dramatically reduced.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Must drain freely — sitting in wet soil causes root rot rapidly.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches between plants. Provide trellis, arbor, or fence — vines will climb 10–20 feet in one season.
care.fertilizer: High phosphorus (bloom-booster) fertilizer every 2–3 weeks during the growing season. Phosphorus promotes flower production. Stop feeding in fall when bringing indoors.
care.notes: Mandevilla produces milky sap when cut — wash hands after pruning. Wear gloves if latex-sensitive. Overwintering: before first frost, bring container indoors to a bright sunny window or greenhouse. Cut back by 1/3, reduce watering dramatically, and keep at 55°F+. Resume feeding and watering in spring.

container.min_size: 12–15 gallon for best results. Smaller containers are possible but limit root growth and bloom count.
container.notes: Container growing is the standard practice in cold climates — allows overwintering indoors. Use a trellis insert or grow on a patio obelisk. Terracotta warms faster than plastic, beneficial for heat-loving mandevilla.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch tip cuttings in spring or summer. Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, place in moist perlite/sand mix. Root in 4–6 weeks in warm conditions (70°F+). Wear gloves — sap causes skin irritation.
Most practical method — purchase established plants in spring after last frost. Immediately available blooms.

harvest.when: Flowers do not need deadheading — spent blooms drop cleanly. Cut stems for arrangements when flowers are fully open.
harvest.how: Cut stems with clean scissors. Wash hands after — milky sap is a skin irritant. Condition cut stems in water for 2–4 hours before arranging.
harvest.storage: Cut flowers last 5–7 days in water. Not primarily a cut flower — best enjoyed on the plant.
harvest.yield: One established plant produces hundreds of flowers over the season. Continuous bloomer without deadheading.

common_mistakes: Planting outdoors before nights are reliably above 50°F — mandevilla is cold-sensitive and will drop leaves and stop blooming if chilled.
Overwatering — the most common killer. Allow soil to partially dry between waterings.
Too little light — in shade it grows but rarely blooms. Full sun is essential for flowering.
Not overwintering — in cold climates many gardeners throw away container plants each fall. Bring indoors and they can live for many years.
Touching eyes after handling cut stems — the milky latex sap is a skin and eye irritant. Always wash hands after pruning.

seed_saving.type: Rarely sets seed in cultivation. Propagate vegetatively from cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: Seed pods occasionally form — long thin pods splitting to reveal silky-plumed seeds like milkweed.
seed_saving.method: Collect pods before they split. Dry seeds from pappus before storing.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope in cool dark place.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings are infinitely more reliable. Named varieties do not breed true from seed.

good.why: Cascading foliage complements mandevilla's upright vining habit in containers. Both love heat.
Same heat and sun requirements. Different texture at the base of a trellis planting.
Both tropical, both love full sun, both attract hummingbirds and butterflies.

bad.why: Mandevilla's heat and sun requirements are incompatible with cool-season plants like pansies or violas.

culinary: Not edible. The milky latex sap is toxic if ingested.
medicinal: Not used medicinally. The sap contains compounds that can cause skin irritation and is toxic if consumed. Traditional use in some South American cultures has been documented but not standardized.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, possible heart effects in large amounts
pet_toxicity.notes: Mandevilla contains compounds similar to other members of the Apocynaceae (dogbane) family. ASPCA lists mandevilla as toxic to dogs and cats. The sap is the most concentrated source. Keep out of reach of all pets. If ingestion is suspected contact a veterinarian immediately.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at the same depth as the nursery container. Do not bury the crown. Ensure excellent drainage at the bottom of the planting hole.
transplant.mulch: none or light gravel (container) / straw (in-ground in warm zones)

varieties.name: Sun Parasol Series
varieties.description: The most widely sold mandevilla series. Large 4–5 inch flowers in deep pink, crimson, white, and bicolor. Compact to large vine options. Extremely free-blooming.
varieties.notes: Best all-around mandevilla for containers. Most readily available at garden centers.

varieties.name: Alice du Pont
varieties.description: Classic large-flowered pink mandevilla. Can reach 20 feet. Rich pink with yellow throat. The original and still beloved.
varieties.notes: Best for large trellises and arbors where size is welcome.

varieties.name: Dipladenia (Bush Mandevilla)
varieties.description: Compact shrubby form rather than vining. Stays 12–18 inches tall. Perfect for pots without a trellis. Same flowers as vining types.
varieties.notes: Best for small containers and window boxes where a vine would be too large.

varieties.name: White Delight
varieties.description: Pure white large trumpet flowers with yellow center. Striking against dark foliage. Less common than pink varieties.
varieties.notes: Most dramatic evening display — white flowers glow at dusk.

varieties.name: Red Riding Hood
varieties.description: Deep crimson-red flowers. More compact growth than Alice du Pont. Very striking color.
varieties.notes: Best red mandevilla — most intense color of all varieties.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: Most common pest — especially indoors during overwintering. Fine webbing, stippled pale leaves.
pests.control: Wipe leaves with damp cloth. Neem oil spray. Increase humidity. Quarantine affected plants indoors.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown or white bumps on stems. Suck plant sap — weaken plant over time.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab. Neem oil. Systemic insecticide for severe infestations.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Clouds of tiny white insects on undersides of leaves.
pests.control: Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil. Insecticidal soap.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.desc: Overwatering causes rapid root rot — plant collapses suddenly.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Allow soil to dry more. Remove from pot, trim rotted roots, repot in fresh mix.

name: Bougainvillea
growing_zones: 9–11 perennial. 4–11 as container plant overwintered indoors.

season.start_indoors: Purchase nursery plant — not practical from seed
season.transplant: After last frost when nights stay above 55°F
season.harvest_window: Blooms on new wood — multiple flushes spring through fall in warm climates

seed.desc: Purchase established nursery transplant. Seeds are rarely available and extremely slow. All garden bougainvilleas are nursery-grown from cuttings.

germination.desc: If growing from cutting: 4–6 inch semi-hardwood cuttings root in 4–6 weeks in warm, humid conditions with rooting hormone.

seedling.desc: Young plants establish quickly. Do not overwater — bougainvillea prefers to dry slightly between waterings. Provide full sun from the start.

young.desc: Growth accelerates in heat. Stress the plant slightly by restricting water to trigger bloom. Feeding with high-phosphorus fertilizer promotes flowering.

adult.desc: Covered in brilliant papery bracts (the showy 'flowers' are actually modified leaves called bracts). Blooms prolifically when stressed. Can reach 20–30 feet on a structure.

care.water: Allow soil to dry between waterings — drought stress triggers blooming. Overwatering causes green lush growth with few flowers. One deep watering per week in summer. Almost none in winter.
care.light: Full sun — minimum 6 hours, 8+ preferred. More sun = more blooms. Will not bloom adequately in shade.
care.soil: Well-draining, slightly acidic to neutral. pH 5.5–6.5. Must not sit in wet soil.
care.spacing: Allow 6–8 feet spread for large varieties. Container: 15+ gallon pot minimum.
care.fertilizer: High phosphorus (bloom booster) every 3–4 weeks during growing season. Avoid high nitrogen — promotes foliage at expense of blooms.
care.notes: The colourful 'petals' are bracts (modified leaves), not true flowers — the tiny white tubes in the center are the actual flowers. Thorns are sharp — wear gloves. Blooms most prolifically when slightly stressed. To trigger blooming: withhold water for 3–4 weeks, then resume. Extremely cold sensitive.

container.notes: Excellent container plant for northern gardeners. Overwinter indoors in a cool, bright location. Cut back by 1/3 before bringing in. Allow to go semi-dormant. Resume watering and feeding in spring.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch cuttings from non-blooming stems in summer. Dip in rooting hormone, insert in perlite/sand mix. Keep warm and humid. Roots in 4–6 weeks.

harvest.when: Cut bract stems when color is fully developed.
harvest.how: Cut with sharp scissors. The bracts last 1–2 weeks in arrangements.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water. Bracts dry beautifully — hang upside down in a warm dry place.
harvest.yield: Hundreds of bract clusters per plant per season.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the most common error. Soggy roots kill bougainvillea quickly and prevent blooming.
Too much nitrogen fertilizer — lush green growth but no blooms. Use bloom booster only.
Not enough sun — 6+ hours minimum. Shaded plants rarely bloom.
Planting outdoors before nights are warm — cold shock causes severe setback.
Repotting too frequently — bougainvillea blooms better when slightly root-bound.

seed_saving.type: Rarely sets viable seed in cultivation.
seed_saving.harvest: Occasionally produces small dry fruits after flowering.
seed_saving.method: Extract seeds, sow at 70°F+ with high humidity.
seed_saving.notes: Propagate by cuttings — seeds not practical.

good.why: Both tropical, both love full sun and heat, both attract butterflies.
Similar care requirements. Beautiful combined in large containers.

bad.why: Bougainvillea's heat requirements incompatible with cool-season plants.

culinary: Not edible. Bracts and sap can cause skin irritation.
medicinal: Traditional medicinal use in Brazil and Mexico for respiratory conditions and blood sugar regulation. Bract extracts show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties in preliminary research. Not used in conventional medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, skin and oral irritation from sap contact. Thorns cause physical injury.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists bougainvillea as mildly toxic. The sap causes irritation. Physical injury from sharp thorns is the greater risk for pets. Keep pets away from the plant.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Handle the root ball gently — bougainvillea resents root disturbance and will drop leaves and bracts after transplanting. Do not loosen roots when transplanting.

varieties.name: Barbara Karst
varieties.description: The most popular bougainvillea. Brilliant magenta-red bracts. Very free-flowering and vigorous. Best for warm climates.

varieties.name: San Diego Red
varieties.description: Deep crimson-red bracts. More compact than Barbara Karst. Excellent for containers.

varieties.name: New River
varieties.description: Deep purple bracts. Large flowers. Very vigorous grower.

varieties.name: Raspberry Ice
varieties.description: Variegated cream and green leaves with raspberry-pink bracts. Compact. Very ornamental.

varieties.name: White Stripe
varieties.description: Pure white bracts — elegant and unusual. Less vigorous than colored varieties.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Cluster on new growth and flower buds.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Insecticidal soap.

pests.name: Scale
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab. Neem oil.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: Fine webbing especially indoors in dry conditions.
pests.control: Increase humidity. Neem oil. Wipe leaves with damp cloth.

name: Tropical Hibiscus
plant_type: Perennial shrub (zones 9–12) / Annual or container plant

season.transplant: After last frost, when nights above 55°F
season.harvest_window: Blooms daily throughout the warm season — each flower lasts one day but new ones open constantly

seed.desc: Purchase nursery transplant for best results. Seeds available but plants take 2+ years to bloom well.

germination.desc: Nick seed coat and soak overnight before sowing. Germinates in 2–3 weeks at 75°F+.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly in warm conditions. Provide consistent moisture and full sun.

young.desc: First blooms appear. Pinch tips to encourage branching and more flowers.

adult.desc: Covered in enormous dinner-plate flowers daily. Each bloom lasts one day but is replaced by new ones. Continuous show from spring to frost.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Never let dry out completely. Drooping leaves signal drought stress. Containers need daily watering in summer heat.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. More sun = more blooms.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 3–6 feet depending on variety. Can be pruned to any size.
care.fertilizer: High potassium fertilizer every 2 weeks during growing season. Avoid high phosphorus — can cause leaf drop. A specialized hibiscus fertilizer is ideal.
care.notes: Each individual flower lasts only one day, opening in the morning and closing by evening. The plant compensates by producing dozens of buds that open in sequence. Prune heavily in spring to encourage bushy new growth — flowers form on new wood only.

container.notes: Excellent container plant. Overwinter indoors in a bright, warm location (60°F+). Reduce watering significantly but don't allow to dry out completely. Resume feeding in spring.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch tip cuttings in summer. Root in moist perlite at 70–80°F. Roots in 3–5 weeks.

harvest.when: Flowers edible and used in beverages and food. Harvest open flowers in the morning.
harvest.how: Simply pluck the open flower. The calyx (green base) is also used.
harvest.storage: Fresh flowers wilt quickly — use same day. Dry for tea storage.
harvest.yield: Daily flowers throughout the season.

common_mistakes: Overwatering or underwatering — both cause bud drop before blooms open.
Too little sun — hibiscus needs full sun to bloom prolifically.
Wrong fertilizer — high phosphorus causes leaf yellowing and drop. Use hibiscus-specific fertilizer.
Cold temperatures — exposure to temperatures below 50°F causes leaf drop and dieback.
Not pruning — unpruned plants become leggy with few flowers. Hard prune in spring.

seed_saving.type: Species hibiscus breeds true. Hybrids do not.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed pods to dry on plant. Brown pods split to reveal seeds.
seed_saving.method: Collect dry seeds. Nick seed coat before sowing.
seed_saving.notes: Named hybrid varieties must be propagated from cuttings.

good.why: Same tropical sun-loving requirements. Both attract hummingbirds.
Beautiful tropical combination for large containers.
All three create a stunning tropical garden display.

culinary: Flowers and calyces edible. Dried calyces used to make hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica), jams, syrups, and the base of many herbal beverages. High in vitamin C and antioxidants. Flavor is tart, cranberry-like.
medicinal: Hibiscus tea clinically shown to lower blood pressure in multiple studies — equivalent to some medications in mild to moderate hypertension. High in anthocyanins (antioxidants). Traditionally used as a diuretic. Anti-inflammatory. Liver-protective compounds identified in research.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, and loss of appetite if ingested in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists hibiscus as mildly toxic to dogs and cats. Usually causes only mild GI upset. The risk is low but keep pets from grazing on it.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Handle root ball gently.

varieties.name: Braided Standard
varieties.description: Tree-form hibiscus with braided trunk. Classic patio plant.
varieties.notes: Most dramatic form for container display.

varieties.name: Disco Belle
varieties.description: Compact variety with extra-large flowers to 9 inches. Multiple colors available.
varieties.notes: Best for smaller spaces and containers.

varieties.name: Luna Series
varieties.description: Compact (2–3 feet), very early blooming. Excellent container plant. Multiple colors.
varieties.notes: Best series for northern container gardeners.

varieties.name: Robert Fleming
varieties.description: Deep crimson-red double flowers. Very showy.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Clouds of tiny flies on undersides of leaves.

pests.name: Japanese Beetle
pests.control: Hand pick. Neem oil. Beneficial nematodes.

name: Wisteria
latin: Wisteria sinensis / W. floribunda / W. frutescens

season.start_indoors: Purchase nursery grafted plant — seeds take 10–15 years to bloom
season.harvest_window: Late spring — spectacular 2–3 week bloom. Reblooms lightly in summer with good care.

seed.desc: IMPORTANT: Purchase a grafted nursery plant, not a seedling grown from seed. Seed-grown wisteria takes 10–20 years to first bloom. Grafted plants bloom in 2–3 years. American wisteria (W. frutescens) is less aggressive and blooms faster.

germination.desc: If growing from seed (not recommended): cold stratify 3 months, then sow at 65°F. Germination unreliable.

seedling.desc: Young plants establish quickly. Provide a very strong support structure — mature wisteria can weigh hundreds of pounds and pulls down fences and gutters.

young.desc: Aggressive growth phase. Prune twice yearly: once in summer (after bloom) to shorten new shoots to 5 leaves, once in winter to 2–3 buds. This pruning cycle is essential for blooming.

adult.desc: Spectacular cascading clusters of fragrant purple/white/pink flowers in late spring. Can grow 25–30 feet. Lives 50–100 years. Some specimens become architectural features.

care.water: Moderate. Drought tolerant once established. Water regularly in first 2 years.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. Blooms best in full sun.
care.soil: Moderately fertile, well-draining. Avoid overly rich soil — promotes foliage over flowers.
care.spacing: One plant can cover 30+ feet. Plant 15 feet from structures you don't want damaged.
care.fertilizer: Low nitrogen. High potassium and phosphorus promotes blooming. Excessive nitrogen = all foliage. Never add compost — too fertile prevents flowering.
care.notes: STRUCTURAL WARNING: Mature wisteria is extremely heavy and powerful. It will destroy gutters, damage wooden fences, and pry apart brick. Provide steel or masonry support only. Prune TWICE yearly — this is non-negotiable for blooming. Consider American wisteria (W. frutescens 'Amethyst Falls') — much less aggressive, blooms younger, native to eastern US.

container.notes: American wisteria ('Amethyst Falls') can be trained as a standard in a large container. Standard wisteria too large for containers.

propagation.desc: In spring, bend a young stem to the ground, wound it slightly, pin it down and cover with soil. Roots form in one growing season. Sever from mother plant the following spring.
Take 4–6 inch cuttings in early summer. Root in moist medium. Less reliable than layering.

harvest.when: Cut flower clusters when half the flowers are open.
harvest.how: Cut stems and immediately condition in water.
harvest.storage: Flowers last 5–7 days in water. The fragrance fills a room.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flower clusters on a mature plant.

common_mistakes: Buying seed-grown plants or not verifying grafted status — 10–20 years to first bloom.
Not pruning — the twice-yearly pruning is essential for flower bud formation.
Planting against wooden structures — wisteria destroys wood.
Too much fertilizer — especially nitrogen. Lean soil promotes flowering.
Planting Chinese/Japanese wisteria (invasive in eastern US) instead of native American wisteria.

seed_saving.type: Rarely worth saving — take 10-20 years to bloom.
seed_saving.harvest: Pea-like seed pods form in summer.
seed_saving.method: Dry pods, remove seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Seeds and pods are toxic. All parts toxic.

good.why: Classic cottage garden pairing — bloom at similar time.
Both climbing vines, can intertwine on a sturdy support.

bad.why: Wisteria's aggressive roots and shade can suppress neighboring plants.

culinary: Flowers edible in small quantities — used in fritters and as garnish in Japan. All other parts TOXIC. Seeds especially dangerous.
medicinal: Not used medicinally. All parts contain toxic lectins and alkaloids. Seeds cause severe vomiting and have caused hospitalizations in children.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — especially seeds and pods
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting (sometimes severe), diarrhea, abdominal pain, depression. Seeds most dangerous — can cause collapse.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists wisteria as toxic to dogs and cats. The beautiful seed pods are particularly attractive to dogs and particularly dangerous. Keep pets away from all parts. Emergency vet if seeds are ingested.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth on prepared, strong support. Do not plant near foundations or wooden structures.

varieties.name: Amethyst Falls (W. frutescens)
varieties.description: Native American wisteria. Much less aggressive than Asian species. Blooms at 2–3 years. Fragrant blue-purple clusters. Repeat blooms in summer. BEST CHOICE for most gardens.
varieties.notes: The only wisteria recommended for most home gardens. Non-invasive, blooms young, just as beautiful.

varieties.name: Blue Moon (W. macrostachya)
varieties.description: Hardy to zone 3. Extremely cold-hardy American wisteria. Blooms 3x per season. Blue-violet fragrant clusters.

varieties.name: Aunt Dee (W. macrostachya)
varieties.description: Pale lilac-blue fragrant clusters. Earlier bloomer than most. Native species.

pests.name: Wisteria Borer
pests.desc: Larvae bore into stems causing dieback.
pests.control: Prune out affected stems. Seal wounds.

name: Clematis

season.transplant: Spring or fall — keep roots cool
season.harvest_window: Spring through fall depending on variety and pruning group

seed.desc: Purchase 1–2 year old nursery plant. 'The first year it sleeps, second year it creeps, third year it leaps' — clematis establishes slowly below ground before showing above-ground growth.

germination.desc: Seeds require cold stratification. Extremely slow and variable. Nursery plants always preferred.

seedling.desc: Year 1: modest above-ground growth while the root system develops. Do not be discouraged. Plant deeply with crown 2–3 inches below soil. Keep roots cool with mulch or shade.

young.desc: Year 2: significant growth begins. First blooms appear. Learn your variety's pruning group — incorrect pruning is the most common reason clematis fails to bloom.

adult.desc: Year 3+: full performance. Vigorous climbing growth with abundant flowers. Some varieties bloom spring and fall. Can live 25+ years.

care.water: Consistent moisture — never let dry out. 1 inch per week minimum. Mulch deeply to retain moisture.
care.light: 'Feet in shade, head in sun' — roots need to stay cool while top grows in full to partial sun. At least 4–6 hours sun for good blooming.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline. pH 6.5–7.5. Add lime if soil is acidic.
care.spacing: 3–4 feet between plants. Provide trellis, fence, or host shrub to climb.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring. High potassium mid-season. Avoid excessive nitrogen.
care.notes: CRUCIAL: Know your pruning group. Group 1 (early bloomers): prune lightly after flowering. Group 2 (large-flowered): light prune in late winter, remove dead wood. Group 3 (late bloomers): cut back hard to 12 inches in late winter. Wrong pruning = no flowers.

container.notes: Choose compact varieties. Keep container cool — insulate against heat. Requires trellis.

propagation.desc: Take cuttings between leaf nodes in early summer. Root in perlite with bottom heat. Takes 6–8 weeks.
Bend flexible stem to ground, pin, cover with soil. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Cut stems with flowers at bud or just-opening stage.
harvest.how: Cut long stems, immediately place in water. Condition overnight before arranging.
harvest.storage: Excellent cut flower — lasts 7–10 days in water.
harvest.yield: Prolific once established — cut freely to encourage more flowers.

common_mistakes: Wrong pruning group — the most common reason clematis fails to bloom.
Planting too shallow — crown should be 2–3 inches below soil surface.
Roots in hot sun — roots must stay cool. Mulch heavily or plant a low-growing plant at the base.
Wilt disease — sudden wilting of stems. Cut back to healthy wood. Usually recovers.
Choosing one plant only — clematis looks best with 3+ plants intertwining on a support.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Hybrids variable.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow feathery seed heads to develop. Harvest when fluffy pappus appears.
seed_saving.method: Separate seeds from pappus. Cold stratify 3 months.
seed_saving.notes: Species clematis are worth seed saving. Hybrid varieties won't come true.

good.why: Classic combination — clematis growing through roses extends the season and adds vertical interest.
Both climbing vines on a shared strong support.
Fills the base of clematis while providing nectar.

bad.why: Clematis is generally a good neighbor when given its own support.

culinary: Not edible. Mildly toxic.
medicinal: Traditionally used in Chinese medicine (Clematis chinensis) for pain and rheumatism. Contains irritating compounds (protoanemonin) that cause skin and mucous membrane irritation. External use only and with caution.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Drooling, vomiting, diarrhea. Sap causes skin and oral irritation.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists clematis as toxic to dogs and cats. Causes primarily GI upset and oral irritation. Usually mild. Contact vet if significant symptoms occur.

transplant.deep_note: Plant crown 2–3 inches BELOW soil level — this protects against clematis wilt. The buried stem nodes can sprout new growth if the top is damaged.

varieties.name: Jackmanii
varieties.description: The classic large-flowered purple clematis. Group 3 pruning. Blooms summer into fall. Very reliable and vigorous. The benchmark clematis.
varieties.notes: Most widely grown clematis in the world.

varieties.name: Nelly Moser
varieties.description: Stunning pale pink with dark pink central bar on each petal. Large flowers to 8 inches. Group 2. Blooms spring and fall.

varieties.name: The President
varieties.description: Rich purple-blue large flowers. Group 2. Reliable and free-blooming.

varieties.name: Sweet Autumn Clematis (C. terniflora)
varieties.description: Masses of small fragrant white flowers in late summer/fall. Very vigorous. Self-seeds aggressively — can become weedy.
varieties.notes: Most fragrant clematis. Deadhead to prevent seeding.

varieties.name: Armandii
varieties.description: Evergreen clematis with white fragrant flowers in early spring. Group 1. Zones 7–9.
varieties.notes: Best evergreen clematis for mild climates.

pests.name: Clematis Wilt
pests.desc: Sudden wilting of entire stems — caused by fungal disease.
pests.control: Cut wilted stems to healthy wood or soil level. Plant often recovers. Improve air circulation.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: On new growth and flower buds.

name: Hydrangea
latin: Hydrangea macrophylla / H. paniculata / H. arborescens
growing_zones: 3–9 (varies by species — panicle hydrangeas zones 3–8, bigleaf zones 5–9)

season.harvest_window: Summer through fall depending on type. Dried flower heads persist through winter.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Hydrangeas rarely grown from seed — propagation by division or cuttings.

germination.desc: If growing from cutting: 4–6 inch softwood cuttings in early summer root in 3–4 weeks under mist or in humid conditions.

seedling.desc: First year: modest growth, establishing root system. May produce a few flowers.

young.desc: Year 2: fuller growth and bloom. Avoid heavy pruning until blooming pattern is established.

adult.desc: Full performance. Massive flower heads of lacecap or mophead type. Some varieties change color based on soil pH. Excellent dried flower.

care.water: Consistently moist — 1–2 inches per week. Wilts dramatically in drought but usually recovers. Morning watering preferred.
care.light: Part shade to full sun depending on species. Bigleaf hydrangeas prefer morning sun and afternoon shade. Panicle hydrangeas tolerate full sun.
care.soil: Rich, moisture-retentive, well-draining. pH affects color of bigleaf varieties: acidic (below 6.0) = blue; alkaline (above 7.0) = pink.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring. To make blue: add aluminum sulfate to lower pH. To keep pink: add lime to raise pH.
care.notes: KEY: Know your pruning rules. Bigleaf (H. macrophylla): blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering or not at all. Panicle (H. paniculata): blooms on new wood — prune hard in early spring. Smooth (H. arborescens): blooms on new wood — cut to ground in early spring. Wrong pruning removes next year's flower buds.

container.min_size: 15 gallon for most varieties. Dwarf varieties in 10 gallon.
container.notes: Excellent container plant. Keep consistently moist — containers dry out rapidly. Overwinter in sheltered location in cold climates.

propagation.desc: Early summer cuttings root easily in 3–4 weeks in moist perlite. One of the easiest shrubs to root from cuttings.
Divide large clumps in early spring. Each division needs several healthy shoots.

harvest.when: For fresh use: cut when flowers fully developed. For drying: cut when flowers begin to feel papery.
harvest.how: Cut long stems. For drying: hang upside down or stand in 2 inches of water and allow to dry slowly.
harvest.storage: Fresh in water 7–10 days. Dried heads last indefinitely — excellent dried flower.
harvest.yield: 10–30+ flower heads per season on an established plant.

common_mistakes: Wrong pruning time for bigleaf varieties — the most common reason for no blooms.
Too much sun for bigleaf types — afternoon shade essential in hot climates.
Inconsistent watering — wilting causes bud abort.
pH not managed — if you want blue blooms on bigleaf types, soil must be acidic.
Planting too close to foundation — crowded plants don't bloom well.

seed_saving.type: Rarely done — cuttings preferred.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds tiny, in dried flower heads.
seed_saving.method: Shake dried heads over paper to collect seeds. Surface sow.
seed_saving.notes: Hybrids won't come true from seed.

good.why: Both love similar moist, shaded conditions. Hosta foliage complements hydrangea flowers beautifully.
Same moisture preferences. Blooms at slightly different time extending the season.
Woodland combination in shaded moist gardens.

bad.why: Hydrangea's constant moisture needs incompatible with drought-tolerant companions.

culinary: Not edible. Contains cyanogenic glycosides — mildly toxic.
medicinal: Hydrangea root used historically as a diuretic and for kidney stones. Contains compounds that may be beneficial for kidney health. Not used in conventional medicine. All parts contain compounds that can cause cyanide toxicity in quantity.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — flower buds most concentrated
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy. Cyanogenic glycosides can cause more serious toxicity in large amounts.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists hydrangea as toxic to dogs and cats. Typically causes GI upset. Large ingestion more serious. Keep pets from chewing flower buds and leaves.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Amend soil with compost. Mulch heavily to retain moisture.

varieties.name: Endless Summer
varieties.description: Reblooming bigleaf hydrangea — blooms on both old and new wood. Resolves the pruning problem. Blue in acid soil, pink in alkaline. Most popular hydrangea variety.
varieties.notes: Best choice for reliability in zone 4–9.

varieties.name: Annabelle (H. arborescens)
varieties.description: Native American hydrangea. Enormous 12-inch white ball-shaped flower heads. Cut to ground each spring. Extremely reliable — blooms every year without fail.

varieties.name: Limelight (H. paniculata)
varieties.description: Panicle hydrangea. Enormous lime-green flower clusters aging to pink and cream. Very hardy (zone 3). Full sun tolerant. Tree-form available.
varieties.notes: Best panicle hydrangea. The most landscape-versatile hydrangea.

varieties.name: Little Lime (H. paniculata)
varieties.description: Compact version of Limelight — 3–5 feet. Same flower performance in a smaller package.

varieties.name: Incrediball (H. arborescens)
varieties.description: Improved Annabelle with stronger stems — flowers don't flop. Huge white balls to 12 inches.
varieties.notes: Better than Annabelle for stem strength.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves in humid conditions.
pests.control: Improve air circulation. Resistant varieties. Potassium bicarbonate spray.

name: Butterfly Bush
plant_type: Perennial shrub (dies to ground in cold climates)

season.harvest_window: Summer through first frost — one of the longest blooming shrubs

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Butterfly bush grows easily from cuttings and self-seeds aggressively — a concern in some regions.

germination.desc: Seeds germinate easily at 65°F+ — so easily that it has become invasive in parts of the Pacific Northwest and Southeast. Check local invasive species lists before planting.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly in warm conditions. First-year plants may bloom lightly.

young.desc: Vigorous growth. First substantial blooming begins.

adult.desc: Covered in long fragrant flower spikes from summer through frost. Attracts clouds of butterflies. Can reach 6–10 feet in one season in warm climates.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established. Do not overwater.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. Thrives in lean conditions.
care.spacing: 4–6 feet. Cut hard each spring — plants regenerate from crown.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: INVASIVE WARNING: Buddleja davidii is invasive in parts of the Pacific Northwest, California, and Mid-Atlantic states. Check your state's invasive species list before planting. Consider sterile cultivars (e.g., Flutterby series) or native alternatives (Cephalanthus, Clethra, Itea) that provide equal butterfly value without invasive risk. Deadhead aggressively to prevent seeding.

container.notes: Excellent container plant — eliminates spread risk. Cut back heavily in fall before overwintering.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch tip cuttings in summer. Root very easily in moist medium. One of the easiest shrubs to propagate.

harvest.when: Cut flower spikes for arrangements when 2/3 of the florets are open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems early morning.
harvest.storage: Conditions in water 4 hours before arranging. Lasts 5–7 days.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flower spikes per plant per season.

common_mistakes: Not deadheading — spent flower spikes must be removed immediately to prevent prolific seeding and extend bloom.
Planting invasive varieties in at-risk regions — check your area before planting.
Not pruning hard in spring — cut to 12 inches. This promotes vigorous growth and maximum flowering.
Expecting immediate establishment — plants may look poor after transplant but recover rapidly.

seed_saving.type: Seeds very viable — but check invasive status before allowing to seed in your area.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow dried seed heads to develop after bloom.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry heads into paper bag.
seed_saving.notes: Do not collect seeds in areas where invasive — dispose of seed heads in trash, not compost.

good.why: Both butterfly magnets. Excellent pollinator combination.
Same full sun conditions. Extends butterfly season.
Both fragrant, both attract pollinators.

bad.why: Main concern is invasive spread, not companion planting.

culinary: Not edible.
medicinal: Traditional Chinese medicine uses Buddleja species for eye conditions and liver disorders. Compounds with anti-inflammatory and liver-protective properties identified in research. Not used in Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported
pet_toxicity.notes: Butterfly bush is not listed as toxic to pets. Generally considered safe. The main concern with butterfly bush is its invasive potential, not pet safety.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

varieties.name: Black Knight
varieties.description: Deep purple-black flower spikes — the darkest butterfly bush. Very striking.

varieties.name: Royal Red
varieties.description: Deep magenta-red flower spikes. Very fragrant.

varieties.name: White Profusion
varieties.description: Pure white flower spikes. Very fragrant. Elegant.

varieties.name: Pugster Blue
varieties.description: Compact (3–4 feet), sterile (does not set seed). Good for invasive-concern areas. Blue-purple flowers.
varieties.notes: Best choice where invasive risk is a concern.

name: Gardenia

season.harvest_window: Late spring through summer, with lighter bloom at other times in warm climates

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Gardenias grown from cuttings for exact replication of named varieties.

germination.desc: Seeds possible but slow. Cuttings strongly preferred.

seedling.desc: Slow growing. Keep warm, humid, and in bright indirect light. Very sensitive to temperature fluctuations.

young.desc: Gradual growth. First buds form. Temperature stability critical — drafts and fluctuations cause bud drop.

adult.desc: One of the world's most intensely fragrant flowers. Creamy white waxy flowers against glossy dark green leaves. A gardenia in bloom fills a room with perfume.

care.water: Consistently moist but never waterlogged. Rain-water or distilled water preferred — gardenias are sensitive to fluoride and chlorine in tap water. High humidity essential.
care.light: Bright indirect light indoors. Partial shade to full morning sun outdoors in warm climates.
care.soil: Acidic, well-draining, peaty. pH 5.0–6.0. Use acidic potting mix for containers.
care.spacing: 3–5 feet outdoors. Individual plants in containers.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer (azalea/rhododendron type) every 2 weeks during growing season. Iron deficiency (yellow leaves with green veins) common in alkaline conditions — treat with chelated iron.
care.notes: Gardenias are notoriously temperamental. The most common problems: bud drop (caused by temperature fluctuation, drafts, low humidity, or inconsistent watering), yellow leaves (usually iron deficiency or pH wrong), and pest infestation indoors. Keep away from heating vents. Mist leaves daily indoors. Run a humidifier nearby.

container.notes: The standard way to grow gardenias in cold climates. Use acidic potting mix. Place on a humidity tray. Overwinter indoors at 60–65°F.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch cuttings in summer. Root in acidic medium with bottom heat and high humidity. Mist-bench ideal. Takes 4–8 weeks.

harvest.when: Cut when flowers are fully open but still fresh — usually in the morning.
harvest.how: Cut short stems. Handle blooms minimally — fingerprints cause brown spots on the waxy petals.
harvest.storage: Float in a bowl of cool water. Refrigerate loosely wrapped in damp tissue. Lasts 2–3 days.
harvest.yield: Dozens of blooms on an established plant per season.

common_mistakes: Bud drop — the most common complaint. Caused by: temperature fluctuation, drafts, low humidity, inconsistent watering, or moving the plant while in bud. Once set, never move a gardenia.
Alkaline water — use rainwater or distilled water if tap water is hard.
Low humidity indoors — gardenias need 50%+ humidity. Mist daily or use humidifier.
Overwatering — roots must not sit in water.
Wrong soil pH — must be acidic. Test and amend regularly.

seed_saving.type: Not practiced — cuttings preferred.
seed_saving.harvest: Red-orange fruits contain seeds.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from fruit. Sow fresh.
seed_saving.notes: Named varieties must be propagated from cuttings.

good.why: Both prefer acidic soil. Complement each other in acidic garden beds.
Same acidic soil requirement. Blooms at different times.

bad.why: Gardenias need acidic soil incompatible with alkaline-preferring plants like lavender.

culinary: Flowers edible and used in Chinese cuisine — steeped in tea, crystallized as confections, used in desserts. Fruity-floral flavor.
medicinal: Gardenia fruit (Zhi Zi) is an important herb in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Used for liver and gallbladder conditions, reducing fever, anti-inflammatory, and treating anxiety. Geniposide — the primary active compound — has been studied for liver protection, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. Used in Traditional Chinese Medicine for 2,000+ years.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Mild vomiting, diarrhea, and hives. Usually mild GI upset.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists gardenia as toxic to dogs and cats. Typically causes only mild GI upset. Contact vet if significant symptoms occur.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Use acidic soil mix. Do not plant near concrete foundations — concrete leaches lime and raises pH.

varieties.name: August Beauty
varieties.description: Large double white flowers, very fragrant. Blooms spring and fall. Classic gardenia.

varieties.name: Radicans (Dwarf)
varieties.description: Compact ground cover form — 1–2 feet tall, spreads to 3 feet. Smaller flowers but equally fragrant. Good for containers and borders.

varieties.name: Crown Jewel
varieties.description: More cold-hardy (to zone 6b with protection). Double white flowers. Repeat bloomer.

varieties.name: Veitchii
varieties.description: Continuous bloomer from spring to fall. Smaller double flowers. Very fragrant.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.desc: Major pest — clouds of tiny flies under leaves.
pests.control: Yellow sticky traps. Insecticidal soap. Neem oil.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown bumps on stems — very common on gardenias.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton. Horticultural oil.

name: Azalea / Rhododendron

season.harvest_window: Spring (most varieties). Repeat bloomers: spring and fall.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Azaleas are slow growing — a 3-gallon nursery plant represents several years of growth.

germination.desc: Seeds extremely fine — surface sow, do not cover. Takes weeks to germinate and years to reach flowering size.

seedling.desc: Very slow growth for 2–3 years. Patient establishment — roots before shoots.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. First substantial flowering. Avoid heavy pruning until after bloom.

adult.desc: Spectacular spring display of flowers covering the entire plant. Some varieties rebloom in fall. Lives 50+ years in good conditions.

care.water: Consistent moisture — shallow roots dry out quickly. 1 inch per week. Mulch deeply to retain moisture and keep roots cool.
care.light: Partial shade — morning sun and afternoon shade is ideal. Full shade reduces flowering. Full sun in hot climates causes stress.
care.soil: Acidic, well-draining, rich in organic matter. pH 4.5–6.0. Never plant near concrete. The most important factor for azalea success.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer (azalea/rhododendron type) immediately after flowering. Never fertilize after midsummer — can damage new growth before frost.
care.notes: NEVER prune after midsummer — flower buds set in late summer for the following spring. Prune only immediately after flowering. The shallow fibrous roots are extremely sensitive to disturbance, drought, and poor drainage.

container.notes: Good in containers with acidic potting mix. Overwinter in sheltered location in cold climates.

propagation.desc: Take 3–4 inch cuttings in late summer. Dip in rooting hormone. Root in acidic medium under humidity. Takes 6–8 weeks.
Bend flexible branch to ground, wound, pin, and cover with soil. Roots in one growing season.

harvest.when: Cut stems with flowers at bud stage just beginning to open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems. Condition in cool water overnight.
harvest.storage: Lasts 7–10 days in water in a cool location.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flower stems on an established plant.

common_mistakes: Wrong soil pH — the #1 cause of azalea failure. Must be acidic. Test before planting.
Planting too deep — crown must be at or above soil level.
Pruning at wrong time — pruning after midsummer removes next year's flower buds.
Drought stress — shallow roots cannot handle dry spells without supplemental water.
Planting near concrete foundations or driveways — lime leaches and raises pH.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Hybrids variable.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow brown seed capsules to develop. Harvest before they split.
seed_saving.method: Collect tiny seeds. Surface sow in acidic medium.
seed_saving.notes: Hybrids won't come true. Species azaleas worth saving.

good.why: Same family, same soil requirements. Layers beautifully.
Same acidic soil preference.
Same acidic soil. Blooms at similar time extending the spring display.
Ideal understory companion — same moisture and shade preference.

bad.why: Azaleas need acid soil incompatible with plants that prefer alkaline conditions.

culinary: TOXIC — do not eat. All parts contain grayanotoxins. Honey produced from azalea nectar ('mad honey') causes toxicity.
medicinal: Grayanotoxins in azalea flowers used in traditional medicine in small doses for hypertension, but extremely dangerous — the therapeutic dose is very close to the toxic dose. Not used in conventional medicine. 'Mad honey' poisoning (from azalea-collected honey) has been documented throughout history.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, low blood pressure, heart rate abnormalities, seizures, coma in severe cases.
pet_toxicity.notes: Azaleas and rhododendrons are among the most toxic plants for dogs and cats. Grayanotoxins are serious cardiac and neurological toxins. Even a few leaves can cause severe toxicity. Seek emergency veterinary care immediately if ingestion is suspected.

transplant.deep_note: Crown must be AT or SLIGHTLY ABOVE soil level. Never bury the root ball. Azaleas planted too deep decline and die slowly.

varieties.name: Encore Series
varieties.description: Reblooming azaleas — bloom in spring and again in fall. Many colors available. Zones 6–9. Revolutionary for extending azalea season.

varieties.name: PJM Rhododendron
varieties.description: Very cold-hardy (zone 4). Compact, lavender-pink flowers in very early spring. Reliable performer in cold climates.

varieties.name: Gibraltar (Exbury)
varieties.description: Deciduous azalea with brilliant orange-flame flowers. Intensely fragrant. Outstanding fall color.
varieties.notes: Best deciduous azalea for fall color.

varieties.name: Delaware Valley White
varieties.description: Classic white evergreen azalea. Very reliable. Pure white flowers. Very hardy for an evergreen azalea.

pests.name: Azalea Lace Bug
pests.desc: Mottled yellow-white stippling on upper leaves. Most serious pest in full sun.
pests.control: Plant in shade. Neem oil. Insecticidal soap on undersides of leaves.

pests.name: Petal Blight
pests.desc: Flowers turn brown and slimy in wet weather.
pests.control: Remove infected flowers immediately. Improve air circulation. Fungicide.

pests.name: Root Rot (Phytophthora)
pests.desc: Sudden wilting and plant death from crown rot in poorly drained soil.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Plant in raised beds. No cure once severe.

name: Jasmine
latin: Jasminum officinale / J. sambac / J. polyanthum
plant_type: Perennial vine/shrub (zones 7–10) / Container plant in colder zones

season.harvest_window: Summer (common jasmine). Year-round in warm climates (Arabian jasmine).

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Jasmine propagated by cuttings for reliability.

germination.desc: Seeds possible but slow. Semi-hardwood cuttings preferred.

seedling.desc: Establishes quickly in warm conditions. Provide support for vining types from the start.

young.desc: Rapid growth with support. First blooms in warm weather.

adult.desc: Covered in intensely fragrant white or yellow flowers. Arabian jasmine (J. sambac) — the source of jasmine tea — blooms almost continuously in warm conditions. One of the most powerfully fragrant plants in cultivation.

care.water: Consistent moisture during growing season. Allow to dry slightly between waterings in winter.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. More sun = more blooms and stronger fragrance.
care.soil: Well-draining, moderately fertile. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.spacing: 5–15 feet depending on type. Provide sturdy support for vining types.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring. High potassium in summer to promote flowering.
care.notes: Jasmine is one of the most powerfully fragrant plants in the world — a single plant can scent an entire garden. The fragrance is strongest in the evening and at night, attracting sphinx moths as pollinators. Overwinter container plants indoors at 55°F+.

container.notes: Excellent container plant for northern gardeners. Overwinter indoors — will bloom through winter if kept at 60°F+ with adequate light. One of the best winter-blooming container plants.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch cuttings in summer. Dip in rooting hormone. Root in moist medium at 70°F+. Roots in 4–6 weeks.
Pin flexible stem to soil. Roots in 2–3 months.

harvest.when: Pick flowers in the morning just as they open — fragrance is strongest then.
harvest.how: Gently pick individual flowers or small clusters.
harvest.storage: Float in water. Dry for potpourri or jasmine-infused oil. Use to scent tea.
harvest.yield: Hundreds of flowers per plant per season.
