common_mistakes: Too little light — jasmine in shade grows but rarely blooms well.
Cold damage — exposure to frost kills most jasmine species. Bring containers indoors before first frost.
Overwatering — roots rot in wet soil.
Not providing support — vining types need a trellis from the beginning.
Expecting fragrance indoors — common jasmine may not bloom well indoors. Arabian jasmine (J. sambac) is the best for indoor fragrance.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Hybrids variable.
seed_saving.harvest: Small black berries contain seeds.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from berries. Sow fresh.
seed_saving.notes: Propagate by cuttings for named varieties.

good.why: Classic fragrant combination. Both climb and fill the air with scent.
Both intensely fragrant. Mediterranean pairing.

bad.why: Jasmine generally well-behaved except invasive star jasmine (Trachelospermum) in warm climates.

culinary: Jasmine flowers used to scent jasmine tea (Arabian jasmine, J. sambac). Also used in desserts, syrups, and liqueurs. Flowers edible as garnish. Distinctive floral flavor.
medicinal: Jasmine tea and extracts used in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine for stress, anxiety, and as an aphrodisiac. Jasmine oil (one of the most expensive essential oils) used in aromatherapy for anxiety and depression. Limited clinical evidence but strong traditional use. Some compounds show mild sedative effects.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Mild vomiting and diarrhea if ingested in quantity.
pet_toxicity.notes: True jasmines (Jasminum species) are generally low-toxicity. Caution: 'Carolina jessamine' (Gelsemium) and 'star jasmine' (Trachelospermum) are NOT true jasmines and have different toxicity profiles. J. officinale considered low risk.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Provide trellis or support immediately after planting.

varieties.name: J. officinale 'Argenteovariegatum'
varieties.description: Common jasmine with silver-edged variegated leaves. White intensely fragrant flowers in summer. Very ornamental foliage year-round.

varieties.name: J. sambac 'Grand Duke'
varieties.description: Arabian jasmine with double white flowers — the source of jasmine tea and jasmine absolute essential oil. The most intensely fragrant jasmine. Nearly continuous bloom in warm climates.
varieties.notes: Most fragrant jasmine. The source of commercial jasmine tea.

varieties.name: J. polyanthum
varieties.description: Pink jasmine — masses of pink buds opening to white flowers. Blooms in late winter and spring. Extremely fragrant. Popular as a houseplant.
varieties.notes: Best jasmine for late winter/early spring fragrance indoors.

varieties.name: J. nudiflorum
varieties.description: Winter jasmine — yellow flowers on bare stems in late winter before leaves. Hardy to zone 6. No fragrance but earliest flowering shrub.
varieties.notes: Most cold-hardy jasmine. First flower of the year.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: On new growth and flower buds.

pests.name: Scale
pests.control: Horticultural oil. Isopropyl alcohol on cotton.

name: Lantana
plant_type: Perennial shrub (zones 8–11) / Annual in colder zones

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm areas
season.transplant: After last frost when nights stay above 50°F
season.harvest_window: Continuous from transplant through hard frost — one of the longest-blooming annuals

seed.desc: Purchase nursery transplant or start from seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost. Soak seeds 24 hours before sowing. Germination at 70–75°F.

germination.desc: Reliable in warm soil. Transplants available everywhere in spring — much easier than growing from seed.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly in warm conditions. Pinch growing tips to encourage branching.

young.desc: Blooming begins. Flowers change color as they age — new flowers brighter, older flowers deeper — creating the multicolor effect.

adult.desc: One of the longest-blooming and most butterfly-attractive plants available. Blooms from transplant to hard frost without deadheading. Attracts an extraordinary range of butterflies, skippers, and hummingbirds.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Water regularly when first planting. Overwatering causes root rot and poor flowering.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. More sun = more blooms. Will not bloom well in shade.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. Thrives in lean conditions — too rich = foliage at expense of flowers.
care.spacing: 18–36 inches. Trailing types 12–18 inches for baskets.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: INVASIVE WARNING: Lantana camara is invasive in Florida, Hawaii, and many subtropical/tropical regions worldwide. It is one of the world's most invasive plants in warm climates. In cold-winter areas (zones 7 and below where it freezes) it is not invasive. Check local invasive status. Consider sterile varieties or alternatives in warm climates.

container.min_size: 10–12 gallon. Trailing varieties excellent in hanging baskets.
container.notes: Outstanding container plant. Overwinter cuttings or the whole plant indoors in a cool, bright location. Cut back by 2/3 before bringing in.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch tip cuttings in summer. Root very easily in moist medium at 70°F. Roots in 2–3 weeks.
Divide established plants in spring where perennial.

harvest.when: Not typically used as cut flower.
harvest.how: N/A.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Continuous bloom — no deadheading required.

common_mistakes: Too much water or rich soil — causes lush green growth with few flowers.
Not enough sun — needs full sun to bloom.
Planting invasive varieties in warm climates — serious environmental concern.
Touching berries — green unripe berries are toxic. Ripe black berries less so but still problematic.
Expecting fragrance — lantana has a distinctive pungent scent that some find unpleasant, especially the leaves.

seed_saving.type: Saves easily but may not come true to parent hybrid.
seed_saving.harvest: Ripe black berries contain seeds.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from berries. Sow fresh or dry.
seed_saving.notes: Do not collect seeds in areas where invasive.

good.why: Both love heat, drought, and full sun. Excellent heat-garden combination.
Same sun and heat requirements. Both attract butterflies.
Both attract butterflies and hummingbirds. Classic Florida combination.

culinary: Unripe green berries TOXIC. Ripe black berries reportedly edible in small amounts but generally not eaten due to toxicity concerns. Not a culinary plant.
medicinal: Traditional medicinal use in many tropical countries for fever, respiratory conditions, and skin problems. Contains compounds with antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antifungal properties in laboratory studies. Not used in conventional Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — especially unripe green berries
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, liver failure with large amounts. Unripe berries most dangerous.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists lantana as toxic to dogs and cats. The unripe green berries are the most dangerous part and can cause liver failure. Ripe black berries are less toxic but still problematic. Keep pets away from all parts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

varieties.name: Miss Huff
varieties.description: Large shrub to 6 feet. Orange and pink bicolor flowers. Sterile (no viable seed). Most cold-hardy lantana — survives to zone 7 with protection.
varieties.notes: Best cold-hardy lantana. Most ecologically responsible — sterile.

varieties.name: New Gold
varieties.description: Bright golden yellow. Compact trailing form. Sterile. Very heat tolerant.

varieties.name: Bandana Series
varieties.description: Very compact (12–14 inches). Multiple colors. Excellent container performance.

varieties.name: Luscious Series
varieties.description: Compact, very heat-tolerant, good for containers and borders. Multiple colors.

pests.name: Lantana Lace Bug
pests.control: Neem oil. Insecticidal soap. Encourage parasitic wasps.

name: Passionflower

season.start_indoors: Start from seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost. Cold stratify first.
season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm areas
season.harvest_window: Summer blooms. Passion fruit (maypops) ripen in late summer/fall.

seed.desc: Cold stratify seeds for 3 months before sowing. Or purchase nursery plant. Native passion vine spreads aggressively by underground runners once established.

germination.desc: Reliable after cold stratification. Warm soil (70°F+) accelerates germination.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly once established. Provide support from the start.

young.desc: Vigorous vining growth. Fascinating buds form — watch them slowly open over several days into the extraordinary flower structure.

adult.desc: One of the most extraordinary flowers in the plant kingdom — elaborate structure of 10 petals, corona of filaments, and prominent reproductive structures. Blooms summer through fall. Produces edible passion fruit (maypops). Dies back to roots in winter, returning vigorously in spring.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established due to deep root system.
care.light: Full sun to light shade.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. Too rich soil promotes foliage over flowers.
care.spacing: Allow 6–8 feet spread on a sturdy trellis. Spreads by underground runners.
care.fertilizer: Light feeding. Avoid nitrogen-heavy fertilizers.
care.notes: Native passionflower is the ONLY host plant for Gulf Fritillary, Zebra Longwing, and Variegated Fritillary butterflies. Planting it directly supports these species. The spreading tendency by runners can be managed with mowing or root barriers. Plant in a contained area or dedicated wildlife garden.

container.notes: Possible in containers but growth is more limited. Deep containers accommodate the extensive root system. Overwinter in a cool location.

propagation.desc: Dig underground runners with attached roots in spring or fall. Replant immediately.
Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer. Root in moist medium.
Cold stratify 3 months. Sow at 70°F+.

harvest.when: Passion fruit (maypops): harvest when yellow-green skin wrinkles slightly. Pick up fallen fruit immediately.
harvest.how: Pick or collect fallen fruit. The wrinkled skin signals ripeness — this is when flavor is best.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 1–2 weeks. Freeze pulp for long-term storage.
harvest.yield: Dozens of maypop fruits per vine in good conditions.

common_mistakes: Expecting the tropical passion fruit store-bought variety — P. incarnata produces maypops, smaller and with different flavor but still delicious.
Not providing support — vines need a sturdy trellis from the start.
Panicking when it disappears in winter — it dies back to the roots and returns from them in late spring. Later than most plants.
Planting where spreading is a problem — underground runners can travel 10+ feet from the mother plant.

seed_saving.type: Seeds from ripe maypops breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Extract seeds from fully ripe fruit. Clean off pulp.
seed_saving.method: Rinse seeds. Cold stratify 3 months before sowing.
seed_saving.drying: Dry seeds on paper 1–2 weeks before storing.
seed_saving.notes: Native species breeds reliably true from seed.

good.why: Similar growing conditions. Combined habitat for butterflies.
Together support an extraordinary range of native butterflies.
Same native plant garden aesthetic.

bad.why: Spreading runners can overtake less vigorous nearby plants.

culinary: Maypop fruits edible — yellow pulp around seeds has sweet-tart tropical flavor. Eaten fresh, used in jellies, juice, and beverages. Young leaves edible cooked as greens in some traditions. One of the few native North American fruits.
medicinal: Passionflower (Passiflora incarnata) is a well-researched herbal sedative. European Medicines Agency approves passionflower preparations for mild anxiety and sleep disturbances. Clinically studied — shows benefits comparable to low-dose benzodiazepines in some studies. Flavonoids (particularly chrysin) bind GABA receptors producing calming effect. Traditional use by Cherokee, Houma, and other southeastern nations for anxiety, insomnia, and pain.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported for P. incarnata. Fruit safe.
pet_toxicity.notes: Native passionflower (P. incarnata) is generally considered safe for pets. The fruit is edible. Some tropical Passiflora species may differ — stick to the native species.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Deep, well-prepared soil recommended for the extensive root system.

varieties.name: P. incarnata (native)
varieties.description: The native North American passionflower. Lavender-purple flowers, edible maypop fruit. Host plant for multiple butterfly species. Hardy to zone 5.
varieties.notes: The ecologically correct choice for eastern US gardens.

varieties.name: P. caerulea
varieties.description: Blue crown passionflower. More cold-hardy than tropical types (zone 7). Smaller orange fruits.

varieties.name: Maypop (P. incarnata 'Betty Myles Young')
varieties.description: Selected variety of native passionflower with larger flowers and improved fruit production.

pests.name: Gulf Fritillary Caterpillars
pests.desc: Orange caterpillars with black spines eating the leaves — these are the butterfly larvae the plant hosts. This is DESIRED not a pest.
pests.control: Do not control. Plant extra passionflower if larvae consume too much.

pests.name: Scale
pests.control: Horticultural oil. Isopropyl alcohol on cotton.

name: Trumpet Honeysuckle

season.harvest_window: Spring through fall — peak in late spring. Red berries in summer.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Native trumpet honeysuckle is the ecologically responsible choice — NOT the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica) which has devastated eastern forests.

germination.desc: Cold stratify seeds 3 months. Germination slow and unreliable. Nursery plants strongly preferred.

seedling.desc: Establishes moderately quickly. Provide support from planting.

young.desc: Growth accelerates in second year. First substantial bloom.

adult.desc: Beautiful coral-red tubular flowers from spring through fall on evergreen to semi-evergreen vines. Red berries in summer attract birds. One of the best native vines for hummingbirds — the flowers are perfectly designed for hummingbird pollination.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Blooms best in full sun.
care.soil: Average, well-draining. Adaptable to most soils.
care.spacing: Allow 8–15 feet spread. Provide sturdy trellis or fence.
care.fertilizer: Light feeding in spring. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: Native trumpet honeysuckle is the ecological alternative to invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica) — which should NEVER be planted. The native version provides exactly the same hummingbird value without destroying the forest understory. The berries are attractive to many bird species but toxic to humans.

container.notes: Good container plant. Provide a sturdy obelisk or trellis. More cold-hardy than most container vines.

propagation.desc: Take cuttings in late summer. Dip in rooting hormone. Root in 4–6 weeks.
Pin stem to ground. Roots readily.

harvest.when: Not a cut flower or culinary plant.
harvest.how: N/A.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Continuous blooms spring through fall.

common_mistakes: Planting invasive Japanese honeysuckle instead of native — a serious ecological mistake. Always verify species before purchasing.
Expecting fragrance — native trumpet honeysuckle is not fragrant. The fragrant species are often invasive.
Insufficient support — needs a sturdy structure to climb.
Allowing Japanese honeysuckle to coexist — if you have invasive honeysuckle on your property, remove it.

seed_saving.type: Native species breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Red berries in summer/fall. Collect when fully red.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from berries (berries toxic to humans — wear gloves). Cold stratify 3 months.
seed_saving.notes: Native species worth propagating to support pollinator habitat.

good.why: Naturalistic native garden combination.
Both native vines supporting different butterfly and hummingbird species.
Both hummingbird plants — together they cover a longer season.

bad.why: Never plant invasive species nearby — they will outcompete native plants.

culinary: Red berries TOXIC to humans. Do not eat. Flowers not typically eaten.
medicinal: Native American peoples used honeysuckle bark and leaves for various medicinal purposes. Not used in conventional medicine. The berries are toxic.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: berries — toxic to pets and humans
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea if berries ingested.
pet_toxicity.notes: Berries are toxic to dogs, cats, and humans. The flowers and leaves are generally considered low-toxicity. Keep pets from eating the berries.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Provide support immediately.

varieties.name: Magnifica
varieties.description: The best selection of native trumpet honeysuckle. Extra-large scarlet flowers. Very free-blooming. Excellent hummingbird plant.

varieties.name: John Clayton
varieties.description: Yellow-flowered form of native honeysuckle. Unusual and beautiful. Same hummingbird value.
varieties.notes: Best yellow honeysuckle. Rare and worth seeking out.

varieties.name: Alabama Crimson
varieties.description: Deep crimson-red flowers. Very striking color. Good hummingbird plant.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Common on new growth — especially the invasive Japanese honeysuckle. Native is less susceptible.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: In humid conditions with poor air circulation.
pests.control: Improve air circulation. Resistant varieties preferred.

name: Bleeding Heart

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root or nursery plant in spring
season.harvest_window: Spring — spectacular but brief 4–6 week bloom. Goes dormant in summer.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant or bare root division. Growing from seed requires patience — takes 2–3 years to bloom. Division is instant.

germination.desc: Seeds need cold stratification (3 months). Germination slow and unreliable.

seedling.desc: Slow growth in year 1. Allow to establish without disturbance.

young.desc: Better growth in year 2. First blooms may appear.

adult.desc: Spectacular arching stems 2–3 feet long with dozens of dangling heart-shaped pink and white flowers in spring. Then — disappears completely in summer heat leaving a gap in the border. Plan surrounding plants to fill the space.

care.water: Consistent moisture in spring. Reduce after plant goes dormant in summer. Never waterlogged.
care.light: Part shade — morning sun with afternoon shade ideal. Full shade acceptable. Will burn in full summer sun.
care.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining, high in organic matter. Slightly acidic to neutral. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: 2–3 feet. Mark the location to avoid disturbing dormant roots in summer.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring as growth emerges.
care.notes: SUMMER DORMANCY: Bleeding heart completely disappears by midsummer in warm climates — leaves yellow, stems die back. This is NORMAL, not a problem. Plant late-emerging perennials (hostas, ferns, astilbe) nearby to fill the gap when bleeding heart goes dormant. Mark the location of dormant clumps to avoid accidentally digging them up.

container.notes: Good in containers. Store containers in a cool, dry location when dormant in summer.

propagation.desc: Divide clumps in early spring when shoots first emerge, or in fall after dormancy. Each division needs several growth buds.
Take root cuttings in fall. Lay horizontally in moist medium. Roots form over winter.

harvest.when: Cut stems with flowers when 1/3 of the flowers are open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems immediately into water. Handle carefully — stems fragile.
harvest.storage: Excellent cut flower — lasts 1–2 weeks in cool water.
harvest.yield: 10–20 arching flower stems per established clump.

common_mistakes: Panicking at summer dormancy — this is completely normal. Mark locations. Plan for it.
Planting in full sun — leaves scorch and plant declines.
Digging dormant roots in summer — easy to accidentally destroy.
Overwatering in summer after dormancy — dormant roots rot in wet soil.
Growing in hot humid climates — prefers cool, moist conditions. Struggles south of zone 8.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true. Named varieties variable.
seed_saving.harvest: Long narrow seed pods form after flowering. Harvest before they split.
seed_saving.method: Split pods and collect seeds. Cold stratify 3 months.
seed_saving.notes: Fresh seeds germinate better. Cold stratification essential.

good.why: Hostas fill the gap when bleeding heart goes dormant in summer — perfect timing and shade tolerance.
Same moist, shaded conditions. Beautiful spring combination.
Takes over as bleeding heart fades. Extends the shade garden season.
Classic cottage garden combination — blue forget-me-nots and pink bleeding hearts.

culinary: Not edible. Contains isoquinoline alkaloids toxic in quantity.
medicinal: Traditional use by several Native American nations for pain relief and as a tonic — the alkaloids have analgesic properties. Eschscholzia-related alkaloids being studied for pain management. Not used in conventional medicine. Toxic in significant quantities.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, tremors, respiratory distress. Isoquinoline alkaloids are the toxic agents.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists bleeding heart as toxic to dogs and cats. The alkaloids can cause significant toxicity. Keep pets away from all parts, especially the roots which are more concentrated. Seek veterinary attention if ingestion is suspected.

transplant.deep_note: Plant crown 1 inch below soil level. Mark location clearly for summer dormancy period.

varieties.name: Gold Heart
varieties.description: Golden yellow foliage with classic pink and white heart flowers. Extraordinary combination. Foliage attractive even without flowers.
varieties.notes: Most ornamental bleeding heart — foliage color exceptional.

varieties.name: Alba
varieties.description: Pure white flowers — elegant and unusual. Same arching form as the classic.

varieties.name: King of Hearts
varieties.description: Compact fern-leaf bleeding heart (D. formosa hybrid). Deep rose-pink flowers. Stays in bloom longer than standard. More heat tolerant.

varieties.name: Valentine
varieties.description: Deep red flowers with white tips. Unusual color. More sun tolerant than standard.

pests.name: Fusarium Wilt
pests.desc: Sudden wilting and yellowing. Soil-borne fungal disease.
pests.control: Remove and destroy infected plants. Improve drainage. Long crop rotation.

name: Salvia (Perennial)
latin: Salvia nemorosa / S. greggii / S. guaranitica
plant_type: Perennial (varies by species — some tender perennials)

season.start_indoors: Start from seed 8–10 weeks before last frost OR purchase nursery plant
season.harvest_window: Late spring through fall — deadhead for continuous bloom. Some varieties rebloom prolifically.

seed.desc: Many perennial salvias easy from seed (S. nemorosa). Others better from nursery plants. Sow 8–10 weeks before last frost at 65°F.

germination.desc: Reliable in warm conditions. Light assists germination — do not cover seeds.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly. Pinch tips to encourage branching.

young.desc: First bloom spikes appear. Deadhead after first bloom for repeat flowering.

adult.desc: Covered in vertical flower spikes in blue, purple, red, pink, or white. One of the most important groups of pollinator plants — attracts native bees, bumblebees, hummingbirds, and butterflies. Some species bloom continuously from spring to frost.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Well-draining soil essential — roots rot in wet conditions. Minimal watering in winter.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. Partial shade in extreme heat (zone 9+).
care.soil: Well-draining, average to lean. pH 6.0–7.0. Avoid wet heavy soils.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: Perennial salvias are among the most important pollinator plants available. They offer rich nectar to bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds throughout the growing season. The key to continuous bloom: deadhead spent spikes by cutting back by 1/3 immediately after the first flush fades. Most will rebloom within 3–4 weeks.

container.notes: Excellent container plants. Overwinter tender species (S. greggii, S. guaranitica) in pots indoors or treat as annuals.

propagation.desc: Divide clumps in spring or fall every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer root easily in 3–4 weeks.
S. nemorosa and species salvias easy from seed. Many hybrids do not come true.

harvest.when: Cut flower spikes when 2/3 of florets are open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems in early morning.
harvest.storage: Excellent cut flower — lasts 7–10 days in water. Dries beautifully — hang upside down.
harvest.yield: Abundant spikes throughout the season with deadheading.

common_mistakes: Not deadheading — removing spent spikes is essential for reblooming.
Wet or poorly-drained soil — roots rot and plant declines rapidly.
Too little sun — salvias in shade are leggy with few flowers.
Not cutting back in fall — leave seed heads for birds but cut back in spring to encourage fresh growth.
Treating cold-hardy salvias (S. nemorosa) the same as tender ones (S. greggii) — know your species.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Many hybrids sterile or variable.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flower spikes to dry on plant. Seeds shed easily when ripe.
seed_saving.method: Shake dry spikes into paper bag. Seeds are tiny.
seed_saving.drying: Not needed — seeds dry on plant.
seed_saving.notes: S. nemorosa cultivars may not come true from seed but produce beautiful plants regardless.

good.why: Same sun and drainage requirements. Both exceptional pollinator plants. Spectacular together.
Same dry, sunny conditions. Beautiful color combination.
Same cultural requirements. Extended bloom season and color harmony.
Same ecological role — both attract bees prolifically with similar appearance.

bad.why: Salvia's drought tolerance and need for well-drained soil is incompatible with plants needing consistent moisture.

culinary: Perennial ornamental salvias generally not used as culinary herbs (that is Salvia officinalis). Some species have aromatic leaves used in herbal teas.
medicinal: Salvia nemorosa extracts show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties. Traditional use in European herbalism for digestive and wound-healing applications. Rosmarinic acid in many salvias is a potent antioxidant. Less extensively studied than culinary sage (S. officinalis).

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported for ornamental salvias
pet_toxicity.notes: Ornamental perennial salvias are generally considered safe for pets. Not listed as toxic by ASPCA. The culinary sage (S. officinalis) is also safe. One of the safer flowering perennials for pet-friendly gardens.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Ensure excellent drainage.
transplant.mulch: gravel or light straw (avoid heavy organic mulch over crown)

varieties.name: May Night (S. nemorosa)
varieties.description: Deep indigo-violet flower spikes. Compact 18 inches. Hardy to zone 4. The most widely grown perennial salvia. Perennial Plant of the Year 1997.

varieties.name: Caradonna (S. nemorosa)
varieties.description: Dark purple flowers on striking dark purple stems. More upright than May Night. Very dramatic.
varieties.notes: Most dramatic stem color of any salvia.

varieties.name: Wendy's Wish (S. hybrid)
varieties.description: Brilliant magenta-red. Continuous bloomer from spring to frost. Hummingbird magnet. Tender perennial — zone 9+.

varieties.name: Black and Blue (S. guaranitica)
varieties.description: Cobalt blue flowers with black calyces — striking bicolor effect. 4–5 feet. Hummingbird specialist. Zone 7–11.

varieties.name: Hot Lips (S. greggii)
varieties.description: Bicolor red and white flowers that change to all-red or all-white in heat or cold. Very long blooming season. Zone 6–9.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating in humid conditions with poor air circulation.
pests.control: Resistant varieties. Improve spacing. Potassium bicarbonate.

name: Mountain Laurel

season.harvest_window: Late May–June spectacular bloom. Evergreen foliage year-round.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Mountain laurel very slow from seed — takes years to bloom. Grafted or rooted cuttings preferred.

germination.desc: Seeds extremely fine — surface sow without covering on acidic, peaty medium. Germination slow.

seedling.desc: Very slow first 2–3 years. Patience required. Deep watering encourages deep root establishment.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. Evergreen foliage becomes attractive. First flowers may appear.

adult.desc: Spectacular clusters of cup-shaped pink and white flowers with the unique catapult stamen mechanism. Evergreen year-round. Lives 50–100+ years.

care.water: Consistent moisture — shallow roots dry quickly. 1 inch per week. Deep mulch essential.
care.light: Partial shade — morning sun, afternoon shade ideal. Full sun in cool climates. Deep shade reduces flowering.
care.soil: Acidic, well-draining, rich in organic matter. pH 4.5–6.0. Never lime. Plant away from concrete.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer after flowering only. Never fertilize after midsummer.
care.notes: State flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania. The unique catapult stamen mechanism flings pollen onto visiting bumblebees. ALL PARTS TOXIC — grayanotoxins are serious cardiac toxins. Toxic honey ('mad honey') has been documented. Never prune after midsummer — flower buds set in late summer for the following spring.

container.notes: Too slow-growing and large for containers.

propagation.desc: Difficult to root. Take cuttings in late summer with rooting hormone and bottom heat. Success rate low.
More reliable. Pin a flexible branch to the ground and cover with acidic soil. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Cut flower clusters when half the flowers are open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems, condition immediately in water.
harvest.storage: 5–7 days in cool water. Striking cut flower.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flower clusters on a mature plant.

common_mistakes: Wrong soil pH — must be acidic. Most common failure reason.
Pruning after midsummer removes next year's buds.
Planting in full sun in hot climates — leaves scorch.
Planting near concrete — lime leaches and raises pH.
Allowing pets or children near — all parts severely toxic.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Small brown seed capsules after bloom.
seed_saving.method: Surface sow on acidic peaty medium.
seed_saving.notes: Very slow from seed — 5+ years to first bloom.

good.why: Same acidic soil. Layered woodland garden.
Same moist shaded conditions.
Same family, same requirements.

culinary: TOXIC — all parts. Do not eat.
medicinal: Grayanotoxins studied for cardiac effects but far too dangerous for medicinal use. Traditional Native American use as a very cautious external pain remedy only.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, drooling, weakness, low blood pressure, heart rhythm abnormalities — grayanotoxins are serious cardiac toxins.
pet_toxicity.notes: Mountain laurel is severely toxic to dogs and cats. Even small amounts can cause serious cardiac effects. Keep pets strictly away from all parts. Emergency vet immediately if ingestion suspected.

transplant.deep_note: Crown must be at or slightly above soil level — same as azalea. Never bury the root ball.

varieties.name: Minuet
varieties.description: Dwarf, 3–4 feet. White flowers with red banding. Very ornamental.

varieties.name: Ostbo Red
varieties.description: Deepest red buds opening to pink. Very striking.

varieties.name: Olympic Fire
varieties.description: Bright red buds opening to pale pink. Very showy.

varieties.name: Snowdrift
varieties.description: Pure white flowers. Clean and elegant.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Improve drainage — no cure once severe.

name: Flowering Dogwood

season.harvest_window: March–May spectacular bloom before leaves. Red berries fall. Outstanding fall color.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery tree. Flowering dogwood from seed takes 5–7 years to first bloom. A 3-gallon nursery tree represents several years of growth and will bloom in 2–4 years.

germination.desc: Cold stratify seeds 3–4 months. Germination slow and unreliable.

seedling.desc: Slow first year. Keep consistently moist and in partial shade.

young.desc: Steady growth 1–2 feet per year. Pyramidal shape develops. First bloom may appear at 3–5 years.

adult.desc: One of the most beautiful flowering trees in North America — white bracts (modified leaves) surround tiny true flowers in early spring before leaves emerge. Brilliant red berries in fall, stunning crimson fall color. Supports 117 moth/butterfly species and 36+ bird species.

care.water: Consistent moisture — especially in first 3 years. Drought stress causes dieback and susceptibility to anthracnose.
care.light: Dappled shade to full sun. Morning sun with afternoon shade ideal. Full sun acceptable in cool climates with adequate moisture.
care.soil: Rich, moist, acidic, well-draining. pH 5.5–6.5. Native to forest edges — replicates those conditions.
care.spacing: 15–20 feet. Do not plant under larger trees — needs some sun.
care.fertilizer: Light acidic fertilizer in early spring. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: State flower/tree of Virginia and North Carolina. Susceptible to dogwood anthracnose fungal disease — worse in cool, wet conditions. Improve air circulation. Stressed, drought-weakened trees most vulnerable. The white 'petals' are bracts — the true flowers are the tiny green-yellow cluster in the center. Kousa dogwood (C. kousa) is more disease-resistant but flowers after leaves emerge.

container.min_size: Too large for long-term container growing.
container.notes: Plant in ground for best results.

propagation.desc: Take cuttings in early summer. Difficult to root — requires mist bench and rooting hormone. Success rate moderate.
Cold stratify 3–4 months. Sow in acidic medium. 5–7 years to bloom.

harvest.when: Cut bract-bearing branches when bracts fully expanded.
harvest.how: Cut long branches. Condition immediately in water.
harvest.storage: 7–10 days in water. Excellent cut branches.
harvest.yield: Dozens of bloom-bearing branches on a mature tree.

common_mistakes: Drought stress — the #1 cause of anthracnose susceptibility. Water deeply in dry spells.
Planting in too much shade — needs some sun to bloom well and stay healthy.
Mechanical damage from mowers/trimmers — wounds allow anthracnose entry. Mulch around the base.
Wrong soil pH — must be acidic.
Planting too deep — flare roots must be at or above soil level.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Red berries in fall. Collect when bright red and firm.
seed_saving.method: Remove pulp from seed. Cold stratify 3–4 months. Sow in spring.
seed_saving.storage: Stratify in moist medium in refrigerator.
seed_saving.viability: 1–2 years — do not let fully dry.
seed_saving.notes: Berries mildly toxic to humans. Birds eat them — clean seeds from bird droppings in the wild.

good.why: Classic woodland combination — blooms at same time, same soil needs.
Naturalistic woodland understory below dogwood canopy.
Spring ephemerals bloom simultaneously under dogwood.
Both early spring bloomers in the same woodland habitat.

culinary: Red berries technically edible but very bitter and astringent. Not a food plant. Berries mildly toxic in large quantities.
medicinal: Dogwood bark used by multiple Native American nations as a quinine substitute for fever and malaria treatment — contains cornin, a compound with some antimalarial activity. Bark tea used for pain relief. Historically important as a substitute for cinchona bark during the Civil War when quinine was unavailable.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: berries may cause mild GI upset in large quantities
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Possible mild vomiting if berries eaten in large amounts.
pet_toxicity.notes: Flowering dogwood is generally considered safe for pets. The berries may cause mild GI upset if eaten in large quantities but are not classically toxic. One of the safer native trees for pet-friendly gardens.

transplant.deep_note: Plant with root flare at or slightly above soil level. Never bury the trunk flare — a common and fatal planting error. Mulch the drip line but keep mulch away from trunk.
transplant.mulch: wood chips (3 inches, away from trunk)

varieties.name: Cherokee Chief
varieties.description: Deep rose-red bracts — the most popular red-bracted dogwood. Outstanding fall color.

varieties.name: Cloud Nine
varieties.description: Extra-large pure white bracts. Abundant bloomer even when young. Excellent disease resistance.

varieties.name: Appalachian Spring
varieties.description: White bracts. Excellent anthracnose resistance — the most important disease-resistant variety.
varieties.notes: Best choice where anthracnose is a concern.

varieties.name: Rainbow
varieties.description: Stunning variegated leaves with yellow, green, and red. White bracts. Three-season interest.

pests.name: Dogwood Anthracnose
pests.desc: Purple-bordered leaf spots, twig dieback, crown dieback. Serious fungal disease.
pests.control: Avoid wounding. Reduce stress. Improve air circulation. Fungicide in severe cases. Plant resistant varieties.

pests.name: Dogwood Borer
pests.desc: Larvae bore into trunk — wounds from mowers are entry points.
pests.control: Mulch widely to prevent mower damage. Pheromone traps.

name: Common Lilac

season.harvest_window: May — spectacular but brief 2–3 week bloom. The most intensely fragrant shrub in the northern garden.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Lilacs from seed take 5–7 years to bloom and rarely match the parent. Named varieties must be propagated vegetatively.

germination.desc: Cold stratify seeds 6 weeks. Germination unreliable.

seedling.desc: Very slow early growth. Do not fertilize heavily.

young.desc: Growth accelerates in years 2–4. Avoid heavy pruning until blooming pattern established.

adult.desc: One of the most intensely fragrant shrubs in the northern hemisphere — the scent of lilac in bloom is unmistakable and powerful. Dense panicles of lavender, purple, pink, white, or bicolor flowers. Lives 100+ years. Some lilacs are 200+ years old in New England.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established. Do not overwater.
care.light: Full sun — minimum 6 hours. Blooms poorly in shade.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining, slightly alkaline to neutral. pH 6.5–7.5. Add lime if soil is acidic.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer immediately after blooming only. Never in fall.
care.notes: State flower of New Hampshire. The key to annual blooming: prune immediately after flowering — remove spent blooms before the plant sets next year's buds (which form within 6 weeks of bloom). Never prune after June. Remove suckers from the base to maintain single-stemmed form. Rejuvenate old lilacs by removing 1/3 of the oldest stems each year for 3 years.

container.notes: Not suitable for containers long-term.

propagation.desc: Dig rooted suckers from base of plant in early spring. Replant immediately.
Take cuttings in late spring/early summer. Root in moist medium — moderate success rate.

harvest.when: Cut panicles when 1/3 of the florets are open — early morning.
harvest.how: Immediately sear the cut ends in boiling water for 30 seconds or smash stems to help water uptake. Lilac wilts quickly.
harvest.storage: 3–5 days in water after proper conditioning. The fragrance fills a room.
harvest.yield: Dozens of panicles on a mature shrub.

common_mistakes: Not deadheading — removing spent flowers is essential for next year's bloom.
Pruning at wrong time — only prune immediately after flowering, before new buds set.
Too much shade — lilac requires full sun.
Acidic soil — lilac prefers neutral to slightly alkaline. Add lime if needed.
Suckers from grafted plants — suckers on grafted lilacs are from the rootstock (often common lilac) and should be removed.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true. Named varieties do not.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed capsules to develop in fall. Collect before they split.
seed_saving.method: Stratify seeds 6 weeks at 40°F. Sow in spring.
seed_saving.notes: Seeds take 5–7 years to bloom. Named varieties must be propagated vegetatively.

good.why: Both bloom in late spring/early summer. Classic cottage garden pairing.
Bloom simultaneously — spectacular fragrant combination.
Tulips bloom just before lilacs — extends the spring sequence.

bad.why: Lilac prefers neutral to alkaline soil.

culinary: Flowers edible — used to make lilac simple syrup, lilac sugar, and as garnish. Distinct floral flavor. Use sparingly.
medicinal: Lilac bark and leaves used in traditional medicine as a bitter tonic and fever reducer. Syringin — the primary active compound — has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Essential oil used in aromatherapy. Not used in conventional medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported.
pet_toxicity.notes: Lilacs are not listed as toxic to dogs or cats. Generally considered safe. One of the more pet-friendly flowering shrubs.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Do not plant too deep — crown at soil level.

varieties.name: Charles Joly
varieties.description: Deep magenta-purple double flowers. Very fragrant. The classic dark lilac. Old French hybrid.

varieties.name: Madame Lemoine
varieties.description: Pure white double flowers. Very fragrant. Elegant. Old French hybrid.

varieties.name: President Lincoln
varieties.description: True sky-blue flowers — the bluest lilac available. Single flowers. Very fragrant.
varieties.notes: Most blue lilac — a collector's plant.

varieties.name: Sensation
varieties.description: Unique: purple flowers edged in white. Single flowers. Very dramatic.
varieties.notes: Most unusual color pattern in lilacs.

varieties.name: Miss Kim (S. patula)
varieties.description: Dwarf Korean lilac — 4–5 feet. Ice-blue flowers. Blooms 2–3 weeks after common lilac. Excellent disease resistance. Hardy to zone 3.
varieties.notes: Best compact lilac for small gardens.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves — cosmetic only, not fatal.
pests.control: Improve air circulation. Resistant varieties. Usually appears after bloom — minimal impact.

pests.name: Lilac Borer
pests.desc: Larvae bore into stems causing dieback.
pests.control: Prune out affected stems. Pheromone traps.

pests.name: Bacterial Blight
pests.desc: Shoots and leaves blacken rapidly in cool wet spring weather.
pests.control: Prune infected shoots immediately. Copper fungicide.

name: Common Blue Violet

season.start_indoors: Purchase plants or allow to self-seed
season.harvest_window: March–May primary bloom. Scattered bloom through season.

seed.desc: Violets self-seed prolifically — allow them to spread naturally. Seeds require cold stratification (occur naturally outdoors). Purchase plants or transplant self-sown seedlings.

germination.desc: After cold stratification. Surface sow — seeds need light. Outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly in cool spring conditions.

young.desc: Spreads by runners and self-seeding. May bloom lightly in first year.

adult.desc: Covered in blue-violet five-petaled flowers in spring — one of the most beloved wildflowers. State flower of Rhode Island, New Jersey, and others. Spreads cheerfully to fill appropriate gaps. Both showy open flowers AND cleistogamous (self-fertilizing, never-opening) flowers that produce abundant seed.

care.water: Moderate — tolerates drought once established.
care.light: Part shade to full sun. More shade-tolerant than most garden flowers.
care.soil: Average, well-draining to moisture-retentive. Adaptable to most soils.
care.spacing: Allow to naturalize freely — 6–12 inches between plants.
care.fertilizer: None needed. Self-sufficient in average soil.
care.notes: State flower of Rhode Island, New Jersey, Illinois, and Wisconsin. THE MOST IMPORTANT HOST PLANT for butterflies: all Fritillary butterfly species (Great Spangled, Meadow, Gulf, Variegated, Regal, Diana) can ONLY reproduce on native violets. Without violets, Fritillary butterflies cannot survive. Also edible — flowers and young leaves used in salads, as garnish, and crystallized as confections.

container.notes: Good container plant. Allow to naturalize freely in garden.

propagation.desc: Allow plants to self-seed naturally. Thin seedlings as needed.
Divide clumps in early spring or fall.

harvest.when: Harvest flowers and young leaves in spring when fully open.
harvest.how: Pick gently. Young leaves before they fully expand are most tender.
harvest.storage: Fresh — use same day. Crystallize flowers for longer storage.
harvest.yield: Abundant flowers throughout spring.

common_mistakes: Treating as a weed — violets are essential butterfly host plants and edible wildflowers.
Not allowing to self-seed — the population should be encouraged, not controlled.
Using herbicides on lawn violets — this destroys critical Fritillary butterfly habitat.

seed_saving.type: Prolific self-seeder — seeds form in two ways: showy spring flowers AND cleistogamous summer flowers that never open but produce abundant seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed pods to mature and pop open.
seed_saving.method: Collect seeds as pods begin to swell. Cold stratify for spring sowing.
seed_saving.notes: Usually not necessary — plants self-seed prolifically.

good.why: Violets fill gaps between tulips and daffodils naturally.
Naturalistic woodland ground cover combination.
Both spring wildflowers of woodland edges.

bad.why: Violets are excellent garden citizens. Main 'problem' is enthusiastic self-seeding.

culinary: Flowers and young leaves edible. Flowers used fresh in salads, as cake decorations, crystallized with egg white and sugar, in violet syrup, violet honey, and jelly. High in vitamin C and A. Mild sweet floral flavor. One of the oldest edible flowers in cultivation.
medicinal: Violet leaves and flowers used medicinally — high in rutin (strengthens capillaries), mucilaginous compounds soothe mucous membranes. Traditional use for coughs, sore throats, and skin irritation. Rutin has documented anti-inflammatory properties. Leaf poultices historically used for skin conditions.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — edible for humans and safe for pets.
pet_toxicity.notes: Common blue violet is completely safe for dogs and cats. Edible for humans. One of the safest garden plants for all species.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth or just below soil surface.

varieties.name: Freckles
varieties.description: White flowers heavily speckled with purple-blue dots. Unusual and charming.

varieties.name: Confederate Violet
varieties.description: White flowers streaked with blue-violet veins. Classic southern US violet.

varieties.name: Albiflora
varieties.description: Pure white flowers. Elegant and unusual.

name: Yellow Jessamine

season.harvest_window: January–March — one of the first flowers of the year in the Southeast. Fills the garden with fragrance before anything else blooms.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagated by cuttings for named varieties.

germination.desc: Seeds possible but slow. Fresh seeds, warm stratification then cold. Nursery plants strongly preferred.

seedling.desc: Establishes quickly once planted. Provide trellis or fence immediately.

young.desc: Rapid growth on support. First blooms may appear in late winter of second year.

adult.desc: Covered in fragrant bright yellow trumpet flowers in late winter and early spring — one of the first flowers of the year. State flower of South Carolina. Blooms from January to March when the garden is otherwise bare. Evergreen vine with glossy leaves throughout the year.

care.water: Moderate — somewhat drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Blooms best in full sun.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. Adaptable to most soils.
care.spacing: Allow 10–20 feet on a sturdy trellis or fence.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: SEVERELY TOXIC — all parts, especially roots and seeds, contain gelsemine and related alkaloids that affect the nervous system. Has caused deaths when confused with edible plants. Nectar can occasionally poison bees producing toxic honey. Keep strictly away from children and pets. Despite its toxicity, it is a valuable early nectar source for native bees emerging in late winter.

container.notes: Possible in containers with trellis. Overwinter indoors in cold climates.

propagation.desc: Take cuttings in late summer. Dip in rooting hormone. Root in moist medium. Takes 4–6 weeks.
Pin flexible stem to soil. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Not harvested — decorative vine only.
harvest.how: N/A — all parts toxic.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Continuous bloom over 2–3 months in late winter.

common_mistakes: Confusing with edible plants — SEVERELY TOXIC. Never consume any part.
Allowing children or pets access — all parts toxic.
Insufficient support — needs a sturdy structure.
Planting in too much shade — minimal flowering.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Seed pods in summer.
seed_saving.method: Collect seeds. Wear gloves — all parts toxic.
seed_saving.notes: Propagate by cuttings — faster and more reliable.

good.why: Both bloom in late winter/early spring in the Southeast.
Yellow jessamine blooms before azaleas — sequential spring display.

bad.why: Severe toxicity risk if grown near food plants that could be confused.

culinary: SEVERELY TOXIC. All parts toxic — do not eat under any circumstances. Has caused human deaths.
medicinal: Gelsemine and related alkaloids have been studied for pain management and neurological conditions but the therapeutic window is extremely narrow — dose very close to toxic dose. Used in homeopathic preparations (highly diluted). Traditional use for neuralgia but dangerous without expert preparation. Not used in conventional medicine.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts — roots and seeds most concentrated
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Muscle weakness, difficulty breathing, seizures, cardiac effects — neurological toxins.
pet_toxicity.notes: Yellow jessamine is severely toxic to dogs and cats. All parts contain gelsemine which affects the nervous system. Emergency veterinary care immediately if any ingestion suspected. Do not grow where pets have unsupervised access.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Provide strong support structure immediately.

varieties.name: Pride of Augusta
varieties.description: Double yellow flowers — more showy than the species. Same fragrance. Sterile — does not set seed.

varieties.name: Plena
varieties.description: Semi-double flowers. More floriferous than species.

name: Orange Blossom

season.harvest_window: February–April bloom (in warm climates). Fruit takes 9–12 months to ripen after bloom.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery grafted tree. Seed-grown trees take 7–15 years to bear fruit and don't come true to parent variety. Grafted trees bear in 3–5 years.

germination.desc: Seeds germinate readily. Often polyembryonic — multiple seedlings per seed, most genetic clones of the mother.

seedling.desc: Grows slowly in first year. Thorns present on seedlings. Requires warm temperatures year-round.

young.desc: Growth accelerates. First blooms may appear. The fragrance of orange blossom is extraordinary.

adult.desc: State flower of Florida. Clusters of intensely fragrant white waxy flowers — the classic scent of Florida. One of the most prized fragrances in perfumery. Blooms yield both oranges and essential oil (neroli). A mature tree is covered in bloom and scents an entire garden.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Allow top inch to dry between waterings. Drip irrigation ideal.
care.light: Full sun — 8+ hours minimum.
care.soil: Well-draining, slightly acidic. pH 6.0–7.0. Sandy loam ideal.
care.spacing: 15–20 feet for standard trees. Dwarf: 6–10 feet.
care.fertilizer: Specialized citrus fertilizer (high nitrogen, with trace elements) 3–4 times per year during growing season. Iron and manganese deficiencies common — use chelated micronutrients.
care.notes: The flowers produce neroli essential oil — one of the most expensive in perfumery. Flower water (orange blossom water) used in Middle Eastern, North African, and Southern European cooking. In containers: use citrus potting mix, pot with good drainage, provide maximum sun. Bring indoors before first frost — citrus cannot tolerate frost.

container.notes: Excellent container plant for northern gardeners. Dwarf varieties ('Calamondin', 'Improved Meyer Lemon') better for containers. Requires very large containers for significant fruit production. Overwinter indoors in bright, warm location (above 50°F).

propagation.desc: All commercial citrus grafted onto rootstock. Grafting requires specialized skill but is the only way to maintain named varieties.
Seeds viable — produce true-to-type plants due to polyembryony in most varieties. 7–15 years to fruit.

harvest.when: Flowers: harvest open flowers in the morning for culinary use or distillation. Fruit: when fully colored and slightly soft.
harvest.how: Gently pick fully open flowers. Fruit: twist and pull or cut with pruners.
harvest.storage: Fresh flowers: use immediately. Flowers for drying: air dry in single layer. Fruit: keeps at room temperature 1–2 weeks, refrigerator 1–2 months.
harvest.yield: A mature tree produces hundreds of pounds of fruit annually. Flowers by the thousands.

common_mistakes: Insufficient sun — citrus needs full sun. Most common failure indoors.
Overwatering in containers — root rot is common. Allow to partially dry.
Not fertilizing — citrus is a heavy feeder. Regular specialized citrus fertilizer essential.
Cold damage — any frost kills citrus. Bring containers in before temperatures approach 35°F.
Using wrong soil — citrus must have excellent drainage. Never standard potting soil alone.

seed_saving.type: Most citrus polyembryonic — seeds produce true-to-type clones of the mother (plus one sexual seedling).
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from ripe fruit. Clean off pulp.
seed_saving.method: Sow fresh — citrus seeds don't store well.
seed_saving.storage: Sow fresh. Will not tolerate drying.
seed_saving.notes: Grafting is far superior for maintaining named varieties.

good.why: Same Mediterranean sun and drainage conditions.
Both fragrant, both love sun and heat.

bad.why: Citrus growing conditions (warm, no frost) apply to all companions in-ground.

culinary: Orange blossom water (distilled flower water) used in baklava, maamoul cookies, Turkish delight, Moroccan pastries, and cocktails. Flowers crystallized as confections. Candied orange peel. Orange juice. Fresh eating. Marmalade. One of the world's most important culinary fruits — essentially the entire orange is used.
medicinal: Orange blossom (neroli) essential oil studied for anxiety reduction — clinical trials show significant anxiolytic effect. Orange blossom water used in aromatherapy for stress and insomnia. Vitamin C in orange juice — one of the most documented nutritional benefits. Hesperidin in orange peel — anti-inflammatory flavonoid with cardiovascular benefits. Limonene in peel — studied for cancer prevention.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: peel essential oils — limonene and linalool; leaves
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, depression, photosensitization — cats more sensitive than dogs.
pet_toxicity.notes: Citrus peel essential oils are toxic to cats and mildly irritating to dogs. The fruit pulp is generally safe in small amounts. The peel, leaves, and stems contain concentrated essential oils. Keep cats away from citrus plants entirely.

transplant.deep_note: Plant with bud union (graft point) above soil level. Never bury the graft. Root flare at soil level.
transplant.mulch: none near trunk / straw at drip line

varieties.name: Navel Orange
varieties.description: Seedless. Best eating orange. Excellent flavor. The most widely grown orange for fresh consumption.

varieties.name: Valencia
varieties.description: Juicing orange. Lower acid, high juice content. Bears fruit and flowers simultaneously (paroaro).

varieties.name: Calamondin
varieties.description: Tiny hybrid mandarin — perfect for containers. Produces prolifically. Very ornamental. Tart flavor used like lime.

varieties.name: Improved Meyer Lemon
varieties.description: Dwarf lemon, excellent for containers. Cold-hardier than standard lemons. Year-round fruit. Sweet lemon flavor.
varieties.notes: Most popular container citrus. Beloved for its sweet-tart flavor.

pests.name: Citrus Leafminer
pests.desc: Winding tunnels in new growth leaves.
pests.control: Neem oil on new growth. Beneficial wasps.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Multiple species attack citrus — one of the most scale-susceptible plants.
pests.control: Horticultural oil. Systemic insecticide for severe infestations.

pests.name: Citrus Greening (HLB)
pests.desc: Bacterial disease spread by Asian citrus psyllid — incurable and deadly. Major threat to Florida citrus.
pests.control: Control psyllid vector. Use certified disease-free trees. No cure.

name: Trailing Arbutus (Mayflower)

season.start_indoors: Not practical to grow from seed or purchase as transplant in most areas
season.transplant: Extremely difficult — do not transplant from the wild
season.harvest_window: March–May — one of the very first wildflowers of spring.

seed.desc: Trailing arbutus is notoriously difficult to cultivate. It requires specific mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. The best approach: purchase from a specialized native plant nursery that propagates it correctly, or allow it to establish naturally where conditions suit.

germination.desc: Seeds require specific fungi to germinate and establish. Success very low without the right mycorrhizal partner.

seedling.desc: Extremely slow growth. A 2-inch plant may represent 2+ years of growth.

young.desc: Very gradual spreading. Do not disturb soil around established plants.

adult.desc: Low, woody, evergreen ground cover with leathery oval leaves and clusters of intensely fragrant pink and white tubular flowers in earliest spring — among the first wildflowers to bloom. State flower of Massachusetts. Named Mayflower because it was among the first flowers Pilgrim settlers found after their difficult winter. Nearly impossible to transplant from the wild.

care.water: Consistent moisture in a well-draining acidic environment. Never waterlogged.
care.light: Part shade — dappled light under pines ideal. Tolerates deep shade.
care.soil: VERY acidic, well-draining, sandy loam with abundant organic matter and leaf litter. pH 4.0–5.5. Requires specific mycorrhizal fungi.
care.spacing: Allow to spread naturally — very slow.
care.fertilizer: None — disturbing soil damages the mycorrhizal relationship.
care.notes: Massachusetts state flower. One of the most difficult native wildflowers to cultivate — nearly impossible to transplant from the wild (and illegal in most states where protected). The specific mycorrhizal fungi in the root zone cannot be replicated in most garden situations. If you have it naturally on your property, protect it. If purchasing, buy only from reputable native plant nurseries propagating from cuttings, not wild-collected.

container.notes: Not suitable for containers.

propagation.desc: 4 inch semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer in specialized acidic medium with mycorrhizal inoculant. Very low success rate.

harvest.when: Never harvest from wild populations — protected in many states.
harvest.how: N/A.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Small clusters of fragrant flowers — appreciate in place.

common_mistakes: Attempting to transplant from the wild — almost always kills the plant and is often illegal.
Wrong soil — must be VERY acidic and well-draining with organic matter.
Disturbing soil around established plants — damages mycorrhizal network.
Expecting rapid growth — this is among the slowest native plants.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true but cultivation from seed very difficult.
seed_saving.harvest: Small berries after bloom contain seeds.
seed_saving.method: Complex — require mycorrhizal inoculant for success.
seed_saving.notes: Not practical for home gardeners.

good.why: Same acidic woodland habitat and mycorrhizal associations.
Same acidic, well-draining, pine-forest habitat.
Same habitat requirements.

bad.why: Trailing arbutus cannot compete with vigorous plants.

culinary: Flowers have a sweet fragrance — not typically eaten. Historical records of Pilgrims gathering and treasuring the flowers, which were one of the first signs of spring after the brutal first winter.
medicinal: Traditionally used by Ojibwe and other nations as a kidney and urinary tract remedy — contains arbutin, a compound that becomes hydroquinone (a urinary antiseptic) in the body. Same compound as uva ursi (bearberry) which is used in European herbal medicine for UTIs.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported.
pet_toxicity.notes: Trailing arbutus is not listed as toxic to pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant purchased nursery specimens only. Do not transplant from wild. Use acidic, well-draining soil with added pine bark and leaf mold.
transplant.mulch: pine needle duff (authentic — matches natural habitat)

varieties.name: Species only
varieties.description: No named varieties in cultivation — all plants are the wild type. Flowers range from white to deep pink.
varieties.notes: The species itself is the treasure.

pests.name: Root disturbance
pests.desc: Not a pest but the main 'problem' — soil disturbance of any kind around established plants causes decline.
pests.control: Never cultivate soil nearby. Apply pine needle mulch gently.

name: Shallot

season.direct_sow: Fall (for spring harvest) or early spring
season.transplant: Plant sets in early spring as soon as soil workable
season.harvest_window: Summer when foliage falls over

seed.desc: Plant sets (small bulbs) 1 inch deep, pointed end up, 6 inches apart. Fall planting in mild climates produces larger bulbs.

germination.desc: Green shoots emerge quickly from sets. Much faster than growing from seed.

seedling.desc: Upright hollow green tops grow. Each bulb multiplies into a cluster of 4–12 new bulbs.

young.desc: Bulbs swell underground. Tops remain green and edible as green onions.

adult.desc: Tops yellow and fall over — the signal to harvest. Cure in a warm, dry, airy location for 2–4 weeks for long storage.

care.water: Moderate — consistent moisture during bulb formation. Reduce as tops die back.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, loose, fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early, then switch to potassium as bulbs form.
care.notes: Shallots are the chef's allium — milder, sweeter, and more complex flavor than onion. Each set multiplies into a cluster. French Gray shallot is considered superior in flavor by many chefs.

container.notes: Good in containers.

propagation.desc: Plant small bulbs from previous year's crop or purchase sets.

harvest.when: When tops yellow and fall over naturally.
harvest.how: Lift entire cluster with fork. Separate bulbs. Cure 2–4 weeks in warm dry location.
harvest.storage: Properly cured shallots store 6–8 months in cool, dry, dark location. Longer than onions.
harvest.yield: Each set produces 4–12 shallots.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too early — wait for tops to fully die back.
Not curing properly — skipping curing causes rot in storage.
Planting too shallowly — tips only just below soil surface.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by bulb division. Rarely from seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Save the smallest bulbs from each harvest for replanting.
seed_saving.method: Store saved sets in cool, dry location until planting time.
seed_saving.storage: Cool, dry, dark — same as food shallots.
seed_saving.notes: The easiest vegetable to 'seed save' — just keep some bulbs back from harvest.

good.why: Classic companion — alliums deter carrot fly.
Alliums deter aphids from tomatoes.
Good space-efficient pairing.

bad.why: Alliums inhibit bean and pea growth.

culinary: The foundation of French cooking — shallots used in vinaigrettes, pan sauces, béarnaise, compound butters, and countless preparations where onion would be too strong. Eaten raw in salads, pickled, caramelized, fried crispy (Southeast Asian cooking), and roasted whole. Milder and sweeter than onion with a hint of garlic.
medicinal: Same allicin-based compounds as garlic and onion — antimicrobial, cardiovascular protective, anti-inflammatory. Quercetin content particularly high — potent anti-inflammatory flavonoid.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Heinz body anemia — same as garlic and onion.
pet_toxicity.notes: All alliums toxic to dogs and cats. No safe amount.

transplant.deep_note: Plant sets 1 inch deep, pointed tip just at soil level.

varieties.name: French Gray (Griselle)
varieties.description: The classic French chef's shallot. Gray-brown skin, pink flesh, complex nuanced flavor. Considered superior by most chefs.

varieties.name: Dutch Yellow
varieties.description: Most common commercial shallot. Yellow-brown skin, mild flavor. Very productive.

varieties.name: Red Sun
varieties.description: Reddish skin, mild sweet flavor. Beautiful raw in salads.

pests.name: Onion Fly
pests.control: Row covers. Companion planting with carrots.

name: Watercress

season.start_indoors: Start cuttings any time in water
season.transplant: Any time in appropriate water/moist conditions
season.harvest_window: Year-round where water doesn't freeze. Best in cool seasons.

seed.desc: Surface sow — seeds need light. Or simply place store-bought watercress stems in water and they root within days. One of the easiest plants to propagate.

germination.desc: Fast germination in cool, moist conditions. Stems placed in water root in 3–5 days.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly in cool conditions. Trailing stems root at nodes in contact with water or moist soil.

young.desc: Begins forming the dense mats characteristic of natural stands.

adult.desc: Dense mats of round, dark green, peppery leaves. Self-maintaining in moving water. Harvest regularly to prevent bolting. Flowers are small and white — signal to cut back.

care.water: REQUIRES constantly moist to wet conditions — grows in stream margins, continuously moist soil, or shallow containers of water changed frequently.
care.light: Part shade — too much sun causes bolting.
care.soil: Very moist to aquatic. pH 6.5–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen feeding. Naturally fertile aquatic environments provide sufficient nutrients.
care.notes: One of the most nutritious vegetables per gram — extraordinarily high in vitamins K, C, and A relative to its weight. Grows naturally along clean streams and springs. Can be grown in a bucket of water changed every few days, in a container with drainage holes sitting in a saucer of water, or in a bog garden. Wild watercress may harbor liver flukes — only eat home-grown or commercially produced watercress.

container.min_size: Wide shallow container in saucer of water.
container.notes: Excellent container plant — grow in a pot sitting in a saucer of clean water, changed every 2–3 days. One of the easiest aquatic vegetables.

propagation.desc: Simply place stems in clean water. Roots form in 3–5 days at every node. The easiest propagation method of any vegetable.
Surface sow in very moist medium. Germinates in 7–14 days.

harvest.when: When stems reach 4–6 inches. Harvest frequently to prevent bolting.
harvest.how: Cut or pinch tips. The more you harvest, the more it grows.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate in a jar with stems in water, loosely covered. Lasts 5–7 days. Wash thoroughly before eating.
harvest.yield: Continuous harvest from established plants.

common_mistakes: Not enough water — the most common failure. Must be constantly wet.
Too much sun — bolts quickly. Partial shade extends harvest season.
Not harvesting frequently enough — plants bolt and become bitter in heat.
Wild watercress — do not eat watercress from unknown wild sources (liver fluke risk).

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow flowering stems to set seed. Collect small seed pods when dry.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dry pods.
seed_saving.notes: Easiest — just let some stems go to flower and collect seed.

good.why: Both love moist conditions. Good container pairing in wet environments.
Watercress thrives alongside other moisture-loving plants.

culinary: Classic English watercress soup. Watercress and orange salad. Sandwiches (traditional English 'watercress sandwiches'). Stirred into pasta. Used like arugula in any application. The peppery bite diminishes with cooking — use raw for maximum flavor and nutrition. One of the most ancient cultivated vegetables — eaten since ancient Rome and Greece.
medicinal: Watercress has one of the highest ORAC (antioxidant capacity) scores of any vegetable. Contains PEITC (phenethyl isothiocyanate) — studied extensively for cancer prevention, particularly lung cancer in smokers. Clinical trial at University of Ulster showed watercress reduced DNA damage markers by 17% in healthy volunteers. Extraordinarily high in vitamin K — blood thinning medication interactions possible.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None.
pet_toxicity.notes: Watercress is safe for dogs and cats in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant cuttings in very moist soil or place directly in shallow water.

varieties.name: Aqua (Common)
varieties.description: The standard commercial watercress. Round dark green leaves. Peppery flavor.

varieties.name: Upland Cress (Land Cress)
varieties.description: Not true watercress but similar flavor — can be grown in regular moist garden soil without standing water. More practical for most gardens.
varieties.notes: Best option for gardens without water features.

name: Broccoli Rabe (Rapini)

season.direct_sow: Early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) or late summer for fall crop
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Bolts in heat.

seed.desc: Direct sow ½ inch deep in cool soil. One of the fastest-maturing vegetables — ready in 6 weeks.

germination.desc: Very fast in cool soil. Germinates readily.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Thin to 6 inches. Thinnings edible.

young.desc: Forms leafy rosette. Begin harvesting outer leaves.

adult.desc: Flower buds form — this is the harvest moment. Cut the central stem with buds before flowers open. Side shoots continue producing for several more weeks.

care.water: Consistent moisture. 1 inch per week.
care.light: Full sun to part shade.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Nitrogen-rich fertilizer at planting.
care.notes: A staple of Italian-American cuisine — bitter, pungent flavor beloved in orecchiette con cime di rapa, sautéed with garlic and olive oil, or in sandwiches. Not the same as broccolini. The bitterness mellows when blanched or cooked with good olive oil and garlic. Harvest before any yellow flowers open — bitterness increases after flowering.

container.notes: Good in containers in cool weather.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only. Fast enough that transplanting is unnecessary.

harvest.when: When central flower bud cluster forms but before any yellow flowers open — usually 40–50 days.
harvest.how: Cut central stem 6 inches below bud cluster. Side shoots produce for 3–4 more weeks.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed in damp paper towel bag for 3–5 days.
harvest.yield: Multiple harvests from one planting via side shoots.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer heat — bolts immediately. Cool-season only.
Waiting too long to harvest — once yellow flowers open, flavor becomes extremely bitter.
Not blanching before sautéing — blanching 2 minutes in salted water removes excessive bitterness.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated. Allow plants to fully flower and set seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed pods to dry on plant. Harvest before splitting.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dry pods.
seed_saving.notes: Cross-pollinates with other Brassica rapa — isolate by ½ mile from turnips, bok choy, etc.

good.why: Cool-season crop that finishes before tomatoes need full space.
Both cool-season, compatible timing.

bad.why: Same pests and diseases. Rotate annually.

culinary: The classic Italian-American preparation: blanch in salted water, sauté in good olive oil with garlic and red pepper flakes, toss with orecchiette pasta. Also: sautéed with sausage, in frittatas, as a pizza topping, in sandwiches (classic Italian beef sandwich). The bitter flavor is the point — it pairs perfectly with rich, fatty ingredients.
medicinal: High in vitamin K, vitamin C, and folate. Glucosinolates (the compounds responsible for bitterness) are studied for cancer prevention. Same brassica family health benefits as broccoli and kale.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — glucosinolates cause GI upset in large amounts
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Gas and GI upset in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Large quantities can cause GI upset in pets due to glucosinolates.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow ½ inch deep. Transplanting not recommended — direct sow only.

varieties.name: Spring Raab
varieties.description: Standard variety. Good for spring planting.

varieties.name: Sessantina Grossa
varieties.description: Slower-bolting variety for longer harvest. Larger plants.

varieties.name: Early Fall Raab
varieties.description: Specially bred for fall planting. Very quick.

name: Turnip

season.direct_sow: Early spring (6 weeks before last frost) or late summer (8 weeks before first frost)
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Best flavor after light frost.

seed.desc: Direct sow ½ inch deep. Turnips dislike transplanting — direct sow only.

germination.desc: Very fast germination in cool soil.

seedling.desc: Thin to 4–6 inches. Thinnings edible as greens.

young.desc: Root begins to swell at soil surface. Leaves (turnip greens) harvestable at any stage.

adult.desc: Root fully formed. Harvest before roots exceed 3 inches — larger roots become woody. Fall-harvested turnips sweeter after frost converts starches to sugar.

care.water: Consistent moisture — drought causes split, bitter roots.
care.light: Full sun to part shade.
care.soil: Loose, well-draining. Remove stones. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer. Excess nitrogen = lush tops, small roots.
care.notes: One of the most cold-hardy vegetables — handles frost better than almost any other root vegetable. Fall-planted turnips taste sweeter after frost. Turnip greens are highly nutritious and often overlooked. Popular in Southern US cooking.

container.notes: Good in containers. Choose small varieties.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only — fast enough that transplanting is unnecessary.

harvest.when: When roots are 2–3 inches diameter. Greens anytime.
harvest.how: Pull roots by hand or loosen with fork. Cut greens separately.
harvest.storage: Remove greens, refrigerate roots up to 2 weeks. Store in root cellar several months.
harvest.yield: One root per plant. Generous greens.

common_mistakes: Planting in summer heat — bolts and becomes extremely bitter.
Letting roots grow too large — over 3 inches becomes woody.
Not harvesting greens — nutritious and delicious.

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties breed true. Biennial — plant overwintered root to flower second year.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow seed pods to dry. Collect before splitting.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dry pods.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other Brassica rapa. Isolate.

good.why: Both cool-season crops. Peas fix nitrogen for turnips.
Onions deter turnip pests.

culinary: Classic in pot roasts and stews. Roasted with root vegetables. Mashed with butter (neeps and tatties — Scottish tradition). Turnip greens sautéed with bacon and vinegar — a Southern US classic. Pickled turnips (bright pink from beets) — Lebanese and Middle Eastern cuisine staple. Turnip soup.
medicinal: High in vitamin C and glucosinolates with cancer-preventive properties. Turnip greens particularly high in vitamins K, A, and C. Historically important as a winter vitamin source in northern Europe.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Glucosinolates can cause GI upset in large quantities.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow ½ inch deep. Does not transplant well.

varieties.name: Purple Top White Globe
varieties.description: The classic turnip — white with purple shoulders. Excellent flavor cooked.

varieties.name: Hakurei
varieties.description: Japanese salad turnip — small, white, sweet, mild. Excellent raw. Fast maturing.
varieties.notes: Best for eating raw. Mild enough for salads.

varieties.name: Golden Globe
varieties.description: Golden-yellow flesh. Slightly sweeter and milder than standard turnip.

pests.name: Cabbage Root Maggot
pests.control: Row covers from transplant. Beneficial nematodes.

name: Parsnip

season.direct_sow: Early spring — as soon as soil can be worked. Needs long season.
season.harvest_window: Fall through winter. Best after hard frost converts starch to sugar. Can leave in ground all winter.

seed.desc: Use FRESH seed — parsnip seed loses viability rapidly. Sow thickly because germination rate can be poor. ½ inch deep in loose, stone-free soil.

germination.desc: SLOW and often patchy — parsnip is one of the most difficult vegetables to germinate reliably. Fresh seed is critical. Soil must not dry out during germination.

seedling.desc: Slow early growth. Thin to 3–4 inches. Mark rows carefully — seedlings resemble weeds.

young.desc: Ferny carrot-like foliage develops. Root grows slowly underground.

adult.desc: Ready after first hard frost — cold converts starches to sugars, creating the sweet, nutty flavor parsnips are prized for. Can be left in ground all winter under mulch and harvested as needed. One of the finest winter vegetables.

care.water: Consistent moisture during germination (critical) and root development.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Deep, loose, stone-free — same as carrots. pH 6.0–7.0. Rocks cause forking.
care.fertilizer: Moderate balanced fertilizer. Avoid excess nitrogen.
care.notes: One of the most underrated vegetables. Sweet, nutty flavor after frost is extraordinary. Requires long growing season (120+ days) and patience with slow germination. Always buy fresh seed each year. Can be left in the ground all winter and harvested as needed — actually improves with successive freezes.

container.min_size: Needs very deep soil — not practical in most containers.
container.notes: Requires 12+ inch soil depth.

propagation.desc: Fresh seed only. Direct sow — taproot makes transplanting impossible.

harvest.when: After first hard frost. Can harvest throughout winter.
harvest.how: Loosen soil with fork, pull roots carefully.
harvest.storage: Leave in ground under mulch for winter harvesting. Or refrigerate up to 4 weeks.
harvest.yield: One root per plant. Worth the wait.

common_mistakes: Old seed — parsnip seed loses viability dramatically after 1 year. Always buy fresh.
Dry soil during germination — the most common failure. Cover with row cover to retain moisture.
