Harvesting before frost — parsnips before frost taste starchy and bland. Wait for frost.
Rocky soil — causes badly forked ugly (but edible) roots.
CAUTION: Parsnip sap causes phototoxic burns in sunlight — wear gloves and long sleeves when working with the plant in sunny conditions.

seed_saving.type: Biennial — needs to overwinter and flower in year 2. Open-pollinated.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow overwintered plant to flower and set seed in year 2.
seed_saving.method: Collect seeds from dried umbels.
seed_saving.storage: Paper envelope — USE WITHIN ONE YEAR.
seed_saving.notes: Save seed ONLY from best roots. Use immediately — viability drops dramatically.

good.why: Rosemary repels carrot fly which also attacks parsnips.
Onions deter carrot/parsnip fly.
Peas fix nitrogen. Good timing — peas done before parsnips need full space.

bad.why: Same family — same pests. Don't plant adjacent.

culinary: Roasted parsnips (caramelized in butter and honey) — a revelation. Parsnip soup — creamy and elegant. Parsnip purée — sweeter and more complex than mashed potato. Classic in British roasts and stews. Parsnip cake (yes — as sweet as carrot cake). Roasted alongside carrots and beets. One of the great autumn and winter root vegetables.
medicinal: High in folate, vitamin C, and potassium. Furanocoumarins in the leaves cause phototoxic burns — a documented and serious hazard. Traditional use of the root as a diuretic. Falcarinol compounds studied for anticancer properties (same as carrots).

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: leaves and stems in sun (phototoxic — affects humans more than pets)
pet_toxicity.symptoms: None from root. Leaf sap + sunlight causes skin burns in humans.
pet_toxicity.notes: Parsnip root is safe for dogs and cats. The leaves contain furanocoumarins — phototoxic to humans in sunlight. Less of a concern for pets but avoid pets chewing the foliage.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow only — taproot makes transplanting impossible.

varieties.name: Hollow Crown
varieties.description: The classic heirloom parsnip. Large, smooth, excellent flavor after frost.

varieties.name: Gladiator
varieties.description: Improved hybrid — better germination, disease resistant, smoother skin.

varieties.name: Albion
varieties.description: Very smooth skin, easier to peel. Good disease resistance.

pests.name: Carrot Fly
pests.control: Row covers. Avoid crushing foliage (releases attractant scent). Companion plant with alliums.

pests.name: Canker
pests.desc: Brown rot at shoulder of root.
pests.control: Resistant varieties. Avoid damage during thinning.

name: Kohlrabi

season.direct_sow: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer
season.harvest_window: Spring and fall. Best in cool weather.

seed.desc: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost. Or direct sow. One of the most space-efficient vegetables.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable germination.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly. Transplant when 3–4 inches tall.

young.desc: The swollen stem (the edible part, technically a swollen hypocotyl) begins to form above ground.

adult.desc: Bulb-like swelling at base of plant reaches 2–3 inches diameter — harvest now. White, purple, or green. Crisp, mild, slightly sweet. One of the most underrated vegetables.

care.water: Consistent moisture — drought causes tough, fibrous texture.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer at planting.
care.notes: Kohlrabi tastes like a cross between broccoli stems and a mild turnip — sweet and crisp when young. The leaves are also edible. Extremely productive per square foot. One of the fastest vegetables — from transplant to harvest in just 6–8 weeks.

container.notes: Excellent container vegetable — compact and fast.

propagation.desc: Start indoors or direct sow. Easy from seed.

harvest.when: When bulb is 2–3 inches diameter — about tennis ball size. Larger becomes woody.
harvest.how: Cut at soil level.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 2–3 weeks. Remove leaves first.
harvest.yield: One bulb per plant. Very productive per square foot.

common_mistakes: Letting bulb grow too large — over 3 inches becomes woody and tough.
Drought stress — causes fibrous, tough texture.
Planting in heat — bolts. Cool season only.

seed_saving.type: Biennial. Cross-pollinates with other B. oleracea (broccoli, cabbage, etc.).
seed_saving.harvest: Overwinter plant, collect seed from year 2 flower.
seed_saving.method: Thresh dry seed pods.
seed_saving.notes: Isolate by ½ mile from other B. oleracea.

good.why: Compatible timing, different root depths.
Good space-sharing companion.
Onions deter brassica pests.

culinary: Raw in slaws and salads — sweeter and more mild than turnip. Roasted or steamed. Kohlrabi fries (cut into matchsticks, roast at high heat). Stuffed kohlrabi (hollow out bulb, fill with meat or vegetable mixture). Pickled. Creamy kohlrabi soup. Grated into fritters. Popular in Germany, Eastern Europe, and India.
medicinal: High in vitamin C and glucosinolates with cancer-preventive properties. Good source of potassium and fiber.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Do not bury the swelling stem — it must develop above ground.

varieties.name: Early White Vienna
varieties.description: Classic white-green variety. Mild sweet flavor. Most widely grown.

varieties.name: Kolibri
varieties.description: Purple skin, white flesh. Very ornamental. Fast maturing.

varieties.name: Superschmelz
varieties.description: Giant variety — grows to 10 pounds without becoming woody. Excellent flavor even at large sizes.
varieties.notes: Best for large production. Stores exceptionally well.

name: Ginger

season.start_indoors: Start rhizomes indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost
season.transplant: After last frost — ginger loves heat
season.harvest_window: Fall — about 8–10 months after planting. Baby ginger (tender, no need to peel) at 4–5 months.

seed.desc: Purchase fresh, plump, firm ginger rhizomes from an Asian grocery or garden center (avoid supermarket ginger which may be treated). Soak overnight. Break into 1–2 inch pieces with visible growth buds (eyes).

germination.desc: Shoots emerge from rhizome eyes. Slow to start — patience required.

seedling.desc: Upright reed-like stalks emerge. Grows well in warm conditions. Keep consistently warm — cold below 50°F causes dormancy.

young.desc: Spreading growth develops. Rhizomes expand underground. Baby ginger can be harvested at 4–5 months — tender, pink-tinged, with edible skin.

adult.desc: Full mature ginger at 8–10 months when leaves yellow and die back in fall. Harvest entire clump. Divide and save some rhizome pieces for next year's planting.

care.water: Consistent moisture — ginger is a tropical plant that needs humidity and regular water. Never let dry out. Never waterlogged.
care.light: Bright indirect light to partial shade — NOT full afternoon sun. Morning sun ideal.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, high organic matter. pH 5.5–6.5.
care.fertilizer: High potassium fertilizer every 3–4 weeks during growing season.
care.notes: One of the world's most important culinary and medicinal plants. Easy to grow in containers in northern climates — bring indoors before first frost and continue growing on a sunny windowsill, or allow to go dormant (leaves die back) and store rhizomes cool and dry until spring.

container.notes: Ideal container plant for northern gardeners. Wide, shallow containers work better than deep ones — ginger spreads horizontally. Overwinter indoors or allow to go dormant.

propagation.desc: Simply break fresh rhizomes into sections with at least one visible growth bud (eye) each. Soak overnight before planting.

harvest.when: Baby ginger: 4–5 months (tender, mild). Mature ginger: when tops yellow and die back (8–10 months).
harvest.how: Lift entire clump with fork. Wash, dry. Save firm sections with eyes for replanting.
harvest.storage: Fresh refrigerates 3 weeks. Freeze whole rhizomes (grate directly from frozen). Pickled. Crystallized. Dried and ground.
harvest.yield: Each planted rhizome section yields 3–5 pounds of mature ginger given good conditions.

common_mistakes: Cold temperatures — ginger stops growing below 55°F. Must stay warm.
Too much direct sun — leaves scorch. Bright indirect or morning sun only.
Shallow containers — ginger needs room to spread horizontally.
Supermarket ginger — may be treated to prevent sprouting. Use fresh organic or seed ginger.
Not starting early enough — needs 8–10 months for mature ginger.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by rhizome division — save plump sections with growth eyes each fall.
seed_saving.harvest: Save firm rhizome sections at harvest.
seed_saving.method: Cure cut surfaces 24 hours before storing.
seed_saving.storage: Cool (55°F), dry, dark location wrapped in paper — not plastic.
seed_saving.notes: Easy to maintain — just save some rhizomes each fall.

good.why: Same tropical requirements. Both rhizome plants grow beautifully together.
Same tropical growing conditions.

culinary: One of the world's most important spices. Fresh ginger: stir-fries, curries, marinades, ginger tea, ginger ale, gingerbread, pickled ginger (sushi accompaniment). Crystallized ginger: confections. Ground dried ginger: baking, spice blends. Ginger juice: cocktails, dressings. Young baby ginger: sliced paper-thin in salads, less pungent.
medicinal: One of the most studied medicinal plants. Gingerols and shogaols: powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds. Clinical evidence for: nausea (pregnancy morning sickness, chemotherapy nausea, motion sickness) — Level A evidence comparable to some medications. Anti-inflammatory effects comparable to ibuprofen in some studies for osteoarthritis. Carminative (reduces gas and bloating). May lower blood sugar and cholesterol.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — may cause GI upset in large amounts
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Possible GI upset in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Ginger is generally considered safe for dogs and cats in small amounts. Actually used by some veterinarians to treat nausea in dogs. Avoid large quantities.

transplant.deep_note: Plant rhizome sections 2 inches deep with growth bud (eye) facing up. Wide, shallow planting — ginger spreads horizontally not vertically.

varieties.name: Common Ginger (Z. officinale)
varieties.description: The standard culinary ginger. Pale yellow flesh, strong flavor.

varieties.name: Baby Ginger
varieties.description: Not a distinct variety but a harvest timing — young ginger harvested at 4–5 months. Pink-tinged, tender, edible skin, milder flavor.
varieties.notes: Excellent for pickling and fresh use.

varieties.name: Hawaiian Red Ginger
varieties.description: Ornamental ginger with brilliant red flower spikes. Not the culinary species but the flower is edible and decorative.

pests.name: Rhizome Rot
pests.desc: Soft, mushy rhizomes from overwatering or poor drainage.
pests.control: Improve drainage. Reduce watering. Remove affected material.

name: Turmeric

season.start_indoors: Start rhizomes indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost
season.transplant: After last frost in warm soil
season.harvest_window: Fall when leaves die back — about 8–10 months after planting

seed.desc: Purchase fresh turmeric rhizomes from Asian grocery or garden center. Break into 1–2 inch sections with visible buds. Soak overnight.

germination.desc: Slower to sprout than ginger. Keep warm (70°F+). Shoots emerge from rhizome nodes.

seedling.desc: Beautiful large paddle-shaped leaves emerge — ornamental as well as productive. Grows well in warm conditions.

young.desc: Rhizomes expand underground. Striking tropical foliage 3–4 feet tall. Some varieties produce spectacular pink or white flower spikes.

adult.desc: Leaves yellow and die back in fall — harvest time. Dig entire clump. Brilliant orange flesh revealed when cut. Fresh turmeric has a much more complex, earthy flavor than dried powder.

care.water: Consistent moisture — tropical plant needs regular watering. Never waterlogged.
care.light: Bright indirect light to partial shade. Morning sun fine.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, high organic matter. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High potassium fertilizer monthly.
care.notes: Even easier than ginger. The same growing conditions apply. More cold-tolerant than ginger (survives to zone 8 in-ground). The fresh rhizomes have a more complex, less pungent flavor than the dried powder and are worth seeking out for cooking. WARNING: turmeric stains intensely — gloves recommended when processing.

container.notes: Excellent container plant. Same approach as ginger. The large ornamental leaves make it an attractive patio plant.

propagation.desc: Break fresh rhizomes into 1–2 inch sections with visible buds. Soak overnight before planting.

harvest.when: When leaves die back — usually October in most climates.
harvest.how: Lift entire clump with fork. Separate main and finger rhizomes from fibrous roots.
harvest.storage: Fresh refrigerates 3 weeks. Freeze (grate directly from frozen). Boil, peel, and dry to make powder. Pickle.
harvest.yield: Each planted section yields 3–7 pounds of rhizomes.

common_mistakes: Impatience — turmeric takes 8–10 months. Plan ahead.
Cold temperatures below 55°F — stop growth, can kill plant.
Too much direct afternoon sun — leaves scorch.
Not wearing gloves when processing — intense permanent staining.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by rhizome division.
seed_saving.harvest: Save firm rhizome sections with buds at harvest.
seed_saving.method: Cure cut surfaces 24 hours before storing.
seed_saving.storage: Cool (55–60°F), dry, dark. Wrapped in paper.
seed_saving.notes: Keep the largest, most vibrant rhizomes for replanting.

good.why: Identical growing requirements. Both tropical rhizome plants.
Same tropical conditions.

culinary: The golden spice — essential in South Asian, Southeast Asian, and Middle Eastern cooking. Gives curry its yellow color. Golden milk (turmeric latte). Fresh turmeric: grated into smoothies, rice dishes, soups. Turmeric rice, turmeric eggs, turmeric hummus. Pickled fresh turmeric. The fresh rhizome has more aromatic complexity than dried powder.
medicinal: Curcumin — turmeric's primary bioactive compound — is one of the most extensively studied natural compounds. Evidence for: anti-inflammatory (rivals ibuprofen in some studies for osteoarthritis without GI side effects), antioxidant, potential anticancer (hundreds of studies), neuroprotective (Alzheimer's prevention research), liver protective. BIOAVAILABILITY CRITICAL: curcumin poorly absorbed alone — always combine with black pepper (piperine increases absorption 2000%) and a fat. Standard curcumin supplements often ineffective without these.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None in small amounts. GI upset possible in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Turmeric is generally safe for pets. Some veterinarians use it as an anti-inflammatory supplement for dogs. Avoid large amounts. The staining properties are the main practical concern.

transplant.deep_note: Plant 2 inches deep with buds facing up. Wide, shallow planting preferred.

varieties.name: Alleppey
varieties.description: Most common commercial variety. High curcumin content. The standard for medicinal use.
varieties.notes: Best for medicinal use — highest curcumin.

varieties.name: Madras
varieties.description: Slightly faster than Alleppey. Good for culinary use.

varieties.name: Hawaiian
varieties.description: Mild flavor, less bitter. Good for smoothies and fresh use.

pests.name: Leaf Blotch
pests.desc: Brown spots on leaves in humid conditions.

name: Lemongrass
plant_type: Perennial tropical grass (zones 9–11) / Annual or container plant

season.start_indoors: Purchase stalks from grocery store and root in water, or buy plants
season.transplant: After last frost in warm soil
season.harvest_window: Throughout growing season once established. Harvest outer stalks continuously.

seed.desc: Easiest propagation: purchase fresh lemongrass stalks from Asian grocery store, trim to 6 inches, place in water on a sunny windowsill. Roots form in 2–3 weeks. Plant outdoors after last frost.

germination.desc: From seed: slow and unreliable. Rooting stalks in water is far superior.

seedling.desc: Establishes quickly in warm conditions. Grows into a substantial clump rapidly.

young.desc: Forms a dense clump of fragrant grass. Harvest outer stalks when pencil-thick at the base.

adult.desc: Large, dramatic clumps of 3–5 foot grass with intensely lemon-fragrant foliage. One plant produces dozens of stalks per season. Mosquito-repellent properties from the citronella oil content.

care.water: Consistent moisture during establishment. Somewhat drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum.
care.soil: Well-draining, fertile. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly during growing season.
care.notes: One of the most useful culinary herbs for Asian cooking — essential in Thai, Vietnamese, and Cambodian cuisine. Also a natural mosquito repellent — the leaves contain citronella oil. Easy to overwinter: pot up before frost, cut back by half, keep on a sunny windowsill in a warm room. Barely water in winter. Resume feeding and watering in spring.

container.notes: Classic container plant for northern gardeners. Dramatic on patios. Overwinter indoors.

propagation.desc: Buy fresh supermarket lemongrass, trim to 6 inches, place in water in sun. Roots form in 2–3 weeks. Plant in soil.
Divide established clumps in spring. Each division with several stalks and roots establishes quickly.

harvest.when: When outer stalks reach pencil thickness at the base — from 90 days.
harvest.how: Grasp outer stalk at base and pull downward firmly, or cut with knife at soil level. Use the white base (lower 4–6 inches). The upper green part used for tea and flavoring stocks (remove before eating).
harvest.storage: Refrigerate wrapped in plastic 2–3 weeks. Freeze trimmed stalks (use directly from frozen). Dry leaves for tea.
harvest.yield: Dozens of stalks per season from an established clump.

common_mistakes: Cold temperatures — any frost kills lemongrass. Bring containers in before frost.
Insufficient sun — needs full sun.
Shallow containers — needs room for large root system.
Not harvesting outer stalks — encourages continuous production.

seed_saving.type: Rarely sets seed in cultivation. Propagate by division.
seed_saving.harvest: Divide clumps each spring for propagation.
seed_saving.method: Division is the standard method.
seed_saving.notes: Simply divide clumps — no seed saving needed.

good.why: Identical tropical growing conditions.
Same tropical requirements.
Both love heat and sun. Mosquito-repellent combination.

culinary: Essential in Thai cooking: Tom Kha Gai (coconut soup), Tom Yum, green and red curry pastes, satay marinades. Vietnamese pho and soups. Lemongrass tea (steep dried or fresh leaves). Grilled fish and chicken. Lemongrass mojito and cocktails. The lower white bulb is finely sliced or pounded into pastes. The upper stalks used to flavor liquids.
medicinal: Citral — the primary essential oil compound — has antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antifungal properties. Lemongrass tea studied for: anxiety reduction, cholesterol lowering, anti-inflammatory effects. Citronella oil (from the leaves) is a proven mosquito repellent. Traditional use throughout Southeast Asia for fever, respiratory conditions, and digestive issues.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Cats: vomiting, lethargy from essential oil compounds. Dogs: usually mild GI upset only.
pet_toxicity.notes: Cats lack liver enzymes to process many essential oils including citronella/lemongrass compounds. Keep cats away from lemongrass plants. Dogs are less sensitive — small contact usually fine but don't allow eating. ASPCA lists lemongrass as toxic to cats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant divisions 1 inch deep. Place rooted stalk sections with roots just covered.

varieties.name: West Indian (C. citratus)
varieties.description: The common culinary lemongrass. Standard for cooking. The grocery store variety.

varieties.name: East Indian (C. flexuosus)
varieties.description: Higher citral content — more intensely lemon-scented. Preferred for essential oil production.
varieties.notes: More fragrant. Good for teas and aromatherapy.

varieties.name: Palmarosa (C. martinii)
varieties.description: Rose-scented cousin. Rosy, geranium-like fragrance. Used in perfumery and aromatherapy.

pests.name: Rust
pests.control: Improve air circulation. Remove affected leaves. Copper fungicide.

name: Horseradish

season.harvest_window: Fall through spring. Best after frost. Can harvest year-round but fall is peak.

seed.desc: Plant root sections (thong cuttings) 4–6 inches long at a 45-degree angle, 2–3 inches deep, thick end up. One plant yields many roots for replanting and eating.

germination.desc: Shoots emerge from root sections. Vigorous growth begins.

seedling.desc: Large, bold leaves emerge. Very vigorous growth.

young.desc: Substantial foliage. Roots expanding underground. Plant spreads by root offshoots.

adult.desc: Large root clump established. Harvest roots in fall for best flavor and heat. A single planting lasts indefinitely — horseradish is nearly indestructible once established.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade.
care.soil: Deep, loose, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. Deep soil produces straight, large roots.
care.spacing: 18–24 inches. PLANT IN A CONTAINED AREA — spreads aggressively by root.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: WARNING: Horseradish spreads aggressively by underground roots and is very difficult to eradicate once established. Plant in a dedicated bed, in a buried container, or at the garden's edge. Even tiny root pieces left in soil regrow. That said — it is virtually indestructible, extremely easy to grow, cold-hardy to zone 2, and the homegrown root is incomparably superior to any bottled horseradish product.

container.notes: Container growing is actually recommended to control spreading. Deep containers (18+ inches) produce best roots.

propagation.desc: Cut side roots (thongs) 4–6 inches long. Plant at 45-degree angle, thick end up, 2–3 inches deep. Angling ensures only the thick end produces shoots.

harvest.when: Fall after first frost for best flavor and heat. Can harvest year-round.
harvest.how: Dig roots with a garden fork. Large main root plus smaller lateral roots.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed roots 6+ months. Process immediately after washing — grate and mix with vinegar to preserve the heat compounds (which dissipate rapidly once grated).
harvest.yield: Large main root plus many lateral roots per plant annually.

common_mistakes: Not containing spreading — horseradish will take over a garden bed.
Waiting to process after grating — the heat compounds oxidize rapidly. Grate and immediately mix with vinegar.
Not harvesting regularly — periodic harvest keeps the plant productive.
Planting where you don't want a permanent plant — it IS permanent.

seed_saving.type: Rarely sets viable seed. Propagate by root division.
seed_saving.harvest: Save lateral root cuttings at harvest time.
seed_saving.method: Store root cuttings in damp sand in a cool location until planting.
seed_saving.drying: Do not dry — keep slightly moist.
seed_saving.notes: Simply save some lateral roots each fall — practically self-propagating.

good.why: Horseradish traditionally planted at corners of potato beds — said to deter Colorado potato beetle.
Horseradish makes an excellent weed-suppressing ground cover under established fruit trees.

bad.why: Horseradish's spreading roots can overtake smaller neighbors. Give it its own space.

culinary: The classic condiment for roast beef, prime rib, and smoked fish. Horseradish cream sauce. Cocktail sauce (mixed with ketchup). Bloody Mary. Prepared horseradish (grated root mixed with vinegar). Horseradish butter. Fresh grated over beets (Eastern European tradition). The heat compounds (isothiocyanates) are different from chili heat — they activate in the nasal passage rather than on the tongue.
medicinal: Glucosinolates (same family as mustard) break down to isothiocyanates — powerful antibacterial, antifungal, and potentially anticancer compounds. Traditional use for sinusitis and upper respiratory infections (the burning sensation clears sinuses). German Commission E approves horseradish for urinary tract infections (antibacterial). Contains more vitamin C than orange juice.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, and GI irritation. The burning sensation deters most pets naturally.
pet_toxicity.notes: Horseradish causes GI irritation in dogs and cats. The strong burning taste naturally deters most pets from eating it. Not severely toxic but keep pets from grazing on it.

transplant.deep_note: Plant 45-degree angle root cuttings with thick end up, 2–3 inches deep.
transplant.mulch: straw (but horseradish will grow through anything)

varieties.name: Bohemian
varieties.description: Most widely grown variety. Smooth, white-fleshed roots. Excellent heat and flavor.

varieties.name: Variegata
varieties.description: Ornamental variety with attractive cream-variegated leaves. Same culinary quality.

varieties.name: Big Top Western
varieties.description: Larger roots, consistent production. Good for commercial-scale harvesting.

pests.name: Flea Beetle
pests.control: Neem oil. Row covers on young plants.

pests.name: White Rust
pests.control: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation.

name: Camellia
growing_zones: 6–10 (C. japonica). Some varieties to zone 6 with protection.

season.harvest_window: Fall through spring depending on variety. Camellias bloom when almost nothing else does.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. From seed: 5–7 years to bloom, and named varieties don't come true.

germination.desc: Fresh seeds, soak 24 hours, sow in acidic medium.

seedling.desc: Very slow first year. Keep in protected location.

young.desc: Gradual growth. Beautiful glossy evergreen foliage year-round.

adult.desc: Spectacular flowers in fall, winter, or spring (depending on variety) when the garden is otherwise bare. One of the most beautiful flowering shrubs — large, perfect flowers in red, pink, white, or bicolor on glossy evergreen foliage. Lives 100+ years.

care.water: Consistent moisture — shallow roots dry quickly. Mulch deeply.
care.light: Part shade — morning sun, afternoon shade ideal. Deep shade reduces flowering.
care.soil: Acidic, well-draining, rich. pH 5.5–6.5. Same as azalea. Never lime.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer after flowering. Never after midsummer.
care.notes: C. sinensis is the tea plant — leaves used to produce all forms of tea (green, black, white, oolong). C. japonica is the ornamental species. Both need same care. Bud drop — the most common complaint — caused by drought stress, temperature fluctuation, or moving the plant while budded. Never move a camellia in bud.

container.notes: Excellent container plant in cold climates. Overwinter in a cool, frost-free, bright location (40–50°F). Keep somewhat dry but not desiccated.

propagation.desc: Take 3–4 inch cuttings in late summer. Dip in rooting hormone, root in acidic medium under mist or high humidity. Takes 6–8 weeks.

harvest.when: For C. sinensis (tea): harvest young leaves (top 2–3 leaves and bud) in spring.
harvest.how: Pinch young leaves. Process immediately for green tea (steam/dry) or allow to oxidize for black tea.
harvest.storage: Process fresh leaves for tea. Store dried tea in airtight container.
harvest.yield: A mature tea camellia produces several pounds of fresh leaves per season.

common_mistakes: Bud drop — caused by drought, temperature fluctuation, or root disturbance. Never move in bud.
Wrong soil pH — must be acidic.
Pruning after summer — removes next season's buds. Prune only immediately after flowering.
Too much sun — leaves scorch in full afternoon sun in warm climates.
Planting near concrete — lime raises pH.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Hybrids do not.
seed_saving.harvest: Round woody seed capsules in fall.
seed_saving.method: Soak seeds 24 hours. Sow in acidic medium.
seed_saving.viability: Short — sow within weeks of harvest.
seed_saving.notes: Named varieties must be propagated from cuttings.

good.why: Same acidic soil. Layered bloom sequence extends flowering season.
Same acidic requirements. Blooms at different times.
Naturalistic woodland combination.

culinary: C. sinensis is the tea plant. All tea — green, black, white, oolong, pu-erh — comes from this one species. Processing method determines tea type: green tea (steamed/dried without oxidation), black tea (fully oxidized), oolong (partially oxidized). Camellia oil from seeds used in East Asian cooking — high smoke point, mild flavor.
medicinal: Tea (C. sinensis) is one of the most researched beverage plants. L-theanine: amino acid unique to tea — promotes calm alertness, reduces anxiety without sedation. EGCG (epigallocatechin gallate): powerful antioxidant studied for cancer prevention, cardiovascular protection, weight management. Caffeine: well-documented cognitive enhancement. Green tea consumption associated with reduced cardiovascular disease and certain cancers in large epidemiological studies.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, increased heart rate from caffeine/theobromine if leaves eaten in quantity.
pet_toxicity.notes: The caffeine and theobromine in camellia leaves can cause toxicity in dogs and cats similar to chocolate (theobromine). Ornamental camellia flowers are generally considered safe. Keep pets from eating leaves of C. sinensis (tea plant) in quantity.

transplant.deep_note: Plant with crown at soil level. Never bury the root flare. Use acidic soil mix.
transplant.mulch: pine bark (acidic, 3 inches away from stem)

varieties.name: Autumn Spirit
varieties.description: Fall-blooming. Rose-pink semi-double flowers October–November. Very cold-hardy for a camellia.

varieties.name: April Kiss
varieties.description: Spring-blooming. Deep red single flowers. Hardy to zone 6b.

varieties.name: Setsugekka
varieties.description: White semi-double flowers with ruffled petals. Very free-blooming. One of the most beautiful camellias.

varieties.name: Korean Fire
varieties.description: Extremely cold-hardy (zone 6). Brilliant red flowers. Developed for northern gardens.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown or white bumps on stems — very common on camellias.
pests.control: Horticultural oil in late winter. Systemic insecticide for severe cases.

pests.name: Tea Scale
pests.desc: White cottony masses on undersides of leaves.

pests.name: Petal Blight
pests.desc: Flowers turn brown rapidly in wet weather.
pests.control: Remove infected flowers immediately. Improve air circulation.

name: Forsythia

season.harvest_window: March–April — one of the first flowering shrubs of spring. Blooms before leaves emerge.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Very easy to propagate from cuttings.

germination.desc: From cuttings: root easily in any moist medium.

seedling.desc: Moderate growth. Can reach 2–3 feet in first year.

young.desc: Vigorous growth. First blooms may appear.

adult.desc: Brilliant golden-yellow flowers covering bare stems in March and April — before any leaves, one of the very first signals of spring. A well-established forsythia is a spectacular, indestructible garden shrub that requires almost no care.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun for best bloom. Tolerates partial shade but flowers reduce.
care.soil: Adaptable — almost any well-draining soil. pH 6.0–8.0.
care.spacing: 5–10 feet depending on variety. Can be kept smaller by pruning.
care.fertilizer: None required — too rich causes lush growth, few flowers.
care.notes: One of the easiest flowering shrubs to grow. Virtually pest-free, disease-free, deer-resistant, and indestructible. The KEY: prune ONLY immediately after flowering (within 3–4 weeks) — forsythia blooms on old wood (previous year's growth). Pruning in fall or winter removes next year's buds. Cut old stems to the ground to rejuvenate. Force branches indoors in February by cutting and placing in warm water — they bloom within 2 weeks.

container.notes: Dwarf varieties work well in large containers.

propagation.desc: Take 6–8 inch cuttings in late fall/winter. Insert in moist medium. Roots by spring. One of the easiest shrubs to propagate.
Pin branch to ground. Roots readily wherever it touches soil.

harvest.when: Cut branches in late winter (February) for forcing indoors.
harvest.how: Cut branches with flower buds. Place immediately in warm water indoors. Flowers open within 1–2 weeks.
harvest.storage: Forced branches last 2 weeks in water. Cut branches in bloom last 5–7 days.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flowering branches on a mature shrub.

common_mistakes: Wrong pruning time — the single most common mistake. ONLY prune immediately after flowering. Never in fall or winter.
Too much shade — dramatically reduces flowering.
Overfertilizing — all foliage, no flowers.
Not rejuvenating old plants — remove 1/3 of oldest stems annually to keep productive.

seed_saving.type: Hybrid — does not breed true.
seed_saving.harvest: Small seed capsules in fall.
seed_saving.method: Propagate by cuttings — much faster and reliable than seed.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings are so easy there is no reason to grow from seed.

good.why: Classic spring combination — bloom simultaneously.
Both early spring bloomers. Good layered effect.
Forsythia provides backdrop for tulips and daffodils.

bad.why: Forsythia is a good garden citizen.

culinary: Flowers edible — used as spring garnish. Mild flavor. Forsythia syrup and cordials. Primarily ornamental.
medicinal: Traditional Chinese medicine uses Forsythia suspensa (lianqiao) — a related species — as one of its most important herbs for fever, inflammation, and infection. The dried fruit is an ingredient in many traditional formulations. Different from ornamental forsythia but related.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported.
pet_toxicity.notes: Forsythia is not listed as toxic to pets. Generally considered safe.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth.

varieties.name: Lynwood Gold
varieties.description: Upright, 8–10 feet. Masses of bright golden-yellow flowers. The most widely grown forsythia.
varieties.notes: Standard forsythia — most reliable and available.

varieties.name: Magical Gold
varieties.description: Compact, 3–4 feet. Same flowering performance in smaller plant.

varieties.name: New Hampshire Gold
varieties.description: Cold-hardy to zone 4. Reliable bloomer even after harsh winters.
varieties.notes: Best for cold climates — flower buds hardy where others lose buds to late frost.

varieties.name: Sunrise
varieties.description: Compact, mounded form. Good for smaller spaces.

pests.name: Practically none
pests.desc: Forsythia is remarkably pest and disease free — one of the most trouble-free shrubs available.

pests.name: Crown Gall
pests.control: Remove and destroy affected plants. Do not replant in same location.

name: Viburnum

season.harvest_window: Spring bloom (most species). Red, orange, or blue-black berries in fall. Some fragrant species bloom in winter.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Viburnums from seed are slow and variable.

germination.desc: Double dormancy — seeds need warm + cold stratification. Very slow.

seedling.desc: Very slow first year.

young.desc: Moderate growth. Beautiful foliage develops.

adult.desc: One of the most ecologically valuable native shrubs — flowers attract pollinators, berries feed dozens of bird species, and dense branching provides nesting cover. Four seasons of interest: spring flowers, summer foliage, fall berries and color, and winter structure.

care.water: Moderate — adaptable. Most species reasonably drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Most species perform well in both.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. Most species adaptable to a range of pH.
care.fertilizer: Light balanced fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: Viburnums are among the most ecologically valuable native shrubs in eastern North America. They support hundreds of native insect species and produce berries eaten by dozens of birds. Many species are fragrant. For most ornamental purposes, native viburnums (V. prunifolium, V. lentago, V. acerifolium) are preferred over Asian species. Plant at least 2 different species for maximum berry production.

container.min_size: 15 gallon for most species. Dwarf varieties 10 gallon.
container.notes: Compact species and cultivars work in containers.

propagation.desc: Late summer cuttings root moderately well in moist medium.
Pin flexible branch to ground. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Berries for birds — leave on plant. Berries for human use — after fully ripe (varies by species, some edible, some not).
harvest.how: Hand pick berries.
harvest.storage: Some species produce edible berries used in jams and wine. Most best left for wildlife.
harvest.yield: Heavy berry production on established plants.

common_mistakes: Planting single specimen expecting berries — most viburnums need cross-pollination from a different viburnum species or cultivar for good berry production.
Choosing Asian species over native — native viburnums provide superior ecological value.
Pruning at wrong time — prune only immediately after flowering.

seed_saving.type: Species breed true. Hybrids variable. Double dormancy required.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect berries when fully colored.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from berries. Warm stratify 3 months, then cold stratify 3 months.
seed_saving.notes: Very slow process — 2 years from seed to transplantable seedling.

good.why: Naturalistic planting combination providing habitat structure.
Both native, both providing berries for birds at different seasons.
Both native woodland plants.

bad.why: Viburnum is an excellent garden citizen.

culinary: V. lentago (nannyberry) and V. prunifolium (black haw) produce edible sweet berries — eaten fresh or used in jams, wine, and preserves. Most other species berries not palatable to humans. Black haw berries have a rich prune-like flavor when fully ripe.
medicinal: Viburnum prunifolium (black haw) bark used medicinally — contains viburnin and salicin (aspirin-related). Traditional uterine antispasmodic — still used by herbalists for menstrual cramps and threatened miscarriage. Studied for its antispasmodic properties. European Medicines Agency is reviewing data.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None.
pet_toxicity.notes: Most viburnum species are not toxic to pets. Generally considered safe. Some species berries may cause mild GI upset if eaten in large quantity.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Crown at soil level.

varieties.name: Arrowwood (V. dentatum)
varieties.description: Native to eastern North America. White flowers, blue-black berries. Outstanding fall color. Adaptable to sun or shade. Very wildlife-valuable.

varieties.name: Blackhaw (V. prunifolium)
varieties.description: Native. White flowers, blue-black edible berries with prune flavor. Small tree form to 15 feet. Excellent wildlife value. Edible berries.
varieties.notes: Best viburnum for edible berries and maximum wildlife value.

varieties.name: Korean Spice (V. carlesii)
varieties.description: Intensely fragrant pink-white flowers in spring — one of the most fragrant shrubs. Asian origin.

varieties.name: Snowball (V. opulus Roseum)
varieties.description: Classic snowball viburnum with large white flower balls. Sterile — no berries but spectacular flowers.
varieties.notes: Most showy flowers. Sterile so no wildlife value.

pests.name: Viburnum Leaf Beetle
pests.desc: Skeletonizes leaves — serious pest, especially on V. opulus and relatives.
pests.control: Destroy egg-laying sites on stems in winter. Neem oil. Insecticidal soap. Choose resistant species (V. prunifolium, V. lentago resistant).

name: Summersweet (Clethra)

season.harvest_window: July–August — blooms in midsummer when few other shrubs are flowering. One of the most important midsummer nectar shrubs.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Native clethra easy from cuttings and readily available.

germination.desc: Seeds sow in moist acidic medium. Surface sow — needs light.

seedling.desc: Moderate growth. Adaptable to wet and shaded conditions.

young.desc: Establishes readily. Spreads slowly by suckering.

adult.desc: One of the finest native shrubs — intensely fragrant white or pink flower spikes in midsummer fill the garden with spicy, clove-like fragrance. Tolerates wet soil and shade better than almost any other flowering shrub. Brilliant gold fall color. Native to the eastern US — excellent ecological value.

care.water: Loves moisture — one of the few flowering shrubs that thrives in consistently wet or boggy soil. Also tolerates normal conditions.
care.light: Part shade to full sun. More shade-tolerant than most flowering shrubs.
care.soil: Acidic, moist, high organic matter. pH 4.5–6.0. Thrives in wet conditions.
care.fertilizer: Light acidic fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: An ideal shrub for difficult spots — wet soil, shade, under trees. Also works in normal border conditions. The fragrance is extraordinary — one of the most intensely and pleasantly scented native shrubs, often compared to cloves and spices. The midsummer bloom fills a gap when few other shrubs are flowering. Bees cover it while in bloom.

container.notes: Works in large containers. Keep consistently moist.

propagation.desc: Early summer cuttings root readily in moist medium.
Dig rooted suckers from base of plant in spring. Replant immediately.

harvest.when: Cut flower spikes when half the florets are open.
harvest.how: Cut long stems early morning. Condition in water.
harvest.storage: Excellent cut flower — lasts 7–10 days. Intensely fragrant in arrangements.
harvest.yield: Dozens of flower spikes on an established plant.

common_mistakes: Not enough moisture — clethra prefers consistently moist conditions. It tolerates normal conditions but never thrives in dry sites.
Wrong soil pH — must be acidic.
Removing suckers — clethra naturally spreads. If spread is unwanted, remove suckers but otherwise allow natural spreading.

seed_saving.type: Species breeds true.
seed_saving.harvest: Tiny seed capsules persist through winter.
seed_saving.method: Surface sow on acidic moist medium.
seed_saving.notes: Propagation by suckers or cuttings is easier and faster.

good.why: Both love moist acidic conditions. Wonderful woodland combination.
Same acidic soil. Bloom at different times — extends the season.
Both love wet conditions. Both excellent pollinator plants.
Both late summer bloomers in moist sites.

bad.why: Clethra needs consistent moisture incompatible with drought-tolerant companions.

culinary: Not edible.
medicinal: Traditional Native American use as an astringent and tonic. Limited modern research.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None reported.
pet_toxicity.notes: Clethra is not listed as toxic to pets. Generally considered safe.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Add organic matter to soil. Keep consistently moist after planting.

varieties.name: Hummingbird
varieties.description: Compact — 3–4 feet. White flowers. The best dwarf clethra for small gardens and containers.

varieties.name: Ruby Spice
varieties.description: Deep rose-pink flowers — the most colorful clethra. Same intense fragrance. 4–6 feet.

varieties.name: Anne Bidwell
varieties.description: Very large white flower spikes. Vigorous grower. Excellent fragrance.

varieties.name: Sixteen Candles
varieties.description: Compact — 3–4 feet. White flowers. Uniform upright habit. Very reliable.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: In dry conditions — unusual for a moisture-loving shrub.
pests.control: Keep moist. Neem oil if severe.

pests.name: Leaf Spot
pests.control: Usually not severe. Improve air circulation.

name: Pieris (Andromeda)

season.harvest_window: March–April — cascading flower clusters appear before most spring shrubs. New foliage often brilliant red.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Slow from seed.

germination.desc: Surface sow on acidic medium. Slow.

seedling.desc: Very slow first year.

young.desc: Moderate growth. New growth often fiery red — one of the best features.

adult.desc: Beautiful evergreen shrub with cascading clusters of white or pink urn-shaped flowers in early spring, and spectacular red new growth that matures to green. A four-season shrub with something of interest year-round. Very long-lived.

care.water: Consistent moisture — shallow roots. Mulch deeply.
care.light: Part shade — morning sun, afternoon shade ideal. Tolerates full shade.
care.soil: Acidic, well-draining, high organic matter. pH 4.5–6.0. Same as azalea.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer immediately after flowering.
care.notes: Excellent companion for azaleas and rhododendrons — same soil requirements, overlapping bloom season. The red new growth is one of the finest features of any shrub — it emerges brilliant red and slowly matures to green over several weeks.

container.notes: Good container plant. Use acidic potting mix.

propagation.desc: Late summer cuttings in acidic medium with rooting hormone. Takes 8–10 weeks.
Pin flexible branch to soil. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Cut branches with flowers when half open.
harvest.how: Cut long branches. Condition in cool water.
harvest.storage: Excellent cut branches — 7–10 days.
harvest.yield: Many flowering branches on established plants.

common_mistakes: Wrong soil pH — must be acidic.
Too much sun — leaves scorch.
Planting near concrete — lime raises pH.
Lace bug damage — most serious pest in sunny, dry conditions.

seed_saving.type: Hybrids don't come true.
seed_saving.harvest: Tiny capsules in fall.
seed_saving.method: Surface sow on acidic medium.
seed_saving.notes: Propagate from cuttings for named varieties.

good.why: Same acidic soil. Sequential bloom extends spring display.
Same family, same requirements.
Same conditions. Bloom overlap.

culinary: TOXIC — all parts. Do not eat.
medicinal: Contains grayanotoxins — same as azalea and rhododendron. Not used medicinally.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, drooling, weakness, heart rate abnormalities — same as azalea.
pet_toxicity.notes: Pieris contains the same grayanotoxins as azalea and rhododendron. All parts severely toxic to dogs and cats. Keep strictly away from all pets.

transplant.deep_note: Crown at soil level — never bury root ball. Same planting rules as azalea.

varieties.name: Mountain Fire
varieties.description: Brilliant fire-red new growth maturing to glossy green. White flowers. One of the most ornamental pieris for foliage effect.

varieties.name: Valley Rose
varieties.description: Deep rose-pink flowers — most colorful pieris in bloom. Good red new growth.

varieties.name: Cavatine
varieties.description: Dwarf compact form — 2–3 feet. White flowers. Perfect for small spaces.

varieties.name: Brouwer's Beauty
varieties.description: Excellent disease resistance. White flowers. Reliable performer. Cold-hardy.

pests.name: Lace Bug
pests.desc: Stippled, silvery leaves — worst in full sun. Most serious pieris pest.
pests.control: Plant in shade. Insecticidal soap on undersides of leaves. Neem oil.

pests.name: Phytophthora Root Rot
pests.control: Improve drainage. No cure once severe.

name: Spirea

season.harvest_window: Spring (bridal wreath types) or summer (Japanese spirea types). Some rebloom.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Very easy to propagate from cuttings.

germination.desc: Easy from cuttings. Seed germination variable.

seedling.desc: Moderate growth. Easy to establish.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Often blooms in year 2.

adult.desc: One of the easiest and most adaptable flowering shrubs. Cascading white flower clusters (spring types) or flat-topped pink/red clusters (summer types) cover the plant. Extremely reliable, virtually pest-free, and tolerates a wide range of conditions.

varieties.name: Pretoria (Bengal Tiger)
varieties.description: Yellow-striped green leaves with orange flowers.

varieties.name: Wyoming
varieties.description: Deep bronze-purple foliage with orange flowers.

varieties.name: Cleopatra
varieties.description: Mottled leaves with mixed bicolor flowers on same plant — fascinating.
varieties.notes: Most unusual — flowers change on a single plant.

name: Pothos

season.harvest_window: Continuous foliage year-round

seed.desc: Propagate from stem cuttings — one of the easiest plants to propagate. Place cuttings in water until roots form.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in water in 1–2 weeks.

seedling.desc: New growth emerges quickly from rooted cuttings.

young.desc: Establishes rapidly. Vining stems begin trailing.

adult.desc: Long trailing vines with heart-shaped leaves in green, variegated yellow, white, or neon green. Nearly indestructible. Tolerates neglect, low light, and irregular watering better than almost any other houseplant. NASA lists as an air-purifying plant.

care.water: Allow top 2 inches of soil to dry between waterings. Tolerates drought well — yellowing leaves signal overwatering, not underwatering.
care.light: Low to bright indirect light. Variegated varieties need more light to maintain colour. Direct sun scorches leaves.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix. pH 6.0–6.5.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Train on a moss pole for larger leaves.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly during spring and summer. None in winter.
care.notes: The most beginner-friendly houseplant. Nearly impossible to kill. Trailing stems root at every node — propagate endlessly for free plants. ALL PARTS TOXIC — keep away from pets and children (calcium oxalate crystals). Wipe leaves monthly to remove dust. In very low light, variegated leaves revert to solid green.

container.notes: Excellent in hanging baskets. Can trail several feet. Train up a moss pole for larger leaves.

propagation.desc: Cut a 4–6 inch stem below a node. Place in water on a bright windowsill. Roots form in 1–2 weeks. Pot when roots reach 1 inch.
Dip cut end in rooting hormone, insert in moist potting mix. Roots in 3–4 weeks.

harvest.when: Trim long vines any time to propagate or tidy.
harvest.how: Cut just below a node with clean scissors.
harvest.storage: Root cuttings immediately in water or soil.
harvest.yield: Unlimited free plants from cuttings.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — yellow leaves with soggy soil means too much water. Wait longer between waterings.
Direct sun — scorches leaves. Indirect or low light only.
Cold drafts — below 50°F causes damage. Keep away from cold windows in winter.
Not propagating — pothos cuttings in water make excellent free gifts.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Stem cuttings in water.
seed_saving.notes: One of the easiest plants to propagate.

good.why: Both tolerant of similar low-light conditions.
Similar care requirements. Good mix of trailing habits.

bad.why: Pothos is an excellent companion plant.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible.
medicinal: NASA Clean Air Study lists pothos as removing formaldehyde, benzene, and carbon monoxide from indoor air.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Oral irritation, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists pothos as toxic. Causes oral irritation and GI upset. Not usually fatal but keep pets away. One of the most common pet toxicity calls to vets — extremely common houseplant.

transplant.deep_note: Repot when roots grow out of drainage holes or the plant becomes rootbound — every 1–2 years. Go up only one pot size.

varieties.name: Golden Pothos
varieties.description: Classic green leaves with yellow variegation. Most common. Very tolerant.

varieties.name: Marble Queen
varieties.description: White and green marbled variegation. Slower growing. Needs more light for variegation.

varieties.name: Neon Pothos
varieties.description: Bright chartreuse-yellow solid leaves. Glows in a dark room.

varieties.name: N'Joy
varieties.description: Crisp white and green patches. More compact. Excellent variegation retention.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.desc: White cottony clusters at leaf joints.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab. Neem oil.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Let dry completely, remove rotten roots, repot in fresh dry mix.

pests.name: Scale
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton. Neem oil.

name: Snake Plant (Sansevieria)

season.transplant: Repot every 2–3 years or when rootbound
season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Propagate by division or leaf cuttings. Division is fastest — pull apart offset pups from the mother plant.

germination.desc: Leaf cuttings take 4–8 weeks to form roots. Division establishes in a few weeks.

seedling.desc: New pups (offsets) emerge from base. Leaf cuttings grow new plants slowly.

young.desc: Upright sword-shaped leaves develop.

adult.desc: Architectural upright leaves with yellow edges or silver-green banding. One of the most tolerant houseplants — survives weeks without water, thrives in low light, and tolerates temperature fluctuations. NASA lists as one of the best air-purifying plants.

care.water: VERY drought tolerant — water only when soil is completely dry. In winter: once a month or less. Overwatering is the only real way to kill it.
care.light: Low to bright indirect light. Tolerates very low light but grows fastest in bright indirect.
care.soil: Well-draining cactus or succulent mix. Must not hold moisture.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Produces pups (offsets) around the base.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer once or twice during spring/summer only. Never in winter.
care.notes: The most indestructible houseplant. Perfect for beginners, travelers, or anyone who forgets to water. NEVER let water sit in the crown of the leaves — causes rot. Toxic to pets. The plant formerly known as Sansevieria — reclassified as Dracaena in 2017.

container.min_size: Any pot with drainage. Heavy pots prevent tipping.
container.notes: Choose heavy ceramic or terracotta to prevent tall plants tipping. Terracotta allows soil to dry faster — ideal for snake plants.

propagation.desc: Remove plant from pot. Pull or cut apart 'pups' (offsets) from the base. Each pup with roots can be potted separately.

Cut a leaf into 3–4 inch sections. Allow cut ends to dry 24 hours. Insert right-side-up in sandy mix. Roots in 4–8 weeks. NOTE: variegated varieties revert to green with this method — divide for true-to-type plants.

harvest.when: Propagate pups when they reach 3–4 inches tall.
harvest.how: Remove plant from pot, separate pups with a clean knife.
harvest.storage: Pot pups immediately or allow cut surfaces to callous 24 hours.
harvest.yield: One plant produces many pups over time.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the only consistent killer of snake plants. When in doubt, don't water.
Water in the leaf crown — causes crown rot, kills the plant.
Too heavy a pot that prevents tilting when rootbound — use drainage check instead.
Repotting too often — snake plants prefer being rootbound and bloom when stressed.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by division or cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A — propagate by division.
seed_saving.method: Division of pups.
seed_saving.drying: Allow cut surfaces to callous 24 hours before potting.
seed_saving.notes: Division maintains variety; leaf cuttings cause variegated types to revert.

good.why: Both tolerate low light and similar watering neglect.
Both extremely drought tolerant. Good drought-neglect duo.

bad.why: Snake plant's dry needs are incompatible with humidity-loving plants.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible.
medicinal: NASA Clean Air Study: one of the most effective plants for removing formaldehyde, xylene, benzene, toluene, and trichloroethylene from indoor air. One of the few plants that converts CO2 to oxygen at night — traditionally recommended for bedrooms.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists snake plant as toxic. Saponins cause GI upset. Rarely severe but keep pets away.

transplant.deep_note: Repot only when severely rootbound — every 2–3 years. Use fast-draining succulent mix. Go up only one pot size.

varieties.name: Laurentii
varieties.description: Classic yellow-edged sword leaves. Most recognizable snake plant.

varieties.name: Moonshine
varieties.description: Soft silvery-pale green leaves. Very architectural.

varieties.name: Cylindrica (African Spear)
varieties.description: Round cylindrical leaves instead of flat. Dramatic architectural form.

varieties.name: Hahnii (Bird's Nest)
varieties.description: Low rosette form — 6 inches tall. Perfect for small spaces.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Allow to dry completely. Remove rotten roots. Repot in dry cactus mix.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.control: Wipe leaves with damp cloth. Neem oil.

name: Peace Lily

season.harvest_window: Flowers typically spring through summer. Some rebloom in fall.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagate by division of established clumps.

germination.desc: Division of clumps establishes quickly.

seedling.desc: New growth from divisions emerges.

young.desc: Dark glossy leaves develop. Plant establishes.

adult.desc: Dark glossy oval leaves with elegant white spathe flowers (the white 'petal' is actually a modified leaf — a spathe — surrounding the tiny true flowers on the spadix). One of the very few houseplants that blooms reliably in low light. Droops dramatically when thirsty — a useful watering indicator. SEVERELY TOXIC.

care.water: Keep evenly moist — peace lilies are one of the few houseplants that appreciate consistently moist (not wet) soil. They wilt dramatically when dry and recover quickly when watered. Use this drooping as a watering reminder.
care.light: Low to medium indirect light. One of the best true low-light flowering plants. Direct sun causes leaf scorch and brown tips.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining potting mix. pH 5.8–6.5.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer every 6 weeks during spring and summer.
care.notes: Brown leaf tips are very common — caused by fluoride in tap water, low humidity, or fertilizer salts. Use filtered or distilled water if tip burn is a problem. To promote rebloom: move to brighter indirect light for 2–3 months. The dramatic wilt is alarming but non-damaging — the plant recovers fully within hours of watering. SEVERELY TOXIC to pets and children.

container.notes: Choose pots without drainage holes only if you are very careful about watering — drainage pots strongly recommended.

propagation.desc: Remove from pot. Pull apart or cut clumps into sections, each with several healthy leaves and roots. Pot separately.

harvest.when: Cut flower spathes for arrangements when fully open.
harvest.how: Cut stems at base.
harvest.storage: 7–10 days in water.
harvest.yield: Multiple flowers per season on established plants.

common_mistakes: Brown leaf tips — use filtered water and increase humidity.
Direct sun — scorches leaves rapidly.
Not enough light to bloom — move to brighter location to stimulate flowering.
Ignoring the dramatic wilt — it looks alarming but recovers quickly. Just water.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by division.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Division of clumps.
seed_saving.notes: Division is the only practical propagation method.

good.why: Both low-light lovers.
Both prefer humid, shaded conditions.

bad.why: Peace lily needs moisture; succulents need drought.

culinary: SEVERELY TOXIC — do not eat.
medicinal: NASA Clean Air Study: top performer for removing ammonia, formaldehyde, trichloroethylene, benzene, and xylene from indoor air. One of the most effective air-purifying houseplants.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Burning and irritation of mouth and throat, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists peace lily as toxic to dogs and cats. Calcium oxalate crystals cause significant oral pain and irritation. Not usually fatal but very uncomfortable. Keep strictly away from pets.

transplant.deep_note: Repot when roots circle the pot or emerge from drainage holes — every 1–2 years. Spring is ideal.

varieties.name: Wallisii (standard)
varieties.description: Classic peace lily — medium size, abundant flowers, excellent air purifier.

varieties.name: Sensation (Mauna Loa)
varieties.description: Giant variety — leaves to 20 inches wide. Very dramatic.
varieties.notes: Largest peace lily for dramatic effect.

varieties.name: Domino
varieties.description: Variegated green and white leaves. More unusual appearance.

varieties.name: Piccolino
varieties.description: Dwarf — 10 inches. Perfect for small spaces.

name: ZZ Plant

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Propagate by division of rhizomes or by single leaf cuttings (extremely slow — 6–9 months).

germination.desc: Division establishes in a few weeks. Leaf cuttings very slow.

seedling.desc: Very slow growth — ZZ plants are among the slowest-growing houseplants.

young.desc: New stems emerge from the underground rhizome.

adult.desc: Architectural glossy dark green compound leaves on graceful arching stems. Nearly indestructible — survives months of neglect. Rhizomes store water like a succulent. Thrives in low light. One of the most stylish and easy houseplants. Historically rare and expensive; now widely available.

care.water: Very drought tolerant — water only when soil is almost completely dry. Every 2–4 weeks in growing season, every 6–8 weeks in winter. Overwatering is the only real problem.
care.light: Low to bright indirect light. One of the best true low-light plants. Survives in offices with only fluorescent light.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix or cactus mix. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer once or twice in spring/summer. Never in winter.
care.notes: The rhizomes store water like a camel — this is why it survives such extreme neglect. Do NOT mist — ZZ plants do not need or appreciate high humidity. Wipe glossy leaves monthly for best appearance. The leaves are extremely shiny naturally — no leaf-shine products needed. ALL PARTS TOXIC.

container.notes: Terracotta or unglazed pots help prevent overwatering.

propagation.desc: Remove from pot. Divide the rhizome cluster. Each section needs at least one stem. Pot in dry mix and water sparingly.
Insert individual leaves in moist mix. A tiny rhizome forms at the base over 6–9 months. Very slow but satisfying.

harvest.when: Propagate by division any time.
harvest.how: Remove from pot, divide rhizomes.
harvest.storage: Allow cut rhizome surfaces to callous 24 hours before potting.
harvest.yield: One plant produces many rhizome divisions over time.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — by far the most common cause of ZZ plant death. Less water than you think.
Too much direct sun — leaves yellow and get sunburned.
Fertilizing in winter — causes weak spindly growth.
Expecting fast growth — ZZ plants are very slow. Be patient.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by division or leaf cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Rhizome division is standard.
seed_saving.notes: Leaf cuttings are slow but rewarding.

good.why: Both extremely drought tolerant. Perfect neglect-proof duo.
Both low-light tolerant.

bad.why: ZZ plant's drought preference is incompatible.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible.
medicinal: Traditional use in East Africa — leaf juice applied to ear for pain relief. Rhizomes used as an anti-inflammatory poultice. Not in Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, oral irritation.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists ZZ plant as toxic. Calcium oxalate crystals cause irritation. Not severely dangerous but keep pets away. Wash hands after handling — the sap can irritate skin.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 2–3 years or when rhizomes push the plant out of the pot. Use well-draining mix.

varieties.name: Standard (green)
varieties.description: Classic glossy dark green. The most tolerant and most available.

varieties.name: Raven (ZZ Raven)
varieties.description: Near-black leaves — one of the most dramatic houseplants. New growth emerges bright green and darkens.
varieties.notes: Most dramatic colour. Highly sought after.

varieties.name: Zamicro
varieties.description: Dwarf compact form. Perfect for small spaces.

varieties.name: Variegata
varieties.description: Cream and green variegated leaves. Rare and slow-growing.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Let dry completely. Remove rotten roots. Repot in dry cactus mix.

name: Spider Plant

season.harvest_window: Year-round. Produces 'spiderettes' on runners throughout the year.

seed.desc: Propagate from 'spiderettes' — the small plantlets that dangle on long runners from the mother plant. The easiest propagation in all of houseplants.

germination.desc: Spiderettes root in water in 1–2 weeks.

seedling.desc: Rooted spiderettes establish quickly in potting mix.

young.desc: Arching leaves develop. Runners begin to appear.

adult.desc: Fountaining rosette of arching green and white striped leaves with long runners bearing dozens of spiderettes. Extremely prolific — one plant produces unlimited free babies. Pet-safe (rare for houseplants). NASA air purifier. Virtually indestructible.

care.water: Moderate — allow top inch to dry between waterings. More drought tolerant than appearance suggests. Reduce in winter.
care.light: Bright to medium indirect light. Tolerates lower light but loses variegation. Avoid direct sun.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix. pH 6.0–6.5.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Excellent in hanging baskets.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer every 2 weeks during growing season.
care.notes: Brown leaf tips are very common — caused by fluoride in tap water, low humidity, or fertilizer. Use rainwater or filtered water if tip burn is a problem. One of the only common houseplants that is pet-safe. One plant can produce 50–100 spiderettes per year — perfect for giving away. Becomes rootbound quickly and benefits from annual repotting.

container.notes: Outstanding hanging basket plant — the runners and spiderettes cascade dramatically.

propagation.desc: The easiest propagation method of any houseplant — simply pin a spiderette to moist soil or place in water. Roots in 1–2 weeks.
Divide the main plant at repotting time.

harvest.when: Harvest spiderettes when they have tiny root nubs visible.
harvest.how: Pin to moist soil while still attached to runner, or snip off and place in water.
harvest.storage: Root immediately.
harvest.yield: One plant produces dozens of spiderettes per year.

common_mistakes: Brown leaf tips — switch to filtered water and increase humidity.
Too little light for good variegation — variegated types need medium to bright indirect light.
Potbound neglect — spider plants benefit from annual repotting.
Not propagating — the spiderettes are a constant resource. Root and share.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by spiderettes — the easiest method in houseplants.
seed_saving.harvest: Harvest spiderettes when root nubs appear.
seed_saving.method: Water or soil rooting.
seed_saving.notes: Endless free plants.

good.why: Both easy, both air purifying.
Both NASA air purifiers with similar care.

culinary: Not edible.
medicinal: NASA Clean Air Study: removes formaldehyde and xylene from indoor air. Traditionally used in Chinese medicine as a wound-healing herb.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none toxic — cats may eat it compulsively
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Cats are mildly attracted to spider plants (similar to catnip effect). May cause mild vomiting if eaten in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: One of the very few common houseplants considered pet-safe. Cats may be attracted and may experience mild stomach upset if they eat large quantities — the hallucinogenic compounds are very mild. Not dangerous.

transplant.deep_note: Repot annually or when roots overflow the pot. The fleshy white roots are normal and store water.

varieties.name: Vittatum
varieties.description: Green leaves with a central white stripe. Classic spider plant. Most common.

varieties.name: Variegatum (Reverse)
varieties.description: White edges with green center — reverse of Vittatum. Very elegant.

varieties.name: Solid Green
varieties.description: All-green no variegation. More tolerant of low light than variegated types.

varieties.name: Curly (Bonnie)
varieties.description: Curly, twisted leaves. More compact. Very unusual appearance.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.control: Increase humidity. Blast with water. Neem oil.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown bumps on stems and leaf bases.

name: Rubber Tree

season.transplant: Repot every 1–2 years when young, less often when mature
season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagate from stem cuttings.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in 4–6 weeks in moist mix.

seedling.desc: New growth from cuttings develops slowly.

young.desc: Large glossy leaves develop. Upright growth begins.

adult.desc: Bold upright tree with enormous glossy leaves in deep green, burgundy, or tricolor. Can reach ceiling height indoors (6–10 feet). One of the most dramatic statement houseplants. Relatively easy to maintain. The milky latex sap is the source of natural rubber — historically one of the most economically important plants.

care.water: Allow top inch to dry between waterings. More drought tolerant than appearance suggests. Yellow leaves signal overwatering.
care.light: Bright indirect light for best growth and leaf colour. Tolerates medium indirect but grows slowly. Avoid direct sun and dark corners.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Allow room for a large plant.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly during spring and summer.
care.notes: Rubber trees are fickle about being moved — they drop leaves after being relocated. Once you find the right spot, leave it there. Wipe large glossy leaves monthly with a damp cloth. The milky white sap (latex) causes skin irritation and is toxic — wear gloves when pruning. To encourage branching: nick the stem just above a node.

container.min_size: 10-inch pot minimum. Grows into large pots over time.
container.notes: Heavy pots prevent tipping as the plant grows large.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch tip cuttings. Allow sap to dry 1 hour (or rinse with warm water). Dip in rooting hormone. Root in moist mix with bottom heat. Takes 4–6 weeks.
Score the stem, wrap with moist sphagnum moss and plastic wrap. Roots form in the moss in 4–8 weeks. Cut below the roots and pot.

harvest.when: Trim for shape any time. Wear gloves — sap irritates skin.
harvest.how: Cut with clean sharp pruners. Allow sap to dry or rinse with warm water.
harvest.storage: Root tip cuttings immediately.
harvest.yield: Can take regular tip cuttings to propagate.

common_mistakes: Moving the plant — rubber trees drop leaves after being moved. Find a spot and leave it.
Overwatering — yellow lower leaves signal too much water.
Low light — loses colour and grows slowly. Bright indirect is ideal.
Sap contact without gloves — causes skin irritation.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by cuttings or air layering.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Stem cuttings or air layering.
seed_saving.drying: Allow sap to dry before rooting.
seed_saving.notes: Air layering produces the largest divisions quickly.

good.why: Both architectural, both low-maintenance.
Trailing pothos at the base complements the rubber tree's height.

culinary: TOXIC — the latex sap is toxic. Not edible.
medicinal: Natural rubber from Hevea brasiliensis (a related tree) is the source of medical-grade latex for gloves, catheters, and many medical devices. F. elastica sap has traditional wound-healing use in its native Asia.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, skin irritation from latex sap.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists rubber plant as mildly toxic. The latex sap causes GI upset if eaten and skin irritation on contact. Keep pets from chewing the leaves and stems.

transplant.deep_note: Repot in spring when rootbound — every 1–2 years when young, less when mature. Go up one pot size. Minimize disturbance to avoid leaf drop.

varieties.name: Robusta (standard green)
varieties.description: Classic deep green glossy leaves. Most available and most tolerant.

varieties.name: Burgundy
varieties.description: Almost black burgundy-dark leaves. Very dramatic. More tolerant of lower light than variegated types.

varieties.name: Tineke
varieties.description: Cream, green, and pink variegated. Stunning but needs brighter light for variegation.

varieties.name: Ruby
varieties.description: Deep red-pink variegation. Extraordinary colour. Rare.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown waxy bumps on stems and leaf undersides.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton. Horticultural oil.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.desc: Fine webbing in dry indoor conditions.

name: Philodendron

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Purchase plant. Propagate from stem cuttings.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in water in 2–3 weeks.

seedling.desc: New growth emerges from rooted cuttings.

young.desc: Heart-shaped or large lobed leaves develop depending on species.

adult.desc: Two main types: heartleaf philodendron (P. hederaceum) — trailing/climbing, easy, heart-shaped leaves, similar to pothos; split-leaf philodendron (P. bipinnatifidum, formerly Monstera — though true Monstera is a different genus) — dramatic large deeply lobed leaves. Both are easy, forgiving, and one of the most popular houseplant families.

care.water: Allow top inch to dry between waterings. Very similar to pothos. More forgiving of drought than overwatering.
care.light: Medium to bright indirect light. Heartleaf tolerates lower light. Split-leaf needs bright indirect for large leaves.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix. pH 5.0–6.0.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Provide a moss pole for climbing types.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly during growing season.
care.notes: Nearly as easy as pothos. Yellow leaves signal overwatering. Heartleaf philodendron can trail or climb — provide a moss pole for larger leaves. Wipe leaves monthly. Very fast grower in good conditions. ALL PARTS TOXIC.

container.notes: Excellent in hanging baskets (heartleaf). Large floor containers for split-leaf.

propagation.desc: Cut below a node. Place in water. Roots in 2–3 weeks. One of the easiest houseplant propagations.
Dip in rooting hormone. Insert in moist mix. Roots in 3–4 weeks.

harvest.when: Propagate stem cuttings any time.
harvest.how: Cut just below a node with clean scissors.
harvest.storage: Root in water immediately.
harvest.yield: Unlimited cuttings.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — yellowing leaves with wet soil.
Too little light for split-leaf types — need bright indirect for large leaves.
No climbing support — heartleaf develops much larger leaves when given a moss pole.
Cold temperatures — below 55°F causes damage.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Stem cuttings in water.
seed_saving.notes: One of the easiest houseplant propagations.

good.why: Nearly identical care. Good mixed tropical display.
Similar light and water preferences.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible.
medicinal: Traditional use in tropical medicine for various conditions. Not in Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Oral irritation, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists philodendron as toxic. Calcium oxalate crystals cause significant oral irritation. One of the most common pet toxicity plants due to widespread use.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 1–2 years when rootbound. Spring is ideal.

varieties.name: Heartleaf (P. hederaceum)
varieties.description: Classic trailing/climbing type. Heart-shaped glossy leaves. Very tolerant of neglect. The most common philodendron.

varieties.name: Brasil
varieties.description: Heartleaf with yellow variegation down the center. Very ornamental.

varieties.name: Micans
varieties.description: Velvety textured heart-shaped leaves in deep green-bronze. Highly sought after.

varieties.name: Xanadu
varieties.description: Compact split-leaf type — deeply lobed leaves, 2–3 feet tall, non-climbing. Excellent floor plant.

name: Aloe Vera

season.transplant: Repot when pups crowd the pot — every 2–3 years
season.harvest_window: Year-round gel harvest from mature outer leaves

seed.desc: Purchase plant. Propagate from pups (offsets) that appear around the base.

germination.desc: Pups removed and potted establish in a few weeks.

seedling.desc: Removed pups establish slowly.

young.desc: Fleshy spiky leaves develop in a rosette.

adult.desc: Rosette of thick fleshy spiky green leaves filled with soothing clear gel. One of the most useful houseplants — the gel has documented wound-healing and burn-soothing properties. Produces tall yellow flower spikes when mature and in bright light. Extremely drought tolerant. Produces many pups over time.

care.water: VERY drought tolerant — water only when soil is completely dry (every 2–4 weeks). In winter: once a month. Overwatering causes root rot and is the primary killer of aloe.
care.light: Bright indirect to direct sun. Aloe can handle more direct sun than most houseplants — a south-facing window is ideal.
care.soil: Cactus/succulent mix. Excellent drainage is essential. pH 7.0–8.5.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Pups appear around the base.
care.fertilizer: Diluted balanced fertilizer once in spring. None in winter. Does not need heavy feeding.
care.notes: The gel inside the leaves is a well-documented first-aid plant — apply fresh gel from a cut leaf to minor burns, sunburn, and skin irritation. Do NOT eat the latex (the yellow layer between the skin and gel) — this is a strong laxative. The clear inner gel is generally safe for skin use.

container.min_size: 6-inch wide pot — aloe spreads more than it grows tall.
container.notes: Unglazed terracotta is ideal — allows the soil to dry quickly. Shallow wide pots preferred over deep narrow ones.

propagation.desc: Gently remove pups from around the base. Allow cut surfaces to callous 24–48 hours. Plant in dry cactus mix. Wait 1 week before first watering.

harvest.when: Harvest outer leaves only from mature plants (at least 3–4 years old). Choose thick outer leaves.
harvest.how: Cut an outer leaf at the base with a clean knife. Slice off the spiky edges. Split the leaf and scoop out the clear gel. Discard the yellow latex layer.
harvest.storage: Fresh gel can be refrigerated 1–2 weeks in a sealed container. Freeze in ice cube trays for longer storage.
harvest.yield: Several leaves per year from a mature plant without damaging it.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the #1 killer. When in doubt, don't water.
No drainage — aloe in a pot without drainage holes will die.
Dark conditions — aloe needs bright light. Low light causes it to slowly stretch and weaken.
Harvesting leaves from young plants — wait until the plant has at least 12 mature leaves.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by pup division.
seed_saving.harvest: Harvest pups when they are 3–4 inches tall.
seed_saving.method: Remove from base, callous, and pot.
seed_saving.drying: Callous cut surface 24–48 hours before potting.
seed_saving.notes: One plant produces many pups over years.
