good.why: Both succulents, both drought tolerant, both architectural.
Both succulents needing the same care.

bad.why: Aloe needs completely dry conditions between waterings.

culinary: The clear inner gel is used in some food and beverage products. The yellow latex layer is a laxative — do not consume. Not generally considered a culinary plant.
medicinal: One of the most extensively studied medicinal plants. Clinical evidence for: wound healing (minor burns, sunburn, abrasions) — the gel contains acemannan which accelerates wound healing. Anti-inflammatory compounds (emodin, aloe-emodin). Moisturizing properties well documented. Topical use for psoriasis and eczema supported by several clinical trials. Oral aloe (the latex) is a powerful laxative — used for constipation historically but now discouraged due to potential kidney damage with long-term use.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: gel and latex — the latex (yellow layer) is most toxic
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, loss of appetite, changes in urine color.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists aloe vera as toxic to dogs and cats. The saponins and anthraquinones in the latex cause GI irritation. The clear gel is less toxic but still not recommended for pets. Keep pets from chewing aloe leaves.

transplant.deep_note: Plant in wide shallow pots. The crown (base of the leaves) should be at soil level. Cactus mix or add 50% perlite to regular potting mix.
transplant.mulch: coarse sand or gravel (top dressing to prevent moisture near crown)

varieties.name: Aloe vera (Barbadensis)
varieties.description: Standard medicinal aloe. The most gel-productive variety. Most widely available.

varieties.name: Aloe arborescens
varieties.description: Tree aloe — more branches, smaller leaves. More cold-hardy (zone 7). Also medicinal.

varieties.name: Aloe aristata
varieties.description: Lace aloe — compact, dark green with white spots. More tolerant of lower light.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Allow to dry completely. Remove rotten roots. Repot in dry cactus mix. May not recover if severe.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol. Repot and inspect roots.

name: Jade Plant

season.transplant: Repot every 2–3 years or when rootbound
season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage. White star-shaped flowers in winter on mature plants.

seed.desc: Purchase plant or take stem/leaf cuttings. One of the easiest succulent cuttings.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in 2–3 weeks in dry mix.

seedling.desc: Slow growth — jade plants are among the slowest-growing houseplants.

young.desc: Very slow growth over years — a 3-inch plant can take 5 years to reach 12 inches.

adult.desc: Eventually becomes a small tree-like succulent with thick woody trunk and jade-green oval leaves. Can live 70–100+ years. Heirloom plants passed between generations. Produces clusters of tiny white star-shaped flowers in winter when mature and stressed by cool temperatures. In parts of South Africa, wild jade plants form small forests.

care.water: VERY drought tolerant — water thoroughly, then allow to dry completely. Every 2–3 weeks in summer, every 4–6 weeks in winter. Overwatering is the primary killer.
care.light: Bright light — 4+ hours of direct sun or very bright indirect. Low light causes weak, leggy growth.
care.soil: Cactus/succulent mix. Excellent drainage essential.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Choose heavy pots to prevent tipping.
care.fertilizer: Diluted balanced fertilizer once in spring and once in summer. Never in winter.
care.notes: Jade plants are incredibly long-lived — some specimens are 50–100 years old. They are often passed as family heirlooms. To encourage flowering: provide cool temperatures (50–55°F) at night in autumn and reduce watering. The thick trunk is a water reservoir. Do not allow water to sit in the leaf axils — causes rot.

container.notes: Choose heavy terracotta or ceramic to prevent tipping as the plant becomes top-heavy. Terracotta dries faster — ideal for succulents.

propagation.desc: Cut a 3–4 inch stem. Allow cut end to dry/callous 24–48 hours. Insert in dry cactus mix. Do not water for 1 week. Roots in 3–4 weeks.
Remove a healthy leaf cleanly. Allow to callous. Lay on dry cactus mix. A tiny new plant grows from the leaf base in 4–8 weeks.

harvest.when: Propagate stem cuttings any time.
harvest.how: Cut with clean scissors. Allow to callous before potting.
harvest.storage: Callous 24–48 hours before potting.
harvest.yield: Many cuttings from a mature plant.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the #1 killer. Mushy leaves and stem base signal root rot.
Too little light — causes weak, leggy, pale growth.
Soft or wrinkled leaves — actually signals underwatering (unusual for succulents). Give a thorough drink.
Forgetting it's a slow grower — be patient.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by stem or leaf cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: Callous stems 24–48 hours before potting.
seed_saving.method: Stem or leaf cuttings.
seed_saving.drying: Essential — allow cut surfaces to dry before planting.
seed_saving.notes: Stem cuttings are fastest. Leaf cuttings produce tiny plants over months.

good.why: Both succulents needing identical care.
Both drought tolerant, both low-maintenance.

bad.why: Jade plants need complete drying between waterings.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible.
medicinal: Traditional South African (Khoi San) use of jade plant leaf juice for epilepsy, diarrhea, and wound healing. Some antimicrobial compounds identified in research. Not in Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, lethargy, loss of coordination, slow heart rate.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists jade plant as toxic. Usually causes mild to moderate symptoms. Keep pets away.

transplant.deep_note: Plant in cactus mix in a heavy pot. Crown at soil level. Do not water for 1 week after transplanting to allow any disturbed roots to callous.
transplant.mulch: coarse gravel (top dressing to prevent moisture near stem base)

varieties.name: Crassula ovata (standard)
varieties.description: Classic round jade-green leaves, thick trunk. Most available.

varieties.name: Hobbit / Gollum
varieties.description: Unusual tubular or curled leaves. Bizarre and fascinating — very popular.

varieties.name: Tricolor (Hummel's Sunset)
varieties.description: Leaves edged in yellow and red. Very ornamental. Needs more light than green types.

varieties.name: Crassula argentea (Silver Jade)
varieties.description: Silvery-blue-green leaves. Elegant and unusual colour.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Allow to dry. Remove rotten roots. Repot in dry cactus mix.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.desc: White cottony masses in leaf joints.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab. Treat every 2 weeks until clear.

name: Fiddle Leaf Fig

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant — preferred. Propagate from stem cuttings, though success rate is lower than most houseplants.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root slowly — 4–8 weeks.

seedling.desc: Very slow early growth.

young.desc: Large violin-shaped leaves develop.

adult.desc: The most photogenic houseplant — enormous violin-shaped (fiddle-shaped) glossy leaves on a tree-like trunk. A design icon. Famous for being difficult and dramatic — it drops leaves in protest at almost any change. Once it finds the right spot and settles in, it is majestic. Can reach 6–10 feet indoors.

care.water: Consistent moisture — allow top inch to dry then water thoroughly. Inconsistent watering (too wet then too dry) causes leaf drop and brown spots.
care.light: Bright indirect light — the brightest spot you can find, without direct sun. A spot near a south or west window is ideal. Low light = leaf drop.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix with good aeration. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: One plant per pot. Allow room for a large plant.
care.fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly during spring and summer.
care.notes: The fiddle leaf fig is notoriously sensitive: it drops leaves when moved, when light changes, when drafts occur, when overwatered, when underwatered, and sometimes for no apparent reason. The key: find the brightest spot in your home, place it there, and NEVER move it. Consistent watering is critical — same amount on the same schedule. Wipe large leaves monthly. New growth is exciting — bright reddish-pink new leaves unfurling.

container.notes: Heavy pots prevent tipping. Terracotta allows faster drying — good for drainage.

propagation.desc: Take 6-inch tip cutting. Allow sap to dry. Dip in rooting hormone. Root in moist mix with bottom heat and high humidity. 60–70% success rate.
Most reliable method. Score the stem, wrap with moist sphagnum moss and plastic. Roots form in 4–8 weeks. Cut below the roots and pot.

harvest.when: Trim for shape with caution — removal of leaves causes stress and possible dropping of remaining leaves.
harvest.how: Wear gloves — sap irritates skin.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: N/A — do not over-prune.

common_mistakes: Moving the plant — leaf drop is almost guaranteed. Find the right spot first.
Inconsistent watering — water the same amount on the same schedule.
Not enough light — needs the brightest indirect spot available.
Cold drafts from windows — keep away from single-pane windows in winter.
Overreacting to leaf drop — let the plant settle in. Some initial drop after purchase is normal.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by cuttings or air layering.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Air layering is most reliable.
seed_saving.drying: Allow sap to dry before propagating.
seed_saving.notes: Air layering produces the most reliable new plants.

good.why: Both architectural statement plants.
Trailing pothos at the base softens the fiddle leaf's formality.

bad.why: The challenge is the fiddle leaf itself, not its companions.

culinary: TOXIC — not edible. The sap causes skin and mouth irritation.
medicinal: Not used medicinally.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Oral irritation, vomiting from latex sap.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists Ficus as mildly toxic. The latex sap causes GI upset and skin irritation. Keep pets from chewing.

transplant.deep_note: Repot very carefully in spring — minimize root disturbance to prevent leaf drop. Go up one pot size only. Return to the EXACT same spot after repotting.

varieties.name: Standard Ficus lyrata
varieties.description: Classic large fiddle-shaped leaves. The most available.
varieties.notes: Most widely available. The iconic form.

varieties.name: Bambino (Dwarf)
varieties.description: More compact leaves and overall smaller plant. Slightly more manageable.
varieties.notes: Best for smaller spaces. Slightly more tolerant.

varieties.name: Variegata
varieties.description: White and green variegated leaves. Extremely rare and expensive.

pests.name: Scale
pests.desc: Brown bumps on stems and leaf undersides — common on all Ficus species.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton. Horticultural oil.

pests.name: Spider Mites
pests.control: Increase humidity. Wipe leaves. Neem oil.

name: Brussels Sprouts

season.harvest_window: Fall through early winter — sweetens after frost

seed.desc: Start indoors 16–20 weeks before your first fall frost date — this is the most important timing note. Brussels sprouts are a fall crop started in summer. Most gardeners start seeds in June–July.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable germination at 65–75°F.

seedling.desc: Grow on in a cool spot — heat causes leggy seedlings.

young.desc: Transplant outdoors in midsummer. The plant grows 2–3 feet tall with large cabbage-like leaves.

adult.desc: Small sprouts (mini cabbages) form in the leaf axils from the bottom of the stalk upward. Harvest from the bottom as sprouts reach golf ball size. Flavor improves dramatically after the first frost — cold converts starches to sugar.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Inconsistent watering causes hollow or loose sprouts.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, firm, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. Firm soil produces tighter sprouts — don't loosen soil too much.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen at planting, then switch to balanced when sprouts begin forming.
care.notes: Timing is everything — count back from your first frost date, not forward from last frost. Sprouts mature from bottom to top. Snap off the lower leaves as you harvest to keep the plant producing upward. To force all sprouts to mature at once, pinch off the growing tip 4 weeks before desired harvest.

container.notes: Not practical in containers.

propagation.desc: Start indoors midsummer. Transplant as seedlings.

harvest.when: When sprouts are firm and 1–2 inches in diameter. Harvest bottom-up over several weeks.
harvest.how: Twist and snap sprouts downward off the stalk. Remove the leaf below each harvested sprout.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed up to 5 weeks on the stalk. Individual sprouts: 1–2 weeks.
harvest.yield: 50–100+ sprouts per plant over several weeks.

common_mistakes: Planting too late — must be started midsummer for fall harvest
Loose or soft sprouts — caused by heat, inconsistent watering, or too much nitrogen
Not harvesting from the bottom up
Skipping the frost — flavor is significantly better after a freeze

seed_saving.type: Biennial — overwinter plant, collect seed year 2.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow overwintered plant to flower and set seed pods.
seed_saving.method: Collect dry pods before they split.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other B. oleracea species. Isolate.

good.why: Attracts beneficial wasps that parasitize caterpillar pests.
Trap crop for aphids.
Deters aphids and other pests.

bad.why: Share all the same pests. Rotate annually.

culinary: Roasted Brussels sprouts with olive oil and balsamic — the dish that converted a generation. Shaved raw in salads. Sautéed with bacon and shallots. Braised in cream. Halved and grilled. The key: high heat and don't overcook.
medicinal: Extremely high in vitamin K, vitamin C, and glucosinolates with well-documented cancer-preventive properties. Among the most nutrient-dense vegetables per calorie.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — glucosinolates cause gas in large amounts
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Gas and GI upset in large quantities.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts. Large quantities cause significant gas in pets.

transplant.deep_note: Plant deeper than nursery pot depth — bury the lower stem for stability. Firm soil well around the base.

varieties.name: Long Island Improved
varieties.description: Classic heirloom. Compact plants, firm sprouts. Best flavor after hard frost.

varieties.name: Jade Cross
varieties.description: Hybrid. Early and uniform. Good disease resistance.

varieties.name: Diablo
varieties.description: Hybrid. Very uniform, large sprouts. Outstanding flavor.

varieties.name: Falstaff
varieties.description: Purple sprouts — striking and ornamental. Same flavor as green.
varieties.notes: Most ornamental — beautiful on the stalk.

pests.name: Cabbage Worm
pests.desc: Green caterpillars eating leaves and sprouts.

pests.name: Clubroot
pests.desc: Soil-borne fungal disease causing swollen roots.

name: Cauliflower

season.start_indoors: 4–6 weeks before last frost (spring) or 10–12 weeks before first fall frost
season.harvest_window: Spring or fall — brief window when conditions are right

seed.desc: Cauliflower is the most temperature-sensitive brassica. It needs consistently cool temperatures (60–70°F) to form a head. Heat, cold stress, or drought at any point causes premature bolting or 'buttoning' (tiny useless heads).

germination.desc: Fast at 65–75°F.

seedling.desc: Grow in cool conditions. Harden off carefully before transplanting.

young.desc: Large blue-green leaves develop. The head (curd) begins to form in the center.

adult.desc: White curd develops. Once the curd reaches the size of an egg, blanch by gathering outer leaves over the curd and securing with a rubber band — this keeps it white and prevents yellowing from sun exposure. Harvest within 7–12 days of blanching.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Drought stress at any stage causes problems.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early, balanced when curd forms.
care.notes: Cauliflower is the pickiest brassica. Any stress — heat spike, cold snap, drought, or pest damage — triggers premature heading or bolting. Spring crops are particularly risky. Fall crops are more reliable in most climates. Blanch the heads as soon as they reach egg size.

container.notes: Needs too much space and consistency.

propagation.desc: Start indoors. Transplant carefully — avoid root disturbance.

harvest.when: When the curd is firm, tight, and white — 6–8 inches across. Before any separation or yellowing.
harvest.how: Cut the entire head with 6 inches of stem and some leaves.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate in plastic bag up to 2 weeks. Freezes well after blanching.
harvest.yield: One head per plant.

common_mistakes: Heat exposure during heading — causes loose, ricey curds
Not blanching — heads turn yellow and develop off-flavor in sunlight
Starting too late for spring crop — must mature before summer heat
Inconsistent watering — stress causes buttoning

seed_saving.type: Biennial. Crosses with other B. oleracea.
seed_saving.harvest: Year 2 seed pods.
seed_saving.method: Allow pods to dry fully.
seed_saving.notes: Very difficult to save true-to-type due to crossing.

good.why: Celery repels cabbage white butterfly.
Deters aphids.
Attracts beneficial wasps.

culinary: Roasted whole cauliflower heads. Cauliflower rice. Cauliflower steaks. Mashed cauliflower. Cauliflower pizza crust. Buffalo cauliflower. Pickled. Raw with dip. One of the most versatile vegetables for low-carb cooking.
medicinal: Very high in vitamin C, vitamin K, and glucosinolates. Same cancer-preventive compounds as broccoli.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Gas in large amounts.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Plant slightly deeper than nursery pot. Firm soil well.

varieties.name: Snowball Y
varieties.description: Classic white. Self-blanching (leaves curl naturally over the curd). Reliable.

varieties.name: Cheddar
varieties.description: Orange curd — naturally high in beta-carotene. Nutty flavor. No blanching needed.
varieties.notes: Best color, best nutrition, easiest to grow.

varieties.name: Graffiti
varieties.description: Purple curd — striking color. No blanching needed. Color fades when cooked.

varieties.name: Romanesco
varieties.description: Chartreuse fractal spiral heads — mathematically stunning. Nutty flavor between broccoli and cauliflower.
varieties.notes: Most unusual and conversation-starting vegetable you can grow.

pests.name: Cabbage Worm
pests.desc: Green caterpillars damage leaves and heads.

name: Artichoke

season.harvest_window: Spring (perennial); midsummer (annual). Harvest before flowers open.

seed.desc: For first-year production: cold stratify seeds in the refrigerator for 2 weeks, then start indoors under lights 8–10 weeks before last frost. This vernalization (cold period) tricks the plant into producing buds in year 1.

germination.desc: After cold stratification. Reliable at 70°F.

seedling.desc: Large architectural plants with silvery deeply-cut leaves. Impressive from an early age.

young.desc: Central bud forms on perennial plants or cold-treated annuals. Side buds follow after central bud is harvested.

adult.desc: Enormous thistle-relative reaching 4–6 feet wide and tall. Multiple buds per plant. In warm climates, perennial artichokes produce for 5–7 years. The flower buds — harvested before they open — are the edible part. Allowed to open, the purple thistle flower is strikingly beautiful.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1–2 inches per week. Drought causes tough, small buds.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, deep, well-draining. pH 6.5–7.5.
care.spacing: 4–6 feet — artichokes are very large plants.
care.fertilizer: Heavy feeder — balanced fertilizer monthly during growing season.
care.notes: Artichokes need room — they are large, bold, architectural plants. In zones 7+, cut back to 12 inches in fall and mulch heavily for winter. In cold climates, dig and store roots or treat as annuals. Perennial plants produce more and better buds each year as they establish.

container.notes: Not practical.

propagation.desc: Perennial plants produce offshoots at the base. Remove with roots and replant in spring.
Cold stratify, then start indoors.

harvest.when: When buds are tight, firm, and fully formed but before any purple flower shows — typically 3–5 inches diameter.
harvest.how: Cut the stem 1–2 inches below the bud with a sharp knife.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate in a bag with a little water for up to 2 weeks.
harvest.yield: 1 central bud plus 4–6 side buds per plant per season. More as plant matures.

common_mistakes: Not providing vernalization (cold period) — annual plants won't produce without it
Harvesting too late — once the purple flower begins to show, the bud is too tough
Not leaving enough room — artichokes need 4–6 feet per plant
Letting them freeze without mulching in zones 7–8

seed_saving.type: Allow one bud to open fully and dry on the plant.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect seeds from the dried flower head.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds from fluffy pappus.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds readily in warm climates — can become weedy.

good.why: Traditional companion.
Both large plants, compatible.

culinary: Steamed whole with melted butter or aioli. Stuffed artichokes. Artichoke hearts in pasta, pizza, and dips. Marinated artichoke hearts. Raw shaved in salads (baby artichokes). The heart (base of the bud) and the meaty base of each leaf are edible. The fuzzy choke in the center is inedible.
medicinal: Cynarin — the primary bioactive compound in artichokes — promotes bile production, supports liver function, and has been clinically studied for cholesterol reduction. Significant antioxidant content. Traditionally used for digestive complaints and liver support.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None.
pet_toxicity.notes: Artichokes are not toxic to pets. The plant itself is large and spiny — physical injury possible.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery depth. Firm soil well. Water immediately.

varieties.name: Green Globe
varieties.description: The classic market artichoke. Large round heads. Most widely grown.

varieties.name: Imperial Star
varieties.description: Bred specifically for annual production — most reliable first-year buds without cold stratification.
varieties.notes: Best for annual production in cold climates.

varieties.name: Violetto
varieties.description: Italian heirloom with purple-tinged buds. Excellent flavor. More cold-hardy.

varieties.name: Tavor
varieties.description: Thornless variety — easier to harvest. Compact.

pests.name: Artichoke Plume Moth
pests.desc: Larvae bore into buds and stems.

name: Okra

season.start_indoors: 3–4 weeks before last frost (or direct sow)
season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.transplant: After last frost — okra hates cold
season.harvest_window: Continuous from midsummer through frost — harvest every 2–3 days

seed.desc: Nick seeds with sandpaper or soak overnight before planting — the hard seed coat delays germination. Okra is a heat lover — soil must be at least 65°F, preferably 70°F+. Sow directly where it will grow — okra dislikes transplanting.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil after scarification. Cold soil causes rot.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly in heat. Large bold leaves.

young.desc: Striking hibiscus-like flowers appear — okra is in the same family as hibiscus and the flower is beautiful. Pods form within days of pollination.

adult.desc: Produces continuously throughout the hot season. The more you harvest, the more it produces. Plants can reach 6–8 feet in long warm seasons. The pods must be harvested every 2–3 days — pods left on the plant become tough and fibrous within days and signal the plant to stop producing.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established. Consistent moisture produces more tender pods.
care.light: Full sun — loves heat.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly. Avoid excess nitrogen — reduces pod production.
care.notes: One of the most heat-tolerant vegetables. Thrives in hot humid Southern summers. Okra plants can become very tall — pinch the tips at 4–5 feet to encourage branching and more production. Wear gloves and long sleeves when harvesting — the fine hairs on the pods and stems irritate skin.

container.notes: Dwarf varieties possible in 15+ gallon containers.

propagation.desc: Direct sow after soil warms. Scarify seeds first.

harvest.when: When pods are 2–4 inches long and still tender — typically 4–5 days after the flower drops. Do not let pods exceed 4 inches.
harvest.how: Cut pods with scissors. Wear gloves — skin irritant.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Freezes well (blanch first). Pickled okra. Dried.
harvest.yield: 30–50+ pods per plant per season with regular harvesting.

common_mistakes: Letting pods get too large — they become tough and fibrous and stop the plant producing
Not harvesting frequently enough — check every 2–3 days
Planting in cold soil — cold causes rotting
Not wearing gloves — the hairs irritate skin significantly

seed_saving.type: Very easy. Allow pods to fully dry and brown on plant.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect dried brown pods before they split.
seed_saving.method: Shell dry pods.
seed_saving.notes: One of the easiest vegetables for seed saving.

good.why: Both love heat. Basil may deter pests.
Same heat requirements. Grow well together.
Same cultural needs.

culinary: Gumbo — the dish that gives okra its fame. Fried okra. Okra and tomatoes. Roasted okra (reduces sliminess). Pickled okra. Okra chips. The mucilaginous texture is the point in gumbo — it thickens the stew. To reduce sliminess: roast at high heat, cook with acidic ingredients (tomatoes, vinegar), or dry-heat methods.
medicinal: High in vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and magnesium. Mucilaginous compounds may help stabilize blood sugar — okra water consumed by diabetics in traditional medicine. Soluble fiber supports gut health and cholesterol reduction.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — okra is edible.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for pets. The plant hairs may cause skin irritation.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep. Avoid transplanting if possible — okra dislikes root disturbance.

varieties.name: Clemson Spineless
varieties.description: The standard okra. Spineless pods (easier to harvest). Very productive.
varieties.notes: Most widely grown. All-America Selections winner.

varieties.name: Burgundy
varieties.description: Red stems, leaves, and pods — beautiful ornamental plant. Pods turn green when cooked.

varieties.name: Jambalaya
varieties.description: Very compact — 3–4 feet. More suitable for smaller gardens.

varieties.name: Star of David
varieties.description: Heirloom with very large fat ribbed pods. Harvest at 3 inches or becomes tough.

name: Tomatillo

season.direct_sow: After last frost in warm soil
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through frost — continuous production

seed.desc: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost. Very similar to growing tomatoes.

germination.desc: Reliable at 65–75°F.

seedling.desc: Grows vigorously. Stake or cage early — plants become large and sprawling.

young.desc: Small yellow flowers appear. IMPORTANT: plant at least 2 tomatillo plants — they require cross-pollination from another plant to set fruit. A single plant will flower abundantly but produce little to no fruit.

adult.desc: Tart green husked fruits form inside the papery lantern-like calyx. The fruit is ready when it fills and slightly splits the husk. Very productive — one or two plants produce enormous quantities.

care.water: Consistent moisture. More drought tolerant than tomatoes.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer monthly.
care.notes: MUST plant at least 2 plants for fruit set — cross-pollination is required. Tomatillos are very vigorous and productive — 2 plants is usually plenty for a family. The papery husk protects the fruit from pests. Harvest when the fruit fills the husk and the husk begins to split or turn brown.

container.notes: Possible but needs a large container and cross-pollinator nearby.

propagation.desc: Start indoors or direct sow after last frost.
Drops abundant seeds — tomatillos self-seed prolifically in warm climates.

harvest.when: When fruit fills and slightly bursts the husk, or husk turns papery and brown.
harvest.how: Pull fruit from plant. Remove husk before using — wash off sticky coating.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate in husks up to 3 weeks. Freeze without husks. Canned salsa verde.
harvest.yield: Enormous — 100+ fruits per plant.

common_mistakes: Planting only one — will not fruit without cross-pollination
Harvesting too early — wait for fruit to fill the husk
Not staking — plants sprawl everywhere without support
Leaving husks on too long — fruit becomes overripe

seed_saving.type: Very easy — seeds save from fully ripe fruit.
seed_saving.harvest: Allow fruit to fully ripen (yellow or purple).
seed_saving.method: Scoop seeds, ferment 1–2 days in water, rinse and dry.
seed_saving.notes: Self-seeds so freely that containment may be needed.

good.why: Required for cross-pollination.
Classic companion for nightshades.
Deters pests.

culinary: Salsa verde — the defining use. Enchilada verde sauce. Chile verde. Roasted tomatillo salsa. Tomatillo soup. Guacamole addition. The tart acidic flavor (more acidic than tomatoes) is essential to Mexican green sauces. Slightly sticky coating on the fruit is normal — rinse before use.
medicinal: Withanolides in tomatillos have been studied for anticancer properties in laboratory research. High in vitamin C and antioxidants.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: leaves, stems, and unripe fruit — solanine (nightshade family)
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy.
pet_toxicity.notes: Same toxicity profile as tomatoes — leaves and unripe fruit are mildly toxic. Ripe fruit in small amounts generally safe.

transplant.deep_note: Plant deeply like tomatoes — bury lower stem for stronger root system.

varieties.name: Verde Puebla
varieties.description: Classic green tomatillo. Large fruit. Most widely available.

varieties.name: Purple de Milpa
varieties.description: Purple when ripe — sweeter, less acidic than green. Beautiful.

varieties.name: Pineapple
varieties.description: Yellow when ripe. Sweeter, tropical flavor notes.

varieties.name: Tigerella
varieties.description: Small fruited. Very productive. Early maturing.

name: Cantaloupe (Muskmelon)

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 70°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer — brief window at peak ripeness

seed.desc: Start indoors 2–3 weeks before last frost (cantaloupe doesn't need a long head start) or direct sow after soil reaches 70°F. Plant in hills of 2–3 seeds.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Thin to 2 plants per hill.

young.desc: Long vining stems spread. Male flowers appear first, then female flowers (distinguished by the tiny melon at the base). Bees transfer pollen from male to female flowers.

adult.desc: Fruits swell rapidly once pollinated. Cantaloupe signals ripeness with a fragrant scent and by slipping easily from the vine (the stem separates with slight pressure). Unlike watermelon, cantaloupe tells you when it's ready.

care.water: Consistent moisture during vine growth and early fruit development. Reduce water significantly as fruit approaches ripeness — too much water dilutes sugar content and reduces flavor.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, warm. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: Hills 3–4 feet apart in rows 5–6 feet apart.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer until fruits set, then switch to low-nitrogen high-potassium.
care.notes: Reduce watering as fruits approach maturity — this concentrates sugars and dramatically improves flavor. A melon grown in rich moist soil with consistent water will be large but bland. Stress the plant slightly as fruits ripen. Growing on black plastic mulch speeds soil warming and boosts production.

container.notes: Dwarf varieties possible with vertical support.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or short indoor start.

harvest.when: When the melon slips easily from the vine with slight pressure, the stem end has a crack, and the blossom end gives slightly. Fragrant smell is the best indicator.
harvest.how: Gently lift and twist — a ripe cantaloupe slips off the vine.
harvest.storage: Room temperature until ripe, then refrigerate up to 5 days.
harvest.yield: 2–4 melons per plant.

common_mistakes: Overwatering near maturity — the most common cause of bland flavorless melons
Harvesting too early — wait for the slip stage
Poor pollination — plant flowers nearby for bee attraction
Too little heat — melons need sustained warmth

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties easy to save.
seed_saving.harvest: Scoop seeds from fully ripe fruit.
seed_saving.method: Ferment seeds in water 2 days, rinse, dry.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other muskmelons — isolate for true seed.

good.why: Corn provides windbreak for melons.
Deters aphids and cucumber beetles.
Deters cucumber beetles.

culinary: Fresh melon with prosciutto — the classic Italian pairing. Melon and fresh mint. Agua fresca. Smoothies. Melon salads. Sorbet. The flavor is best at room temperature — refrigeration mutes the aroma.
medicinal: High in beta-carotene, vitamin C, potassium, and adenosine (has anticoagulant properties studied for cardiovascular health). High water content for hydration.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset from rind.
pet_toxicity.notes: Cantaloupe flesh is safe for pets. Remove rind.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery depth. Melons resent root disturbance — handle transplants gently.
transplant.mulch: black plastic (for soil warming) or straw

varieties.name: Hale's Best
varieties.description: Classic heirloom. Excellent sweet flavor. Netted orange flesh.

varieties.name: Ambrosia
varieties.description: Very sweet, salmon-orange flesh. Small seed cavity. Exceptional flavor.

varieties.name: Minnesota Midget
varieties.description: Very small melons (4 inch) on compact vines. Great for small gardens and short seasons.
varieties.notes: Best for small gardens and short seasons.

varieties.name: Charentais
varieties.description: Classic French cantaloupe — no netting, smooth green rind, intensely fragrant orange flesh. The melon of French farmers markets.
varieties.notes: Best fragrance and European flavor profile.

pests.name: Cucumber Beetle
pests.desc: Yellow and black beetles spread bacterial wilt.
pests.control: Row covers until flowering, neem oil.

pests.name: Squash Vine Borer
pests.desc: Less susceptible than squash but possible.

name: Watermelon

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 70°F+
season.harvest_window: Late summer — watermelon does not signal ripeness as clearly as cantaloupe

seed.desc: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow in warm soil. Watermelon needs a longer warm season than cantaloupe — in short-season areas, choose ice box or short-season varieties.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil (70°F+).

seedling.desc: Handle transplants very gently — watermelon is sensitive to root disturbance.

young.desc: Long vines spread aggressively — give them space. Males flower first, then females. Pollination by bees is critical.

adult.desc: Fruits swell rapidly. Unlike cantaloupe, watermelon does NOT slip from the vine when ripe. Ripeness indicators: thump test (hollow sound), the tendril nearest the fruit turns dry and brown, the ground spot turns from white to creamy yellow, the skin becomes dull rather than shiny.

care.water: Consistent moisture during growth. Reduce water in the final 2 weeks before harvest — improves sweetness.
care.light: Full sun. Needs maximum heat.
care.soil: Sandy, well-draining, warm. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.spacing: Hills 4–6 feet apart in rows 6–8 feet apart. Needs significant space.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen early. Switch to low-nitrogen high-potassium once fruits set.
care.notes: Watermelons need heat, space, and time. Growing on black plastic mulch significantly boosts yield in northern gardens. Place a board or straw under developing fruit to prevent rot where the melon contacts the ground.

container.min_size: Only dwarf varieties in very large containers.
container.notes: Not practical for standard varieties.

propagation.desc: Start indoors or direct sow in warm soil.

harvest.when: Thump test (hollow sound), brown tendril nearest fruit, yellow ground spot, dull skin — look for all four signs together.
harvest.how: Cut stem with a sharp knife — watermelons do not slip like cantaloupe.
harvest.storage: Room temperature up to 2 weeks. Refrigerate cut melon up to 5 days.
harvest.yield: 2–4 melons per plant.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too early — the most common mistake. Use multiple ripeness indicators.
Not enough space — watermelons need 6+ feet in every direction
Poor soil warmth — grow on black plastic in northern gardens
Not placing fruit on straw or board — ground contact causes rot

seed_saving.type: Open-pollinated varieties easy to save.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from fully ripe fruit.
seed_saving.method: Rinse seeds from flesh, dry on paper.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other watermelons. Isolate by ½ mile.

good.why: Deters cucumber beetles.
Pest deterrent.
Windbreak.

culinary: Fresh sliced. Watermelon granita. Agua fresca. Watermelon and feta salad with mint. Pickled watermelon rind. Grilled watermelon. Watermelon juice. The rind is edible and delicious pickled — a Southern tradition.
medicinal: High in lycopene — the antioxidant that makes watermelon red. Lycopene associated with reduced prostate cancer risk in epidemiological studies. High in citrulline — an amino acid that relaxes blood vessels, studied for cardiovascular benefit and athletic performance. Excellent hydration (92% water).

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Seeds and rind can cause GI upset or blockage.
pet_toxicity.notes: Watermelon flesh is safe for pets. Remove seeds and rind.

transplant.deep_note: Handle root ball very gently — watermelon is sensitive to transplant shock.

varieties.name: Sugar Baby
varieties.description: Small ice-box watermelon — 8–10 lbs. Very sweet. Compact vines. Most popular small watermelon.
varieties.notes: Best for small gardens and short seasons.

varieties.name: Crimson Sweet
varieties.description: Classic large watermelon — 20–25 lbs. Red crisp flesh. Excellent flavor. Most widely grown heirloom.

varieties.name: Charleston Gray
varieties.description: Grey-green rind. 25–35 lbs. Very sweet red flesh. Classic Southern heirloom.

varieties.name: Yellow Doll
varieties.description: Yellow flesh — sweet and honey-flavored. Small fruit. Conversation piece.

varieties.name: Orangeglo
varieties.description: Orange flesh. 20+ lbs. Sweet tropical flavor distinct from red watermelons.

name: Pumpkin

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Fall — harvest before hard freeze

seed.desc: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 2–3 weeks early. Count back from first fall frost — pumpkins need 100+ days. Most people plant too late.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Large leaves emerge.

young.desc: Long vines spread dramatically. In small gardens, train vines in a spiral or grow vertically on a sturdy trellis (support fruit with slings).

adult.desc: Fruit swells rapidly. Pumpkins change from green to orange as they mature. Leave on the vine until the first hard frost threatens — the longer on the vine, the better the cured skin.

care.water: Consistent moisture during vine growth. Reduce as fruit approaches maturity.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.spacing: 4–8 feet depending on variety. Very large varieties need 10+ feet.
care.fertilizer: High nitrogen at planting. Potassium when fruits set.
care.notes: Pumpkins need space — plan carefully. Pollination requires bees — hand-pollinate in the morning if bee activity is low. To limit vine spread, pinch the growing tips after 2–3 fruits have set. Cure pumpkins at 80–85°F for 10–14 days after harvest to harden the skin for storage.

container.notes: Standard varieties not practical.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or short indoor start.

harvest.when: When fully colored, the skin resists fingernail scratching, the stem is dry and corky, and the vine near the fruit begins to die back.
harvest.how: Cut the stem with 3–4 inches attached — never carry by the stem.
harvest.storage: Cure 10–14 days at 80–85°F, then store at 50–55°F in a dry location. Properly cured pumpkins store 3–6 months.
harvest.yield: 2–5 pumpkins per plant depending on variety.

common_mistakes: Planting too late — count back 100+ days from first frost
Breaking the stem — pumpkins without stems rot faster
Not curing — uncured pumpkins rot within weeks
Carrying by the stem — stems break easily

seed_saving.type: Very easy. Seeds from fully ripe pumpkins.
seed_saving.harvest: Scoop seeds from mature pumpkin.
seed_saving.method: Rinse, remove strings, dry on paper.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with squash. Isolate for true seed.

good.why: Traditional Three Sisters — corn provides structure.
Nitrogen fixing supports pumpkins.
Deters squash bugs and cucumber beetles.

culinary: Pumpkin pie. Pumpkin soup. Roasted pumpkin seeds (salt and roast). Pumpkin puree. Pumpkin bread. Pumpkin curry. The seeds are arguably more nutritious than the flesh — high in zinc, magnesium, and beneficial fats.
medicinal: Pumpkin seeds are one of the richest plant sources of zinc — important for immune function and testosterone production. Cucurbitin in seeds used traditionally for intestinal parasites. Beta-carotene in flesh. Pumpkin seed oil studied for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Canned pumpkin is actually used as a digestive remedy for dogs.
pet_toxicity.notes: Pumpkin is not only safe but beneficial for pets — the fiber helps with both diarrhea and constipation. Plain canned pumpkin (not pie filling) is a common veterinary recommendation.

transplant.deep_note: Handle root ball gently. Plant at nursery depth.

varieties.name: Jack O'Lantern
varieties.description: Classic carving pumpkin. Orange, uniform, medium size (8–15 lbs).

varieties.name: Sugar Pie
varieties.description: Small (6–8 lb), thick sweet flesh, few strings. Best pumpkin for cooking.
varieties.notes: Best for eating — pie, soup, puree.

varieties.name: Atlantic Giant
varieties.description: The giant competition pumpkin — record holders exceed 2,000 lbs. Needs heavy feeding and perfect conditions.

varieties.name: Jarrahdale
varieties.description: Blue-grey skin, vibrant orange flesh. Beautiful and delicious.
varieties.notes: Best heirloom for flavor and appearance.

varieties.name: Baby Boo
varieties.description: Tiny white miniature pumpkins — perfect for decoration.

pests.name: Squash Vine Borer
pests.desc: Larvae bore into main stem causing sudden wilt.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves — very common late season.

name: Acorn Squash

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 65°F+
season.harvest_window: Late summer through fall. Stores well through winter.

seed.desc: Direct sow or short indoor start. Acorn squash has a shorter season than butternut or pumpkin — good for northern gardens.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil.

seedling.desc: Vigorous rapid growth.

young.desc: Vining growth. Male then female flowers. Bees pollinate.

adult.desc: Distinctive ribbed dark green (or gold) acorn-shaped fruits. Skin hardens as it matures. Harvest when skin is deep dark green and stem is dry and corky.

care.water: Consistent moisture. Reduce as fruits mature.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.spacing: 3–4 feet between hills. Vines spread 6–8 feet.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer. Potassium when fruits set.
care.notes: More compact than most winter squash — better for smaller gardens. Can be trained on a trellis with fruit supported in slings. One of the most reliable and easy winter squashes.

container.notes: Not practical.

propagation.desc: Direct sow or short indoor start.

harvest.when: When skin is deep green (or gold for golden varieties), firm, and resists scratching. Stem is dry and corky. Vine at attachment point dies back.
harvest.how: Cut stem with 2 inches attached.
harvest.storage: Cure at 80°F for 10 days. Store at 50–55°F, 6–8 weeks.
harvest.yield: 3–5 squash per plant.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too early — green skin should be dark, not light
Not curing — uncured squash deteriorates quickly
Planting in cool soil — wait for warm conditions

seed_saving.type: Easy. Seeds from fully mature fruit.
seed_saving.harvest: Scoop seeds from ripe squash.
seed_saving.method: Rinse, dry on paper.
seed_saving.notes: Crosses with other C. pepo. Isolate.

good.why: Deters squash bugs and cucumber beetles.
Windbreak and shade for squash roots.
Three Sisters combination.

culinary: Halved, seeded, and roasted with butter and maple syrup — the definitive preparation. Stuffed acorn squash (with wild rice, cranberries, and nuts). Acorn squash soup. Roasted seeds like pumpkin seeds. The skin is edible when roasted.
medicinal: High in beta-carotene, vitamin C, potassium, and magnesium. Good source of fiber.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None.
pet_toxicity.notes: Safe for pets. Plain cooked acorn squash is fine.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow or transplant carefully. Squash resents root disturbance.

varieties.name: Table Queen
varieties.description: Classic dark green ribbed acorn squash. Heirloom. Reliable.

varieties.name: Honey Bear
varieties.description: Very compact vine — great for smaller gardens. Sweet flesh. All-America Selections winner.

varieties.name: Carnival
varieties.description: Multicolored mottled orange and cream. Beautiful.

varieties.name: Golden Acorn
varieties.description: Gold-orange skin. Same sweet flavor. Very attractive.

pests.name: Squash Vine Borer
pests.desc: Sudden wilt from larvae in stem.

name: Edamame (Soybean)

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 60°F+
season.harvest_window: Midsummer through fall depending on planting time. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks.

seed.desc: Direct sow only — soybeans do not transplant well. Sow 1–1.5 inches deep, 2–3 inches apart. Inoculate with soybean rhizobium inoculant for nitrogen fixation.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil (60°F+).

seedling.desc: Rapid growth. Bushy upright habit.

young.desc: Small purple-white flowers appear. Fuzzy bean pods begin forming.

adult.desc: Pods fill out — harvest when pods are plump and bright green, before they start to yellow. The beans inside should feel firm when you squeeze the pod. This harvest window is brief — check daily.

care.water: Consistent moisture — especially during pod fill. Drought during pod fill causes shriveled beans.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Average, well-draining. pH 6.0–6.8. Nitrogen fixer — don't over-fertilize with nitrogen.
care.fertilizer: Inoculant at planting only. No additional nitrogen needed.
care.notes: Edamame is simply a soybean harvested at the fresh green stage before it dries. The same seeds used for dried soybeans work — the difference is only harvest timing. Inoculate seeds with rhizobium before planting for maximum nitrogen fixation. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest.

container.notes: Good container crop. Compact bushy habit.

propagation.desc: Direct sow only. Inoculate before planting.

harvest.when: When pods are plump, bright green, and beans feel firm inside — typically 80 days from planting. Before any yellowing begins.
harvest.how: Pull entire pods from the plant. Boil whole pods in salted water 5–6 minutes. Squeeze beans out to eat.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate pods up to 5 days. Blanch and freeze for longer storage.
harvest.yield: About 1/2 pound per plant. Grow many plants.

common_mistakes: Harvesting too late — yellowing pods means overripe beans
Not inoculating seeds — dramatically reduces yield
Transplanting — soybeans need to be direct sown
Under-planting — need many plants for a meaningful harvest

seed_saving.type: Very easy. Allow pods to dry completely on plant.
seed_saving.harvest: Collect dry brown pods before they shatter.
seed_saving.method: Shell dry pods.
seed_saving.notes: One of the easiest legumes for seed saving.

good.why: Classic Three Sisters companion.
Three Sisters — soybeans fix nitrogen for all.

culinary: Boiled in salted water and eaten as a snack (the defining Japanese preparation). Edamame hummus. Shelled in grain bowls, salads, and rice dishes. Edamame dip. Frozen edamame available year-round from Asian grocery stores.
medicinal: One of the most nutritious vegetables — complete protein (all essential amino acids), high in iron, calcium, folate, and vitamin K. Isoflavones (plant estrogens) studied extensively for cardiovascular health, bone density, and menopausal symptom reduction. One of the richest plant protein sources available.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Digestive upset in large amounts due to high protein and fiber.
pet_toxicity.notes: Edamame is safe for pets in small amounts. Large amounts can cause gas and digestive upset.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep. Does not transplant well.

varieties.name: Envy
varieties.description: Early, compact, excellent flavor. Most widely available edamame variety.

varieties.name: Midori Giant
varieties.description: Very large plump beans. Three beans per pod. Outstanding flavor.

varieties.name: Sayamusume
varieties.description: Japanese heirloom. Exceptional sweet flavor. Three beans per pod.

varieties.name: Beer Friend
varieties.description: Very productive. Large pods. Good flavor.

name: Blueberry

season.start_indoors: Purchase nursery plant — bare root or container
season.harvest_window: July–August (highbush). June–July (lowbush). Berries ripen over several weeks.

seed.desc: Purchase 2-year-old nursery plants — blueberries from seed take 5+ years to fruit. Most importantly: purchase at least 2 different varieties for cross-pollination. A single blueberry plant produces very little fruit.

germination.desc: If growing from seed: cold stratify 3 months. Very slow.

seedling.desc: Years 1–3: focus on establishment. Pinch off all flowers in years 1–2 to encourage root development rather than fruit production. Patience is rewarded.

young.desc: Year 3–5: increasing fruit production. The plant establishes its framework of productive canes.

adult.desc: Full production from year 5+. A mature blueberry bush can produce 5–10 pounds of berries per season and live 50+ years. One of the most long-lived and productive fruit bushes available.

care.water: Consistent moisture — blueberries have shallow fibrous roots that dry out quickly. 1–2 inches per week. Drip irrigation is ideal. Consistent moisture is the most important cultural factor.
care.light: Full sun — 6+ hours minimum. Fewer hours = fewer berries.
care.soil: VERY ACIDIC — pH 4.5–5.5. This is non-negotiable. Most garden soil is too alkaline. Test before planting. Amend with elemental sulfur, peat moss, or pine bark. Never plant near concrete.
care.spacing: 4–6 feet between plants (highbush). Plant at least 2 different varieties.
care.fertilizer: Acidic fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or fertilizer formulated for blueberries) in early spring and early summer. Never limestone or wood ash.
care.notes: Soil pH is the #1 success factor — blueberries simply won't grow well above pH 6.0. Test your soil before planting. Use a pine bark mulch to acidify soil over time. Net plants when fruiting — birds will take every berry if given the chance. Prune out oldest canes (over 6 years old) annually to maintain productive younger wood.

container.notes: Excellent container plants — allows perfect soil pH control. Use acidic potting mix. Plant 2 varieties in separate containers for cross-pollination.

propagation.desc: Take 4–6 inch cuttings in early summer. Root in acidic peat-perlite mix. Difficult — low success rate.
In late winter. Better success rate than softwood.

harvest.when: Berries are fully blue (no red tinge), separate easily from the cluster, and are slightly soft. Taste one — flavor is the best indicator.
harvest.how: Gently roll berries off the cluster with your fingers. Ripe berries fall easily.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate unwashed up to 2 weeks. Freeze for year-round use — blueberries freeze better than almost any other fruit.
harvest.yield: 5–10+ pounds per mature bush per season.

common_mistakes: Wrong soil pH — the most common failure. Test before planting.
Only one plant — poor fruit set without cross-pollination
Birds — net before fruit ripens or lose everything
Not mulching — pine bark mulch is essential for moisture and pH
Over-pruning young plants — don't prune heavily until year 4

seed_saving.type: Seeds possible but 5+ years to fruit. Cuttings are preferred.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from fully ripe berries.
seed_saving.method: Mash berries, ferment 2 days, rinse seeds.
seed_saving.notes: Not practical — buy plants.

good.why: Cross-pollination is essential — different varieties required.
Same acidic soil requirements. Good planting partners.
Maintains the acidic conditions blueberries need.

bad.why: Lime leaches from concrete raising pH.

culinary: Fresh eating. Blueberry pancakes, muffins, pies. Jam and preserves. Smoothies. Blueberry sauce for meats. Dried blueberries. Wine. One of the most versatile fruits for both fresh eating and cooking.
medicinal: Blueberries have one of the highest antioxidant capacities of any fruit — primarily from anthocyanins (the pigments that make them blue). Clinical studies show: improved memory and cognitive function in older adults, reduced blood pressure, improved insulin sensitivity. One of the most extensively studied functional foods. Native peoples used blueberries extensively as food and medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — blueberries are safe and nutritious for pets.
pet_toxicity.notes: Blueberries are completely safe for dogs and cats. Many dogs love them as treats.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth or slightly higher — blueberries planted too deep decline. The crown must be at or slightly above soil level. Acidic pine bark mulch 4 inches deep over roots is essential.

varieties.name: Bluecrop
varieties.description: The most widely grown highbush blueberry. Mid-season. Very reliable, productive, and disease resistant. Zone 4–7.

varieties.name: Duke
varieties.description: Early season. Excellent flavor. Very productive. Good for short seasons.

varieties.name: Jersey
varieties.description: Late season. Large berries. Good flavor. Excellent for extending harvest season.
varieties.notes: Best late season for extending harvest.

varieties.name: Sunshine Blue
varieties.description: Southern highbush for zones 5–10. Self-fertile (one plant produces reasonably). Semi-evergreen. Good for warm climates.

varieties.name: Northblue (Lowbush hybrid)
varieties.description: Very cold-hardy to zone 3. Compact 2 feet. Excellent flavor. Good for northern gardens.

pests.name: Birds
pests.desc: Will take every ripe berry — the #1 blueberry problem.
pests.control: Bird netting over the entire plant when fruit begins to color. The only reliable solution.

pests.name: Blueberry Maggot
pests.control: Kaolin clay spray, yellow sticky traps.

pests.name: Mummyberry
pests.control: Remove mummified berries, copper fungicide in spring.

pests.name: Spotted Wing Drosophila
pests.desc: Tiny fly lays eggs in ripe fruit.

name: Raspberry

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root canes in early spring
season.harvest_window: Summer-bearing: June–July. Everbearing: June–July and August–October.

seed.desc: Purchase bare root canes in early spring — the most economical way to start a raspberry patch. One plant quickly becomes many through suckering.

germination.desc: Bare root canes establish within a few weeks of planting.

seedling.desc: Year 1: primocanes (first-year canes) grow vigorously. Summer-bearing types don't fruit until year 2. Everbearing types fruit in late summer/fall of year 1.

young.desc: Year 2: floricanes (second-year canes) bear fruit, then die. New primocanes grow to replace them. This is the natural cane cycle.

adult.desc: A fully established raspberry patch produces abundantly and spreads by underground runners. Annual pruning is essential to maintain productivity and manageability. Can produce for 15–20 years.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1 inch per week minimum. Shallow roots dry quickly. Drip irrigation is ideal.
care.light: Full sun for best production. Tolerates light shade with reduced yield.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 5.5–6.5. Slightly acidic. High organic matter.
care.spacing: 2–3 feet between canes. 6–8 feet between rows. Grow against a fence or trellis.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring. Avoid excess nitrogen — promotes cane growth at expense of fruit.
care.notes: Raspberries have a two-year cane cycle: first-year canes (primocanes) grow; second-year canes (floricanes) fruit, then die. Pruning: remove all dead floricanes after fruiting. Thin remaining primocanes to 4–6 per foot of row. For everbearing types, the simplest management is to mow everything to the ground each fall — you lose the summer crop but the fall crop is excellent.

container.notes: Possible in large containers. Requires regular watering and trellis. Compact varieties preferred.

propagation.desc: Dig rooted suckers that emerge from underground runners. Transplant in spring or fall. Raspeberries spread and self-propagate readily.
For black raspberries: bend tip of cane to ground in late summer. Cover with soil. Roots by fall. Sever from mother plant.

harvest.when: When berries pull away from the central plug easily and are fully colored (red, gold, or black depending on variety). The berry should release with very slight pressure.
harvest.how: Pick gently — raspberries are fragile. Pick every 2–3 days during peak season.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate in a single layer up to 3 days. Freeze on a baking sheet then bag — frozen raspberries are excellent.
harvest.yield: 1–2 quarts per foot of row per season on established plants.

common_mistakes: Not pruning — overcrowded canes reduce yield and increase disease
Wrong pruning time — summer-bearing: prune floricanes after summer fruiting. Everbearing: mow all to ground in fall.
Letting suckers run everywhere — contain the patch or it takes over
Birds — net during ripening

seed_saving.type: Propagated by suckers and tip layering.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from ripe fruit — but not practical.
seed_saving.method: Suckers from the patch.
seed_saving.notes: Sucker division is free and unlimited.

good.why: Deters Japanese beetles and aphids.
Pest deterrent.
Traditional companion for raspberries.

bad.why: Cross-pollinates and can hybridize. Keep separate.
Share Verticillium wilt — rotate away from Solanaceae.

culinary: Fresh eating. Raspberry jam and preserves. Raspberry vinaigrette. Raspberry sauce (coulis) for desserts and meats. Raspberry lemonade. Baked into pies, tarts, and muffins. Raspberry wine and liqueur.
medicinal: High in ellagic acid — a polyphenol with documented anticarcinogenic properties in laboratory studies. High in vitamin C, manganese, and dietary fiber. Raspberry leaf tea used throughout history for pregnancy support, menstrual cramps, and as a uterine tonic — one of the most widely used women's herbs globally.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Trace amounts of xylitol in raspberries are far below toxic thresholds.
pet_toxicity.notes: Raspberries are safe for pets. The fruit is fine in moderation. The canes have thorns — physical injury possible.

transplant.deep_note: Plant bare root canes 2 inches deeper than they grew in the nursery. The crown should be just below soil level.

varieties.name: Heritage
varieties.description: Everbearing. The most widely grown raspberry. Produces summer and fall crops. Very reliable.

varieties.name: Latham
varieties.description: Summer-bearing heirloom. Very hardy (zone 3). Excellent flavor. Very productive.
varieties.notes: Best for cold climates. Outstanding flavor.

varieties.name: Anne
varieties.description: Everbearing golden raspberry. Sweet, mild flavor. Beautiful color.

varieties.name: Jewel (Black)
varieties.description: Black raspberry — intense, complex flavor. Different from red raspberry. Excellent for jam.

varieties.name: Polka
varieties.description: Everbearing. Very large berries. Excellent flavor. Good disease resistance.

pests.name: Spotted Wing Drosophila
pests.desc: Tiny fly lays eggs in ripe fruit — devastating in many areas.
pests.control: Harvest daily during peak, netting, spinosad spray.

pests.name: Cane Borer
pests.desc: Larvae bore inside canes causing wilting.
pests.control: Prune wilted canes 6 inches below damage.

pests.name: Raspberry Crown Borer
pests.desc: Larvae at crown cause plant death.

name: Blackberry

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root canes in early spring
season.harvest_window: July–August. Berries ripen over 3–4 weeks.

seed.desc: Purchase bare root canes in early spring. Same two-year cane cycle as raspberries — primocanes grow year 1, floricanes fruit year 2 then die.

germination.desc: Bare root establishes quickly.

seedling.desc: Vigorous first-year cane growth.

young.desc: Second-year canes flower and fruit in early summer.

adult.desc: Highly productive mature canes. Spreads aggressively by runners and tip layering — contain the patch. Thornless varieties much easier to manage but slightly less vigorous.

care.water: Consistent moisture. 1–2 inches per week.
care.light: Full sun for best production.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining. pH 5.5–7.0. More pH tolerant than raspberries.
care.spacing: 4–6 feet between plants. Grow against a trellis or wire system.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer early spring.
care.notes: Similar care to raspberries. Thornless varieties (Triple Crown, Navaho) are much easier to prune and harvest. Thorned varieties (Apache, Natchez) may be slightly more productive. Blackberries are more drought tolerant than raspberries once established. Train canes to a trellis — arching canes become a tangled thicket without support.

container.notes: Thornless varieties in large containers work well.

propagation.desc: In late summer, bend a cane tip to the ground. Bury the tip 4 inches deep. It roots by fall. Sever from the mother plant in spring.
Dig rooted suckers from established plants.

harvest.when: Berries are fully black, glossy, and pull away from the plant without resistance. Slightly soft to the touch.
harvest.how: Pick every 2–3 days during peak season. Wear long sleeves with thorned varieties.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate up to 5 days. Freeze well.
harvest.yield: 10–20 pounds per mature plant per season.

common_mistakes: Not trellising — canes become an impenetrable thicket
Letting runners spread unchecked
Not wearing protective clothing with thorned varieties
Birds — net when fruit begins to ripen

seed_saving.type: Propagated by tip layering and suckers.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Tip layering is the standard method.
seed_saving.notes: Free unlimited propagation by tip layering.

good.why: Dynamic accumulator — deep roots mine nutrients.
Pest deterrent.

culinary: Fresh eating. Blackberry jam — one of the finest. Blackberry cobbler and crumble. Blackberry wine. Blackberry sauce. Blackberry vinegar. Dried blackberries.
medicinal: High in anthocyanins, ellagic acid, and vitamin C. Same cancer-preventive polyphenols as raspberries. Blackberry leaf tea used in traditional medicine for diarrhea, sore throat, and as an astringent. Native peoples throughout North America used blackberries extensively as food and medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — blackberries are safe for pets.
pet_toxicity.notes: Blackberries are safe for pets. The canes have thorns — physical injury possible.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at same depth as nursery or slightly deeper. Crown just below soil level.

varieties.name: Triple Crown (Thornless)
varieties.description: The most widely grown thornless blackberry. Excellent flavor. Very productive. Erect canes.

varieties.name: Navaho (Thornless)
varieties.description: Upright thornless. Very sweet, mild flavor. Good disease resistance.

varieties.name: Apache (Thorned)
varieties.description: Very large berries. Excellent sweet flavor. Very productive. Zone 6–9.

varieties.name: Natchez (Thornless)
varieties.description: Very early ripening thornless. Large fruit. Good flavor.

varieties.name: Chester (Thornless)
varieties.description: Very cold hardy (zone 5). Large firm berries. Excellent for northern gardens.

pests.name: Spotted Wing Drosophila
pests.desc: Tiny fly lays eggs in ripe fruit.

name: Elderberry
plant_type: Perennial large shrub or small tree

season.direct_sow: Not practical for the home gardener
season.harvest_window: August–September. Harvest entire berry clusters when fully dark purple-black.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plants — at least 2 for cross-pollination. Bare root plants or container-grown. Elderberries establish quickly and grow very fast.

germination.desc: Seeds require cold stratification. Cuttings are far more practical.

seedling.desc: Year 1: significant growth, 3–6 feet possible from a bare root plant. May produce some flowers in year 1.

young.desc: Year 2: good production begins. Plants can reach 8–12 feet and spread by suckers.

adult.desc: Very productive. Enormous flat-topped white flower clusters (umbels) in June — intensely fragrant. Followed by heavy clusters of small dark purple-black berries in August–September. One of the most ecologically valuable native plants — flowers support hundreds of pollinators, berries feed dozens of bird species.

care.water: Moderate — more drought tolerant than most berry plants. Tolerates wet conditions better than most plants.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade. Full sun produces most berries.
care.soil: Average to rich, moist, adaptable. pH 5.5–6.5. Tolerates wet sites.
care.spacing: 6–8 feet between plants. Plant at least 2 for cross-pollination.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring.
care.notes: Elderberry is one of the easiest and most vigorous fruit plants. Grows 6–10 feet per year when established. Prune to keep manageable — cut oldest canes to ground annually. The flowers are edible and used to make elderflower cordial and fritters. ALL parts of the plant EXCEPT ripe cooked berries are toxic — including raw berries, leaves, bark, and roots.

container.notes: Not practical long-term.

propagation.desc: Take 8–10 inch cuttings in late winter. Insert in moist soil. Roots readily.
Dig rooted suckers from established plants in spring.

harvest.when: When the entire cluster is dark purple-black. Individual berries ripen unevenly — harvest when 95%+ are ripe.
harvest.how: Cut entire clusters with scissors. Process promptly.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate clusters up to a week. Process into juice, syrup, or jam immediately. Freeze whole clusters.
harvest.yield: 10–15 pounds of berries per mature plant per season.

common_mistakes: Eating raw berries — TOXIC. Cook or process before consuming.
Planting only one — cross-pollination improves yield significantly
Not harvesting promptly — birds take ripe clusters fast
Letting plants grow without pruning — become very large and unwieldy

seed_saving.type: Cuttings and suckers preferred.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from fully ripe berries.
seed_saving.method: Clean and cold stratify.
seed_saving.notes: Cuttings root so easily there is no reason to grow from seed.

good.why: Cross-pollination dramatically improves yield.
Naturalistic planting — both thrive together.
Attracts same beneficial insects.

bad.why: Elderberry is an excellent garden citizen.

culinary: Elderberry syrup — must be cooked. Elderberry jam and jelly. Elderflower cordial (flowers). Elderberry wine. Elderberry gummies. Elderberry tea. The berries must be cooked to destroy the cyanogenic glycosides — never eat raw. Elderflower fritters are a classic spring delicacy.
medicinal: Elderberry is one of the most extensively studied plants for immune support. Clinical trials show elderberry syrup reduces duration and severity of influenza (two meta-analyses confirm this). Sambucol — the proprietary elderberry extract — is the most studied formulation. Anthocyanins have antiviral properties confirmed in laboratory studies. Historically used throughout Europe and Native America as the 'medicine chest' of the hedgerow. Root, bark, leaves — toxic. Berries — must be cooked.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: all parts except ripe cooked berries — raw berries, leaves, bark, and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, weakness from cyanogenic glycosides.
pet_toxicity.notes: All green parts and raw berries are toxic to pets and humans. Cooked elderberry products are safe. Keep pets away from the plant and raw berries.

transplant.deep_note: Plant slightly deeper than nursery pot. Firm soil well.

varieties.name: Bob Gordon
varieties.description: American elderberry (S. canadensis). Exceptional berry yield. Large clusters. Bred specifically for commercial syrup production.
varieties.notes: Highest berry yield. Best for medicinal syrup production.

varieties.name: Adams
varieties.description: Large berries, very productive. Good cross-pollinator for Bob Gordon.

varieties.name: Nova
varieties.description: Canadian selection. Very cold-hardy. Large sweet berries.

varieties.name: Black Lace
varieties.description: Deeply cut purple-black foliage — extraordinarily ornamental. White-pink flowers. Full berry production.

varieties.name: Instant Karma (Variegated)
varieties.description: Cream and green variegated foliage. White flowers. Good berry production. Very ornamental.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: Black bean aphids colonize stems in spring.
pests.control: Blast with water. Neem oil. Usually resolved by beneficial insects.

pests.name: Birds
pests.desc: Take ripe berries — also desirable for wildlife value.
pests.control: Net if you want to harvest. Consider leaving some for birds.

name: Fig
growing_zones: 7–11 outdoors. 4–11 in containers or with protection.

season.harvest_window: Two crops possible: Breba crop (June–July on previous year's wood) and main crop (August–October on current year's wood).

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Figs root easily from cuttings — ask a neighbor with a fig tree for a cutting. Most edible figs sold in the US are self-fertile — no pollinator needed.

germination.desc: Hardwood cuttings root in 4–6 weeks.

seedling.desc: Vigorous first-year growth. May produce some fruit in year 2.

young.desc: Increasing production each year. The tree develops its characteristic multi-stemmed shrubby form.

adult.desc: A mature fig is one of the most productive fruit plants available. Can produce 40–80 pounds of fruit per season. Extraordinary flavor — fresh figs are nothing like dried. Long-lived — many fig trees in the US are over 100 years old, often planted by immigrants.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established. Consistent moisture during fruit development improves flavor. Reduce water as fruit ripens.
care.light: Full sun. Loves heat.
care.soil: Well-draining, average to rich. pH 6.0–8.0. Very adaptable.
care.spacing: 10–15 feet for free-standing trees. Can be grown as a bush, espalier, or container plant.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring. Too much nitrogen causes lush growth and poor fruit.
care.notes: Figs need heat to ripen — the longer and hotter the summer, the better. In cool climates, grow against a south-facing wall which reflects heat. In zones 4–6: grow in containers and bring indoors for winter (need only minimal light in dormancy), or bury the entire plant (!) — traditional Italian immigrant technique of wrapping and mounding soil over the plant for winter.

container.notes: Outstanding container plant — one of the best fruit trees for containers. Overwinter in a cool garage or basement (no leaves needed — just above freezing).

propagation.desc: Take 8–10 inch pencil-thick cuttings in late winter. Allow ends to dry 24 hours. Insert in moist potting mix. Roots in 4–6 weeks. The easiest fruit tree to propagate.
Pin a low branch to the ground. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: When fruit is soft to the touch, slightly drooping on the stem, and the skin begins to crack slightly. The color change (depending on variety) and drop in neck are good indicators. Taste one — a ripe fresh fig is unforgettable.
harvest.how: Twist gently and pull. Wear gloves — the milky sap irritates skin.
harvest.storage: Fresh figs are extremely perishable — eat within 2–3 days. Refrigerate up to 5 days. Dry, jam, or freeze.
harvest.yield: 40–80 pounds per mature tree per season.

common_mistakes: Picking too early — figs don't ripen after picking. Wait until fully soft.
Not enough heat — figs ripen poorly in cool climates.
Overwatering — reduces sugar content. Reduce water as fruit ripens.
Sap contact without gloves — causes skin irritation.

seed_saving.type: Propagated by cuttings — the easiest fruit tree to propagate.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Hardwood cuttings in late winter.
seed_saving.drying: Allow cut surface to dry 24 hours.
seed_saving.notes: Get a cutting from a neighbor's favorite fig — many heirloom varieties are passed this way.

good.why: Dynamic accumulator — mines nutrients for fig.
Ground cover, pest deterrent.
Attracts pollinators.

bad.why: Figs are generally compatible with most plants.

culinary: Fresh figs eaten out of hand — transcendent when fully ripe. Fig and prosciutto. Fig jam and preserves. Dried figs. Fig tarts and galettes. Roasted figs with honey. Fig and blue cheese. Fig wine. Fresh figs with ricotta. The difference between fresh and dried is extreme — fresh figs are a fleeting seasonal delicacy.
medicinal: High in fiber — used traditionally as a laxative (fig syrup of figs). High in calcium, potassium, and antioxidants. Ficin — a proteolytic enzyme in fig latex — used as a meat tenderizer and has been studied for its anti-inflammatory properties. Traditional use throughout the Mediterranean for digestive health and skin conditions.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: leaves and sap — ficin enzyme causes skin and GI irritation
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Skin irritation from sap. Vomiting and diarrhea if leaves or sap eaten.
pet_toxicity.notes: Fig fruit is safe for pets in small amounts. The sap and leaves cause skin irritation and GI upset. Keep pets from chewing on fig plants.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth. Figs planted in containers can be planted slightly deeper.

varieties.name: Brown Turkey
varieties.description: The most cold-hardy common fig. Brown-purple skin, pinkish flesh. Sweet. Very productive. Best for zones 6–9.
varieties.notes: Most widely available and most cold-hardy.

varieties.name: Chicago Hardy
varieties.description: Extremely cold-hardy — survives to zone 5 with protection. Brown fruit. Very sweet.

varieties.name: Celeste
varieties.description: Small to medium purple-brown fruit. Very sweet, honey-like flavor. Very productive. Closed eye — resistant to souring. Excellent in humid climates.
varieties.notes: Best flavor. Best for humid climates (eye doesn't collect water).

varieties.name: Kadota
varieties.description: Green-yellow skin when ripe. Amber-pink flesh. Very sweet, mild flavor. Used commercially for canning.

varieties.name: Black Mission
varieties.description: The classic California fig. Deep purple-black skin. Rich, intense flavor. Best in hot dry climates.
varieties.notes: Best for hot dry climates (California, Southwest).

pests.name: Fig Beetle
pests.desc: Large green beetle eats ripe fruit.

name: Grape
latin: Vitis vinifera / V. labrusca / V. rotundifolia

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root or container vines in early spring
season.harvest_window: Late summer to fall depending on variety — typically August–October.

seed.desc: Purchase 1–2 year old grafted or own-rooted vines. Named varieties must be grafted onto rootstocks resistant to phylloxera (a devastating root louse). Own-rooted American and muscadine grapes are resistant.

germination.desc: Seeds require cold stratification. Cuttings preferred.

seedling.desc: Year 1: establish the root system. Remove all fruit clusters in years 1–2.

young.desc: Years 2–5: training the vine structure. Grapes produce best on 1-year-old wood — pruning each year to maintain appropriate fruiting wood.

adult.desc: Full production from year 4–5. Grapevines are extremely long-lived — some European vines are 100+ years old. Annual pruning is the most important maintenance task. Grapes require 70–80% of wood removed each year for best production.

care.water: Moderate — grapes are drought tolerant once established. Reduce water as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars.
care.light: Full sun. Needs maximum heat and light.
care.soil: Average to poor, well-draining. pH 5.5–7.0. Deep soil. Avoid overly rich soil — promotes foliage over fruit.
care.spacing: 6–10 feet between vines. Require substantial trellis or arbor.
care.fertilizer: Minimal. Excess nitrogen promotes foliage over fruit. Potassium is the most important nutrient for fruit quality.
care.notes: Grapes are beautiful but demanding. The two requirements for success: full sun and annual pruning. Two-thirds to three-quarters of each vine must be cut away every winter — this seems brutal but grapes only fruit on one-year-old wood. Grapes on an overgrown unpruned vine produce almost nothing. For table grapes, American and hybrid varieties (Concord, Reliance, Marquette) are much easier than wine grapes.

container.notes: Compact table grape varieties in large containers. Requires significant pruning and trellis.

propagation.desc: Take 12–18 inch cuttings in winter. Insert in moist soil in spring. American and hybrid varieties root easily.
Grafted vines for phylloxera resistance — especially for wine grapes.

harvest.when: When berries are fully colored, slightly soft, and taste sweet with no greenness. Taste is the best guide — a brix meter (sugar refractometer) gives an exact reading.
harvest.how: Cut entire clusters with scissors.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate clusters up to 2 weeks. Process into juice, jelly, wine, or raisins.
harvest.yield: 5–15 pounds per vine depending on variety and training system.

common_mistakes: Not pruning — the most common reason for poor or no fruit
Too little sun — grapes need maximum light
Phylloxera — devastating root pest in many areas. Use grafted vines or American varieties.
Disease — European wine grapes require frequent fungicide applications in humid climates

seed_saving.type: Not practical for named varieties.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Hardwood cuttings for propagation.
seed_saving.notes: American and hybrid varieties propagate easily from hardwood cuttings.

good.why: Traditional companion — said to improve grape health and flavor.
Nitrogen fixer between vine rows.
Traditional companion for repelling pests.
