culinary: Fresh eating (table grapes). Wine (wine grapes). Grape juice. Raisins. Grape jelly and jam. Grape leaves for cooking (dolmades). Verjuice (unfermented grape juice). Grapes for drying. Grape seed oil.
medicinal: Resveratrol in grape skins — one of the most studied polyphenols for cardiovascular health, longevity, and cancer prevention. Grape seed extract — rich in proanthocyanidins with antioxidant and cardiovascular benefits. Red wine polyphenols associated with reduced cardiovascular disease in Mediterranean populations (the 'French Paradox'). Quercetin and other flavonoids throughout the fruit.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Acute kidney failure — potentially fatal. The mechanism is unknown but toxicity is well established. Even small amounts can be fatal to dogs.
pet_toxicity.notes: Grapes and raisins are severely toxic to dogs — can cause acute kidney failure and death. Keep strictly away from dogs. The toxic compound has not been identified and there is no safe dose. This applies to all grape varieties, all forms (fresh, dried/raisins, juice). Emergency vet immediately if a dog eats any grapes or raisins.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery pot depth or slightly deeper. Build or install the trellis or arbor BEFORE planting.

varieties.name: Concord
varieties.description: The classic American grape. Deep blue-black. Intense 'foxy' grape flavor. The Welch's grape. Excellent for juice, jelly, and juice. Zone 4–7.

varieties.name: Reliance
varieties.description: Seedless red table grape. Very sweet mild flavor. Good disease resistance. Zone 4–8.
varieties.notes: Best seedless table grape for cold climates.

varieties.name: Marquette
varieties.description: Cold-hardy wine grape (zone 3). Excellent wine quality — used for premium cold-climate wines. Disease resistant.
varieties.notes: Best wine grape for cold climates.

varieties.name: Muscat Blanc
varieties.description: White wine grape. Intensely fragrant floral flavor. Makes extraordinary wine and fresh eating. Zone 6–9.

varieties.name: Muscadine (Carlos / Noble)
varieties.description: Native southeastern US grape (Vitis rotundifolia). Extremely heat and disease resistant. Required for humid southeastern gardens. Different flavor from Vitis vinifera.
varieties.notes: Only practical grape for the humid Southeast. Use in zone 6–10 South.

pests.name: Black Rot
pests.desc: Circular brown leaf spots and mummified fruit — the most devastating grape disease in humid climates.
pests.control: Copper or sulfur fungicide, remove mummified fruit, improve air circulation.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves and fruit.

pests.name: Phylloxera
pests.desc: Root louse devastating to Vitis vinifera.

name: Apple

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root or container tree
season.harvest_window: July–November depending on variety

seed.desc: Purchase a grafted nursery tree — apples grown from seed do not come true and may take 8–12 years to fruit. A grafted tree on a dwarfing rootstock fruits in 2–4 years. Rootstock controls tree size: M.9 (dwarf 8–10ft), M.26 (semi-dwarf 12–15ft), MM.111 (standard 20–25ft).

germination.desc: Seeds require cold stratification. Not practical — buy grafted trees.

seedling.desc: Years 1–2: establish root system. Stake firmly. Prune to create an open-centered or central-leader framework. Remove any fruit that sets in year 1.

young.desc: Years 2–5: scaffold branches develop. Crop increases annually. Annual pruning while dormant shapes the tree and maintains productivity.

adult.desc: Full production from year 4–5 (dwarf) or 6–8 (standard). A well-managed apple tree produces for 50–100 years. Annual pruning, thinning, and pest management are the keys to consistent crops.

care.water: Consistent moisture — 1 inch per week during the growing season. Deep watering preferred. Drought stress reduces fruit size and triggers biennial bearing.
care.light: Full sun — 6–8 hours minimum. More sun = better fruit colour and flavour.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining, fertile. pH 6.0–7.0. Avoid low spots where frost settles.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring. Avoid excess nitrogen — promotes disease-susceptible lush growth over fruiting.
care.notes: Most apples require cross-pollination from a different variety blooming at the same time. Plant at least 2 compatible varieties. Crabapples work as pollinators. Thin fruit to one per cluster (6 inch spacing) in June for larger, better quality apples and to prevent biennial bearing.

container.min_size: 25–30 gallon. Dwarf varieties on M.9 rootstock only.
container.notes: Columnar and dwarf varieties excellent in large containers. Require annual root pruning or repotting.

propagation.desc: Bud or whip-and-tongue graft named varieties onto rootstocks. Requires skill but is the standard commercial method.
Buy grafted trees from reputable nurseries. Always verify rootstock for size control.

harvest.when: When fruit separates easily with a gentle upward twist, seeds are brown, and flesh has developed full colour. Taste is the final test.
harvest.how: Twist upward — ripe apples release cleanly. Never pull straight down.
harvest.storage: Cool storage (32–40°F) extends shelf life weeks to months depending on variety. Wrapped individually in newspaper in a cool cellar. Controlled atmosphere storage for commercial keeping.
harvest.yield: Dwarf: 40–160 lbs/year. Semi-dwarf: 200–400 lbs. Standard: 400–800 lbs at peak.

common_mistakes: Skipping thinning — overcrowded fruit is small and promotes biennial bearing
No cross-pollinator — many varieties are self-sterile
Planting in a frost pocket — late frosts kill blossoms
Not pruning annually — unpruned trees become unproductive thickets
Ignoring fire blight — spread rapidly, must be pruned out immediately

seed_saving.type: Not practical — apple seeds don't come true. Propagate by grafting.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Grafting only.
seed_saving.notes: Every apple seed is genetically unique — a tree grown from a Honeycrisp seed will not produce Honeycrisp apples.

good.why: Repel aphids. Traditional orchard companion.
Trap crop for aphids. Attracts beneficial insects.
Dynamic accumulator — mines nutrients. Excellent orchard ground cover.
Nitrogen fixer. Supports beneficial insects.

bad.why: Competes for water and nutrients. Keep a mulched circle.

culinary: Fresh eating. Apple pie and crumble. Cider (fresh and fermented). Apple butter and sauce. Dried apple rings. Cider vinegar. Cheese pairings. Pork and apple — the classic savoury combination. Tarte tatin. The variety determines the best use — cooking apples vs eating apples vs cider apples have very different characteristics.
medicinal: Quercetin — abundant in apple skin — is one of the most studied flavonoids for anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular effects. Pectin (soluble fibre) feeds beneficial gut bacteria and lowers cholesterol. 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away' has some clinical basis — regular apple consumption associated with reduced cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and certain cancers in epidemiological studies.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Seeds contain amygdalin which releases cyanide when metabolised. Apple flesh is safe and nutritious for pets.
pet_toxicity.notes: Apple flesh is safe and healthy for dogs and cats. The seeds and core contain amygdalin — remove before giving to pets. A few seeds are not dangerous but habitual seed consumption is not recommended.

transplant.deep_note: Plant with the graft union 2 inches ABOVE soil level — if buried, the scion rootstocks and the dwarfing effect is lost. Flare roots at soil surface.

varieties.name: Honeycrisp
varieties.description: Explosively crisp texture. Sweet-tart balanced flavour. Mid-season. The most popular modern apple. Zone 3–7.
varieties.notes: Best fresh eating. Most in-demand variety.

varieties.name: Fuji
varieties.description: Very sweet, dense, slow to brown. Late season. Excellent keeper — stores 5–6 months. Zone 6–9.
varieties.notes: Best for warm climates and long storage.

varieties.name: Granny Smith
varieties.description: Tart green apple. Excellent for baking — holds shape. Long keeper. Zone 5–8.

varieties.name: Liberty
varieties.description: Disease resistant — immune to apple scab, highly resistant to fire blight. Red sweet-tart. Excellent for organic growing.
varieties.notes: Best disease-resistant variety for low-spray growing.

varieties.name: Esopus Spitzenburg
varieties.description: Thomas Jefferson's favourite apple. Rich complex flavour. Heirloom. Zone 5–8.

pests.name: Apple Scab
pests.desc: Dark scabby lesions on fruit and leaves — most common apple disease.
pests.control: Resistant varieties, copper or sulfur spray in spring, remove fallen leaves.

pests.name: Fire Blight
pests.desc: Shepherd's crook shoot dieback — bacterial disease.
pests.control: Prune 12 inches below infection sterilising tools between cuts.

pests.name: Codling Moth
pests.desc: Wormy apples — larvae tunnel into fruit.
pests.control: Pheromone traps, kaolin clay, spinosad spray.

name: Pear

season.transplant: Early spring bare root or spring/fall container
season.harvest_window: August–October. European pears must be picked underripe and ripened off the tree.

seed.desc: Purchase grafted tree. European pears on Quince A or C rootstock (semi-dwarf). Asian pears on OHxF rootstock.

germination.desc: Propagated by grafting. Grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years.

seedling.desc: Years 1–3: establish. Train to central leader. Remove competing shoots.

young.desc: Years 3–5: increasing crops. Thin fruit for size. Fire blight is the primary threat.

adult.desc: Full production. Long-lived — pear trees commonly reach 75–100 years. Very productive per square foot when trained as an espalier on a wall.

care.water: Regular watering especially first 3 years. Established trees are somewhat drought tolerant.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Pears are more tolerant of wet soils than apples.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen in spring. Excess nitrogen dramatically increases fire blight susceptibility.
care.notes: European pears are picked BEFORE ripe — they ripen from the inside out and must be brought indoors to ripen. Test by lifting the fruit horizontal — if it releases with gentle pressure, pick it. Asian pears ripen on the tree like apples. Most pears require cross-pollination.

container.notes: Pears espalier beautifully against walls — excellent for small spaces.

propagation.desc: Chip budding or whip-and-tongue grafting onto rootstocks.
Buy grafted trees specifying rootstock for size control.

harvest.when: European: when fruit lifts easily at horizontal. Still firm, not soft. Ripen indoors at room temperature 1–2 weeks. Asian: when fully coloured and slightly soft on tree.
harvest.how: Lift gently to horizontal and twist. If it releases — pick it.
harvest.storage: Unwaxed European pears: 2–7 months in cool storage (32°F) before ripening. Asian pears: 1–3 months refrigerated.
harvest.yield: Dwarf: 50–100 lbs. Standard: 150–400 lbs at peak.

common_mistakes: Picking European pears ripe — they turn mealy inside. Always pick underripe.
Not cross-pollinating — most pears require a second variety
Too much nitrogen — fire blight devastates fertilizer-driven lush growth
Not thinning — small fruit and biennial bearing

seed_saving.type: Not practical — propagate by grafting.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Grafting.
seed_saving.notes: Pear seeds don't come true to parent.

good.why: Excellent orchard ground cover.
Attracts pollinators.
Trap crop for aphids.

culinary: Poached pears in red wine — the classic dessert. Pear and blue cheese. Pear tart. Pear butter and preserves. Pear cider (perry). Fresh eating. Pear and ginger jam. Asian pears: crisp fresh eating, sliced in salads, Korean BBQ accompaniment.
medicinal: High in pectin (soluble fibre) supporting gut health and cholesterol reduction. Sorbitol content gives pears mild laxative properties. Chlorogenic acid — an antioxidant — studied for blood sugar regulation. One of the lowest-allergen fruits — often recommended for elimination diets.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Flesh safe. Seeds contain trace amygdalin. Leaves toxic.
pet_toxicity.notes: Pear flesh is safe for pets. Remove seeds before giving to pets. Keep pets from eating fallen leaves.

transplant.deep_note: Graft union 2 inches above soil — same as apple. Never bury the graft union.

varieties.name: Bartlett (Williams)
varieties.description: The classic canning and fresh pear. Sweet musky flavour. Most widely grown. Self-fertile.
varieties.notes: Most widely grown. Good self-fertile option.

varieties.name: Bosc
varieties.description: Long russet-brown pear. Rich complex flavour. Excellent for baking — holds shape when cooked.

varieties.name: Anjou
varieties.description: Green or red. Mild sweet flavour. Excellent keeper — stores 6+ months. Good fresh eating.

varieties.name: Harrow Sweet
varieties.description: Fire blight resistant. Sweet buttery flavour. Productive. Best for organic growing.

varieties.name: Hosui (Asian)
varieties.description: Large round Asian pear. Crisp, very juicy, sweet. Ripens on tree. Excellent fresh.

pests.name: Fire Blight
pests.desc: The primary pear disease — more susceptible than apples.
pests.control: Resistant varieties, copper spray at bloom, aggressive pruning.

pests.name: Pear Psylla
pests.desc: Tiny insects causing yellowing and honeydew.
pests.control: Kaolin clay, insecticidal soap, dormant oil.

name: Peach

season.harvest_window: June–September depending on variety and zone

seed.desc: Purchase a grafted tree — varieties on Lovell or Guardian rootstocks. Peaches are generally self-fertile — one tree produces fruit. Peach trees are short-lived by fruit tree standards (15–25 years) but fruit quickly, often in year 2–3.

germination.desc: Grafted trees. Peach pits can be cold stratified and grown but produce highly variable results.

seedling.desc: Years 1–2: vigorous growth. Train to an open-center (vase) shape — 3–5 main scaffold branches with no central leader. This allows light into the center.

young.desc: Years 2–4: first crops. Peaches fruit on one-year-old wood — annual pruning is critical to keep generating new productive wood.

adult.desc: Peak production years 4–15. Requires more annual pruning than apples or pears — remove about 40% of the previous year's growth every winter to maintain fruiting wood. Heavy thinning to one fruit per 6 inches produces much larger fruit.

care.water: Consistent moisture — especially during fruit development. Drought during pit hardening causes split pits and gummy bark.
care.light: Full sun. Needs heat to ripen well.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining, sandy loam preferred. pH 6.0–6.5. Peaches hate wet feet.
care.fertilizer: Nitrogen in early spring only. Measure shoot growth — 12–18 inches per year is ideal. More = too much nitrogen.
care.notes: Peaches require a chilling requirement (hours below 45°F) to bloom and fruit properly. Low-chill varieties for zones 8–9. Brown rot is the most destructive disease — avoid wetting fruit, harvest promptly.

container.notes: Genetic dwarf peaches ('Bonanza', 'El Dorado') bred specifically for containers — reach 5–6ft and produce full-sized fruit.

propagation.desc: T-budding in summer onto rootstock. Standard commercial method.
Cold stratify pit 3–4 months. Germinates spring. Variable result — not recommended for named varieties.

harvest.when: When fruit gives slightly to pressure, is fully coloured, and separates easily from the branch. Peaches do not continue to ripen off the tree significantly — harvest at the right moment.
harvest.how: Cup the fruit and lift gently with a slight twist.
harvest.storage: Room temperature 2–3 days. Refrigerate up to 1 week (refrigeration halts ripening and reduces flavour). Freeze, can, or make preserves immediately.
harvest.yield: Standard tree: 100–200 lbs at peak. Genetic dwarf: 30–50 lbs.

common_mistakes: Not thinning — small fruit and broken branches from weight
Not pruning annually — fruit moves to canopy top, out of reach
Harvesting too early — peaches must be fully ripe. Refrigerate immediately after picking.
Brown rot — harvest all fruit promptly, never leave rotting fruit on tree or ground

seed_saving.type: Pit stratification possible but highly variable results.
seed_saving.harvest: Clean pit from ripe fruit.
seed_saving.method: Cold stratify in damp peat 3–4 months. Sow in spring.
seed_saving.notes: Seedling trees are genetically unique — may not resemble parent. Buy grafted trees for known varieties.

good.why: Orchard ground cover, nutrient accumulator.
Deters peach leaf curl and borers.
Deters aphids and pests.

bad.why: Share brown rot and other diseases.

culinary: Fresh eating — a perfectly ripe peach from the tree is one of the finest fruits. Peach pie and cobbler. Peach jam and preserves. Peach ice cream. Grilled peaches with burrata. Peach salsa. Bellini cocktail. Peach schnapps. Dried peaches.
medicinal: High in vitamin C, vitamin A (as beta-carotene), and potassium. Chlorogenic acid — same antioxidant as in coffee — is abundant in peaches. Peach kernel oil used in cosmetics. Traditional Chinese medicine uses dried peach kernel (tao ren) as a blood-moving herb for pain and menstrual conditions.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: pit, leaves, and stems — amygdalin (cyanide precursor)
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Pit: choking hazard and cyanide toxicity. Leaves/stems: vomiting, difficulty breathing.
pet_toxicity.notes: Peach flesh is safe for pets. The pit is extremely dangerous — choking hazard and contains amygdalin. Leaves and stems also toxic. Keep fallen fruit and leaves picked up if pets have access.

transplant.deep_note: Graft union 2–3 inches above soil. Flare roots at soil level. Stake for first 2 years.
transplant.mulch: straw or wood chips (away from trunk)

varieties.name: Reliance
varieties.description: Extremely cold-hardy (zone 4–5). Freestone, yellow flesh. Sweet and juicy. Very reliable in northern climates.

varieties.name: Redhaven
varieties.description: Classic mid-season peach. Freestone, firm yellow flesh. Excellent flavour. The benchmark variety.

varieties.name: Contender
varieties.description: Cold-hardy (zone 4). Good disease resistance. Large freestone fruit. Mid-late season.
varieties.notes: Best combination of cold hardiness and disease resistance.

varieties.name: Arctic Supreme
varieties.description: White-fleshed peach — sweeter, less acidic than yellow. Complex flavour. Zone 6–9.
varieties.notes: Best white peach for flavour complexity.

varieties.name: Bonanza (Genetic Dwarf)
varieties.description: 4–5ft genetic dwarf. Full-sized freestone yellow fruit. Perfect for containers.

pests.name: Brown Rot
pests.desc: Fuzzy brown mould on ripening fruit — most destructive peach disease.
pests.control: Remove all infected fruit immediately. Never leave rotting fruit. Copper spray at petal fall.

pests.name: Peach Leaf Curl
pests.desc: Red blistered distorted leaves in spring.
pests.control: Copper spray in late winter before buds swell. The only effective timing.

pests.name: Oriental Fruit Moth
pests.desc: Larvae in shoot tips then fruit.

name: Cherry

season.transplant: Early spring bare root or spring/fall container
season.harvest_window: June–July (sweet). July–August (sour).

seed.desc: Purchase grafted tree. Sweet cherries on Gisela 5 (semi-dwarf) or Mazzard (standard) rootstocks. Most sweet cherries require cross-pollination — plant 2 compatible varieties or choose self-fertile varieties. Sour cherries are self-fertile.

germination.desc: Grafted trees. Cherries fruit in 3–5 years.

seedling.desc: Years 1–3: vigorous establishment. Train sweet cherries to a central leader or modified central leader. Sour cherries to an open center.

young.desc: Years 3–5: increasing crop. Birds become a serious problem as fruit ripens — netting is essential.

adult.desc: Full production. Sweet cherries are the most vigorous and potentially largest fruit trees — standard trees can reach 30–35ft. Gisela rootstocks keep them manageable at 10–15ft. Sour cherries are naturally compact (12–15ft).

care.water: Consistent moisture. Avoid overhead irrigation — promotes brown rot. Water at base.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Cherries are extremely sensitive to wet feet — never plant in low spots.
care.spacing: Sweet standard: 25–30ft. Sweet Gisela semi-dwarf: 10–15ft. Sour: 15–20ft.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen in spring. Measure shoot growth — 10–18 inches for sweet, 8–12 for sour is ideal.
care.notes: Birds will take every ripe cherry if not netted. Begin netting when fruit starts to colour. Sweet cherries split badly if it rains during ripening — grow in a location with some overhead protection or choose split-resistant varieties. Sour cherries are far easier than sweet for most home gardeners.

container.notes: Sweet cherries on Gisela 5 work in large containers. Genetic dwarf varieties also available.

propagation.desc: Standard commercial propagation method. Buds inserted onto rootstock in summer.

harvest.when: When fully coloured and sweet (taste one). Sweet cherries: fully dark red. Sour: fully red and slightly soft. Cherries do not ripen after picking.
harvest.how: Pick with stems attached — stemless cherries deteriorate rapidly.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate immediately. Last 1–2 weeks with stems. Freeze, make jam, or preserve promptly.
harvest.yield: Semi-dwarf sweet: 40–80 lbs. Sour: 30–60 lbs at maturity.

common_mistakes: No bird netting — birds take the entire crop in hours
Sweet cherry splitting in rain — harvest before heavy rain if possible
No cross-pollinator for sweet cherries — research compatibility before buying
Wet soil — cherries decline and die in poorly drained soil

seed_saving.type: Not practical — propagate by budding.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Budding.
seed_saving.notes: Cherry seedlings do not come true.

good.why: Deter aphids and borers.
Ground cover, nutrient accumulator.
Pest deterrent at base.

culinary: Fresh eating — sweet cherries are a fleeting seasonal luxury. Sour cherry pie — considered by many the finest of all fruit pies. Morello cherry jam. Black Forest cake. Kirsch (cherry brandy). Cherries jubilee. Maraschino cherries. Cherry compote. Dried sour cherries in salads and baked goods.
medicinal: Tart cherry juice is one of the most studied sports nutrition foods — multiple clinical trials confirm it reduces exercise-induced muscle soreness and inflammation. Anthocyanins in sour cherries have documented anti-inflammatory effects comparable to ibuprofen in some studies. High in melatonin — tart cherry juice studied for improving sleep quality. Traditional use for gout — anthocyanins reduce uric acid levels, confirmed in clinical research.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: pits, leaves, stems, and bark — amygdalin
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Cherry flesh safe in small amounts. Pits, leaves, stems: cyanide precursor causes vomiting, difficulty breathing, collapse.
pet_toxicity.notes: Cherry flesh is safe for pets in small amounts — remove pit first. All other parts are toxic. The wilted leaves of Prunus species are particularly dangerous. Keep fallen fruit and leaves cleaned up.

transplant.deep_note: Graft union 2 inches above soil. Never bury.

varieties.name: Stella (Sweet)
varieties.description: Self-fertile sweet cherry — rare. Large dark red fruit. Excellent flavour. Zone 5–8.
varieties.notes: Best self-fertile sweet cherry — no pollinator needed.

varieties.name: Bing (Sweet)
varieties.description: The classic large dark red sweet cherry. Firm, sweet, excellent flavour. Requires pollinator.

varieties.name: Rainier (Sweet)
varieties.description: Yellow-red bicolor. Very sweet, delicate flavour. Premium market cherry. Requires pollinator.
varieties.notes: Highest-value sweet cherry. Most delicate flavour.

varieties.name: Montmorency (Sour)
varieties.description: The standard sour/tart cherry. Self-fertile. The variety used in tart cherry juice research. Most widely grown sour cherry.
varieties.notes: Best all-around sour cherry. Self-fertile. The medicinal research variety.

varieties.name: Morello (Sour)
varieties.description: Very tart, dark red-black. Self-fertile. Excellent for cooking, jam, and liqueur. More shade tolerant than other cherries.
varieties.notes: Best for cooking and preserves. Most shade tolerant.

pests.name: Birds
pests.desc: Take every ripe cherry — the #1 cherry problem.
pests.control: Bird netting from when fruit begins to colour. The only reliable solution.

pests.name: Brown Rot
pests.desc: Fuzzy mould on ripening fruit — worse in rain.
pests.control: Copper spray, remove infected fruit, avoid overhead watering.

name: Plum

season.harvest_window: July–September. Japanese plums ripen earlier than European.

seed.desc: Purchase grafted tree. European plums on Myrobalan or St. Julien rootstock. Japanese plums on Myrobalan. Plums are among the easiest and most reliable fruit trees for beginners.

germination.desc: Grafted trees. Fruit in 3–6 years.

seedling.desc: Years 1–3: vigorous establishment. European plums can reach 20ft if unpruned. Japanese are slightly smaller. Train to open center.

young.desc: Years 3–6: increasing crops. Plums tend to overbear — thin to 4–6 inches between fruit for best size.

adult.desc: Full production. Plums are among the most productive and reliable of all fruit trees. Brown rot is the main disease concern. Otherwise relatively problem-free compared to apples and peaches.

care.water: Moderate — plums are somewhat drought tolerant once established. Consistent moisture during fruit development improves size.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Deep, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. More tolerant of clay than apples or peaches.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in spring. Plums are moderate feeders.
care.notes: European plums are mostly self-fertile. Japanese plums usually require cross-pollination. Plums are more tolerant of difficult conditions than other stone fruits — a good choice for beginning orchardists.

container.notes: Dwarf plums on Pixy rootstock work well in large containers.

propagation.desc: T-budding onto rootstock. Standard commercial method.

harvest.when: Slightly soft to the touch, fully coloured, and sweet. Plums continue to ripen slightly after picking but are best tree-ripened.
harvest.how: Gently cup and twist upward. Pick with stems.
harvest.storage: Room temperature 3–5 days. Refrigerate up to 2 weeks. Excellent for jam, preserves, and drying (prunes).
harvest.yield: Standard: 100–150 lbs at peak. Semi-dwarf: 50–80 lbs.

common_mistakes: Not thinning — overbearing causes small fruit and broken branches
Brown rot — remove all infected fruit promptly
Japanese plums needing cross-pollinator
Letting fruit overripen on tree — pick slightly underripe if leaving for more than a day

seed_saving.type: Not practical — propagate by budding.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Budding.
seed_saving.notes: Plum seeds highly variable — buy grafted trees.

good.why: Deters borers and aphids.
Orchard ground cover.
Trap crop for aphids.

bad.why: Brown rot spreads on wind spores.

culinary: Fresh eating. Plum jam — one of the finest preserves. Plum tart and galette. Slivovitz (plum brandy — central European tradition). Umeboshi (Japanese pickled plum — technically apricot). Plum sauce (Chinese). Dried Italian plums (prunes). Roasted plums with vanilla. Plum chutney.
medicinal: Prunes (dried plums) are clinically proven to prevent and treat constipation — more effective than psyllium in clinical trials. High in sorbitol (natural laxative) and phenolic compounds that stimulate intestinal motility. Prune consumption associated with improved bone density in postmenopausal women in several clinical trials. High in vitamin K and potassium.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Flesh safe in small amounts. Pit is a choking hazard and contains cyanide precursor.
pet_toxicity.notes: Plum flesh is safe for pets in small amounts — always remove pit. All other parts toxic. Clean up fallen fruit and leaves.

transplant.deep_note: Graft union 2 inches above soil. Stake first 2–3 years.

varieties.name: Stanley (European)
varieties.description: Self-fertile. Blue-purple freestone. Classic prune/plum. Very reliable and productive. Zone 4–8.

varieties.name: Italian Prune (European)
varieties.description: The classic drying plum. Freestone, sweet, low moisture. Self-fertile.

varieties.name: Methley (Japanese)
varieties.description: Self-fertile Japanese plum — rare. Red-purple sweet fruit. Very early. Zone 5–9.

varieties.name: Santa Rosa (Japanese)
varieties.description: The benchmark Japanese plum. Large, red, excellent sweet-tart flavour. Zone 5–9.

varieties.name: Damson
varieties.description: Small, tart, blue-black. Self-fertile. Classic jam and gin plum. Very productive.
varieties.notes: Best for jam and sloe-gin style preserves.

pests.name: Brown Rot
pests.desc: Most serious plum disease. Fuzzy mould on ripening fruit.
pests.control: Remove infected fruit immediately, copper spray.

pests.name: Plum Curculio
pests.desc: Crescent-shaped scars on fruit from egg-laying weevil.
pests.control: Kaolin clay, spinosad, pick up fallen fruit.

name: Gooseberry

season.start_indoors: Purchase bare root canes in early spring
season.harvest_window: July — brief 2–3 week harvest window. Berries ripen progressively.

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plants — 1–2 year old bare root or container. Self-fertile — one plant produces fruit. Begins fruiting in year 2–3.

germination.desc: Seeds require cold stratification. Cuttings preferred.

seedling.desc: Year 1: establishes quickly. Thorned varieties — wear gloves when handling.

young.desc: Year 2: first crop. Gooseberries are among the fastest-producing fruit shrubs.

adult.desc: Productive from year 3+. Long-lived shrub reaching 4–5ft with annual pruning. Very cold hardy — one of the few fruit crops that succeeds in very cold climates.

care.water: Moderate — more drought tolerant than currants. Consistent moisture during fruit development.
care.light: Full sun to partial shade — more shade tolerant than most fruit crops.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, moist. pH 6.0–7.0. High organic matter.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring.
care.notes: Gooseberries are self-fertile — one plant fruits well. Prune out oldest canes (over 4 years) annually, keep 8–12 of the best young canes. Thorned varieties are more vigorous; thornless easier to harvest. American varieties (R. hirtellum) resist powdery mildew better. Note: gooseberries were banned in some US states for decades as an alternate host for white pine blister rust — check your state's current regulations.

container.notes: Good container plant. Use thornless varieties for easier harvest.

propagation.desc: Take 8–10 inch cuttings in late autumn/winter. Insert in soil with 2 buds above ground. Root by spring. Very easy.
Pin cane to soil. Roots in one season.

harvest.when: Green gooseberries for cooking: when full-sized but still firm and tart (June). Ripe gooseberries for fresh eating: when fully coloured and slightly soft (July).
harvest.how: Pick individually with gloves on thorned varieties. The thorns are sharp.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 2–3 weeks. Freeze well — freeze on trays then bag. Excellent for jam.
harvest.yield: 3–8 lbs per mature plant.

common_mistakes: Not wearing gloves on thorned varieties — the thorns cause real injury
Powdery mildew — space well, choose resistant varieties
Harvesting all at once — pick progressively as berries ripen
Overcrowding — gooseberries need good air circulation

seed_saving.type: Propagated by hardwood cuttings.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Hardwood cuttings — extremely easy.
seed_saving.notes: Free propagation from cuttings every winter.

good.why: Nutrient accumulator ground cover.
Attracts pollinators and beneficial insects.

bad.why: Alternate host for white pine blister rust — a legal restriction in some states.

culinary: Classic English gooseberry fool (pureed with cream). Gooseberry jam — tart and jewel-bright. Gooseberry crumble. Gooseberry wine. Gooseberry sauce for mackerel and oily fish — the tartness cuts the fat. Gooseberry chutney. Green gooseberries for cooking; ripe for fresh eating.
medicinal: High in vitamin C (comparable to citrus), vitamin A, and flavonoids. Traditional use in Ayurvedic medicine as amla (Indian gooseberry — a different species but same genus) for liver support, digestion, and immunity. European gooseberries used historically as a cooling medicinal food for fevers.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None. The thorns cause physical injury.
pet_toxicity.notes: Gooseberries are not toxic to pets. The thorned canes can cause physical injury — keep pets away from the plant structure.

transplant.deep_note: Plant 2 inches deeper than nursery pot depth — encourages multiple basal shoots and a bushier habit.

varieties.name: Invicta (Thornless)
varieties.description: Large pale green berries. Good mildew resistance. Thornless — easy harvest. Very productive.

varieties.name: Pixwell
varieties.description: American variety. Pink when ripe. Nearly thornless. Good mildew resistance. Very cold-hardy to zone 3.
varieties.notes: Best for cold climates. Best disease resistance.

varieties.name: Hinnonmaki Red
varieties.description: Finnish heirloom. Dark red ripe berries. Excellent sweet-tart flavour. Good mildew resistance.

varieties.name: Whinham's Industry
varieties.description: Large dark red berries. Rich flavour. Vigorous. Thorned but manageable.
varieties.notes: Classic English variety with excellent flavour.

pests.name: Powdery Mildew
pests.desc: White coating on leaves and fruit tips — most serious gooseberry problem.
pests.control: Improve air circulation, resistant varieties, potassium bicarbonate spray.

pests.name: Gooseberry Sawfly
pests.control: Inspect undersides of leaves weekly in May–June. Hand-pick larvae. Spinosad.

name: Persimmon

season.harvest_window: October–November. After first frost for American. Before frost for most Asian.

seed.desc: Purchase grafted nursery tree. American persimmon (D. virginiana) is native to the eastern US, extremely cold-hardy (zone 4), and produces small but intensely flavoured fruit. Asian persimmon (D. kaki) produces large supermarket-type fruit but requires zone 7+.

germination.desc: Seeds cold stratify naturally outdoors. Grafted trees strongly preferred for named varieties.

seedling.desc: Long establishment period — persimmons are slow to bear. First fruit in 3–7 years from grafted trees.

young.desc: Years 5–7: first significant crops. Persimmons are worth the wait — they require almost zero care once established.

adult.desc: One of the most trouble-free fruit trees available. No significant pest or disease problems. Drought tolerant once established. Long-lived. The fruit hangs on the tree like orange ornaments long after the leaves fall.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established. Water during establishment and during fruit development.
care.light: Full sun for best fruit production. Tolerates partial shade.
care.soil: Adaptable — tolerates poor, clay, and dry soils better than almost any other fruit tree. pH 6.0–7.5.
care.fertilizer: Minimal — persimmons thrive in lean conditions. Light balanced fertilizer if growth is poor.
care.notes: American persimmon may be male, female, or both — plant multiple seedlings or choose named grafted varieties. Asian persimmons are mostly self-fertile. Astringent types (Hachiya) must be fully soft before eating — biting into an unripe astringent persimmon is a memorably unpleasant experience. Non-astringent types (Fuyu) can be eaten firm.

container.min_size: Too large for practical container growing.
container.notes: Not practical long-term.

propagation.desc: T-budding onto D. virginiana rootstock.
American persimmon from seed — cold stratify, plant in spring. Variable but interesting results.

harvest.when: Astringent types: when fully soft (after frost or after cold storage to remove astringency). Non-astringent: when fully orange and firm. American: after frost when fruit drops or is nearly black-orange.
harvest.how: Harvest by hand. American persimmons fall when ripe.
harvest.storage: Refrigerate 1 month. Freeze for longer. Dry for persimmon chips.
harvest.yield: Mature tree: 50–200+ lbs per season.

common_mistakes: Eating astringent persimmons before fully ripe — extremely astringent and unpleasant
Confusing astringent and non-astringent varieties — know which you have
Not waiting for frost on American persimmons — frost breaks down tannins
Ignoring the taproot — persimmons have deep taproots. Transplant young or buy container-grown.

seed_saving.type: American persimmon from seed is worthwhile.
seed_saving.harvest: Seeds from fully ripe fallen fruit.
seed_saving.method: Clean seeds, cold stratify 3 months, sow in spring.
seed_saving.notes: Named varieties don't come true from seed. But American persimmon seedlings are interesting and valuable as rootstocks.

good.why: Naturalistic planting — American persimmon is a native understory tree.
Ground cover, nutrient accumulator.

culinary: Asian persimmon: fresh eating, persimmon bread and pudding, dried persimmon (hoshigaki — Japanese air-dried delicacy). Non-astringent Fuyu: sliced in salads, eaten like an apple. Astringent Hachiya: baked into pudding and bread when fully soft. American persimmon: persimmon pudding (a classic American frontier dessert), jam, beer.
medicinal: High in vitamin A (beta-carotene), vitamin C, and manganese. Betulinic acid — a compound in persimmon skin — has shown anticancer activity in laboratory studies. Traditional Chinese medicine uses the calyx (dried stem base) for hiccups. Very high in dietary fibre. Persimmon tannins have antimicrobial properties.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: seeds and pit cause intestinal blockage
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Seeds can cause intestinal obstruction if swallowed whole.
pet_toxicity.notes: Persimmon flesh is safe for pets. Remove seeds — they can cause intestinal blockage. Do not feed large quantities.

transplant.deep_note: Plant at nursery depth. Persimmons have a deep taproot — minimise root disturbance. Plant young trees.

varieties.name: Hachiya (Asian astringent)
varieties.description: Large, acorn-shaped, deep orange. Must be completely soft before eating. Excellent for baking and pudding.
varieties.notes: Most widely available Asian astringent. Best for cooking.

varieties.name: Fuyu (Asian non-astringent)
varieties.description: Flat-bottomed, tomato-shaped. Eaten firm like an apple. The most popular fresh-eating persimmon.
varieties.notes: Best for fresh eating. Non-astringent — no waiting.

varieties.name: Meader (American)
varieties.description: Self-fertile American persimmon — rare. Small sweet fruit after frost. Zone 4. Very productive.
varieties.notes: Best American persimmon for cold climates and guaranteed fruit set.

varieties.name: Early Golden (American)
varieties.description: Earlier ripening American persimmon. Good flavour. Zone 4–9.
varieties.notes: Best American persimmon for earlier ripening.

pests.name: Practically none
pests.desc: Persimmons are remarkably pest and disease free — one of the lowest-maintenance fruit trees.

pests.name: Persimmon Gall Midge
pests.control: Clean up fallen fruit. Usually not severe.

name: Calathea (Prayer Plant)

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage — leaves open in morning, fold upward at night (nyctinasty)

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagate by division at repotting. Calatheas are notoriously fussy but pet-safe.

germination.desc: Division establishes in 2–4 weeks.

seedling.desc: New growth slowly emerges. Keep warm and humid.

young.desc: Plant establishes. New leaves unfurl — each one a unique artwork.

adult.desc: One of the most visually spectacular houseplants — intricate geometric patterns on leaves in green, white, pink, purple, and silver. Leaves move daily (prayer plant movement). Reclassified from Calathea to Goeppertia botanically but still universally sold as Calathea.

care.water: Consistently moist but never waterlogged. Use filtered or distilled water — calatheas are very sensitive to fluoride and chlorine in tap water (causes brown leaf tips). Allow top inch to dry between waterings.
care.light: Low to medium indirect light. No direct sun — leaves bleach and scorch. One of the better low-light houseplants.
care.soil: Rich, well-draining, moisture-retentive. Peat-free mixes with perlite.
care.fertilizer: Diluted balanced fertilizer every 4 weeks during growing season. Never in winter.
care.notes: Calatheas are the houseplant that teaches patience. They are fussy about water quality (use rainwater or filtered), humidity (50%+), and temperature (no drafts, no cold). The reward is extraordinary foliage that few other houseplants match. The nightly leaf movement (prayer movement) is charming — leaves fold upward at dusk and open at dawn. One of the only common houseplants that is completely pet-safe.

container.notes: Repot every 2 years or when rootbound. Spring repotting.

propagation.desc: Divide clumps at repotting. Each division needs several healthy stems and roots. Keep humid after dividing.

young.desc: Dramatic growth in good conditions. Large paddle-shaped leaves on long petioles.

adult.desc: One of the most dramatic indoor plants — large blue-green paddle-shaped leaves reaching 4–6ft indoors. Orange and blue crane-like flowers possible indoors with sufficient light. The giant white bird of paradise (S. nicolai) can reach 6ft+ indoors with enormous split leaves.

care.water: Allow top 2 inches to dry between waterings. Drought tolerant once established — errs on the side of underwatering. Yellow leaves signal overwatering.
care.light: Bright indirect to direct indoor light — one of the highest-light-requirement houseplants. South or west facing window. More light = faster growth and possible flowering.

name: Dracaena

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage

seed.desc: Purchase nursery plant. Propagate by stem cuttings.

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage — extremely slow-growing but virtually indestructible

seed.desc: Purchase plant or divide established clump. The slowest-growing common houseplant.

germination.desc: Division establishes slowly.

seedling.desc: Very slow growth — one leaf per month is typical.

young.desc: Gradual increase in leaf count. Do not rush repotting.

adult.desc: The most tolerant houseplant in existence — tolerates deep shade, irregular watering, temperature extremes, dust, and near total neglect. Dark green strap-like leaves reaching 2ft. care.water: Very drought tolerant — water only when soil is nearly dry. Monthly in winter. Overwatering is the only real way to harm this plant.
care.light: Low to very low light — the benchmark for low-light tolerance. Tolerates deep shade that would kill virtually any other plant. Will also grow in brighter indirect light but doesn't need it.
care.soil: Any well-draining potting mix.
care.fertilizer: Fertilize only 2–3 times per year. Slow grower doesn't need much.
care.notes: The cast iron plant earned its name. If you have a dark corner that has killed every other plant, this is the answer. One new leaf per month is considered good growth. Do not repot often — it prefers being rootbound and rarely needs a larger pot. One of the few pet-safe houseplants.

container.notes: Rarely needs repotting — every 4–5 years maximum. Uses heavy pots to prevent tipping from large leaves.

name: Boston Fern

season.harvest_window: Year-round lush foliage — dramatic in hanging baskets

seed.desc: Purchase plant or divide established clump. One of the most popular hanging basket plants.

germination.desc: Division establishes quickly.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly with humidity and indirect light.

young.desc: Arching fronds develop. Plant fills out rapidly in good conditions.

adult.desc: Dramatic cascading arching fronds reaching 2–3ft. One of the finest hanging basket plants. NASA top air purifier — one of the most effective plants for removing formaldehyde and xylene. Drops fronds aggressively in dry conditions — this is the most important care consideration.

care.water: Keep consistently moist — never allow to dry out. Ferns wilt and drop fronds rapidly when dry. Check daily in summer. Bottom watering works well — set pot in water 30 minutes.
care.light: Bright indirect light to medium indirect. No direct sun — fronds burn. Can tolerate lower light but grows slowly.
care.soil: Rich, moisture-retentive, well-draining. Peat-based or coco coir mix.
care.spacing: One per pot. Hanging basket ideal.
care.fertilizer: Diluted balanced fertilizer monthly during growing season.
care.notes: The primary enemy of Boston ferns is dry air. In heated indoor environments in winter, misting daily or using a humidifier is often necessary. Fronds drop aggressively without adequate humidity — the plant usually recovers with improved conditions. One of the best pet-safe air purifiers. Overwintering: trim back and keep barely moist in a cool bright location.

container.notes: The classic hanging basket fern. Also good in decorative urns or elevated pots where fronds can cascade.

propagation.desc: Divide clumps at repotting. Each division needs several healthy fronds and roots.
Boston ferns produce long stolons (runners) that can be pinned to moist soil to produce new plants.

harvest.when: N/A.

Heated drafts — from heating vents cause rapid frond drop.

name: Air Plant (Tillandsia)

season.harvest_window: Year-round — blooms once in lifetime then produces pups

seed.desc: Purchase plants — no soil or pot needed. One of the most unusual and low-maintenance houseplants.

germination.desc: Tillandsias don't need propagation setup — they produce pups (offsets) after blooming.

seedling.desc: Pups appear around the base after the mother plant blooms.

young.desc: Pups slowly grow into new plants.

adult.desc: Tillandsias are epiphytes — they grow without soil, absorbing water and nutrients through their leaves. Mount on driftwood, cork bark, shells, or arrange in terrariums. Each plant blooms once (a spectacular event) then produces 2–8 pups before slowly dying. The pups continue the colony.

care.water: Soak in room-temperature water for 20–30 minutes 1–2 times per week (or more in dry conditions). Shake off excess water and allow to dry completely within 4 hours — water trapped at the base causes rot. Misting alone is rarely sufficient.
care.light: Bright indirect light. Some direct morning sun acceptable. Avoid harsh afternoon sun.
care.soil: No soil needed. Mount or display on any decorative surface.
care.spacing: Individual plants or clusters on mounts.
care.fertilizer: Diluted bromeliad or orchid fertilizer monthly — mist or add to soaking water.
care.notes: The soaking method is far superior to misting alone. After soaking, always shake dry and rest upside down briefly to prevent water pooling at the base — this causes rot. The bloom spike is a once-in-a-lifetime event — spectacular colour. After blooming, focus care on the pups. One of the only completely pet-safe houseplants requiring no soil.

container.min_size: No container needed — mount on driftwood, cork, rocks, shells, or display in open terrariums.
container.notes: No pot or soil required. This is the defining feature.

propagation.desc: Separate pups from mother plant when they are 1/3 the size of the mother. Gently twist and pull to detach.

harvest.when: N/A.
harvest.how: N/A.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Each plant blooms once — spectacular. Then produces 2–8 pups.

common_mistakes: Misting only — insufficient moisture. Soak weekly.
Water trapped at base — causes rot. Always shake dry and rest upside down briefly.
No light — needs bright indirect light despite the 'air plant' name.
Buried in a closed terrarium — needs air circulation to dry properly after watering.

seed_saving.type: Pup division after blooming.
seed_saving.harvest: Separate pups when 1/3 of mother's size.
seed_saving.method: Gentle twist and pull.
seed_saving.notes: Colony perpetuates naturally through pups.

name: Moth Orchid (Phalaenopsis)

season.harvest_window: Blooms November–May typically. Each flower spike lasts 2–4 months.

seed.desc: Purchase blooming or near-blooming nursery plant. Phalaenopsis is the most beginner-friendly orchid — far easier than its exotic reputation suggests.

germination.desc: Orchid seeds require laboratory conditions — propagate by keiki (plantlet) division.

seedling.desc: After bloom: cut spike above a node. With luck a new spike or keiki (baby plant) will develop.

young.desc: After bloom, enter a rest period. Continue regular care. New flower spike typically emerges in autumn in response to cooler temperatures.

adult.desc: With proper care, Phalaenopsis blooms annually or more. Each spike carries 10–20 flowers lasting 2–4 months. The key to reblooming: a 10–15°F temperature drop at night in autumn triggers new spike formation.

care.water: Water weekly — thoroughly drench the bark medium, then allow to drain completely. Never allow to sit in water. Between waterings allow bark to nearly dry. Ice cube watering method (place 3 ice cubes on bark weekly) works but room-temperature water is better.
care.light: Bright indirect light. East-facing window is ideal. No direct sun — leaves yellow and burn. Sufficient light: if leaves are dark green, more light is needed; yellow-green leaves indicate good light.
care.soil: Orchid bark or sphagnum moss — never regular potting soil. The roots need air and excellent drainage.
care.spacing: Individual plants in clear pots (orchid roots are photosynthetic — they need light).
care.fertilizer: 'Weakly, weekly' — diluted orchid fertilizer (1/4 strength) every watering, or full strength monthly.
care.notes: To trigger reblooming: move to a cooler location (60–65°F nights) for 4–6 weeks in autumn. This temperature differential is the most reliable rebloom trigger. After blooming ends, cut the spike just above a node (triangular bump) — a new side branch may develop. Or cut to the base to allow the plant to rest.

container.min_size: 5–7 inch clear orchid pot with drainage holes.
container.notes: Clear pots allow light to reach the green photosynthetic roots. The roots turning silver-grey indicates it's time to water; green roots = adequately moist.

propagation.desc: Occasionally a keiki (baby plant) grows from a node on the flower spike. Allow it to develop 2–3 roots of 2 inches before removing and potting in orchid bark.

harvest.when: Flowers can be cut for arrangements.
harvest.how: Cut spike with clean scissors.
harvest.storage: 10–14 days in water. Some of the longest-lasting cut flowers available.
harvest.yield: One or two spikes per plant per year carrying 10–20 flowers lasting months.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the most common killer. Roots rot in constantly wet bark.
No rebloom trigger — needs cool nights (60–65°F) in autumn to initiate new spike.
Too little light — dark green leaves signal insufficient light.
Regular potting soil — always use orchid bark. Regular soil causes root suffocation.
Cutting spike to base immediately after bloom — leaving nodes allows possible secondary spikes.

seed_saving.type: Keiki propagation only.
seed_saving.harvest: Keiki develops on flower spike nodes.
seed_saving.method: Allow keiki to grow 2–3 roots of 2 inches, then remove and pot in orchid bark.
seed_saving.notes: Keikis are genetically identical to the mother plant.

good.why: Similar care and display aesthetic.
Both epiphytes with similar display approach.

bad.why: Orchids prefer moderate humidity — not the extreme humidity calatheas need.

culinary: Flowers edible as garnish — used in high-end food presentation. Vanilla extract comes from a different orchid genus (Vanilla planifolia).
medicinal: Not used medicinally. Traditional Chinese medicine uses other orchid species.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None.
pet_toxicity.notes: Phalaenopsis orchids are non-toxic to pets. One of the safest flowering houseplants.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 1–2 years when bark breaks down. Use fresh orchid bark. Repot after bloom — never during. Roots growing outside the pot are normal and healthy — only repot if bark is decomposing.

varieties.notes: Most available. Most reliable. Best for beginners.

varieties.notes: Best for small spaces. More bloom cycles.

varieties.description: Striped, harlequin, and spotted patterns. Same care. Very collectible.

pests.desc: From overwatering or poor drainage — most common problem.
pests.control: Repot in fresh bark. Remove rotten roots. Reduce watering.
