name: String of Pearls

season.harvest_window: Year-round trailing bead-like foliage. Tiny white cinnamon-scented flowers possible.

seed.desc: Purchase plant or propagate from stem cuttings. One of the most striking and unusual succulents.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root quickly in dry mix.

seedling.desc: New growth extends from cutting.

young.desc: Trailing stems lengthen. Each spherical bead is a modified leaf storing water.

adult.desc: Long cascading strings of perfect spherical beads hanging 2–3ft from a hanging basket or elevated pot. Tiny white flowers with cinnamon fragrance. One of the most distinctive-looking succulents. The spherical bead shape reduces surface area to minimise water loss — a remarkable adaptation.

care.water: Allow soil to dry completely between waterings — this is a true succulent. Overwatering causes the beads to burst and rot. Every 2–3 weeks in growing season, monthly in winter.
care.light: Bright indirect to some direct morning sun. Insufficient light causes the beads to shrink and the plant to become sparse.
care.soil: Cactus/succulent mix. Excellent drainage essential.
care.spacing: One per pot. Hanging basket preferred.
care.fertilizer: Diluted succulent fertilizer once in spring and once in summer only.
care.notes: String of pearls is fussier than most succulents — it needs brighter light and less water than it might seem. The most common problem is overwatering which causes shrivelling and rot. It also dislikes being moved — find a good spot and leave it. The stems are fragile — handle minimally. TOXIC to pets.

container.notes: Hanging baskets show off the cascading strings beautifully. Shallow pots preferred — the shallow root system doesn't need depth.

propagation.desc: Lay 4–6 inch stem sections on dry cactus mix. Pin lightly. Roots form at nodes within 2–3 weeks without any watering for the first week.

harvest.when: N/A.
harvest.how: N/A.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Cascading strings of spherical beads.

common_mistakes: Overwatering — the primary killer. Beads burst when overwatered.
Insufficient light — beads become small and widely spaced.
Moving too often — dislikes being relocated.
Fragile stems — handle minimally.

seed_saving.type: Stem cutting propagation.
seed_saving.harvest: N/A.
seed_saving.method: Lay stem cuttings on dry succulent mix. Do not water for 1 week.
seed_saving.drying: Allow cutting ends to callous 24 hours before placing on soil.
seed_saving.notes: Very easy to propagate from cuttings.

good.why: Same drought conditions.
Compatible watering schedule.

bad.why: Completely incompatible — ferns need constant moisture.

culinary: Not edible — toxic.
medicinal: Not used medicinally.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, drooling.
pet_toxicity.notes: ASPCA lists string of pearls as toxic to dogs and cats. Usually causes mild GI upset. The spherical beads may be attractive to pets. Keep out of reach.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 2 years in shallow containers with cactus mix. Fragile — handle very gently.

varieties.name: String of Pearls (standard)
varieties.description: Classic perfectly spherical green beads. The original.

varieties.name: String of Bananas
varieties.description: Banana-shaped (curved) beads instead of round. More tolerant and faster growing.
varieties.notes: More vigorous and more tolerant than string of pearls.

varieties.name: String of Tears
varieties.description: Teardrop-shaped beads with a translucent 'window'. Very delicate appearance.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Allow to dry completely. Remove rotten sections. Repot in dry fresh mix.

name: Hoya (Wax Plant)

season.harvest_window: Year-round foliage. Flowers typically spring and summer — intensely fragrant clusters.

seed.desc: Purchase plant. Hoyas are long-lived and eventually become generous bloomers. The older and more rootbound, the more they flower.

germination.desc: Stem cuttings root in water or moist mix in 3–4 weeks.

seedling.desc: Young plants establish. Vining growth begins.

young.desc: Trailing or climbing stems lengthen. Thick waxy leaves develop.

adult.desc: Eventually produces clusters of waxy star-shaped flowers with an extraordinary fragrance — sweet, honey-like, sometimes chocolate or citrus notes depending on species. The peduncles (flower stalks) must never be removed — hoyas rebloom from the same peduncles year after year. One of the finest fragrant houseplants. Very long-lived — some specimens are 30–50 years old.

care.water: Allow top inch or two to dry between waterings. More drought tolerant than it appears. Overwatering is the main problem.
care.light: Bright indirect light for best flowering. Tolerates medium indirect but flowers less.
care.soil: Well-draining potting mix with added perlite. pH 6.0–7.0.
care.spacing: One per pot. Provide a small trellis or hoop for climbing varieties.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer every 2–3 weeks during growing season. High phosphorus when budding to promote flowers.
care.notes: Never remove the flower peduncles (the short stubby stalks that flowers grew from) — hoyas reuse the same peduncle for new flower clusters year after year. Hoyas prefer to be rootbound — the most potbound plants bloom most prolifically. Do not repot unless truly necessary. The flowers drip nectar — place a tray beneath. The fragrance is strongest at night.

container.min_size: 6-inch pot. Prefers being rootbound — don't rush to increase pot size.
container.notes: Small pots actually promote blooming. Hanging baskets for trailing types, small trellis for climbing types.

propagation.desc: 4–6 inch cuttings with 2 nodes root readily in water in 3–4 weeks.
Dip in rooting hormone, insert in moist perlite mix. Cover with plastic bag for humidity.

harvest.when: Flowers can be enjoyed in place — they drop cleanly when done.
harvest.how: N/A — never cut peduncles.
harvest.storage: N/A.
harvest.yield: Multiple flower clusters per peduncle per season on mature plants.

common_mistakes: Removing peduncles — the most costly mistake. Never cut the old flower stalks.
Repotting too often — hoyas bloom most when rootbound. Leave them alone.
Overwatering — the most common cause of decline.
Insufficient light for flowering — needs bright indirect.

seed_saving.type: Stem cuttings — very easy.
seed_saving.harvest: Stem cuttings from healthy growth.
seed_saving.method: Root in water or moist perlite.
seed_saving.notes: Hoyas are widely traded as cuttings — a generous and easy plant to share.

good.why: Hoya collectors often build collections — same care across hundreds of species.
Similar care, different texture.

bad.why: Hoyas are more succulent-like and prefer to dry out between waterings.

culinary: Not edible — the nectar drip from flowers is harmless but not culinarily significant.
medicinal: Traditional use in parts of Asia — leaf poultices for skin conditions and ear infections. Not in Western medicine.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None — the sap may cause mild skin irritation in sensitive individuals.
pet_toxicity.notes: Hoyas are generally considered non-toxic to pets. ASPCA does not list hoyas as toxic. The waxy leaves are unlikely to be eaten. One of the safer flowering houseplants.

transplant.deep_note: Repot every 3+ years only when severely rootbound. Go up only one pot size. Smaller pots promote flowering.

varieties.name: Hoya carnosa
varieties.description: The classic wax plant. Thick succulent leaves. Pink and white star flowers with intense sweet fragrance.
varieties.notes: Most widely available. Most reliable bloomer.

varieties.name: Hoya kerrii (Sweetheart)
varieties.description: Heart-shaped succulent leaves. Very popular Valentine's Day plant. Single-leaf cuttings (sold everywhere) will never grow into plants — must have a node.
varieties.notes: Most popular as a gift. Buy only plants with stems and nodes.

varieties.name: Hoya pubicalyx
varieties.description: Speckled silver leaves. Dark red-purple flowers with chocolate fragrance. Very prolific bloomer.
varieties.notes: Best chocolate fragrance. Most prolific bloomer.

varieties.name: Hoya bella
varieties.description: Small delicate leaves. White and purple star flowers. More compact trailing habit.

varieties.name: Hoya obovata
varieties.description: Large round leaves, often with silver speckles. Pink flowers. Very vigorous.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.desc: The most common hoya pest — white cottony masses in leaf axils.
pests.control: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab. Neem oil.

pests.name: Root Rot
pests.control: Allow to dry completely. Repot in dry fresh mix.

name: Wheat

season.direct_sow: Winter wheat: September–November. Spring wheat: March–April.
season.harvest_window: Winter wheat: June–July. Spring wheat: July–August.

seed.desc: Direct sow. Winter wheat is sown in fall, overwinters as a young plant, and is harvested the following summer — this is the most common and highest-yielding type. Spring wheat is sown in early spring and harvested in summer. Purchase seed wheat from a farm supplier or seed company — grocery store wheat is often treated and may not germinate.

germination.desc: Fast in cool, moist soil. Shoots emerge quickly.

seedling.desc: Grass-like seedlings tiller (spread) forming a dense clump.

young.desc: Winter wheat overwinters in a low rosette. In spring, jointing begins — the stem starts to elongate rapidly.

adult.desc: The wheat head (ear) emerges and fills with grain. The plant turns golden as it dries. Harvest when the grain is firm and the straw is golden — before heavy rains can cause lodging (falling over) or grain shattering.

care.water: Rainfall generally sufficient. Needs 1 inch per week during grain fill. Very drought tolerant once established.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, fertile. pH 6.0–7.0. Deep tillage before sowing. Remove weeds — wheat competes poorly with weeds early on.
care.spacing: Broadcast seed at 2–3 lbs per 1000 sq ft or sow in rows 6–8 inches apart.
care.fertilizer: Nitrogen at sowing and again at jointing (spring) is the most important input. 1 lb actual nitrogen per 1000 sq ft.
care.notes: A 10×10ft plot of wheat produces roughly 10 lbs of grain — enough for about 10 loaves of bread. Growing wheat in small plots is more of an educational and self-sufficiency experience than a productive food source unless you have significant acreage. Hand threshing by beating bundles against a barrel, then winnowing in the wind, separates grain from chaff.

container.notes: Can be grown decoratively in containers but harvest is negligible.

propagation.desc: Direct sow. Save seed from your own harvest for next year's crop.

harvest.when: When stalks are golden, the heads are full, and the grain is hard (bite test — should not dent). Before heavy autumn rains.
harvest.how: Cut stalks with a scythe or sickle. Bundle into sheaves. Allow to dry further in stooks (teepee-like bundles) for 1–2 weeks. Thresh by beating against a barrel or tarp. Winnow in the wind to separate grain from chaff.
harvest.storage: Clean dry grain stores for years in sealed containers.
harvest.yield: Approximately 1 lb of grain per 10 sq ft of productive bed.

common_mistakes: Planting grocery store wheat — buy seed wheat, not flour or whole wheat berries from supermarkets (may be irradiated or treated)
Not controlling weeds — wheat is a poor early competitor
Harvesting too late — grain shatters and falls if left too long
Not drying properly before storage — moisture causes mould

seed_saving.type: Very easy — save 10% of harvest for next year's seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Save the best, fullest heads from the healthiest plants.
seed_saving.method: Clean and dry grain completely. Store in sealed container.
seed_saving.drying: Dry to below 12% moisture (grain should be hard and not indent when bitten).
seed_saving.storage: Sealed containers in cool dry location. Lasts years.
seed_saving.notes: Seed saving is central to wheat growing — heritage varieties are preserved this way.

good.why: Clover between rows fixes nitrogen. Classic grain-clover rotation.
Legume companion for nitrogen.

bad.why: Wheat needs its nutrients. Don't crowd with other heavy feeders.

culinary: The foundation of Western civilization's diet — bread, pasta, pastry, noodles, couscous, bulgur, freekeh, semolina. Whole wheat berries: cooked as grain, sprouted, or ground. Home milling with a grain mill produces flour far superior to commercial flour. Wheat beer. Wheat grass juice.
medicinal: Whole wheat is nutritionally superior to refined wheat — retains bran (fibre, B vitamins, minerals) and germ (vitamin E, essential fatty acids). High-fibre diets consistently associated with reduced cardiovascular disease, colorectal cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Wheat germ oil is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin E.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — gluten can cause issues in rare sensitive animals
pet_toxicity.symptoms: GI upset in animals with gluten sensitivity.
pet_toxicity.notes: Wheat grain is generally safe for pets. Some dogs have gluten sensitivity. The green wheat grass shoots are safe and some pets enjoy them.

transplant.deep_note: Sow seed 1–1.5 inches deep. Firm soil contact with seed is critical for germination.

varieties.name: Hard Red Winter Wheat
varieties.description: Most widely grown wheat in the US. High protein. Excellent bread flour. Sown in fall, harvested in summer.

varieties.name: Soft White Winter Wheat
varieties.description: Lower protein. Better for pastry and cake flour. Mild flavour.

varieties.name: Einkorn (Ancient Wheat)
varieties.description: The oldest cultivated wheat. Lower gluten, different gluten structure — tolerated by some with non-celiac gluten sensitivity. Nutty flavour. Lower yield but higher nutrition.
varieties.notes: Best ancient grain. Most nutritious. Tolerated by some gluten-sensitive people.

varieties.name: Emmer (Farro)
varieties.description: Ancient hull-less wheat. Nutty flavour. Used in Italian farro dishes. Good drought tolerance.
varieties.notes: Best for farro dishes. Good drought tolerance.

pests.name: Wheat Rust
pests.desc: Orange or yellow powdery pustules on leaves and stems.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.desc: On new growth, especially the Hessian fly.
pests.control: Delay planting (after Hessian fly date for your area), resistant varieties.

name: Oats

season.direct_sow: Early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) or late summer for a cover crop
season.harvest_window: Midsummer — oats mature 90–100 days from sowing

seed.desc: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked — oats tolerate frost. One of the earliest cool-season grain crops. Also widely used as a cover crop/green manure.

germination.desc: Fast and reliable in cool, moist soil.

seedling.desc: Grass-like seedlings tiller to form a dense clump.

young.desc: Rapid growth. Oat heads (panicles) emerge — more open and feathery than wheat.

adult.desc: Grain fills in the distinctive drooping panicles. Harvest when kernels are firm and golden, before the panicles shatter. Oats are hull-less or hulled depending on variety.

care.water: Tolerates wet conditions better than wheat. 1 inch per week.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Tolerates poor, wet, and acidic soils better than most grains. pH 5.5–7.0.
care.spacing: Broadcast at 3 lbs per 1000 sq ft or sow in rows 6 inches apart.
care.fertilizer: Light nitrogen at sowing. Oats are not heavy feeders.
care.notes: Oats are the most forgiving grain crop — they tolerate poor soils, wet conditions, and late frosts better than wheat or barley. Also an excellent cover crop: sow in late summer, oats winterkill, leaving dead mulch that suppresses weeds and is easily tilled in spring.

container.notes: Can grow decoratively.

propagation.desc: Direct sow. Save seed from harvest.

harvest.when: When grain is firm and golden and the panicles begin to drop. Harvest in sections as they ripen.
harvest.how: Cut stalks, bundle, dry for 1–2 weeks. Thresh against a barrel or with a flail. Winnow to separate grain from hull and chaff.
harvest.storage: Dry, sealed containers. Store as whole oat groats for best nutrition.
harvest.yield: Approximately 1 lb per 10 sq ft.

common_mistakes: Planting too late — oats need cool temperatures to set grain well
Letting panicles shatter — harvest as soon as grain is firm
Not drying properly before storage

seed_saving.type: Very easy — save from your own harvest.
seed_saving.harvest: Save fullest heads from healthiest plants.
seed_saving.method: Clean and dry completely.
seed_saving.storage: Sealed container in cool dry location.
seed_saving.notes: Hull-less varieties are easier to use — no dehulling needed.

good.why: Classic oat-pea companion for nitrogen.
Undersow clover for nitrogen-fixing ground cover.

culinary: Porridge/oatmeal — one of the most nutritious breakfasts. Rolled oats (steamed and flattened). Steel-cut oats (most nutritious, least processed). Overnight oats. Oat flour for baking (gluten-free if certified). Granola. Oatmeal cookies. Oat milk. Scottish oatcakes. Bircher muesli.
medicinal: Beta-glucan in oats is one of the most studied dietary fibre compounds. Clinical evidence for: lowering LDL cholesterol (FDA approved health claim), reducing blood sugar spikes after meals, feeding beneficial gut bacteria. Avenanthramides — compounds unique to oats — have anti-inflammatory and anti-itch properties (used in skin care products). One of the best foods for cardiovascular health with the most clinical evidence.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: None. Oatmeal is commonly used as a pet food ingredient.
pet_toxicity.notes: Oats are safe and nutritious for pets. Oatmeal baths are used to soothe skin irritation in dogs. Plain cooked oats are a healthy occasional pet food.

transplant.deep_note: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep. Firm soil contact essential.

varieties.name: Hull-less Oats (Naked Oats)
varieties.description: Grain falls free from the hull at harvest — no dehulling needed for home use. Best for small-scale growing.
varieties.notes: Best for home growing — no special processing needed.

varieties.name: Common Oats (Hulled)
varieties.description: Standard commercial type. Hull must be removed before eating — requires a grain dehuller.
varieties.notes: Standard type. Need dehuller for eating.

varieties.name: Jumbo Oats
varieties.description: Large kernel variety. Good for rolled oats production.

pests.name: Crown Rust
pests.desc: Orange rust on leaves and stems.

name: Amaranth

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is warm (65°F+)
season.harvest_window: Late summer through fall

seed.desc: Surface sow or barely cover — very small seeds need light and warmth to germinate. Direct sow after soil warms. Thin aggressively — amaranth plants need 18 inches to produce full heads.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil. Seeds very small — sow thickly and thin.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly in heat. Distinctive broad leaves.

young.desc: Spectacular growth — amaranth can reach 6–8ft in a single season.

adult.desc: Enormous plume or head of tiny seeds in gold, red, purple, or multicolor. One of the most visually dramatic food plants. The grain is a true superfood — complete protein (all essential amino acids), gluten-free, extremely nutritious. Both the seeds and leaves are edible.

care.water: Drought tolerant once established — one of the most heat and drought resilient grain crops.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Average to rich, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.5. Surprisingly adaptable.
care.spacing: 18 inches between plants for grain production. Can be grown densely for leaf production.
care.fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer at planting. Moderate feeder.
care.notes: One of the most ancient cultivated grains — a staple of Aztec and Inca civilization. Gluten-free complete protein. Both the seeds and the leaves (used like spinach) are edible and nutritious. The ornamental varieties (Love Lies Bleeding, etc.) are the same genus and their seeds are equally edible. Very easy to grow — thrives where other crops struggle.

container.min_size: Too large for containers for grain production.
container.notes: Not practical for grain harvest.

propagation.desc: Surface sow directly. Very easy.

harvest.when: When the seed heads are dry, the seeds are firm, and they rub off easily between your palms.
harvest.how: Cut heads and place in paper bags to dry further. Rub heads between hands to release seeds. Winnow in the wind to remove chaff.
harvest.storage: Dry seeds in sealed containers. Last years.
harvest.yield: One plant can produce 50,000–500,000 seeds. A 10×10ft plot can produce several pounds of grain.

common_mistakes: Not thinning — crowded plants produce small heads
Harvesting too early — wait until seeds rub off easily
Not winnowing — chaff is bitter

seed_saving.type: Extremely easy — one plant produces enormous quantities of seed.
seed_saving.harvest: Cut dry heads into paper bags.
seed_saving.method: Rub between palms. Winnow.
seed_saving.notes: One plant produces more seeds than you could ever save. Share with neighbours.

good.why: Both heat lovers. Traditional companion.
Three Sisters-style combination.
Both love heat.

culinary: Popped amaranth — pop like popcorn in a dry pan. Cooked whole grain like rice. Ground into gluten-free flour. Amaranth porridge. Alegría (Mexican popped amaranth and honey candy). Leaves cooked like spinach — milder flavour. Amaranth in soups and stews. Mixed with other flours for baked goods.
medicinal: One of the most nutritious grains: complete protein (18–19% protein), high in lysine (limiting amino acid in most grains), iron, calcium, magnesium, and vitamins. Gluten-free. Squalene in amaranth oil — studied for cardiovascular and anticancer properties. Phytosterols that reduce cholesterol absorption. Traditionally used by indigenous peoples of the Americas for strength and endurance.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: none — cooked seeds and leaves safe
pet_toxicity.symptoms: None in normal amounts.
pet_toxicity.notes: Amaranth grain and cooked leaves are safe for pets. Raw leaves contain oxalic acid — cook before feeding to pets.

transplant.deep_note: Surface sow or barely cover. Thin to 18 inches when 3 inches tall.

varieties.name: Golden Giant
varieties.description: Large gold seed heads. Very high yield. One of the most productive grain amaranths.

varieties.name: Burgundy
varieties.description: Deep red-burgundy leaves and heads. Both ornamental and edible grain. Striking.

varieties.name: Green Tails
varieties.description: Drooping green flower tails — very ornamental. Seeds edible.

varieties.name: Plainsman
varieties.description: Developed for mechanised harvest. Good grain yield. Shorter plant.

name: Quinoa

season.start_indoors: Start indoors 4 weeks before last frost for northern gardens
season.direct_sow: Early spring (cool soil) or late summer for fall crop
season.harvest_window: Late summer — a narrow window before fall rains. Timing is critical.

seed.desc: Surface sow or barely cover — seeds need light. Cool-season plant that bolts in high heat. Start early for a spring crop or time for a fall harvest in warm climates.

germination.desc: Very fast in cool moist soil.

seedling.desc: Grows quickly in cool conditions.

young.desc: Upright plants reaching 4–6ft with distinctive diamond-shaped leaves. In dry hot conditions, saponin coating on the seed heads gives a frosted appearance.

adult.desc: Large seed heads form at the top. The seeds have a natural saponin coating that makes them bitter and soapy when raw — must be rinsed thoroughly before eating. Harvest is time-critical — seeds can sprout on the plant if wet weather arrives during ripening.

care.water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established. Too much water causes disease.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Well-draining, lean to average. pH 6.0–7.5. Rich soil causes tall floppy plants.
care.fertilizer: Light fertilization. Excess nitrogen causes lodging.
care.notes: Quinoa is challenging to harvest at home — the seed heads must be completely dry at harvest, which often coincides with fall rains in many climates. The saponin coating makes the seeds taste soapy unless very thoroughly rinsed (or the seeds are pre-rinsed varieties). Growing quinoa is rewarding and educational but requires attention to harvest timing.

container.notes: Not practical.

propagation.desc: Direct sow in cool weather.

harvest.when: When seeds are hard, the seed heads are dry, and seeds rub off easily. The plant yellows and looks finished. Beat heads gently — ripe seeds should fall freely.
harvest.how: Cut heads into paper bags. Allow to dry further in a warm, airy place. Thresh by rubbing between hands or in a pillowcase. Winnow. Rinse thoroughly before eating or storing.
harvest.storage: Thoroughly rinsed and dried grain stores for years.
harvest.yield: One plant can yield 1/4–1/2 lb of grain. 100 sq ft can yield several pounds.

common_mistakes: Harvest timing — the most critical challenge. Wet weather during ripening ruins the crop.
Not rinsing — saponins taste terrible. Rinse very thoroughly.
Too much nitrogen — tall floppy plants that lodge
Heat — quinoa doesn't set seed well above 95°F

seed_saving.type: Very easy. Save seed from best plants.
seed_saving.harvest: Fully dry heads.
seed_saving.method: Thresh, winnow, rinse, dry before storing.
seed_saving.drying: Must be completely dry before storage.
seed_saving.notes: Save seed before rinsing — saponins help preserve the seed.

good.why: Both cool-season, nitrogen fixing companion.
Both cool season.

culinary: Cooked like rice — rinse thoroughly, cook 1:2 with water, 15 minutes. Quinoa salads. Quinoa bowls with roasted vegetables. Ground into flour. Quinoa porridge. Popped quinoa (tiny). Quinoa in soups. The leaves are also edible — cooked like spinach.
medicinal: One of the most nutritious grains: complete protein (14% protein), high in all essential amino acids especially lysine and methionine. High in iron, magnesium, fibre, and antioxidants. Gluten-free. Saponins have antimicrobial and antifungal properties. Betacyanins (the red pigments) are potent antioxidants. Sacred Incan grain with 5,000 years of cultivation.

pet_toxicity.symptoms: Unrinsed quinoa causes GI upset from saponins.
pet_toxicity.notes: Cooked, rinsed quinoa is safe for pets. Always rinse before cooking and before feeding to pets. Plain cooked quinoa can be a nutritious addition to pet food in small amounts.

transplant.deep_note: Surface sow or barely cover. Thin to 12–18 inches.

varieties.name: Temuco
varieties.description: Chilean variety. Good for wetter, cooler climates. Good disease resistance.
varieties.notes: Best for wet or cool climates.

varieties.name: Brightest Brilliant Rainbow
varieties.description: Multicolour seed heads — orange, red, yellow, purple. Ornamental and edible.

varieties.name: Cherry Vanilla
varieties.description: Red and white seed heads. Good for short seasons. Pre-rinsed variety (low saponin).
varieties.notes: Best low-saponin variety for short seasons.

name: Dry Beans

season.direct_sow: After last frost when soil is 60°F+
season.harvest_window: Late summer through fall — when pods are fully dry and papery

seed.desc: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil. The same species as green (snap) beans — simply grown to maturity until the pods dry on the plant. One of the most important and versatile food crops.

germination.desc: Fast in warm soil (60°F+). Cold soil causes rotting.

seedling.desc: Grows rapidly. Bush types stay compact; pole types vine and need support.

young.desc: Flowers appear. Pods develop quickly after pollination.

adult.desc: Pods fill with beans, then dry. Leave on the plant until the pods are completely papery and dry, the seeds rattle inside, and the vines die back. Wet weather at this stage is the primary risk.

care.water: Moderate — consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill. Drought during flowering reduces yield.
care.light: Full sun.
care.soil: Average, well-draining. pH 6.0–7.0. Being legumes, they fix their own nitrogen — don't over-fertilize.
care.spacing: Bush types: 4–6 inches. Pole types: 6–8 inches at the base of poles.
care.fertilizer: Inoculate with rhizobium bacteria before planting for maximum nitrogen fixation. No additional nitrogen needed.
care.notes: The most important calorie-producing crop for food self-sufficiency after grains. High in protein, fibre, and complex carbohydrates. Store for years. Easy to grow, harvest, and process with no special equipment. The diversity of dry beans is extraordinary — from navy to black to pinto to kidney to cannellini to heirloom varieties of every colour.

container.notes: Bush dry beans possible in large containers. Pole beans need tall support and very large containers.

propagation.desc: Direct sow. Save seed from harvest — the easiest of all seed saving.

harvest.when: When pods are completely dry, papery, and the seeds rattle inside — typically 4–6 weeks after the snap bean stage.
harvest.how: Pull entire plants when mostly dry. Hang upside down in a warm, dry, airy location for 2–4 weeks. Thresh by beating plants inside a pillowcase or barrel. Winnow or hand-sort.
harvest.storage: Dry beans store for years in sealed containers. Best eaten within 2 years for cooking quality (older beans take longer to cook).
harvest.yield: Approximately 1 lb of dry beans per 10 row-feet.

common_mistakes: Wet weather at harvest — the pods rehydrate and the beans may mould. Harvest early and finish drying indoors.
Not drying completely before storage — causes mould in storage
Planting in cold soil — causes rotting
Over-fertilizing with nitrogen — reduces nitrogen fixation and yield

seed_saving.type: The easiest of all seed saving — save your best dry beans.
seed_saving.harvest: Save the largest, most perfect beans from the best-yielding plants.
seed_saving.method: Already processed — just keep some back before eating.
seed_saving.notes: Every dry bean you eat is technically a seed. Saving beans is simply not eating some.

good.why: Classic Three Sisters — beans climb corn, fix nitrogen for it.
Three Sisters — squash shades ground, retains moisture.
Beans fix nitrogen, carrots benefit.

bad.why: Garlic and onion inhibit legume growth.

culinary: The most important legume in global cuisine. Black beans: Mexican, Cuban, Brazilian cooking. Pinto beans: refried beans, burritos. Navy beans: baked beans, cassoulet. Kidney beans: chilli con carne. Cannellini: Italian soups and stews. Chickpeas (a close relative): hummus, falafel. Dry beans can replace meat in most contexts — higher protein per dollar than any meat.
medicinal: One of the most nutritious foods available: 22% protein, high in fibre (both soluble and insoluble), iron, folate, potassium, and magnesium. Resistant starch feeds beneficial gut bacteria. Epidemiological studies consistently show legume consumption associated with reduced rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer. The 'Blue Zones' (populations with highest longevity) all consume legumes as a dietary cornerstone.

pet_toxicity.toxic_parts: raw or undercooked beans contain lectins — cook thoroughly
pet_toxicity.symptoms: Lectins in raw beans cause severe GI upset. Fully cooked beans are safe.
pet_toxicity.notes: Fully cooked dry beans are safe for pets. Never feed raw or undercooked beans — lectins are toxic. Small amounts of cooked beans are fine as an occasional addition to pet food.

transplant.deep_note: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep. Inoculate with rhizobium bacteria before planting.

varieties.name: Black Turtle Bean
varieties.description: The classic black bean. Bush type. Very productive. Foundation of Mexican and Brazilian cooking.

varieties.name: Pinto
varieties.description: The most widely grown bean in the US. Speckled tan-brown. Foundation of Southwestern cooking. Bush type.

varieties.name: Jacob's Cattle
varieties.description: Heirloom speckled red and white. Excellent flavour. Very ornamental.

varieties.name: Dragon Tongue
varieties.description: Yellow pods with purple streaks (colour fades when cooked). Can be used as snap or dry bean. Very productive.

varieties.name: Cherokee Trail of Tears
varieties.description: Small black pole bean with deep historical significance. Cherokee people carried these seeds on the Trail of Tears. Excellent flavour.
varieties.notes: Most historically significant. Excellent flavour and cultural heritage.

pests.name: Bean Weevil
pests.control: Freeze dry beans for 3 days before long-term storage to kill any weevil eggs.

pests.name: Mexican Bean Beetle
pests.desc: Yellow spotted beetle and larvae skeletonize leaves.
pests.control: Hand-pick, neem oil, row covers early.
